title: German C1
description: The fifth step in German, from B2 to CEFR level C1, the level of the Goethe-Zertifikat C1. Lessons cover modal verbs in every tense and their subjective use about the past, the Konjunktiv II of the past with modal verbs and the passive, the Konjunktiv I in academic and legal reporting, focus and modal particles, advanced nominal style, Funktionsverbgefüge and participial constructions, every alternative to the passive, the word es and other pointing words, text cohesion, idioms, register and advanced word formation, and the texts of law, economics, science, politics and culture. Writing and speaking reach C1: summaries, graph descriptions, the Erörterung, forum posts and half-formal messages, talks and discussions, and mediation, with a look at regional German and literature. About 1,000 new words build on the roughly 3,400 core words of German A1 to B2 for about 4,400 in all, and a reading list suggests books, newspapers and podcasts at this level. Unlocks when German B2 is complete.
author: Erudior
changelog: Comma-rule references use the 2024 numbering of the official rules.

lessons.title: Had to, would have been able to: modal verbs in every tense
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

You have used modal verbs since your first weeks of German: *Ich kann schwimmen. Du musst um acht da sein.* At A2 you learned their Präteritum (*musste, konnte, durfte*), at B1 the Konjunktiv II of the past with two infinitives (*Ich hätte anrufen sollen*), and at B2 you saw how a long verb cluster is read from the right and where the finite verb goes when a clause ends in two infinitives (B2 lesson 27).

At C1 you need the whole system and you need it fast, because formal German uses modal verbs in every tense, in the passive and in subordinate clauses, often all at once: *…, weil der Vertrag zuerst von beiden Parlamenten hatte ratifiziert werden müssen.* This lesson sets out that system tense by tense, shows how the passive fits in, explains where the finite verb goes in each kind of clause, and helps you choose between the Präteritum and the Perfekt. It also covers the verbs that behave like modals in the perfect (*lassen, sehen, hören, helfen, brauchen*).

All the modal verbs in this lesson are used in their **[[objective use]]**: they say what the subject must, can, may, should or wants to do. Lesson 02 turns to the other use, in which the speaker judges how likely something is (*Er muss es gewusst haben*). Keep the difference in mind; it decides which past form you need.

The theme is diplomacy and international relations: summits, treaties, sanctions and the long nights in which compromises are found.

## Text: Zwölf Nächte in Genf

This is a background article (*Hintergrundbericht*) of the kind you find in a weekly paper. The two states and everyone in them are invented.

> **Zwölf Nächte in Genf**
>
> *Wie das Wasserabkommen zwischen Velarien und Tarsien zustande kam – ein Rückblick*
>
> Als die beiden Delegationen Anfang März in Genf eintrafen, rechnete kaum jemand mit einem Ergebnis. Seit Jahren stritten Velarien und Tarsien um das Wasser des Saro, und die letzte Gesprächsrunde hatte ohne jede Annäherung abgebrochen werden müssen. Die tarsische Außenministerin hatte damals nicht einmal anreisen dürfen, weil ihr das Parlament das Mandat verweigert hatte.
>
> Diesmal war vieles anders. Beide Regierungen standen unter Druck: Nach zwei Dürresommern hatten die Bauern auf beiden Seiten des Flusses ihre Felder kaum noch bewässern können. Schon das Verhandlungsmandat hatte in beiden Hauptstädten vom Parlament genehmigt werden müssen, und diesmal ging es ohne Streit durch. Als Vermittlerin trat eine erfahrene Schweizer Diplomatin auf, die schon andere bilaterale Konflikte deeskaliert hatte. „Ich habe die Delegationen zwölf Nächte lang in getrennten Räumen verhandeln lassen“, erzählt sie heute. „Direkt miteinander reden wollten sie erst ganz am Ende.“
>
> Leicht war es für keine Seite. Velarien hat auf einen Teil seiner Staudammpläne verzichten müssen, Tarsien hat internationale Beobachter an seinen Pegelstationen zulassen müssen. Der Vertragstext hat dreimal neu übersetzt werden müssen, weil die beiden Sprachfassungen voneinander abwichen. Ein velarischer Diplomat räumt ein, man habe die Krise kommen sehen und trotzdem zu lange gezögert. Dass seine Regierung am Ende hat nachgeben müssen, sei für viele zu Hause schwer zu akzeptieren.
>
> Unterschrieben ist das Abkommen, in Kraft ist es noch nicht. Es muss von beiden Parlamenten ratifiziert werden; in Velarien ist das inzwischen geschehen, in Tarsien steht die Abstimmung noch aus. Scheitert die Ratifizierung dort, wird man von vorn beginnen müssen. Die Vereinten Nationen haben bereits angeboten, die Umsetzung zu begleiten.
>
> Ob der Kompromiss hält, weiß niemand. Doch Genf hat eines gezeigt: Diplomatie braucht Zeit, und manchmal muss man die Gegner einfach reden lassen, bis sie müde genug sind, einander zuzuhören.

**Translation.** *Twelve nights in Geneva. How the water agreement between Velaria and Tarsia came about: a look back.* When the two delegations arrived in Geneva at the beginning of March, hardly anyone expected a result. For years Velaria and Tarsia had been arguing over the water of the Saro, and the last round of talks had had to be broken off without any rapprochement. At that time the Tarsian foreign minister hadn't even been allowed to travel, because parliament had refused her a mandate. This time much was different. Both governments were under pressure: after two summers of drought, the farmers on both sides of the river had hardly been able to irrigate their fields any more. Even the negotiating mandate had had to be approved by parliament in both capitals, and this time it went through without a fight. The mediator was an experienced Swiss diplomat who had already de-escalated other bilateral conflicts. "I had the delegations negotiate in separate rooms for twelve nights," she says today. "They only wanted to talk to each other directly at the very end." It was easy for neither side. Velaria had to give up part of its dam plans; Tarsia had to allow international observers at its gauging stations. The text of the treaty had to be translated anew three times because the two language versions differed. A Velarian diplomat admits that they saw the crisis coming and still hesitated too long. That his government had to give way in the end, he says, is hard for many people at home to accept. The agreement is signed, but it isn't in force yet. It has to be ratified by both parliaments; in Velaria that has now happened, in Tarsia the vote is still pending. If ratification fails there, they will have to start again from scratch. The United Nations has already offered to oversee the implementation. Whether the compromise will hold, nobody knows. But Geneva showed one thing: diplomacy takes time, and sometimes you simply have to let opponents talk until they are tired enough to listen to each other.

Read the article again and underline every modal verb. You'll find one in almost every tense, four in the passive, and two verbs (*lassen, sehen*) that behave like modals. The rest of the lesson goes through them.

## One verb, every tense

Here is *verhandeln müssen* (to have to negotiate) in every tense, in a main clause and in a subordinate clause.

| tense | main clause | subordinate clause |
|---|---|---|
| Präsens | *Sie muss verhandeln.* | *…, weil sie verhandeln muss.* |
| Präteritum | *Sie musste verhandeln.* | *…, weil sie verhandeln musste.* |
| Perfekt | *Sie hat verhandeln müssen.* | *…, weil sie hat verhandeln müssen.* |
| Plusquamperfekt | *Sie hatte verhandeln müssen.* | *…, weil sie hatte verhandeln müssen.* |
| Futur I | *Sie wird verhandeln müssen.* | *…, weil sie wird verhandeln müssen.* (also *verhandeln müssen wird*) |

Three things to notice:

1. **Perfekt and Plusquamperfekt use the double infinitive.** When a modal verb has an infinitive with it, its participle (*gemusst, gekonnt, gedurft, gewollt, gesollt, gemocht*) is replaced by the infinitive: *hat verhandeln müssen*, never ~~hat verhandeln gemusst~~. German grammar calls this the *Ersatzinfinitiv* ("replacement infinitive"). The participle survives only when the modal stands alone: *Das hat sie nicht gewollt.* — She didn't want that.
2. **The auxiliary is always *haben*.** The auxiliary belongs to the modal verb, not to the verb that depends on it, so even verbs that take *sein* get *haben*: *Sie ist angereist* but *Sie hat nicht anreisen dürfen.* — She wasn't allowed to travel there.
3. **In a subordinate clause the finite verb doesn't go to the very end.** With a double infinitive, *hat/hatte* comes in front of the whole verb group: *…, weil sie hat verhandeln müssen.* Everything else in the clause (subject, objects, adverbs, *nicht*) stays before *hat*: *…, dass seine Regierung am Ende hat nachgeben müssen.*

The Futur I is the one case where two orders are found. *…, dass man von vorn wird beginnen müssen* follows the same rule as the Perfekt and is the order that grammars recommend for writing; *…, dass man von vorn beginnen müssen wird* puts *wird* at the end and is common in speech. Both are understood. Many writers avoid the question by using the present with a time word: *…, dass man im Herbst von vorn beginnen muss.*

### A tense you can mostly skip

In theory there is also a Futur II with a modal: *Bis Juni wird man den Vertrag haben ratifizieren müssen* (by June they will have had to ratify the treaty). You may meet it in very formal prose, but even careful writers avoid it. Recognize it, and in your own writing say *Bis Juni muss der Vertrag ratifiziert sein.*

## Präteritum or Perfekt?

Both past tenses are correct, but they are not used the same way.

- **In writing**, the Präteritum is the normal narrative tense, and with modal verbs it is also the lighter form: *Die Ministerin durfte nicht anreisen* reads more easily than *Die Ministerin hat nicht anreisen dürfen.* News reports and articles use the Perfekt mainly for something that has just happened and still matters now. That is why the article tells the history in the Präteritum (*stritten, rechnete, standen*) and switches to the Perfekt for the results that count today: *Velarien hat auf einen Teil seiner Staudammpläne verzichten müssen.*
- **In speech**, most speakers in the north and centre of Germany prefer the Präteritum of modal verbs even when they tell everything else in the Perfekt: *Gestern bin ich nach Bonn gefahren, ich musste da einen Vertrag abholen.* The Perfekt *ich habe einen Vertrag abholen müssen* is correct but sounds heavier. In the south of Germany and in Austria, where the Präteritum is rare in speech, you'll hear the Perfekt with the double infinitive much more often.
- **The Plusquamperfekt** marks what had happened before another past event: *Die letzte Runde hatte abgebrochen werden müssen* (before the delegations arrived this time).

A practical rule for your own German: in a written narrative, use the Präteritum of the modal; in conversation, use the Präteritum of the modal and the Perfekt of other verbs; use the Perfekt of the modal when you want to stress a present result (*Wir haben nachgeben müssen, und damit müssen wir jetzt leben*).

## Futur I with a modal verb

*werden* + infinitive + modal infinitive talks about a future obligation, permission or possibility:

- *Scheitert die Ratifizierung, wird man von vorn beginnen müssen.* — If ratification fails, they will have to start again from scratch.
- *Die Delegation wird erst morgen abreisen können.* — The delegation won't be able to leave until tomorrow.
- *Beobachter werden die Pegelstationen jederzeit besuchen dürfen.* — Observers will be allowed to visit the gauging stations at any time.

Don't confuse *wird* (future) with *will* (wants): *Sie will verhandeln* means "she wants to negotiate", not "she will negotiate".

As without a modal, *werden* can also express an assumption about the present, especially with *wohl* (B2 lesson 04): *Die Ministerin wird jetzt wohl unterschreiben müssen.* — The minister will probably have to sign now.

## Modal verb + passive, in every tense

Formal German often combines a modal verb with the passive: a treaty *must be ratified*, sanctions *can be lifted*. The passive part is always Partizip II + *werden*, and *werden* stays in the infinitive because the modal is the finite verb. Then the modal takes the tense:

| tense | main clause | subordinate clause |
|---|---|---|
| Präsens | *Der Vertrag muss ratifiziert werden.* | *…, dass der Vertrag ratifiziert werden muss.* |
| Präteritum | *Der Vertrag musste ratifiziert werden.* | *…, dass der Vertrag ratifiziert werden musste.* |
| Perfekt | *Der Vertrag hat ratifiziert werden müssen.* | *…, dass der Vertrag hat ratifiziert werden müssen.* |
| Plusquamperfekt | *Der Vertrag hatte ratifiziert werden müssen.* | *…, dass der Vertrag hatte ratifiziert werden müssen.* |
| Futur I | *Der Vertrag wird ratifiziert werden müssen.* | *…, dass der Vertrag wird ratifiziert werden müssen.* |
| Konjunktiv II past (lesson 03) | *Der Vertrag hätte ratifiziert werden müssen.* | *…, dass der Vertrag hätte ratifiziert werden müssen.* |

Read each cluster from the right, as at B2: *müssen* (obligation) → *werden* (passive) → *ratifiziert* (what happens). English reads from the left: "has had to be ratified". The German order is the mirror image.

The article has two examples: *Die letzte Gesprächsrunde hatte abgebrochen werden müssen* (the last round had had to be broken off) and *Der Vertragstext hat dreimal neu übersetzt werden müssen* (the text had to be translated anew three times). The agent, if there is one, goes in a *von* phrase before the verbs: *Das Mandat hatte vom Parlament genehmigt werden müssen.*

Four verbs at the end of a subordinate clause are about the limit of what a reader can take in. If a sentence gets heavier than that, use the Präteritum (*…, weil der Text dreimal neu übersetzt werden musste*) or turn it around with *man* (*…, weil man den Text dreimal neu übersetzen musste*).

## Verbs that behave like modals: lassen, sehen, hören, helfen, brauchen

A few other verbs take a bare infinitive and can form their perfect with a double infinitive too.

*lassen* (to let, to have something done) uses the double infinitive whenever an infinitive depends on it:

- *Die Vermittlerin hat die Delegationen in getrennten Räumen verhandeln lassen.* — The mediator had the delegations negotiate in separate rooms.
- *Der Botschafter hat seinen Pass beim Konsulat verlängern lassen.* — The ambassador had his passport renewed at the consulate.

Without an infinitive, *lassen* has its normal participle: *Er hat die Akten im Büro gelassen.* — He left the files in the office.

*sehen* and *hören* (perception verbs) allow both forms. The double infinitive is the traditional written form; the participle is common and also standard:

- *Man hat die Krise kommen sehen.* / *Man hat die Krise kommen gesehen.* — They saw the crisis coming.
- *Ich habe die Delegierten im Flur streiten hören / gehört.* — I heard the delegates arguing in the corridor.

With *helfen* both forms are common: *Sie hat mir den Text übersetzen helfen* or *… übersetzen geholfen*. With *fühlen* and *spüren*, the participle is usual: *Er hat sein Herz schlagen gefühlt.*

*brauchen* + *zu* + infinitive replaces *müssen* after a negation or a restriction (*nicht, kein, nur, erst*): *Sie brauchen nicht zu warten.* — You don't have to wait. *Sie brauchen nur zu unterschreiben.* — You only have to sign. Its perfect usually has the double infinitive as well: *Die Delegation hat nicht lange zu warten brauchen* (the participle *gebraucht* is also found). You only need to recognize this form; in your own writing, the Präteritum is easier: *Die Delegation brauchte nicht lange zu warten.* In speech many people drop the *zu* (*Du brauchst nicht warten*); in writing, keep it.

## Objective or subjective? A first look

The double-infinitive Perfekt is always objective. Compare:

- *Der Diplomat hat von dem Plan wissen müssen.* — The diplomat had to know about the plan (it was his job, he was obliged to be informed).
- *Der Diplomat muss von dem Plan gewusst haben.* — The diplomat must have known about the plan (I'm sure he did).

The first is a past obligation; the second is the speaker's present conclusion about the past. The forms are different: the objective past puts the modal in the past (*hat … müssen, musste*), the subjective past keeps the modal in the present and puts the other verb in the past (*muss … gewusst haben*). Lesson 02 is about the second kind.

## Words: diplomacy and international relations

*die Diplomatie* is the art and the profession; *der Diplomat / die Diplomatin* works in it, at the head of a mission *der Botschafter / die Botschafterin* (from *die Botschaft*, which means both "message" and "embassy"). A *Konsulat* is a smaller mission that looks after citizens abroad: passports, visas, emergencies. At home, *die Außenpolitik* is run by *das Außenministerium* under *der Außenminister / die Außenministerin*; in Germany the ministry's official name is *das Auswärtige Amt*. The adjective *außenpolitisch* means "to do with foreign policy": *eine außenpolitische Krise, außenpolitisch erfahren.*

Relations can be *bilateral* (between two states) or *multilateral* (among many, as in *die Vereinten Nationen*). A *Staatsbesuch* is the most formal visit a head of state makes; a *Gipfeltreffen* (short: *der Gipfel*) brings leaders together. In the UN, *der Sicherheitsrat* has fifteen members, five of them permanent with a veto, and passes *Resolutionen*; under *das Völkerrecht* some of its resolutions are binding. Something *völkerrechtlich verbindlich* is binding under international law.

Pressure works through *Sanktionen* or a full *Embargo*, which a state or the EU *verhängt* (imposes) and later lifts (*aufheben*). Agreements still have to be *ratifiziert* by parliament before they take effect; in Germany, treaties on political relations or on matters of federal law need a federal statute (Article 59(2) of the Basic Law), so the *Ratifizierung* goes through the Bundestag and the Bundesrat, as every federal statute does. A *Bündnis* is an alliance, its members are *Verbündete* (adjectival nouns: *der Verbündete, ein Verbündeter*). Some states stay outside alliances: *die Neutralität* of Switzerland and Austria is part of their identity.

When conflicts escalate, someone has to *deeskalieren*: *die Deeskalation* often starts with a cautious *Annäherung* (rapprochement), helped by a *Vermittler* or *Vermittlerin* and carried out by *Delegationen* that negotiate (*verhandeln*, B2) for nights on end.

## Pronunciation

- *die Diplomatie*: di-plo-ma-TIE, four syllables, stress on the last, with a long *ie*. *der Diplomat*: di-plo-MAHT.
- *das Konsulat* (kon-zu-LAHT), *das Embargo* (em-BAR-go), *die Sanktion* (zank-TSIOHN).
- *ratifizieren*: ra-ti-fi-TSIE-ren; every *-ieren* verb is stressed on *-ie-*.
- *deeskalieren*: de-es-ka-LIE-ren; *de-* and *es-* are separate syllables, with a small break between the two *e*s.
- *das Völkerrecht*: VÖL-ker-recht, stress on the first part, as in most compounds.
- In fast speech the double infinitive is smoothed: *hat nicht kommen dürfen* sounds like *hat nich' komm' dürf'n*. Listen for the second infinitive at the end; it tells you which modal it was.

## Common mistakes

- Using the participle of the modal before an infinitive: ~~Sie hat verhandeln gemusst.~~ → *Sie hat verhandeln müssen.*
- Taking *sein* because the main verb takes *sein*: ~~Sie ist nicht anreisen dürfen.~~ → *Sie hat nicht anreisen dürfen.*
- Putting the finite verb at the end of a subordinate clause with a double infinitive: ~~…, weil sie nachgeben müssen hat.~~ → *…, weil sie hat nachgeben müssen.*
- Putting other parts of the clause between *hat* and the infinitives: ~~…, dass die Regierung hat am Ende nachgeben müssen.~~ → *…, dass die Regierung am Ende hat nachgeben müssen.*
- Forgetting *werden* in the modal passive: ~~Der Vertrag hat ratifiziert müssen.~~ → *Der Vertrag hat ratifiziert werden müssen.*
- Reading *wird … müssen* as the past or *will* as the future: *Sie wird verzichten müssen* = she will have to do without; *Sie will verzichten* = she wants to do without.
- Writing *brauchen* without *zu* in formal texts: ~~Sie brauchen den Antrag nicht unterschreiben.~~ → *Sie brauchen den Antrag nicht zu unterschreiben.*

## Key points

- Perfekt and Plusquamperfekt of a modal with an infinitive: *hat/hatte* + infinitive + modal infinitive (*hat verhandeln müssen*). The auxiliary is always *haben*.
- In a subordinate clause the finite verb goes in front of the double infinitive (*…, weil sie hat nachgeben müssen*); in the Futur, *wird* usually does too, but *… müssen wird* is also found.
- Modal + passive: Partizip II + *werden* + modal, in every tense (*musste ratifiziert werden, hat ratifiziert werden müssen, wird ratifiziert werden müssen*). Read the cluster from the right.
- *lassen* always uses the double infinitive with an infinitive; *sehen* and *hören* allow both forms; *helfen* takes either; *fühlen* and *spüren* usually take the participle. *brauchen + zu* replaces *müssen* after *nicht* and *nur*.
- In writing and in northern speech the Präteritum of modals is the lighter, more common past; the Perfekt stresses a present result and is frequent in the south.
- The double-infinitive past is objective (a past obligation). *Er muss es gewusst haben* is subjective (lesson 02).

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete the lesson.

lessons.title: She must have known: subjective modal verbs about the past
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Lesson 01 was about the **[[objective use]]** of modal verbs: what someone had to do, was allowed to do or wanted to do. At B2 (lesson 03) you also met the other use, in which a modal verb says how sure the speaker is or where the information comes from: *Er soll reich sein* (he is said to be rich), *Das muss ein Irrtum sein* (that must be a mistake). You saw the perfect infinitive (*gelogen haben, zurückgetreten sein*) and a scale from *muss* to *kann nicht*.

This lesson takes that system into the past and makes it precise. You will learn

- the full scale of certainty for past events, with each step's typical paraphrase;
- how the subjective past (*Er muss gegangen sein*) differs from the objective past (*Er musste gehen, Er hat gehen müssen*), and the few forms that can be read both ways;
- the subjective modals with the passive (*Die Urkunde muss gefälscht worden sein*);
- where *werden* + perfect infinitive fits in, and the rarer *mögen*;
- the word order when these clusters stand in a subordinate clause.

No text type uses subjective modals as much as historical writing. Historians rarely know; they infer, estimate, report what a source claims and say what can't have happened. The theme is history and historiography: chronicles, sieges, plagues and the critical reading of sources.

## How the past form is built

A subjective modal judges the past from the present. So the modal stays in the present (or in the Konjunktiv II), and the event itself moves into the past with the perfect infinitive: Partizip II + *haben* or *sein*.

| | present | past |
|---|---|---|
| active, *haben* | *Er muss es wissen.* | *Er muss es gewusst haben.* |
| active, *sein* | *Sie dürfte schon unterwegs sein.* | *Sie dürfte bereits abgereist sein.* |
| *sein* itself | *Das kann nicht wahr sein.* | *Das kann nicht wahr gewesen sein.* |
| passive | *Die Urkunde muss gefälscht werden.* (objective!) | *Die Urkunde muss gefälscht worden sein.* |

The choice between *haben* and *sein* is the same as in the Perfekt: *abreisen, gehen, entstehen, geschehen, sterben* take *sein* (*abgereist sein, entstanden sein*), most other verbs *haben*. In the passive the perfect infinitive is always Partizip II + *worden sein*.

Note the passive row. In the present, *Die Urkunde muss gefälscht werden* can only be objective (the document has to be forged), which is why subjective modals in the passive almost always appear in the past form. *Die Urkunde muss gefälscht sein* (Zustandspassiv) is subjective again: "the document must be a forgery", describing its state now.

## The scale of certainty, for the past

From most to least certain. Each line gives a paraphrase without a modal, which you can use for variety or when a modal would be ambiguous.

| modal + perfect infinitive | meaning | paraphrase |
|---|---|---|
| *Er muss es gewusst haben.* | conclusion: I'm sure | *Er hat es sicher / bestimmt / zweifellos gewusst.* |
| *Er dürfte es gewusst haben.* | probable | *Er hat es wahrscheinlich / vermutlich gewusst.* |
| *Er wird es (wohl) gewusst haben.* | assumption | *Ich nehme an, dass er es gewusst hat.* |
| *Er müsste es gewusst haben.* | expected: by all logic | *Nach allem, was wir wissen, hat er es gewusst.* |
| *Er kann / könnte es gewusst haben.* | possible | *Er hat es vielleicht / möglicherweise gewusst.* |
| *Er mag es gewusst haben (, aber …).* | possible, conceded | *Es ist möglich, dass er es gewusst hat, aber …* |
| *Er muss es nicht gewusst haben.* | not necessarily | *Es ist nicht sicher, dass er es gewusst hat.* |
| *Er kann es nicht gewusst haben.* | impossible | *Es ist ausgeschlossen, dass er es gewusst hat.* |

Grammars don't all rank the middle steps the same way, and in real texts *dürfte*, *wird wohl* and *müsste* are close. What matters is the clear difference between the ends of the scale and the three negative forms:

- *kann nicht* = impossible: *Die Inschrift kann nicht vor 1200 entstanden sein.* — The inscription can't have been made before 1200.
- *muss nicht* = not necessarily (never "must not"): *Der Chronist muss nicht gelogen haben.* — The chronicler didn't necessarily lie.
- *dürfte nicht* = probably not: *Die Belagerung dürfte nicht lange gedauert haben.* — The siege probably didn't last long.

*darf* (indicative) has no subjective use: *Er darf es gewusst haben* is not a way of saying "he probably knew".

### müsste: what the evidence leads you to expect

*müsste* + perfect infinitive is typical of argument: if X were true, we would expect Y, and Y is missing. *Ein Heer, das monatelang vor der Stadt lag, müsste Spuren hinterlassen haben.* — An army that lay before the town for months ought to have left traces. Don't confuse it with *hätte … müssen*, the objective Konjunktiv II of lesson 03: *Er hätte es wissen müssen* is a reproach (he should have known, it was his job).

### mögen: possible, but …

Subjective *mögen* (B2: recognize only) is formal and mostly concessive: it grants a possibility in order to limit it. *Die Belagerung mag stattgefunden haben, aber sicher nicht sieben Monate lang.* — The siege may have taken place, but certainly not for seven months. It also gives rough estimates: *Sie mag damals vierzig gewesen sein* (she may have been about forty then). In older literature you will occasionally meet *möchte* in the same sense (*Es möchte gegen Mitternacht gewesen sein* — it may have been about midnight); today that use is old-fashioned, and *möchte* means "would like".

### werden + perfect infinitive

At B2 (lesson 04) you learned the Futur II as an assumption about the past: *Er wird den Zug verpasst haben.* — He'll have missed the train (I assume). It is a conversational way of guessing, often with *wohl* or *schon*: *Das wird schon seine Gründe gehabt haben.* — There'll have been reasons for that. In academic writing *dürfte* is the more usual choice.

## Where the information comes from: sollen and wollen

Two subjective modals don't express certainty but the source of a statement.

*sollen* passes on what others say (hearsay): *Das Heer soll die Stadt sieben Monate lang belagert haben.* — The army is said to have besieged the town for seven months. The writer neither confirms nor denies; it is the modal equivalent of *angeblich* or *Es heißt, dass …*.

*wollen* reports the subject's own claim, usually with doubt: *Der Chronist will die Belagerung mit eigenen Augen gesehen haben.* — The chronicler claims to have seen the siege with his own eyes. Compare *Er behauptet, die Belagerung gesehen zu haben.* Subjective *wollen* always reports what the subject claims about himself or herself. With a *dass* clause, *wollen* is the ordinary objective verb: *Der Chronist will, dass man ihm glaubt* (he wants people to believe him).

These two are common in history, journalism and court reports, because they let the writer report a claim without taking responsibility for it. Lesson 04 shows the other tool for that job: the Konjunktiv I.

## Objective or subjective? Telling the past forms apart

The form usually tells you which use you have.

| | objective (what the subject had to do) | subjective (what the speaker concludes) |
|---|---|---|
| form | modal in the past, main verb in the infinitive | modal in the present, main verb in the perfect infinitive |
| example | *Er musste gehen. / Er hat gehen müssen.* | *Er muss gegangen sein.* |
| meaning | He had to go. | He must have gone. |
| example | *Sie konnte die Inschrift lesen. / Sie hat sie lesen können.* | *Sie kann die Inschrift gelesen haben.* |
| meaning | She was able to read the inscription. | She may (could) have read the inscription. |
| example | *Er sollte die Stadt verteidigen.* | *Er soll die Stadt verteidigt haben.* |
| meaning | He was supposed to defend the town. | He is said to have defended the town. |

A few strings need context:

- *sollte* + perfect infinitive is mostly the Konjunktiv II of expectation: *Der Bote sollte längst angekommen sein.* — The messenger should have arrived long ago (and I'm surprised he hasn't). This is not hearsay.
- *musste* + perfect infinitive appears in past-tense narratives for a conclusion drawn at that time: *Der Graf war wütend. Jemand musste ihn verraten haben.* — Someone must have betrayed him (so he thought). In a narrative this is the subjective *muss* moved into the past along with everything else.
- *Er muss es wissen* can be either: "he has to know it" (objective: it's his job) or "he must know it" (subjective: surely he does). In the past the forms separate: *Er hat es wissen müssen* vs *Er muss es gewusst haben*.

## Word order in subordinate clauses

With the perfect infinitive there is no double infinitive, so the normal rule applies: the finite verb, here the modal, goes to the very end.

- *Ich glaube, dass er es gewusst haben muss.* — I think he must have known.
- *Man vermutet, dass die Chronik um 1410 abgeschrieben worden sein dürfte.* — It is assumed that the chronicle was probably copied around 1410.
- *Es ist unklar, ob die Kaiserin den Brief selbst geschrieben haben kann.* — It is unclear whether the empress can have written the letter herself.

Read the cluster from the right as usual: *dürfte* (probably) → *sein* (perfect) → *worden* (passive) → *abgeschrieben*. Clusters like this are correct but heavy, and the second example is clumsy because the main verb *vermuten* already expresses the assumption. Good writers keep the subjective modal in a main clause (*Die Chronik dürfte um 1410 abgeschrieben worden sein*) or use an adverb in the subordinate clause (*…, dass die Chronik vermutlich um 1410 abgeschrieben wurde*).

## Text: Eine Belagerung, die es nicht gab?

This is an excerpt from an article in a regional history journal (*Zeitschrift für Landesgeschichte*). The monastery, the chronicle and the town are invented; the methods are those of real source criticism.

> **Eine Belagerung, die es nicht gab? Zur Quellenkritik der Chronik von Hohenwart**
>
> Die Chronik des Klosters Hohenwart gilt seit dem 19. Jahrhundert als wichtigste Quelle für die Geschichte der Region im Spätmittelalter. Ihr Verfasser, ein Mönch namens Konrad, will die Belagerung der Stadt im Jahr 1349 mit eigenen Augen gesehen haben. Das Heer des Grafen soll die Mauern sieben Monate lang belagert haben, bis die Bürger wegen einer Hungersnot aufgaben.
>
> Die neuere Geschichtswissenschaft ist skeptischer. Zunächst zur Datierung: Die Handschrift, die wir besitzen, kann nicht vor 1396 entstanden sein, denn ihr Papier stammt aus einer Mühle, die erst in diesem Jahr gegründet wurde. Sie kann also nicht Konrads eigene Niederschrift sein; ein späterer Schreiber muss eine ältere Fassung abgeschrieben haben. Dabei dürfte er den Text auch ergänzt haben, denn einige Ortsnamen erscheinen in einer Form, die erst um 1400 belegt ist.
>
> Auch inhaltlich gibt es Zweifel. Im Sommer 1349 erreichte die Pest die Region. Ein Heer, das sieben Monate vor der Stadt lag, müsste in den Steuerlisten und Urkunden der Nachbarorte Spuren hinterlassen haben. Solche Spuren fehlen. Die Belagerung mag stattgefunden haben; sie kann aber kaum so lange gedauert haben, wie die Chronik behauptet.
>
> Bemerkenswert ist schließlich eine Inschrift am Stadttor, die auf das Jahr 1352 datiert ist und den „treuen Bürgern“ für ihren Widerstand dankt. Sie galt lange als Beweis für die Belagerung. Inzwischen weiß man, dass sie im 19. Jahrhundert erneuert und dabei wohl verändert worden ist. Die ursprüngliche Inschrift könnte ganz anders gelautet haben, und die Bürger werden die Geschichte von ihrem Widerstand gern weitererzählt haben.
>
> Was bleibt? Konrad muss kein Lügner gewesen sein. Chronisten schrieben, um ihr Kloster und ihre Herrscher in gutem Licht erscheinen zu lassen, und die Überlieferung hat das Ihre dazu getan. Für die Historikerin heißt das: Eine Chronik erzählt, was man glauben sollte – nicht unbedingt, was geschah.

**Translation.** *A siege that never happened? On the source criticism of the Hohenwart chronicle.* Since the 19th century the chronicle of Hohenwart monastery has been regarded as the most important source for the region's history in the late Middle Ages. Its author, a monk called Konrad, claims to have seen the siege of the town in 1349 with his own eyes. The count's army is said to have besieged the walls for seven months, until the citizens gave up because of a famine. Recent historical scholarship is more sceptical. First, the dating: the manuscript we have can't have been written before 1396, because its paper comes from a mill that was only founded in that year. So it can't be Konrad's own copy; a later scribe must have copied an older version. He probably added to the text while doing so, because some place names appear in a form that is attested only from around 1400. There are doubts about the content too. In the summer of 1349 the plague reached the region. An army that lay before the town for seven months ought to have left traces in the tax lists and charters of the neighbouring places. There are no such traces. The siege may have taken place, but it can hardly have lasted as long as the chronicle claims. Finally, there is a notable inscription on the town gate, dated 1352, which thanks the "loyal citizens" for their resistance. For a long time it was considered proof of the siege. We now know that it was renewed in the 19th century and probably altered in the process. The original inscription may have read quite differently, and the citizens will have been glad to keep telling the story of their resistance. What remains? Konrad wasn't necessarily a liar. Chroniclers wrote to show their monastery and their rulers in a good light, and the process of transmission did the rest. For the historian this means: a chronicle tells you what people were meant to believe, not necessarily what happened.

### How the text uses the modals

The article climbs up and down the scale of certainty, and each step is chosen on purpose:

- *will … gesehen haben* and *soll … belagert haben*: the chronicle's claims, reported without being confirmed. *will* is Konrad's own claim; *soll* is what the chronicle says happened.
- *kann nicht … entstanden sein*: a firm exclusion, based on hard evidence (the paper).
- *muss … abgeschrieben haben*: a logical conclusion from that evidence.
- *dürfte … ergänzt haben*: a probable explanation, backed by a weaker argument (the place names).
- *müsste … hinterlassen haben*: what one would expect if the chronicle were right; the missing traces then count against it.
- *mag … stattgefunden haben; … kann aber kaum … gedauert haben*: a concession followed by a restriction.
- *könnte … gelautet haben* and *werden … weitererzählt haben*: possibilities and plausible assumptions, clearly marked as such.
- *muss kein Lügner gewesen sein*: "not necessarily", the negative of *muss*. *Er kann kein Lügner gewesen sein* would say something much stronger: that he certainly wasn't one.

Compare *was man glauben sollte* in the last sentence: here *sollte* is objective (Präteritum: what people were supposed to believe).

## Words: history and historiography

*die Geschichte* (A1) means both "story" and "history"; the academic discipline is *die Geschichtswissenschaft*, and the people who practise it are *Historiker* and *Historikerinnen*. Their method starts with *die Quellenkritik*: who wrote a source, when, for whom and with what aim. That includes *die Datierung* (dating): a historian *datiert* a document *auf* a year (*Die Urkunde wird auf 1352 datiert*). What reaches us from the past is *die Überlieferung*, from *überliefern* (B1, to hand down): *Die Chronik ist nur in einer Abschrift überliefert.*

The big periods: *die Antike* (Greek and Roman antiquity; the adjective *antik* also means "antique"), then *die Völkerwanderung*, the Migration Period of the 4th to 6th centuries, then *das Mittelalter* (*mittelalterlich*, medieval), and from about 1500 *die Neuzeit*. A long period named after what shaped it is *ein Zeitalter* (*das Zeitalter der Reformation*); *die Epoche* (B1) is the more general word.

Power and society: *die Herrschaft* of a *Herrscher* or *Herrscherin* over a *Reich* (empire, realm; not the adjective *reich*), with *der Kaiser* (B1) or *die Kaiserin* at the top and *der Adel* (the nobility; *adlig* or *adelig*, noble) below. Many peasants lived in *Leibeigenschaft*, serfdom, bound to their lord's land. War: *ein Feldzug* (campaign), *die Belagerung* of a town (*eine Stadt belagern*), and finally *die Eroberung* (*erobern*, to conquer). *Der Untergang* is the fall of an empire, a dynasty or a ship: *der Untergang des Weströmischen Reiches.* And the great disasters of the late Middle Ages: *die Pest*, which killed a large part of Europe's population after 1347 (estimates range from about a third to a half), and repeated *Hungersnöte*. Our knowledge of them comes from *Chroniken* written by *Chronisten*, from charters, tax lists and *Inschriften*.

## Pronunciation

- *die Chronik*: KROH-nik, with *ch* = *k*, as in most Greek words (*Chor, Charakter*). *der Chronist*: kro-NIST.
- *der Historiker*: his-TOH-ri-ker; *die Geschichtswissenschaft*: ge-SCHICHTS-wis-sen-schaft, stress on the first part.
- *die Antike*: an-TIE-ke; *antik*: an-TIEK.
- *die Leibeigenschaft*: LEIB-ei-gen-schaft; *die Völkerwanderung*: VÖL-ker-wan-de-rung.
- In speech the perfect infinitive is often reduced: *muss gewusst haben* sounds like *muss gewusst ham*. The modal is unstressed; the stress goes on the participle (*Er muss es geWUSST haben*) or on a contrasting word.

## Common mistakes

- Putting the modal in the past to talk about a conclusion now: ~~Er hat es gewusst haben müssen.~~ → *Er muss es gewusst haben.*
- Using the present infinitive for a past event: ~~Die Stadt soll 1349 belagern werden.~~ → *Die Stadt soll 1349 belagert worden sein.*
- Forgetting *worden* in the passive: ~~Die Urkunde muss gefälscht sein worden.~~ → *Die Urkunde muss gefälscht worden sein.* (*worden* before *sein*)
- Moving the modal forward in a subordinate clause, as with the double infinitive: ~~…, dass er es muss gewusst haben.~~ → *…, dass er es gewusst haben muss.*
- Reading *muss nicht* as "must not": *Er muss nicht gelogen haben* = he didn't necessarily lie. For "he can't have lied" say *Er kann nicht gelogen haben.*
- Reading subjective *wollen* as a wish: *Sie will nichts gesehen haben* = she claims to have seen nothing, not "she wants to have seen nothing".
- Using *darf* for probability: ~~Er darf das gewusst haben.~~ → *Er dürfte das gewusst haben.*

## Key points

- Subjective modal about the past = modal in the present (or *dürfte, müsste, könnte*) + perfect infinitive: *muss gewusst haben, dürfte abgereist sein*. Passive: *muss gefälscht worden sein*.
- The scale: *muss* (sure) > *dürfte* / *wird wohl* / *müsste* (probable, assumed, expected) > *kann / könnte / mag* (possible) > *kann nicht* (impossible). *muss nicht* = not necessarily; *dürfte nicht* = probably not.
- *soll* = it is said (hearsay); *will* = the subject claims.
- The objective past puts the modal in the past (*musste gehen, hat gehen müssen*); the subjective past keeps it in the present (*muss gegangen sein*). *sollte* + perfect infinitive is usually an expectation, *musste* + perfect infinitive a conclusion inside a past narrative.
- In a subordinate clause the modal goes to the very end: *…, dass er es gewusst haben muss.*
- Historians use the whole scale to separate what they know, infer, assume and merely report.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete the lesson.

lessons.title: It could have been prevented: Konjunktiv II of the past
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

At B1 (lesson 22) you learned the Konjunktiv II of the past: *hätte* or *wäre* + Partizip II (*Ich hätte es gewusst; Sie wäre geblieben*), unreal conditions (*Wenn ich das gewusst hätte, …*), *hätte … sollen* and *hätte … können* as patterns, and *beinahe* + Konjunktiv. Lesson 01 of this course showed how modal verbs and the passive combine in every tense.

This lesson puts the two together. Public debate after any disaster is full of sentences like *Das hätte verhindert werden können* and *Man hätte die Menschen früher warnen müssen*, and you need to understand them at speed, build them yourself and choose the right modal. You will also learn the other unreal structures that C1 texts use: conditions without *wenn*, wishes, comparisons (*als hätte es nie geregnet*) and unreal consequences (*zu stark, als dass man …*). Finally, there is a section on the look-alikes (*hatte/hätte, war/wäre*) that decide whether something happened or not, which matters most when you only hear it.

The theme is natural hazards and civil protection: floods, landslides, warning systems, evacuation and what happens afterwards.

## The basic form, briefly

| | indicative (it happened) | Konjunktiv II past (it didn't) |
|---|---|---|
| *haben* verbs | *Man hat gewarnt.* | *Man hätte gewarnt.* |
| *sein* verbs | *Der Damm ist gebrochen.* | *Der Damm wäre gebrochen.* |
| passive | *Das Dorf ist evakuiert worden.* | *Das Dorf wäre evakuiert worden.* |

There is only one past form: *hätte/wäre* + Partizip II, with *worden* in the passive. Note that the passive takes *wäre*, because the passive auxiliary *werden* takes *sein* in the perfect.

## With a modal verb: hätte + infinitive + modal infinitive

As soon as a modal verb is involved, the auxiliary is always *hätte*, and the modal appears as an infinitive (the double infinitive of lesson 01):

- *Man hätte die Bewohner früher warnen müssen.* — The residents should have been warned earlier. (literally: one would have had to warn them)
- *Sie hätte es wissen können.* — She could have known it.
- *Die Gemeinde hätte die Arbeiten nicht verschieben sollen.* — The council shouldn't have postponed the work.
- *Die Familien hätten in der Turnhalle übernachten dürfen.* — The families would have been allowed to spend the night in the gym.

Even verbs that take *sein* get *hätte* here, because the auxiliary belongs to the modal: *Sie wäre geflohen* but *Sie hätte fliehen können.*

### sollen, müssen, können: which one?

All three are about something that didn't happen, but they judge it differently.

| pattern | meaning | typical use | example |
|---|---|---|---|
| *hätte … sollen* | it would have been right or advisable | reproach, regret, advice that comes too late | *Wir hätten auf die Warnung hören sollen.* — We should have listened to the warning. |
| *hätte … müssen* | it was necessary (rules, facts, duty) | stronger reproach; consequences in a condition | *Nach den Vorschriften hätte der Krisenstab sofort tagen müssen.* — Under the rules the crisis team should have met at once. |
| *hätte … können* | it was possible | missed chance; "you could have …" | *Mit einem Frühwarnsystem hätte man die Menschen warnen können.* — With an early warning system people could have been warned. |
| *hätte … dürfen* | it would have been allowed | permission that wasn't used | *Wir hätten früher nach Hause gehen dürfen.* — We would have been allowed to go home earlier. |

*hätte … sollen* and *hätte … müssen* both translate as "should have". The difference is the source of the obligation: *sollen* is what someone thinks would have been right; *müssen* is what the rules, the facts or one's duty required. A report that says *Die Sirenen hätten um 21 Uhr ausgelöst werden müssen* says that the warning plan demanded it, not just that it would have been a good idea.

In a condition, *hätte … müssen* also means "would have had to": *Wäre der Damm gebrochen, hätte man das ganze Dorf evakuieren müssen.* — If the dam had broken, the whole village would have had to be evacuated.

*hätte … können* can also be a reproach in conversation: *Du hättest mich anrufen können!* — You could have called me!

## With the passive: the four-verb cluster

| | main clause | meaning |
|---|---|---|
| passive, no modal | *Das Dorf wäre evakuiert worden.* | would have been evacuated |
| passive + *können* | *Das hätte verhindert werden können.* | could have been prevented |
| passive + *müssen* | *Die Sirenen hätten früher ausgelöst werden müssen.* | should have been set off earlier |
| passive + *sollen* | *Die Deiche hätten längst erhöht werden sollen.* | should have been raised long ago |

Read from the right as always: *können* (possibility) → *werden* (passive) → *verhindert* (the event), all under *hätte* (unreal past). English has the same four parts in the opposite order: *could have been prevented*.

## In subordinate clauses

With a double infinitive, *hätte* goes in front of the infinitives, not to the end (lesson 01); everything else stays before it:

- *…, obwohl man die Gefahr hätte vorhersehen können.* — although the danger could have been foreseen.
- *…, dass die Sirenen viel früher hätten ausgelöst werden müssen.* — that the sirens should have been set off much earlier.
- *…, weil man die Altstadt rechtzeitig hätte räumen können.* — because the old town could have been cleared in time.

Without a modal there is no double infinitive, so the finite verb goes to the end as usual: *…, wenn die Sirenen früher ausgelöst worden wären.*

| | main clause | subordinate clause |
|---|---|---|
| no modal | *Man hätte gewarnt.* | *…, dass man gewarnt hätte.* |
| passive | *Man wäre gewarnt worden.* | *…, dass man gewarnt worden wäre.* |
| modal | *Man hätte warnen müssen.* | *…, dass man hätte warnen müssen.* |
| modal + passive | *Das hätte verhindert werden können.* | *…, dass das hätte verhindert werden können.* |

## Conditions without wenn

Formal German often drops *wenn* and puts the verb first: the verb-first conditional you met at B1 and B2. In the past this is very common, because *hätte* and *wäre* make the condition unmistakable:

- *Hätte die Gemeinde die Deiche erhöht, wäre das Wasser nicht in die Altstadt gelangt.* — Had the council raised the dikes, the water would not have reached the old town.
- *Wäre der Damm gebrochen, hätte es Dutzende Todesopfer geben können.* — Had the dam broken, there could have been dozens of deaths.
- *Hätte man früher evakuieren können, hätte man es getan.* — If it had been possible to evacuate earlier, it would have been done.

In formal writing the main clause can begin with *so* or *dann*: *Hätte man die Warnung ernst genommen, so wäre niemand ums Leben gekommen.*

A condition can also be packed into a phrase, with no clause at all:

- *Mit einem Frühwarnsystem hätten die Menschen rechtzeitig gewarnt werden können.* — With an early warning system …
- *Ohne die Sandsäcke wäre der Damm gebrochen.* — Without the sandbags …
- *Bei rechtzeitiger Warnung hätte niemand sterben müssen.* — With a timely warning nobody would have had to die.

## Wishes and regrets

An unreal wish about the past uses the same forms, usually with *doch*, *nur* or *bloß* (or a combination):

- *Hätten wir doch nur auf die Warnungen gehört!* — If only we had listened to the warnings!
- *Wäre ich bloß früher losgefahren!* — If only I had set off earlier!
- *Wenn man die Deiche doch rechtzeitig erhöht hätte!* — If only the dikes had been raised in time!
- *Hätte man das doch früher wissen können!* — If only it had been possible to know that earlier!

With *wenn* the verb goes to the end; without *wenn* it comes first. The particles are what make it a wish rather than the first half of a condition. *Ich wünschte, ich hätte …* (B1) says the same thing in a full sentence.

## Unreal comparisons: als hätte …

A comparison with something that isn't true takes *als* + the finite verb directly after it, or *als ob* / *als wenn* with the verb at the end (B2 lesson 18):

- *Am nächsten Morgen schien die Sonne, als hätte es nie geregnet.* — … as if it had never rained.
- *…, als ob es nie geregnet hätte.* (same meaning)
- *Wer jetzt so tut, als hätte niemand etwas ahnen können, macht es sich zu leicht.* — Anyone who now acts as if nobody could have suspected anything is making it too easy for themselves.

In formal texts the Konjunktiv I also appears here: *Er tat, als sei nichts geschehen.* Both forms are standard.

## Unreal consequences

Some sentences state that a consequence did not follow, because a condition was too strong or too weak. The consequence clause is then in the Konjunktiv II. This is the **[[irreal consequence clause]]**, and C1 texts use three patterns.

*zu …, als dass* (B2 lesson 17): something was too X for Y to happen.

- *Der Regen war zu stark, als dass man alle Schäden hätte verhindern können.* — The rain was too heavy for all the damage to be prevented.
- *Die Zeit war zu knapp, als dass alle Häuser hätten geräumt werden können.* — There was too little time for all the houses to be cleared.

Compare the infinitive alternative, possible when the subjects match: *Die Feuerwehr war zu schlecht ausgerüstet, um alle Schäden verhindern zu können* (= *…, als dass sie alle Schäden hätte verhindern können*).

*nicht so …, dass*: something was not so X that Y would have followed. With a negated main clause, the *dass* clause describes a consequence that didn't happen, so it often takes the Konjunktiv II:

- *Das Unwetter kam nicht so überraschend, dass niemand hätte reagieren können.* — The storm didn't come so unexpectedly that nobody could have reacted.

*ohne dass*: something happened without something else happening. Here the Konjunktiv II is common but not required; the indicative is also correct.

- *Der Fluss stieg stundenlang, ohne dass jemand Alarm geschlagen hätte.* (or: *… Alarm schlug.*) — The river rose for hours without anyone raising the alarm.

## Almost: beinahe and fast

*beinahe* or *fast* + Konjunktiv II past says that something nearly happened (B1). It works with every form of this lesson:

- *Beinahe wäre der Damm gebrochen.* — The dam almost broke.
- *Fast wäre das ganze Dorf überflutet worden.* — The whole village was almost flooded.
- *Beinahe hätten die Rettungskräfte umkehren müssen.* — The rescue workers almost had to turn back.

The indicative (*Der Damm ist beinahe gebrochen*) is also common, especially in speech. The Konjunktiv makes it unmistakable that it didn't happen.

## Look-alikes: did it happen or not?

The Konjunktiv II past and the Plusquamperfekt differ in one vowel. In writing you see the umlaut; in speech you have to hear it.

| Plusquamperfekt (it happened) | Konjunktiv II past (it didn't) |
|---|---|
| *Man hatte gewarnt.* — They had warned. | *Man hätte gewarnt.* — They would have warned. |
| *Der Damm war gebrochen.* — The dam had broken. | *Der Damm wäre gebrochen.* — The dam would have broken. |
| *Das Dorf war evakuiert worden.* — The village had been evacuated. | *Das Dorf wäre evakuiert worden.* — The village would have been evacuated. |
| *Man hatte warnen müssen.* — They had had to warn. | *Man hätte warnen müssen.* — They should have warned. |

*hatte* has a short [a], *hätte* the open [ɛ] of *Bett*; *war* has a long [aː], *wäre* the long [ɛː] of *Käse*. In fast speech the difference is small, so check the context too: a sentence that continues *…, aber niemand hat reagiert* or follows a *wenn* clause is usually unreal.

Two modals have no visible difference at all: *sollte* and *wollte* are both Präteritum and Konjunktiv II. *Man sollte die Deiche erhöhen* can mean "the dikes were supposed to be raised" or "the dikes ought to be raised". In the past, use the unambiguous *hätte … sollen*.

## Text: Die Katastrophe, die man hätte kommen sehen können

This is a newspaper commentary (*Kommentar*) after a flood. The valley, the town and the report are invented.

> **Kommentar: Die Katastrophe, die man hätte kommen sehen können**
>
> Drei Wochen nach dem Hochwasser im Velbachtal ist die Frage nicht mehr, ob Fehler gemacht wurden, sondern wie viele. Der Bericht des Krisenstabs, der am Montag vorgestellt wurde, liest sich wie eine Liste verpasster Gelegenheiten.
>
> Die Sirenen etwa hätten schon um 21 Uhr ausgelöst werden müssen, als der Pegel die Warnstufe überschritt. Stattdessen stieg der Fluss stundenlang, ohne dass jemand Alarm geschlagen hätte. Ausgelöst wurden die Sirenen erst nach Mitternacht, zu spät für die Bewohner der unteren Altstadt, die man rechtzeitig hätte evakuieren können. Dass man die Häuser am Fluss nicht früher geräumt hat, obwohl man die Gefahr hätte vorhersehen können, ist der schwerste Vorwurf des Berichts.
>
> Auch die Vorsorge war lückenhaft. Hätte die Gemeinde die Deiche nach der Risikobewertung von 2015 erhöht, wäre das Wasser wohl gar nicht in die Altstadt gelangt. Das Geld dafür war bewilligt worden; der Bau wurde trotzdem zweimal verschoben. Man hätte die Arbeiten nicht verschieben sollen, räumt inzwischen sogar der Bürgermeister ein.
>
> Glimpflich ist das Tal dennoch nicht davongekommen: Zwei Menschen sind ums Leben gekommen, der Sachschaden wird auf mehrere Hundert Millionen Euro geschätzt. Beinahe wäre auch der alte Damm oberhalb von Ried gebrochen; die Rettungskräfte sicherten ihn die ganze Nacht mit Sandsäcken. Wäre er gebrochen, hätte es Dutzende Todesopfer geben können.
>
> Natürlich ist man hinterher immer klüger, und kein Frühwarnsystem macht ein Unwetter harmlos. Der Regen war zu stark, als dass man alle Schäden hätte verhindern können. Aber er kam nicht so überraschend, dass niemand hätte reagieren können: Der Wetterdienst hatte zwei Tage vorher gewarnt.
>
> Wer jetzt so tut, als hätte niemand etwas ahnen können, macht es sich zu leicht. „Hätten wir doch nur auf die Warnungen gehört!“ – dieser Satz hilft den Betroffenen nicht mehr. Helfen würde es, die Lehren des Berichts umzusetzen, bevor das nächste Unwetter kommt.

**Translation.** *Commentary: The disaster that could have been seen coming.* Three weeks after the flood in the Velbach valley, the question is no longer whether mistakes were made, but how many. The crisis team's report, presented on Monday, reads like a list of missed opportunities. The sirens, for example, should have been set off as early as 9 p.m., when the water level passed the warning mark. Instead the river rose for hours without anyone raising the alarm. The sirens were only set off after midnight, too late for the residents of the lower old town, who could have been evacuated in time. That the houses by the river weren't cleared earlier, although the danger could have been foreseen, is the report's most serious charge. Prevention was patchy too. Had the council raised the dikes after the 2015 risk assessment, the water would probably not have reached the old town at all. The money had been approved; the work was nevertheless postponed twice. The work shouldn't have been postponed, even the mayor now admits. Even so, the valley didn't get off lightly: two people died, and the property damage is estimated at several hundred million euros. The old dam above Ried almost broke too; the rescue workers secured it all night with sandbags. Had it broken, there could have been dozens of deaths. Of course, hindsight is always wiser, and no early warning system makes a storm harmless. The rain was too heavy for all the damage to be prevented. But it didn't come so unexpectedly that nobody could have reacted: the weather service had issued a warning two days before. Anyone who now acts as if nobody could have suspected anything is making it too easy for themselves. "If only we had listened to the warnings!": that sentence no longer helps those affected. What would help is putting the report's lessons into practice before the next storm comes.

Look at how the commentary moves between real and unreal. The facts are in the indicative (*stieg, wurden ausgelöst, sind ums Leben gekommen, hatte gewarnt*); the missed alternatives are all in the Konjunktiv II. Note especially *Der Wetterdienst hatte zwei Tage vorher gewarnt*: Plusquamperfekt, because the warning really was given. *Hätte* there would turn the whole argument upside down.

## Words: natural hazards and civil protection

A *Naturgefahr* (natural hazard: flood, storm, landslide, avalanche) becomes a *Naturkatastrophe* when it hits people and things. In Central Europe the typical hazards are *das Hochwasser* (B1), *die Sturmflut* on the coasts, *die Lawine* in the Alps and *der Erdrutsch* after long rain. *Erdbeben* (with *Nachbeben*, aftershocks), *Vulkanausbrüche* and *Tsunamis* are rarer here but common in the news. Protection is built: *der Deich* holds back rivers and the sea, *der Damm* holds back water in a valley or carries a road over wet ground.

Organized protection has two names in Germany. *Der Katastrophenschutz* (disasters in peacetime) is the responsibility of the federal states; *der Zivilschutz* (protecting the population in war) is the federal government's. When disaster strikes, a *Krisenstab* takes charge, *Rettungskräfte* (fire brigades, relief organizations, police) carry out *die Evakuierung* (people are *evakuiert*) and set up *Notunterkünfte*. A government can declare *den Ausnahmezustand*, the official state of emergency; *der Notstand* is the acute shortage or crisis itself (*Pflegenotstand*, a staffing emergency in care) and also a legal term.

Warning: *die Sirene*, apps, and since 2023 messages sent to every mobile phone in an area (Cell Broadcast); a nationwide warning day (*bundesweiter Warntag*) tests the system once a year. A good *Frühwarnsystem* gives time, a careful *Risikobewertung* tells you where to build, but a *Restrisiko* (residual risk) always remains, and some events are simply *unvorhersehbar*.

After the event: *das Ausmaß* of the damage, *Todesopfer* and *Sachschaden*, *verheerende* consequences (devastating) or, with luck, an outcome that is *glimpflich* (*glimpflich davonkommen*, to get off lightly). People *verschüttet* under rubble or snow must be *geborgen* (*bergen*: *barg, hat geborgen*); *die Bergung* is the work of getting them, or a wreck, out. In July 2021 floods in western Germany, especially in the Ahr valley, killed more than 180 people; much of the debate since has been about warnings that came too late.

## Pronunciation

- *die Lawine*: la-WIE-ne; *der Vulkan*: vul-KAHN; *der Tsunami*: tsu-NAH-mi, with *ts* as in *Zeit*.
- *die Evakuierung*: e-va-ku-IE-rung (*v* as in English *v*); *evakuieren*: e-va-ku-IE-ren.
- *die Sirene*: si-REH-ne, with a voiced *s* at the start.
- *glimpflich*: GLIMPF-lich; the *pf* is clearly heard.
- *hätte* [ˈhɛtə] vs *hatte* [ˈhatə], *wäre* [ˈvɛːʁə] vs *war* [vaːɐ̯]. Practise them in pairs: *Man hatte gewarnt. – Man hätte gewarnt.*

## Common mistakes

- *wäre* with a modal: ~~Sie wäre fliehen können.~~ → *Sie hätte fliehen können.*
- Participle of the modal: ~~Man hätte warnen gemusst.~~ → *Man hätte warnen müssen.*
- *hätte* at the end with a double infinitive: ~~…, obwohl man es vorhersehen können hätte.~~ → *…, obwohl man es hätte vorhersehen können.*
- Wrong order of *worden* and *wäre*: ~~…, wenn das Dorf evakuiert wäre worden.~~ → *…, wenn das Dorf evakuiert worden wäre.*
- Using the indicative in a *zu …, als dass* clause: the Konjunktiv II is the norm there, because the consequence didn't happen: *Der Regen war zu stark, als dass man alles hätte verhindern können.* The indicative (*… verhindern konnte*) is rare and sounds wrong to many speakers.
- Verb-second after *als* in a comparison: ~~als es hätte nie geregnet~~ → *als hätte es nie geregnet* (or *als ob es nie geregnet hätte*).
- Confusing *hätte … sollen* (it would have been right) with *sollte … haben* (expectation or hearsay, lesson 02): *Er hätte anrufen sollen* = he should have called; *Er sollte längst angerufen haben* = he should have called by now (I'm surprised he hasn't).

## Key points

- Konjunktiv II past: *hätte/wäre* + Partizip II; passive *wäre* + Partizip II + *worden*.
- With a modal: always *hätte* + infinitive + modal infinitive (*hätte warnen müssen*); with the passive, *hätte* + Partizip II + *werden* + modal (*hätte verhindert werden können*). In a subordinate clause *hätte* comes before the infinitives.
- *hätte … sollen* = it would have been right; *hätte … müssen* = it was required (or "would have had to"); *hätte … können* = it was possible.
- Verb-first conditions (*Hätte man …, wäre …*), wishes with *doch / nur / bloß*, comparisons with *als* + verb, and unreal consequences with *zu … als dass*, *nicht so …, dass* and *ohne dass* all use these forms.
- *hatte/war* (it happened) vs *hätte/wäre* (it didn't): listen for the umlaut and check the context.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete the lesson.

lessons.title: According to the author: Konjunktiv I in academic and extended reports
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

At B2 you learned the Konjunktiv I and indirect speech (lessons 01–02): the forms (*er sei, sie habe, es gebe*), the replacement rule (*sie haben* → *sie hätten*), the single past form (*sie habe gesagt, er sei gegangen*) and the reporting verbs that frame a statement (lesson 05). Those lessons mostly worked sentence by sentence: *Die Sprecherin sagte, das Büro sei geschlossen.*

Academic and journalistic texts go further. A review, a literature report or a summary of a study can stay in the Konjunktiv I for a whole paragraph, with the source named only once. Inside that paragraph there are relative clauses, *weil* clauses and modal verbs in the past, all in the Konjunktiv I or its replacement. And the writer keeps switching between the author's voice and their own, signalled only by the verb form. This lesson teaches you to follow that switching and to do it yourself.

You will learn

- **[[berichtete Rede]]**: reported speech that runs on without a reporting verb;
- the Konjunktiv I in subordinate clauses inside reported speech, including the past with modal verbs (*…, die man habe einführen müssen*);
- the replacement rule over a long text, including the cases where only *würde* is unambiguous;
- what Konjunktiv I, Konjunktiv II and indicative signal about the writer's distance;
- the standard frames of academic reporting and the rules for quoting.

The theme is religion and worldviews in a secular society. As in any academic text, the aim is to describe and report, not to judge.

## Forms you need: a quick review

The Konjunktiv I is used where it is distinct from the indicative, and in practice that means the third person singular and *sein* throughout. Everything else is replaced.

| | singular (KI) | plural (replacement) |
|---|---|---|
| present | *sie sei, habe, glaube, könne, werde* | *sie seien* (KI), *hätten, glaubten* → *würden glauben*, *könnten*, *würden* |
| past | *sie habe geglaubt, sei gegangen* | *sie hätten geglaubt, seien gegangen* |
| past with a modal | *sie habe nicht verhindern können* | *sie hätten nicht verhindern können* |
| passive past | *es sei eingeführt worden* | *sie seien eingeführt worden* |
| modal + passive past | *es habe eingeführt werden müssen* | *sie hätten eingeführt werden müssen* |
| future | *sie werde zeigen* | *sie würden zeigen* |

Two points from the table matter in long texts:

- **The past with a modal** uses the double infinitive, so it is *habe* + infinitive + modal infinitive: *Die Kirche habe die Austritte nicht verhindern können.* — The church, she says, was unable to prevent the departures. In the plural *haben* is replaced by *hätten*: *Die Kirchen hätten … nicht verhindern können.*
- **Weak verbs in the plural** have a Konjunktiv II that looks like the Präteritum (*sie glaubten, beteten, suchten*). The replacement rule then asks for *würde*: *Viele Konfessionslose würden beten oder meditieren.* In practice many writers use the Präteritum-looking form anyway when the context makes it clear (*Viele, so die Autorin, beteten regelmäßig*); both are found in published texts. If you want to be unambiguous, use *würde*.

## Reporting for a whole paragraph

Once a source has been named, the Konjunktiv I itself says "according to her". The writer doesn't need to repeat *sagt sie, schreibt sie, meint sie* in every sentence. German grammars call this **[[berichtete Rede]]** (reported speech without a reporting verb):

> Die Autorin hält die Säkularisierung für unumkehrbar. Die Bindung an die Kirchen nehme seit Jahrzehnten ab, und daran werde auch keine Reform etwas ändern. Entscheidend sei nicht die Lehre, sondern das Vertrauen. Wer dieses einmal verloren habe, kehre selten zurück.

Every sentence after the first is the author's view, even though no verb of saying appears. An English translation has to add "she argues", "in her view" or "she says" now and then, because English has no verb form that does this job.

The writer can interrupt the report with short reminders: *so die Autorin, heißt es in der Studie, wie sie schreibt.* And the moment the writer speaks in their own voice, the verb returns to the indicative:

> Entscheidend sei nicht die Lehre, sondern das Vertrauen. **Das ist eine plausible These.** Allerdings stütze sie sich, so die Autorin selbst, vor allem auf Interviews in Großstädten.

The bold sentence is the reviewer's own judgement; the next sentence returns to what the author says. A careful reader follows the verb forms like a change of speaker in a play.

## Konjunktiv I in subordinate clauses

Inside reported speech, subordinate clauses normally take the Konjunktiv I too, because they are part of what the source says:

- *Die Kirchen verlören Mitglieder, weil sie zu spät auf Kritik reagiert hätten.* — The churches, she says, are losing members because they reacted to criticism too late.
- *Was den Menschen fehle, sei nicht der Glaube, sondern das Vertrauen in die Institution.* — What people lack, she says, is not faith but trust in the institution.
- *Gemeint seien die Missbrauchsskandale, die man jahrelang habe vertuschen wollen.* — What is meant, she says, are the abuse scandals that people tried to cover up for years (literally: wanted to cover up).

The last example combines three things: a relative clause, the Konjunktiv I past with a modal verb, and the subordinate-clause order of lesson 01, in which *habe* comes before the double infinitive: *…, die man jahrelang habe vertuschen wollen*, never ~~vertuschen wollen habe~~.

When a subordinate clause states a fact the writer shares, it may stay in the indicative: *Sie betont, dass seit 2021 weniger als die Hälfte der Bevölkerung einer der beiden großen Kirchen angehört.* This is a statistic, not a claim, so the writer doesn't distance themselves from it. Both choices are correct; the form tells the reader how the writer sees the statement.

## Konjunktiv I, Konjunktiv II or indicative?

After a verb of saying, all three moods occur. In formal writing, they send different signals:

| | example | what it signals in formal writing |
|---|---|---|
| Konjunktiv I | *Sie behauptet, die Kirchen seien selbst schuld.* | neutral reporting: this is her claim |
| Konjunktiv II | *Sie behauptet, die Kirchen wären selbst schuld.* | either the replacement rule (where KI = indicative) or, where KI would have been available, a hint of doubt; in speech simply the usual form |
| indicative | *Sie behauptet, die Kirchen sind selbst schuld.* | informal; in writing it can suggest that the writer accepts the content |

Treat the second and third rows with care. The idea that the Konjunktiv II expresses doubt is a traditional rule of style; many writers use *wäre* simply because it sounds more natural to them, and in everyday speech the Konjunktiv II and the indicative are the normal forms of reported speech. In an academic text, the safest practice is: Konjunktiv I for the views of others, indicative for facts you accept and for your own view.

The reporting verb itself carries a lot of attitude, more than the mood does. *Sie zeigt, dass …* accepts the result (indicative is natural: *Sie zeigt, dass die Austritte zugenommen haben*); *Sie behauptet, dass …* reports a claim the writer doesn't vouch for; *Sie räumt ein, dass …* reports a concession.

## Frames for academic reporting

In a summary, review or seminar paper, you report what an author thinks, and you need more than *sagt*. These frames are standard; note which mood usually follows.

| frame | meaning | mood that follows |
|---|---|---|
| *Die Autorin vertritt die These, dass …* | the author argues that | KI (or indicative) |
| *Ihre zentrale These lautet, …* | her central thesis is that | KI, without *dass* |
| *Nach Auffassung von Sandvoß …* / *Nach Sandvoß …* | in Sandvoß's view | KI or indicative |
| *Sandvoß zufolge …* / *Laut Sandvoß …* | according to Sandvoß | KI or indicative |
| *Wie Sandvoß zu bedenken gibt, …* | as Sandvoß points out (as a caution) | indicative |
| *Wie die Autorin zeigt, …* | as the author shows | indicative |
| *Sie geht davon aus, dass …* | she assumes that | KI or indicative |
| *Sie kommt zu dem Schluss, dass …* | she concludes that | KI or indicative |
| *Sie weist darauf hin, dass …* | she points out that | KI or indicative |
| *Sie wendet sich gegen die Annahme, dass …* | she argues against the assumption that | KI |

Two notes:

- **wie-clauses take the indicative.** *Wie die Autorin zeigt, nimmt die Bindung ab.* By writing *wie*, the writer agrees: "as she shows (and it is so)". The *wie* clause itself is never in the Konjunktiv I (~~Wie die Autorin zeige~~), and careful writers keep the main clause in the indicative too.
- **Academic reporting uses the present.** The author *argues*, *shows*, *concludes*, even if the book appeared years ago: *Sandvoß zeigt, dass …*. The past (*Sandvoß zeigte*) is used for a specific event, such as a lecture or an interview.

## Quoting or reporting?

Reporting rephrases; quoting reproduces. Academic German has clear conventions for quotation:

- Quotation marks „…“ (opening low, closing high) and the page: *Die Kirchen seien zu „Dienstleistern für Lebenswenden“ geworden (S. 87).*
- Omissions are marked with three dots in square brackets: *„Der Glaube ist nicht verschwunden, […] er ist umgezogen.“*
- Changes that fit the quotation into your sentence go in square brackets: *Sie spricht von „eine[r] stille[n] Abwanderung“.* (The original said *eine stille Abwanderung*; the endings have been changed to fit the dative after *von*.)
- *[sic]* (Latin "thus") after a word shows that a mistake or odd form is in the original and not yours: *„die Kirchenaustrite [sic] der letzten Jahre“.*
- Quotation marks around a single word can also distance the writer from a term: *der Glaube sei ins Private „ausgewandert“.* This is common and useful, but don't overdo it.

A short quotation can be built into a sentence in reported speech: the reported part stays in the Konjunktiv I, the quoted words keep their original form. Mixing the two is normal: *Die Autorin schreibt, der Glaube sei nicht verschwunden, sondern „umgezogen“ (S. 214).*

## Text: Glauben ohne Kirche?

This is a book review from a specialist journal for sociology. The book, its author and the study are invented; the general facts about church membership and church tax in Germany are real.

> **Miriam Sandvoß: Glauben ohne Kirche? Religiöse Praxis im säkularen Deutschland. 312 Seiten.**
>
> In ihrer Studie geht die Religionssoziologin Miriam Sandvoß der Frage nach, was von der Religion bleibt, wenn die Kirchen ihre Mitglieder verlieren. Ihre zentrale These lautet, die Säkularisierung bedeute nicht das Ende des Glaubens, sondern seine Verlagerung ins Private.
>
> Grundlage sind eine Befragung von rund 3.000 Erwachsenen sowie sechzig ausführliche Interviews. Wie Sandvoß zeigt, gehört seit 2021 weniger als die Hälfte der Bevölkerung einer der beiden großen Kirchen an. Konfessionslos heiße aber nicht ungläubig: Viele Befragte ohne Konfession würden gelegentlich beten, meditieren oder in der Natur nach Sinn suchen. Was diesen Menschen fehle, sei nicht die Spiritualität, sondern das Vertrauen in die Institution. Den Kirchenaustritt begründeten die meisten mit der Kirchensteuer und mit den Missbrauchsskandalen, die man jahrelang habe vertuschen wollen. Die Kirchen hätten diese Entwicklung nicht aufhalten können, weil sie zu spät auf Kritik reagiert hätten.
>
> Anders sei die Lage in vielen kleineren Glaubensgemeinschaften. Dort spiele die Religion oft eine größere Rolle für die Identität, vor allem in Familien, die nach Deutschland eingewandert seien. Ob das für die nächste Generation noch gelte, lasse sich, so die Autorin, noch nicht sagen.
>
> Die Studie ist gründlich und gut lesbar. Fraglich bleibt allerdings, ob sich ihre These verallgemeinern lässt. Sandvoß räumt selbst ein, die Interviews seien überwiegend in Großstädten geführt worden. Zudem gibt sie zu bedenken, dass sich Spiritualität kaum messen lässt. Umso vorsichtiger sollte man mit der Formulierung sein, der Glaube sei ins Private „ausgewandert“ (S. 214). Ob er dort überlebt oder langsam verblasst, wird die Forschung erst noch zeigen müssen.

**Translation.** *Miriam Sandvoß: Faith without church? Religious practice in secular Germany. 312 pages.* In her study, the sociologist of religion Miriam Sandvoß explores what remains of religion when the churches lose their members. Her central thesis is that secularization does not mean the end of faith but its shift into private life. The study is based on a survey of about 3,000 adults and sixty in-depth interviews. As Sandvoß shows, since 2021 less than half of the population has belonged to one of the two large churches. But, she argues, belonging to no church doesn't mean having no faith: many respondents without a denomination pray, meditate or look for meaning in nature now and then. What these people lack is not spirituality but trust in the institution. Most respondents gave the church tax and the abuse scandals, which people tried to cover up for years, as their reasons for leaving the church. The churches, she says, were unable to stop this development because they reacted to criticism too late. The situation is different, in her view, in many smaller religious communities. There religion often plays a greater part in people's identity, especially in families who immigrated to Germany. Whether that will still hold for the next generation can't yet be said, according to the author. The study is thorough and readable. It remains questionable, however, whether its thesis can be generalized. Sandvoß herself admits that the interviews were mostly conducted in large cities. She also points out that spirituality can hardly be measured. All the more reason to be cautious about saying that faith has "emigrated" into private life (p. 214). Whether it survives there or slowly fades is something research will still have to show.

### Following the voices

Go through the review and mark each sentence as A (the author's view) or R (the reviewer's own voice):

- Paragraph 1: *bedeute* → A. The frame *Ihre zentrale These lautet* names the source.
- Paragraph 2: *gehört* after *Wie Sandvoß zeigt* → R (the reviewer accepts the statistic). From *heiße* to *hätten … reagiert* → A, all Konjunktiv I or its replacement: *würde … beten, meditieren … suchen* (weak verbs in the plural, so *würde*), *fehle, sei, begründeten* (plural: *begründen* → *begründeten*, here understood as Konjunktiv II from the context), *habe … vertuschen wollen* (KI past with a modal, in a relative clause), *hätten … aufhalten können* and *reagiert hätten* (plural replacement).
- Paragraph 3: A throughout (*sei, spiele, eingewandert seien, gelte, lasse*), with *so die Autorin* as a reminder.
- Paragraph 4: *ist, bleibt, lässt* → R. *seien … geführt worden* → A (her admission). *gibt … zu bedenken, dass sich … lässt*: indicative, because the reviewer agrees. The last two sentences → R.

Note the one form that is ambiguous on paper: *begründeten* could be Präteritum ("most respondents gave as their reason") or Konjunktiv II ("they gave, she says"). Here both readings say almost the same thing. When it matters, writers use *würden … begründen* or switch to the singular: *Die Mehrheit begründe den Austritt mit …*

## Words: religion and worldviews

Germany is described as religiously neutral but not strictly secular: the state favours no religion or *Weltanschauung* (worldview), but it cooperates with religious communities, for example by collecting *die Kirchensteuer* for them. Church tax is paid only by members, at 8 percent of income tax in Bavaria and Baden-Württemberg and 9 percent in the other states. Leaving a church officially (*der Kirchenaustritt*, *aus der Kirche austreten*) is declared at the registry office or the local court, depending on the state.

Christian *Konfessionen* (denominations): *katholisch* and *evangelisch* (in Germany this means the mainstream Protestant churches, not "evangelical" in the American sense). *Das Christentum* is the religion, *christlich* the adjective. The other religions most present in Germany are *der Islam* (*muslimisch*; *der Muslim, die Muslimin*) and *das Judentum* (*jüdisch*); they worship in *die Moschee* and *die Synagoge*. Religious leaders: *der Pfarrer / die Pfarrerin* (in the Catholic church only men are ordained; *der Priester* is the general word), *der Imam*, *der Rabbiner / die Rabbinerin*. *Eine Glaubensgemeinschaft* is any religious community.

Belief and practice: someone who believes is *gläubig*, a *Gläubiger* or *Gläubige* (adjectival noun: *ein Gläubiger*, but careful, *der Gläubiger* in finance is a creditor). They *beten* (pray; *das Gebet*), listen to a *Predigt* (*predigen*) and keep *Rituale*. Something *heilig* is holy or sacred. People without a church are *konfessionslos*; some call themselves *Atheist* or *Atheistin*, others prefer *Spiritualität*, being *spirituell* without being religious. The long process in which religion loses its public role is *die Säkularisierung*; a *säkular* state keeps religion and politics apart. In eastern Germany, after forty years of state atheism in the GDR, most people today belong to no church.

## Pronunciation
