Das Argument, eine Pflicht verbessere die Diskussion, greift deshalb zu kurz: Eine gute Diskussion entsteht durch Vorbereitung, nicht durch eine Unterschrift auf einer Liste.
>
> Wägt man die Argumente ab, so zeigt sich, dass beide Seiten einen wahren Kern haben, nur dass sie sich auf unterschiedliche Veranstaltungen beziehen. Zwar ist eine allgemeine Pflicht kaum zu rechtfertigen, doch in Laborpraktika oder Sprachkursen, in denen das gemeinsame Arbeiten der eigentliche Inhalt ist, erscheint sie durchaus sinnvoll. Unterm Strich spricht daher vieles für eine differenzierte Lösung: keine Pflicht für Vorlesungen, wohl aber für Veranstaltungen, die ohne Anwesenheit ihren Zweck verfehlen.

In English:

> Compulsory attendance at universities: paternalism or a precondition of good teaching?
>
> Anyone who goes to an eight o'clock lecture often sees more empty seats than students. Some universities therefore lay down compulsory attendance in their study regulations; others reject such an obligation on principle. The following discusses whether students should be required to attend classes.
>
> In favour of compulsory attendance, it is often argued that a seminar lives from discussion. If half the participants are missing, the quality suffers to such an extent that even those present hardly benefit any more. In addition, many teachers report that students who come regularly pass their exams more often. Even if this correlation doesn't prove that attendance is the cause, it is still a hint to be taken seriously.
>
> Against an obligation, on the other hand, is the fact that students are adults who can decide for themselves how to use their time. Many of them work on the side or look after children; for them a rigid rule would be such a heavy burden that some might have to drop out. A second argument carries more weight, however: attendance alone doesn't guarantee learning. Someone who is only physically present learns at most how to look at their phone without being noticed. The argument that an obligation improves discussion therefore falls short: good discussion comes from preparation, not from a signature on a list.
>
> If one weighs up the arguments, it becomes clear that both sides have a grain of truth, except that they refer to different kinds of class. Admittedly a general obligation is hard to justify, but in lab courses or language courses, where working together is the actual content, it seems perfectly sensible. On balance, therefore, much speaks for a differentiated solution: no obligation for lectures, but one for classes that miss their purpose without attendance.

## Erörterung or Stellungnahme?

| | Erörterung | Stellungnahme |
|---|---|---|
| Purpose | examines a question from several sides and reaches a weighed judgement | states and justifies a position on a question or a text |
| Length | longer (often 400 words or more) | shorter (often 150–250 words) |
| Counterarguments | treated in full | named and answered, but the focus is your own view |
| Typical places | school, university, essay tasks | letters to the editor, forum posts, meetings, the C1 writing tasks |

There are two kinds of Erörterung:

- The **[[linear Erörterung]]** follows one line: only the arguments for (or only against) one position, building up from the weakest to the strongest. It suits a question like *Welche Folgen hat …?* or *Warum sollte man …?*
- The **[[dialectical Erörterung]]** sets the arguments for and against against each other and ends with a synthesis or a decision. It suits a yes/no question like *Sollte …?* The model above is dialectical.

## The structure

**Einleitung.** Start with a hook (*der Aufhänger*): a scene, a current event, a figure, a provocative question. The model opens with empty seats at eight in the morning. Then lead to the question itself: *Im Folgenden soll erörtert werden, ob …*; *Es stellt sich die Frage, ob …*. Don't give your answer yet in a dialectical Erörterung.

**Hauptteil.** Each argument has three parts: the claim (*These*), the reason (*Begründung*) and an example or evidence (*Beispiel, Beleg*). In a dialectical Erörterung, put the side you will reject (or rate lower) first and your own side second, so that the reader goes into the conclusion with your strongest point in mind. Within each side, go from the weaker argument to the stronger one, and say so: *Schwerer wiegt jedoch …*; *Entscheidend ist aber …*; *Gewichtiger noch ist …*.

There are two ways to arrange a dialectical Hauptteil. In the block pattern (as in the model), all the arguments on one side come first, then all those on the other. In the alternating pattern, each argument is followed directly by its counterargument. The block pattern is clearer for beginners; the alternating one suits topics where arguments answer each other point by point.

**Schluss.** Weigh, don't repeat. A good conclusion says which arguments carry more weight and why, and may propose a compromise or an outlook. It brings in no new argument.

## Two-part connectors: conceding and restricting

Concession admits a point and then limits its force. You know *obwohl, zwar … aber* and *sosehr … auch* from B1 and B2. C1 adds more weight and nuance.

| Pattern | Use | Example |
|---|---|---|
| *zwar …, doch / aber / jedoch …* | admit, then counter (neutral) | *Zwar ist eine allgemeine Pflicht kaum zu rechtfertigen, doch in Laborpraktika erscheint sie sinnvoll.* |
| *wenn … auch, so … doch* | admit, then insist (formal) | *Wenn das Verfahren auch aufwendig ist, so ist es doch gerecht.* |
| *mag … auch, (so) …* | admit even a strong point (formal, written) | *Mag dieser Zusammenhang auch nichts beweisen, so ist er doch ein Hinweis.* |
| *sosehr … auch* (B2) | however much | *Sosehr ich die Freiheit auch schätze, eine Grenze braucht es.* |
| *…, nur dass …* | everything holds, except one thing | *Der Vorschlag ist gut, nur dass er Geld kostet.* |
| *…, außer dass …* | except that | *Über das Treffen weiß ich nichts, außer dass es stattgefunden hat.* |
| *allenfalls* | at most, at best; if at all | *Das lohnt sich allenfalls für Vorlesungen.* |
| *insofern …, als* (B2) | in that, to the extent that | *Er hat insofern recht, als …* |
| *es sei denn* (B2) | unless | *Eine Pflicht ist unnötig, es sei denn, es geht um Laborarbeit.* |

Notes on word order:

- In *wenn … auch, so … doch*, the *wenn* clause has its verb at the end; *auch* sits inside it, and *so* opens the main clause, followed by the verb: *Wenn das Verfahren auch aufwendig ist, so ist es doch gerecht.* *Wenn auch* can also introduce a short phrase: *eine, wenn auch kleine, Verbesserung* (an improvement, albeit a small one).
- The *mag* clause puts *mag* first (like a conditional without *wenn*) and the infinitive at the end: *Mag die Pflicht auch lästig sein, …*. The main clause can begin with *so* and the verb (*so ist sie doch notwendig*), or keep its normal order after a comma (*…, notwendig ist sie trotzdem*).
- *nur dass* and *außer dass* follow the main clause; the verb goes to the end. *nur dass* restricts a positive judgement (everything is fine, only …); *außer dass* names the single exception (nothing, except that …).
- *allenfalls* is an adverb. It means "at most" with numbers and amounts (*allenfalls zehn Teilnehmende*) and "at best, if anything" with judgements (*Das ist allenfalls ein Anfang*). In both senses it restricts downwards: whatever it names is the upper limit. (Especially in Switzerland, *allenfalls* also often means "possibly, if need be": *Allenfalls rufe ich Sie an.*)

## Consequence: so, derart, dermaßen

To say that something happens to such an extent that it has a consequence, German puts an intensifying word in the main clause and a *dass* clause after it.

| Pattern | Example |
|---|---|
| *so* + adjective / adverb …, *dass* | *Die Regel ist so starr, dass viele sie umgehen.* |
| *derart* + adjective / verb …, *dass* | *Die Qualität leidet derart, dass niemand profitiert.* *eine derart hohe Hürde, dass …* |
| *dermaßen* + adjective …, *dass* | *eine dermaßen große Belastung, dass manche abbrechen müssten* |
| *zu* + adjective …, *als dass* + Konjunktiv II (B2) | *Die Pflicht ist zu starr, als dass sie allen gerecht werden könnte.* |

*derart* and *dermaßen* mean "to such a degree"; both are a step more emphatic than *so*. *derart* is the more formal and can also go with a verb (*leidet derart*); *dermaßen* goes mostly with adjectives and is common in speech as well (*Das war dermaßen peinlich!*). The comma before *dass* is obligatory. Don't confuse these with *sodass* (also *so dass*), which joins a result directly without an intensifier: *Viele fehlten, sodass das Seminar ausfiel.*

## Refuting and weighing

Answering a counterargument is the heart of the dialectical Erörterung.

Refuting:

- *Dem ist entgegenzuhalten, dass …* — Against this it must be said that …
- *Dieses Argument greift zu kurz, weil / denn …* — This argument falls short because …
- *Hierbei wird übersehen, dass …* — What this overlooks is that …
- *Das überzeugt nur bedingt, denn …* — That is only partly convincing, because …
- *Daraus folgt keineswegs, dass …* — It by no means follows that …

Weighing and concluding:

- *Wägt man die Argumente ab, so zeigt sich, dass …* — If one weighs up the arguments, it becomes clear that … (*abwägen* is separable: in the verb-first conditional, *wägt* comes first and *ab* at the end.)
- *Bei aller Berechtigung der Kritik …* — However justified the criticism may be …
- *Letztlich überwiegen die Argumente gegen …* — Ultimately the arguments against … prevail.
- *Unterm Strich spricht vieles für …* — On balance, a lot speaks for … (*unterm Strich*, "below the line", from accounting, is common in journalism; in a formal exam essay *alles in allem* or *insgesamt* is the safer register.)
- *Eine differenzierte Lösung könnte darin bestehen, dass …* — A differentiated solution could consist in …

Look at how the model uses these: *Für … wird häufig angeführt* introduces the side the writer will rate lower, in an impersonal passive that keeps a distance; *Mag … auch …, so … doch* concedes it fairly; *Gegen … spricht hingegen* switches sides; *Schwerer wiegt jedoch* marks the climax; *greift deshalb zu kurz* refutes; *Wägt man … ab* and *Unterm Strich* open the weighed conclusion.

## Words for academic life

- The doctorate: *die Promotion* (doctorate, and the process of getting one), *promovieren* (to do a doctorate: *Sie promoviert in Soziologie; Er hat 2024 promoviert*), *der Doktorand / die Doktorandin* (doctoral student; *Doktorand* is an n-noun: *des Doktoranden*), *die Dissertation* (doctoral thesis, everyday word *die Doktorarbeit*), *das Promotionsstudium* (a structured doctoral programme).
- The way to a chair: *die Habilitation* is a further qualification after the doctorate, traditionally the route to a professorship in Germany. *die Juniorprofessur*, introduced in 2002, is a path to a professorship without it. *die Professur* is a professorship as a post; *der Lehrstuhl* is a chair, a professorship with its own staff.
- Money and contracts: *die Drittmittel* (plural only) are research funds from outside the university's own budget (research foundations, the EU, companies). *die Befristung* is the time limit on a contract; many younger researchers work on fixed-term contracts, regulated by a special law (*Wissenschaftszeitvertragsgesetz*) whose reform has been debated for years. *die Exzellenzinitiative* (from 2005/06) funded selected top universities and projects; it has been continued as the *Exzellenzstrategie*.
- *die Forschungsfreiheit* (freedom of research) is protected by the Basic Law: *„Kunst und Wissenschaft, Forschung und Lehre sind frei.“* (Art. 5 Abs. 3 Satz 1 GG)
- *der Wissenschaftsbetrieb* is the academic world as a system, often in a critical tone: *Der Wissenschaftsbetrieb belohnt Veröffentlichungen, nicht gute Lehre.*
- Admission and studying: *die Zulassungsbeschränkung* (restricted admission) and *der Numerus clausus* (NC): in subjects with more applicants than places, the grade needed results from each round's applications, so it isn't fixed in advance. *die Immatrikulation* (enrolment; everyday *die Einschreibung*) and *die Exmatrikulation* (leaving the university's register). *die Studienordnung* sets out how a degree is organized; *die Regelstudienzeit* is the standard length of a degree, which matters, for example, for how long student finance is normally paid. *die Lehrveranstaltung* is any taught class (lecture, seminar, tutorial). *die Hochschulleitung* is the university's management.
- People: *der Stipendiat / die Stipendiatin* (scholarship holder; n-noun: *des Stipendiaten*), *der Gaststudent / die Gaststudentin* (visiting student).
- For the essay itself: *erörtern* (to discuss a question thoroughly: *eine Frage erörtern*), *dialektisch*, *die Abwägung* (weighing up, from *abwägen*), *das Für und Wider* (the pros and cons, a nominalized pair).

## Pronunciation

- *die Promotion*: pro-mo-TSJOHN; *promovieren*: pro-mo-VIE-ren (*v* as English *v*).
- *die Habilitation*: ha-bi-li-ta-TSJOHN; *die Dissertation*: di-ser-ta-TSJOHN.
- *der Numerus clausus*: NOO-me-rus KLAU-sus (Latin, *au* as in *Haus*).
- *dialektisch*: di-a-LEK-tisch.
- *der Doktorand*: dok-to-RAND, stress at the end; *der Stipendiat*: shti-pen-DJAHT (*st* as in *Stipendium*).

## Common mistakes

- No own position in the Schluss of a dialectical Erörterung: weighing means deciding, even if the decision is "it depends on …", explained.
- New arguments in the Schluss.
- Mixing the two *mag* patterns. With *mag* in second position (*Die Pflicht mag lästig sein*), the sentence is an ordinary main clause and continues with *aber*: *Die Pflicht mag lästig sein, aber sie ist notwendig.* The continuation with *so … doch* belongs to the verb-first clause: *Mag die Pflicht auch lästig sein, so ist sie doch notwendig.*
- Forgetting *so* + verb inversion after the *wenn … auch* clause: ~~Wenn es auch teuer ist, so es ist doch gerecht.~~ → *so ist es doch gerecht*.
- *allenfalls* for "in any case": ~~Ich komme allenfalls~~ means "I'll come at most / if at all", not "I'll come anyway" (*jedenfalls*).
- *derart* without *dass* clause, or without the comma: *Die Qualität leidet derart, dass …*.
- Counting instead of weighing: "three arguments for, two against, so yes" is not an argument.

## Key points

- The Erörterung weighs a question (linear: one line, building up; dialectical: for and against, then a synthesis); the Stellungnahme is shorter and centred on your own position.
- Einleitung with a hook and the question; Hauptteil from weaker to stronger; Schluss weighs and decides, with no new arguments.
- Concede and restrict: *zwar … doch*, *wenn … auch, so … doch*, *mag … auch, so …*, *sosehr … auch*, *nur dass*, *außer dass*, *allenfalls*.
- Consequence of degree: *so / derart / dermaßen …, dass*; *zu …, als dass* + Konjunktiv II.
- Refute with *Dem ist entgegenzuhalten*, *greift zu kurz*, *Hierbei wird übersehen*; weigh with *Wägt man … ab, so …*, *Letztlich überwiegt*, *Unterm Strich* (journalistic) or *Alles in allem*.
