lessons.title: Kriegen, bekommen, erhalten: register and stylistic levels
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

At B2 (lesson 29) you compared formal written, neutral and colloquial German and saw some features of spoken German (*weil* + verb second, tag questions, Anglicisms). At C1 the question is no longer "formal or informal?" but "exactly how high or low is this word, and does it fit the text around it?". A C1 writer chooses between *bekommen, erhalten* and *kriegen* on purpose, uses an educated foreign word where it adds precision and avoids it where it only shows off, and notices when a sentence breaks the style of its text.

This lesson covers the stylistic levels as German dictionaries label them, synonym ladders from elevated to coarse, the grammar that marks register, the educated foreign words (*bildungssprachliche Fremdwörter*) of academic and professional German, connotation, and how to spot and repair a break in style. The words of the lesson are those educated foreign words and the vocabulary for talking about style.

## A newspaper language column

Many German newspapers run a column in which a linguist answers readers' questions about language. Read this (invented) one.

> **Die Sprachsprechstunde**
>
> *Leserin K. aus Kassel fragt: „Mein Sohn schreibt in seinen Bewerbungen ‚kriegen‘ statt ‚bekommen‘. Ich finde das unmöglich, er sagt, meine Haltung sei obsolet. Wer hat recht?“*
>
> Liebe Frau K.,
> zunächst die gute Nachricht: Falsch ist „kriegen“ nicht. Das Wort steht im Wörterbuch, ist grammatisch einwandfrei und im Gespräch völlig legitim. Die Frage ist also nicht, ob es korrekt ist, sondern ob es in den Text passt. Und hier ist der Befund evident: In einer Bewerbung wirkt „kriegen“ wie Turnschuhe zum Anzug, nämlich wie ein Stilbruch.
>
> Wörter haben nicht nur eine Bedeutung, sondern auch eine Stilebene. „Erhalten“, „bekommen“ und „kriegen“ bezeichnen dieselbe Sache, doch ihre Konnotationen divergieren deutlich: „Erhalten“ klingt förmlich, „bekommen“ neutral, „kriegen“ locker. Wer in einem formellen Text zum lockeren Wort greift, sagt implizit: Ich nehme diese Situation nicht ganz ernst. Das mag Ihr Sohn nicht beabsichtigen, aber der Leser hört es mit.
>
> In einem Punkt hat Ihr Sohn allerdings recht: Die Grenzen verschieben sich sukzessive. Manche Wörter, die vor dreißig Jahren als salopp galten, sind heute neutral, und manche gehobenen Ausdrücke wirken inzwischen eher steif. Von einem Paradigmenwechsel würde ich trotzdem nicht sprechen; die Diskrepanz zwischen gesprochener und geschriebener Sprache ist nach wie vor beträchtlich.
>
> Umgekehrt gilt: Wer jeden Satz mit Fremdwörtern spickt, macht es auch nicht besser. „Wir müssen die Optionen eruieren“ ist nicht präziser als „Wir müssen herausfinden, was möglich ist“, nur schwerer zu lesen. Ein Fremdwort ist adäquat, wenn es eine Nuance trifft, die das deutsche Wort nicht hat. Sonst ist es redundant oder schlicht Imponiergehabe.
>
> Mein Rat an Ihren Sohn: Er soll prägnant und konsistent schreiben, in einer Bewerbung also durchgehend neutral bis gehoben. Ein einziges „kriegen“ diskreditiert keinen Bewerber. Es kann aber einen sonst fundierten Eindruck trüben, wenn auch nur marginal, und manchmal entscheidet genau das.
>
> Ihre Sprachsprechstunde

*The Language Surgery.* Reader K. from Kassel asks: "My son writes *kriegen* instead of *bekommen* in his job applications. I think it's impossible; he says my attitude is obsolete. Who's right?"
Dear Ms K., first the good news: *kriegen* is not wrong. The word is in the dictionary, grammatically flawless and entirely legitimate in conversation. So the question isn't whether it is correct, but whether it fits the text. And here the finding is evident: in an application, *kriegen* looks like trainers with a suit, in other words like a break in style.
Words don't just have a meaning; they also have a stylistic level. *Erhalten, bekommen* and *kriegen* denote the same thing, but their connotations diverge clearly: *erhalten* sounds formal, *bekommen* neutral, *kriegen* casual. Anyone who reaches for the casual word in a formal text is implicitly saying: I'm not taking this situation entirely seriously. Your son may not intend that, but the reader hears it.
On one point, though, your son is right: the boundaries are gradually shifting. Some words that were considered slangy thirty years ago are neutral today, and some elevated expressions now seem rather stiff. I still wouldn't speak of a paradigm shift; the discrepancy between spoken and written language is still considerable.
Conversely, stuffing every sentence with foreign words doesn't make it any better. "We must ascertain the options" is no more precise than "We must find out what is possible", only harder to read. A foreign word is appropriate when it captures a nuance that the German word lacks. Otherwise it is redundant, or simply showing off.
My advice to your son: he should write concisely and consistently, in an application that means neutral to elevated throughout. A single *kriegen* won't discredit any applicant. But it can cloud an otherwise solid impression, if only marginally, and sometimes that is exactly what decides.

## Stylistic levels: how dictionaries label words

German dictionaries such as Duden mark words that are not neutral with a label (*Stilebene* or *Gebrauch*). Unmarked words are neutral: they fit almost any text. The labels you will meet most often:

| Label | Meaning | Typical examples |
|---|---|---|
| *gehoben* | elevated: solemn, literary, formal speeches | *das Antlitz* (face), *speisen* (to dine), *entschlafen* (to pass away), *grollen* (lesson 16) |
| *bildungssprachlich* | educated: needs a certain education to be understood; academic and professional texts | *eruieren, evident, obsolet, ambivalent* |
| (no label) | neutral | *bekommen, Geld, sterben, Gesicht* |
| *umgangssprachlich* | colloquial: everyday speech, informal writing | *kriegen, gucken, eh, die Nase voll haben* |
| *salopp* | very casual, slangy; careless in tone | *pennen* (to sleep), *den Löffel abgeben* (to kick the bucket) |
| *derb* | coarse, crude | *abkratzen* (to croak), *fressen* used of people |
| *vulgär* | vulgar, offensive (often sexual) | (no examples needed) |

Dictionaries add further labels about use, not level: *veraltend* (going out of use), *veraltet* (obsolete), *scherzhaft* (jocular), *abwertend* (disparaging, pejorative), *verhüllend* (euphemistic: honors lesson 20h1), *Fachsprache* (technical language, often with the field: *Medizin, Rechtssprache*), and regional labels (*süddeutsch, österreichisch*: lesson 26). Dictionaries sometimes disagree about a label, and labels change over time, so treat them as a guide, not a law.

Two points are easy to misunderstand. *bildungssprachlich* is not the same as formal: a word like *ambivalent* is educated but can be used in a relaxed conversation among students. And *gehoben* is not the same as correct: in an e-mail to a colleague, *Ich würde gern mit Ihnen speisen* sounds stilted or ironic.

## Synonym ladders

Many everyday meanings have a whole ladder of words. Choosing the rung is choosing the register.

| Meaning | gehoben / formal | neutral | umgangssprachlich / salopp | derb |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| to die | *entschlafen, verscheiden*; *versterben* (official, mostly *verstorben*) | *sterben* | *den Löffel abgeben, ins Gras beißen* | *abkratzen, verrecken* |
| to get | *erhalten* | *bekommen* | *kriegen* | — |
| money | *finanzielle Mittel* (official) | *das Geld* | *die Kohle, die Knete, der Zaster* | — |
| to eat | *speisen, dinieren* | *essen* | *futtern* | *fressen* (of people; neutral for animals) |
| to look | *betrachten, erblicken* | *sehen, schauen* | *gucken*; *glotzen* (to gawp, disparaging) | — |
| face | *das Antlitz* | *das Gesicht* | — | *die Visage, die Fresse* |

Notice that *fressen* is perfectly neutral for animals (*Der Hund frisst*) and only coarse when used of people. And the solemn noun *das Ableben* (passing, decease) belongs to the obituary and the condolence letter (honors lesson 20h2).

## Grammar that marks register

Register isn't only vocabulary. Some grammatical choices place a sentence on the scale too.

| More formal / written | Neutral / spoken | Regional or colloquial (not for writing) |
|---|---|---|
| *das Auto meines Vaters* (genitive) | *das Auto von meinem Vater* | *meinem Vater sein Auto* (possessive dative) |
| *Er kam, sah und ging.* (Präteritum in narration) | *Er ist gekommen, hat geguckt und ist gegangen.* (Perfekt) | — |
| *Sie sagte, sie habe keine Zeit.* (Konjunktiv I) | *Sie hat gesagt, sie hätte keine Zeit / sie hat keine Zeit.* | — |
| *der Mann, dessen Auto hier steht* | — | *der Mann, wo dem sein Auto hier steht* (southern dialect) |
| *…, weil ich keine Zeit habe.* | *…, weil ich hab keine Zeit.* (spoken only) | — |
| *Du brauchst nicht zu kommen.* | *Du brauchst nicht kommen.* (colloquial) | — |
| *Hast du es gesehen?* | *Hast du's gesehen? Hab ich nicht.* | *Haste das gesehen?* |

The genitive with *wegen* (*wegen des Wetters*) is standard in writing; *wegen dem Wetter* is common in speech and accepted as colloquial by Duden. Formal texts also prefer the nominal style of module 2 (*nach Eingang der Zahlung*) where speech has a clause (*wenn das Geld da ist*).

## Educated foreign words

Academic, professional and journalistic German uses a layer of foreign words, mostly from Latin, Greek and French, that has no place in everyday chat. At C1 you need to understand them all and use the common ones with confidence. Each has a plainer German equivalent, but the two are not always interchangeable.

| Fremdwort | Plainer German | Note |
|---|---|---|
| *eruieren* | *herausfinden, ermitteln* | find out through careful investigation |
| *evident* | *offensichtlich, klar erkennbar* | |
| *obsolet* | *überholt, nicht mehr nötig* | |
| *marginal* | *geringfügig, am Rande* | *marginalisiert* (lesson 12) is "pushed to the margins" |
| *adäquat* | *angemessen* | |
| *ambivalent* | *zwiespältig* | feelings or judgements that pull both ways |
| *plausibel* | *einleuchtend, nachvollziehbar* | |
| *explizit* / *implizit* | *ausdrücklich* / *unausgesprochen, mitgemeint* | |
| *prägnant* | *knapp und treffend* | false friend: "pregnant" is *schwanger* |
| *redundant* | *überflüssig, doppelt* | in technology also "duplicated as a backup" |
| *sukzessive* | *nach und nach, schrittweise* | adverb; the adjective is *sukzessiv* |
| *tangieren* | *berühren, betreffen* | colloquially ironic: *Das tangiert mich nicht* (I couldn't care less) |
| *implizieren* | *einschließen, mit sich bringen* | |
| *diskreditieren* | *in Verruf bringen* | |
| *legitim* / *legitimieren* | *berechtigt* / *rechtfertigen* | |
| *fundiert* | *gut begründet, solide* | *fundierte Kenntnisse* (thorough knowledge) |
| *konsistent* | *widerspruchsfrei, einheitlich* | |
| *divergieren* | *auseinandergehen* | |
| *die Diskrepanz* | *das Missverhältnis* | |
| *das Paradigma* | *das Denkmuster, das Modell* | plural *die Paradigmen* |
| *der Paradigmenwechsel* | *ein grundlegender Wandel* | from the philosophy of science; often overused |

**When they help.** A Fremdwort earns its place when it is more precise or is the term of a field: in logic and statistics *konsistent* has an exact meaning that *einheitlich* doesn't; *implizit* is shorter than *nicht ausdrücklich gesagt, aber mitgemeint*. **When they hurt.** If the plain word says the same, the Fremdwort only makes the sentence harder and can sound pompous (*Imponiergehabe*, showing off). The column's example, *die Optionen eruieren*, is the classic case.

**Watch the false friends.** *konsistent* means "free of contradictions"; English "consistent" in the sense of "acting the same way every time" is usually *konsequent* (*Sie handelt konsequent*). *prägnant* is not "pregnant". *evident* in German is rather bookish; in many contexts *offensichtlich* is better.

## Denotation and connotation

The **[[denotation]]** of a word is what it refers to; its **[[connotation]]** is everything it suggests on top: feelings, judgements, associations, register. *Hund* and *Köter* denote the same animal, but *Köter* is disparaging. *sparsam* (thrifty) and *geizig* (stingy) describe the same behaviour, one approvingly, the other not. *Regierung* (government) is neutral, *Regime* suggests an illegitimate or authoritarian one.

A word with a negative connotation is *pejorativ* (dictionary label: *abwertend*). Connotations change over time: *Weib* was the neutral word for "woman" in medieval German and is disparaging today, while *geil* moved from "lustful" to youth slang for "great". When you are unsure about a word's connotation, look at the dictionary label and at its typical contexts (DWDS and Duden show example sentences).

## Spotting and repairing a break in style

A **[[Stilbruch]]** is a word, phrase or construction that doesn't fit the level of the text around it. It can be upward (*Ich speise heute Abend mit meinen Kumpels*: an elevated verb among friends) or downward, which is far more common in learners' formal texts. Here is an e-mail to a university office with three breaks:

> ~~Hallo~~ Sehr geehrte Frau Weber,
> leider habe ich das Formular für die Rückmeldung noch nicht ~~gekriegt~~ erhalten. ~~Ist ja auch egal,~~ Könnten Sie es mir bitte noch einmal zuschicken? Die Frist läuft am 15. Juli ab, und ich möchte sie ungern versäumen.
> Mit freundlichen Grüßen
> Ana Pereira

*Hallo* is too casual for a first message to an office, *gekriegt* is colloquial, and *Ist ja auch egal* is spoken and dismissive. The repaired version is neutral and polite throughout. Note that the repair doesn't need any elevated words: *erhalten* and *versäumen* are standard in letters, and that's enough.

A Stilbruch can also be deliberate. Columnists and comedians mix levels for humour and irony: *Der Herr Minister geruhte, sich zu verplappern* (*geruhen* is mock-solemn, *sich verplappern* colloquial). In your own texts, keep one level unless you have a reason not to.

## The words of this lesson

- The register labels themselves are adjectives: *gehoben, bildungssprachlich, salopp, derb, vulgär* (plus *umgangssprachlich* from B2). *salopp* also describes clothes: *ein salopper Pullover* (casual). *gehoben* also means "upmarket" or "higher-level": *gehobene Gastronomie, der gehobene Dienst* (a higher grade of the civil service).
- *die Stilebene* (stylistic level), *die Konnotation, die Nuance* (a fine shade of meaning: *in allen Nuancen*), *nuanciert* (nuanced: *eine nuancierte Darstellung*), *der Stilbruch* (break in style).
- The verbs in *-ieren* (*eruieren, tangieren, implizieren, diskreditieren, legitimieren, divergieren*) are all weak, stressed on *-ie-*, and form their participle without *ge-*: *hat eruiert, hat tangiert, hat divergiert* (*Die Meinungen haben stark divergiert*).
- *sukzessive* is an adverb; *pejorativ* and *explizit* are adjectives and adverbs: *Das Wort wird pejorativ gebraucht.*

## Pronunciation

Foreign words keep their stress near the end:

- -ieren verbs: e-ru-IE-ren, tan-GIE-ren, im-pli-ZIE-ren, dis-kre-di-TIE-ren, le-gi-ti-MIE-ren, di-ver-GIE-ren.
- Adjectives: e-vi-DENT, ob-so-LET, mar-gi-NAL, ad-ä-QUAT (*ä* and *a* in separate syllables), am-bi-va-LENT, plau-SI-bel, ex-pli-ZIT, im-pli-ZIT, präg-NANT, re-dun-DANT, le-gi-TIM, kon-sis-TENT, pe-jo-ra-TIV (final *v* sounds like *f*).
- *sukzessive*: suk-tses-SI-ve, four syllables. *die Diskrepanz*: dis-kre-PANZ. *das Paradigma*: pa-ra-DIG-ma.
- *die Nuance* is French: nü-ANG-se, with a nasal vowel; *die Konnotation*: kon-no-ta-TSION.

## Common mistakes

- Using *kriegen* or other colloquial words in applications, complaints and official e-mails.
- Overcorrecting with a Fremdwort in every sentence: ~~Wir müssen die Divergenz der Optionen eruieren~~ when you mean *Wir müssen herausfinden, wie sich die Möglichkeiten unterscheiden*.
- Confusing *konsistent* (free of contradictions) with *konsequent* (sticking to a line).
- Taking *prägnant* for "pregnant".
- Using *fressen* or *abkratzen* about people without meaning to be coarse.
- Writing the possessive dative or relative *wo* in standard texts: ~~meinem Bruder sein Fahrrad~~ → *das Fahrrad meines Bruders* / *von meinem Bruder*.

## Key points

- Dictionaries label non-neutral words: *gehoben, bildungssprachlich, umgangssprachlich, salopp, derb, vulgär*; plus usage labels such as *veraltend, abwertend, verhüllend, Fachsprache*. Unlabelled words are neutral.
- Synonym ladders (*erhalten / bekommen / kriegen*; *versterben / sterben / den Löffel abgeben / abkratzen*) let you pick the level; choose one and keep it.
- Grammar marks register too: genitive vs *von* vs possessive dative, Präteritum vs Perfekt, Konjunktiv I vs *hätte*/indicative, *dessen* vs dialect *wo*.
- Educated foreign words (*eruieren, evident, obsolet, adäquat, implizit …*) belong to academic and professional texts; use one when it is more precise, not to impress.
- Denotation is what a word refers to; connotation is what it suggests. Pejorative words carry the label *abwertend*.
- A Stilbruch is a word or form that breaks the level of its text; repair it with the neutral word, not necessarily an elevated one.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete the lesson.

lessons.title: Blitzschnell, spottbillig, Unmenge: advanced word formation
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

At B2 (lessons 21 and 22) you learned how German builds nouns and adjectives: suffixes such as *-ung, -heit, -bar, -los*, compounds with linking elements, short forms. This lesson looks at the expressive side of word formation, the side that advertising, journalism and everyday speech love: compounds that intensify (*blitzschnell, spottbillig*), prefixes that inflate (*Riesenauswahl, Mordsspaß, Unmenge*), foreign prefixes that combine with *-ieren, -ität* and *-ismus*, words made from other parts of speech (*das Aus, das Hin und Her*), blends (*Denglisch*) and new coinages.

The theme is advertising and marketing, the domain where new words are produced fastest and where the effects of word choice can be measured in sales.

## A feature article on the language of advertising

> **Blitzschnell im Kopf: Wie die Werbung Wörter baut**
>
> Wer morgens die Zeitung aufschlägt, begegnet ihr spätestens auf Seite drei: der Sprache der Werbung. Hier ist nichts einfach billig, sondern spottbillig, kein Angebot nur neu, sondern brandneu. Die Waschmaschine schleudert blitzschnell, der Laptop ist hauchdünn, die Bedienung kinderleicht. Werbetexter greifen zu solchen verstärkenden Zusammensetzungen, weil sie in wenigen Silben ein Bild erzeugen: Der Blitz steht für Tempo, der Hauch für Leichtigkeit, das Kind für Einfachheit.
>
> Ähnlich arbeiten Vorsilben wie *Riesen-*, *Mega-* oder *Top-*. Ein Möbelhaus wirbt mit einer Riesenauswahl, ein Freizeitpark verspricht einen Mordsspaß für die ganze Familie. Dass darin das Wort „Mord“ steckt, stört niemanden: Die ursprüngliche Bedeutung ist längst verblasst, übrig bleibt die Verstärkung. Auch *Un-* kann verstärken statt verneinen. Eine Unmenge Spielzeug ist nicht „keine Menge“, sondern eine sehr große.
>
> Besonders beliebt sind Neuschöpfungen. Manche Marken prägen eigene Wörter, die sich in der Alltagssprache festsetzen; andere verschmelzen zwei Wörter zu einem Kofferwort, etwa „Kurlaub“ aus Kur und Urlaub. Von einem Neologismus spricht die Sprachwissenschaft, solange ein Wort noch als neu empfunden wird. Ob es bleibt, entscheidet allerdings nicht die Werbebranche, sondern die Sprachgemeinschaft.
>
> Überschätzen sollte man die Wirkung solcher Wörter nicht. Viele Werbeforscher betonen, dass Konsumentinnen und Konsumenten Werbeversprechen heute mit einer gesunden Skepsis begegnen. Ein Slogan, der zu dick aufträgt, wirkt schnell unglaubwürdig. Ein guter Blickfang ist deshalb oft schlichter, als man denkt: ein einziges treffendes Wort statt dreier Superlative.
>
> Und manchmal greift die Werbung auch daneben. Als „steinreich“ spricht man Kunden besser nicht an, und wer im Werbespot todmüde Angestellte zeigt, verkauft eher Kaffee als Bürostühle.

*Lightning-fast in the mind: how advertising builds words.* Anyone who opens the newspaper in the morning meets it by page three at the latest: the language of advertising. Here nothing is simply cheap, it's dirt cheap; no offer is just new, it's brand new. The washing machine spins at lightning speed, the laptop is wafer-thin, using it is child's play. Copywriters reach for such intensifying compounds because they create an image in a few syllables: the lightning stands for speed, the breath for lightness, the child for simplicity.
Prefixes such as *Riesen-* (giant), *Mega-* or *Top-* work in a similar way. A furniture store advertises a huge selection, a theme park promises tremendous fun for the whole family. Nobody minds that the word *Mord* (murder) is inside it: the original meaning faded long ago, and what remains is the intensification. *Un-*, too, can intensify instead of negating. *Eine Unmenge Spielzeug* is not "no amount" of toys but a huge one.
New coinages are especially popular. Some brands create their own words, which take root in everyday language; others fuse two words into a portmanteau, such as *Kurlaub* from *Kur* (spa cure) and *Urlaub*. Linguists speak of a neologism as long as a word is still felt to be new. Whether it stays, however, is decided not by the advertising industry but by the language community.
One shouldn't overestimate the effect of such words. Many advertising researchers stress that consumers today meet advertising promises with healthy scepticism. A slogan that lays it on too thick quickly seems untrustworthy. A good eye-catcher is therefore often simpler than you'd think: a single apt word instead of three superlatives.
And sometimes advertising misses the mark. It's better not to address customers as *steinreich* (filthy rich), and an ad that shows dead-tired employees is more likely to sell coffee than office chairs.

## Intensifying compounds: blitzschnell, todmüde

An adjective can be intensified by a noun (or another adjective) in front of it. The first part doesn't keep its literal meaning; it adds "extremely" through an image.

| Compound | Literally | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| *blitzschnell* | lightning-fast | extremely fast |
| *hauchdünn* | breath-thin | wafer-thin; also *ein hauchdünner Vorsprung* (a razor-thin lead) |
| *kinderleicht* | child-easy | dead easy |
| *spottbillig* | mockery-cheap | dirt cheap (so cheap it's laughable) |
| *brandneu* | from English *brand-new* (fresh from the fire) | brand new |
| *steinreich* | stone-rich | immensely rich |
| *todmüde* | death-tired | dead tired |
| *stockdunkel* | (*stock-* only intensifies) | pitch-dark |
| *kerngesund* | core-healthy | in perfect health, fit as a fiddle |
| *erzkonservativ* | arch-conservative | ultra-conservative |

Three things to know about them.

**They are largely fixed.** You can't combine freely: *blitzschnell* but not ~~blitzbillig~~, *todmüde* but not ~~steinmüde~~. Some first parts are productive, mostly in colloquial speech: *tod-* (*todernst, todsicher, todschick, todlangweilig*), *stink-* (*stinklangweilig, stinknormal*), *brand-* (*brandaktuell, brandgefährlich*), *grund-* (*grundverschieden, grundfalsch*), *hoch-* (*hochgefährlich, hochmotiviert*), *ur-* (*uralt*), *super-, mega-* (*supergünstig, megacool*).

**They are stressed on both parts.** *BLITZ-SCHNELL, STEIN-REICH, TOD-MÜDE.* This can change the meaning: *steinreich* with stress on both parts means "immensely rich"; stressed only on *Stein-* it means "full of stones" (*ein steinreicher Acker*, a stony field).

**They are rarely compared.** Since they already mean "extremely", a comparative is odd: ~~blitzschneller~~ as a comparative, ~~am kinderleichtesten~~. As attributive adjectives they take normal endings: *ein brandneues Modell, mit einem hauchdünnen Vorsprung*.

Their register varies: *kinderleicht, brandneu, blitzschnell* are fine in a newspaper; *spottbillig* and *stinklangweilig* are colloquial.

## Augmentative prefixes: Riesen-, Mords-, Un-

Nouns, too, have intensifying first parts. They mean "huge, great, tremendous" and are mostly colloquial.

| Prefix | Examples | Note |
|---|---|---|
| *Riesen-* | *die Riesenauswahl, der Riesenerfolg, ein Riesenhunger* | very common, also in ads |
| *Mords-* | *der Mordsspaß, ein Mordshunger, ein Mordskrach* | colloquial; *Mord* (murder) is no longer felt |
| *Heiden-* | *ein Heidenlärm, eine Heidenangst, eine Heidenarbeit* | colloquial |
| *Bomben-* | *die Bombenstimmung, ein Bombenerfolg* | colloquial |
| *Spitzen-* | *die Spitzenqualität, die Spitzenleistung* | neutral, positive |
| *Top-* | *das Topangebot, die Topqualität* | advertising, colloquial |
| *Erz-* | *der Erzfeind, erzkonservativ* | "arch-", usually negative |
| *Un-* | *die Unmenge, die Unsumme, die Unzahl* | huge amount, sum, number |

*Un-* deserves attention, because it normally negates: *unklug* (unwise), *die Unruhe* (unrest). In a few nouns of quantity it does the opposite and intensifies: *eine Unmenge Arbeit* (a huge amount of work), *eine Unsumme Geld* (a vast sum). In *das Unwetter* (severe weather) it means "bad"; in *die Untat* (atrocity) "evil". Context and the noun tell you which.

In compounds the second part decides the gender, as always: *der Spaß → der Mordsspaß, die Auswahl → die Riesenauswahl, die Menge → die Unmenge*.

## Foreign prefixes

Educated and technical German (lesson 18) uses a set of prefixes from Latin and Greek. They combine mainly with foreign stems and with the suffixes *-ieren* (verbs), *-ität* (feminine nouns), *-ismus* (masculine nouns, plural *-ismen*) and *-ierung*.

| Prefix | Meaning | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| *anti-* | against | *antiautoritär, antibakteriell, der Antisemitismus* |
| *pro-* | for, in favour of | *proeuropäisch, prowestlich* |
| *post-* | after | *postfaktisch, die Postmoderne* |
| *prä-* | before | *prähistorisch, präventiv* |
| *de-/des-* | removing, reversing | *dezentral, deeskalieren* (lesson 1), *die Desinformation, demotivieren* |
| *dis-* | apart, not | *disqualifizieren* (lesson 5), *die Disharmonie* |
| *in-* (*il-, im-, ir-*) | not | *inkompetent, illegal, immobil, irrelevant* |
| *re-* | again, back | *reorganisieren, die Rekonstruktion, reaktivieren* |
| *ex-* | former | *der Exfreund, die Expräsidentin* (colloquial; formal *ehemalig*) |
| *non-* | not | *nonverbal, nonkonformistisch* |

*in-* assimilates to the next sound: *il-* before *l* (*illegal*), *im-* before *m, b, p* (*immobil, impulsiv*), *ir-* before *r* (*irrelevant, irreal*). These words are mostly stressed at the end, as foreign words usually are: *in-kom-pe-TENT, ir-re-le-VANT*.

Stem, suffix and prefix combine into word families: *real → die Realität, realisieren, der Realismus, irreal*; *legal → die Legalität, legalisieren, illegal, die Illegalität*; *aktiv → die Aktivität, aktivieren, der Aktivismus, inaktiv, reaktivieren*.

## Conversion: das Aus, das Hin und Her

**[[Conversion]]** (*Konversion*) makes a new word from another part of speech without adding anything except, for nouns, the article and a capital letter. You know nominalized infinitives (*das Lesen*, B2). Other parts of speech can be converted too:

- *das Aus* (the end): *Das Aus für das Werk kam überraschend.*
- *das Hin und Her* (back-and-forth): *Nach langem Hin und Her wurde der Vertrag unterschrieben.*
- *das Für und Wider* (pros and cons, lesson 14): *Wir haben das Für und Wider abgewogen.*
- *ohne Wenn und Aber* (without ifs and buts): *Die Firma muss den Schaden ohne Wenn und Aber ersetzen.*
- *das Ja / das Nein*: *Sie gab ihr Ja zum Kompromiss.*
- *ein Muss* (a must): *Für Fans ist das Album ein Muss.*

Converted words are capitalized and usually neuter. Headlines love them because they are short: *Aus für Kohlekraftwerk*. The Gesellschaft für deutsche Sprache chose *Ampel-Aus*, the end of the "traffic-light" coalition government, as its Word of the Year 2024.

## Blends and new coinages

A **[[portmanteau word]]** (*das Kofferwort*, a "suitcase word") fuses parts of two words into one: *Denglisch* (*Deutsch + Englisch*), *jein* (*ja + nein*), *Kurlaub* (*Kur + Urlaub*), and from English *der Brunch* (*breakfast + lunch*) and *der Smog* (*smoke + fog*). *Teuro* (*teuer + Euro*), the grumble about price rises after the euro arrived, was chosen as the German Word of the Year 2002 by the Gesellschaft für deutsche Sprache.

A **[[neologism]]** (*der Neologismus*, plural *die Neologismen*; also *die Neuschöpfung*) is any new word, whether a blend, a compound, a borrowing or a new meaning. Advertising and technology create many; most disappear again. Some brand names became the ordinary word for the product (*das Tempo* for a paper tissue, *der Tesafilm* for sticky tape), which is why companies sometimes fight to protect their trademarks.

## Reading long advertising compounds

The B2 rule still works: read a compound from the right, because the last part is the head and decides the gender.

- *die Zielgruppenanalyse* = die Analyse + der Zielgruppe(n): an analysis of the target group.
- *das Werbeversprechen* = das Versprechen + in der Werbung: an advertising promise or claim.
- *die Markenbotschaft* = die Botschaft + der Marke: the message a brand wants to send.
- *die Schleichwerbung* = die Werbung + *schleichen* (to creep): covert advertising, hidden in a programme or article. German media law prohibits it; product placement is allowed only under conditions and must be labelled.
- *der Werbeträger* = der Träger + der Werbung: an advertising medium (a poster, a bus, a website).

## The words of this lesson

- *das Marketing* has no plural; *die Vermarktung* is the marketing of something particular (*die Vermarktung des neuen Modells*), from *vermarkten* (inseparable: *hat vermarktet*).
- *die Reklame* is an older word for advertising, still used (*die Leuchtreklame*, neon sign), but in many contexts it sounds old-fashioned or slightly disparaging; the neutral word is *die Werbung* (A2).
- *der Werbespot* is a TV or radio commercial, *die Werbeanzeige* a print or online advertisement, *die Werbekampagne* a whole campaign, *der Slogan* (plural *die Slogans*) its catchphrase.
- *der Konsument, die Konsumentin* are a little more formal and more economic than *der Verbraucher, die Verbraucherin* (B1).
- *die Markentreue* is brand loyalty, *der Blickfang* an eye-catcher (*als Blickfang dienen*).

## Pronunciation

- Intensifying compounds: both parts stressed, BLITZ-SCHNELL, KIN-DER-LEICHT, SPOTT-BIL-LIG.
- *die Unmenge, die Unsumme*: stress on *Un-*: UN-men-ge, UN-sum-me.
- *der Neologismus*: ne-o-lo-GIS-mus. *die Reklame*: re-KLA-me.
- *der Slogan* is pronounced roughly as in English, SLOH-gen; *das Marketing* MAR-ke-ting.

## Common mistakes

- Building new intensifiers by analogy: ~~blitzbillig~~, ~~steinmüde~~. Use the fixed ones, or plain *sehr, extrem, äußerst*.
- Comparing intensifying compounds: ~~Das neue Modell ist noch blitzschneller.~~ → *noch schneller*.
- Reading *Un-* as always negative: *eine Unmenge* is a huge amount.
- Getting the gender of an augmented noun wrong: ~~das Riesenauswahl~~ → *die Riesenauswahl* (the last part decides).
- Using colloquial augmentatives in formal writing: ~~Das Projekt war ein Bombenerfolg~~ in a report → *ein großer Erfolg*.
- Forgetting assimilation: ~~inlegal~~ → *illegal*, ~~inrelevant~~ → *irrelevant*.

## Key points

- Intensifying compounds (*blitzschnell, kinderleicht, todmüde, steinreich*) add "extremely" through an image; they are largely fixed, stressed on both parts and not compared.
- Augmentative first parts (*Riesen-, Mords-, Heiden-, Bomben-, Spitzen-, Top-, Erz-*) inflate nouns, mostly in colloquial style; *Un-* intensifies in *Unmenge, Unsumme, Unzahl*.
- Foreign prefixes (*anti-, pro-, post-, prä-, de-, dis-, in-/il-/im-/ir-, re-, ex-, non-*) combine with *-ieren, -ität, -ismus* into word families.
- Conversion makes nouns from other parts of speech: *das Aus, das Hin und Her, ohne Wenn und Aber*.
- Blends (*Denglisch, jein*) and other neologisms come and go; the language community decides which stay.
- Long compounds are read from the right: the last part is the head.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete the lesson.

lessons.title: Was mich stört, ist …: emphasis, information structure and negation
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

German word order is famously flexible: only the verb has a fixed place. At B2 you learned the fields of the sentence (**Vorfeld**, **Mittelfeld**, the verb bracket) and met **Ausklammerung**. At C1 the question is how to use that flexibility: what to put first, how to give one element extra weight, how to keep a long sentence readable, and how to say "not" with the right strength and scope. This is called **[[information structure]]**: the arrangement of what is known and what is new, what is in focus and what is background.

The lesson covers the Vorfeld, cleft sentences (*Es war die Stadt, die …*) and pseudo-cleft sentences (*Was mich stört, ist …*), the Nachfeld, right dislocation in speech (*Der ist gut, der Kompost*), and the finer points of negation: *keineswegs, mitnichten, nicht einmal, geschweige denn, keinerlei*, the scope of *nicht*, litotes and double negation. The theme is the circular economy: waste, recycling and repair.

## A radio report from a repair café

> **Radioreportage: „Kaputt? Nicht mit uns!“**
>
> *Sprecherin:* Samstagvormittag in einem Gemeindesaal in Kassel. Auf den Tischen liegen Toaster, Lampen, ein Staubsauger ohne Kabel. Einmal im Monat wird der Saal zum Reparaturcafé. Was hier zählt, ist nicht der Preis eines Geräts, sondern die Frage, ob es sich retten lässt.
>
> *Werner Kluge, 71, ehemaliger Elektriker:* Wissen Sie, was mich am meisten ärgert? Dass die Leute so schnell aufgeben. Der ist doch nicht kaputt, der Toaster. Da ist nur die Sicherung durch. Das dauert keine fünf Minuten.
>
> *Sprecherin:* Werner Kluge ist von Anfang an dabei. Es war seine Frau, die ihn vor acht Jahren überredet hat mitzumachen. Bereut hat er es keineswegs.
>
> *Kluge:* Mitnichten! Hier lerne ich mehr als in vierzig Jahren Beruf.
>
> *Sprecherin:* Nicht alles lässt sich reparieren. Bei vielen neuen Geräten sind die Akkus verklebt, Ersatzteile gibt es keine, geschweige denn eine Anleitung. Seit Ende Juli 2026 gilt zwar ein Recht auf Reparatur, das die Hersteller bestimmter Geräte, etwa von Waschmaschinen, Kühlschränken und Smartphones, verpflichtet, diese auf Wunsch zu reparieren. Für Toaster und Lampen gilt es aber nicht. Was die Helferinnen und Helfer fordern, ist deshalb ein Recht auf Reparatur für alle Geräte.
>
> *Selma Arslan, 34, Softwareentwicklerin:* Wir sind keine Nostalgiker. Es geht uns nicht ums Basteln, sondern um Ressourcen. Ein Laptop, der zehn Jahre hält, hat eine ganz andere Ökobilanz als einer, der nach drei Jahren auf dem Wertstoffhof landet. Und das Argument, Reparieren lohne sich nicht, stimmt oft nicht einmal finanziell.
>
> *Sprecherin:* Und die Bilanz des Vormittags? Von 23 Geräten funktionieren 15 wieder. Nicht schlecht, findet Werner Kluge, und für die Umwelt nicht unwichtig. Den Staubsauger ohne Kabel nimmt er übrigens mit nach Hause. Aufgegeben hat er ihn nämlich noch nicht.

*Radio report: "Broken? Not with us!"*
*Narrator:* Saturday morning in a parish hall in Kassel. On the tables lie toasters, lamps, a vacuum cleaner with no cable. Once a month the hall becomes a repair café. What counts here is not what a device costs, but whether it can be saved.
*Werner Kluge, 71, retired electrician:* Do you know what annoys me most? That people give up so quickly. It isn't broken, this toaster. The fuse has just blown. That takes less than five minutes.
*Narrator:* Werner Kluge has been here from the start. It was his wife who persuaded him to join eight years ago. He has by no means regretted it.
*Kluge:* Not in the least! I learn more here than in forty years at work.
*Narrator:* Not everything can be repaired. In many new devices the batteries are glued in, there are no spare parts, let alone instructions. Since the end of July 2026 there has been a right to repair, which obliges the manufacturers of certain devices, such as washing machines, fridges and smartphones, to repair them on request. But it doesn't apply to toasters and lamps. So what the volunteers are calling for is a right to repair for all devices.
*Selma Arslan, 34, software developer:* We're not nostalgics. For us it's not about tinkering, it's about resources. A laptop that lasts ten years has a completely different life-cycle assessment from one that ends up at the recycling centre after three years. And the argument that repairing doesn't pay often isn't even true in financial terms.
*Narrator:* And the result of the morning? Of 23 devices, 15 work again. Not bad, Werner Kluge thinks, and for the environment not unimportant. By the way, he's taking the vacuum cleaner with no cable home with him. He hasn't given up on it yet, you see.

## The Vorfeld: what comes first

The Vorfeld (position 1) holds exactly one element. By default it is the subject, but any part of the sentence can go there, and the choice is not random. Three things typically come first:

1. **A link to what was just said** (known information, the "topic"): *Werner Kluge ist von Anfang an dabei.* The report has just been about the café; the next sentence picks up a person in it. *Den Staubsauger ohne Kabel nimmt er übrigens mit nach Hause.* The vacuum cleaner was mentioned at the start, so it can open the sentence.
2. **A scene-setter** (time, place): *Einmal im Monat wird der Saal zum Reparaturcafé.*
3. **A contrast**: *Bereut hat er es keineswegs.* Here even the participle moves to the Vorfeld. This is only possible when it stands in contrast to something (his wife persuaded him; regretted it he has not). The same with an infinitive: *Reparieren kann man vieles, aber nicht alles.* Spoken, the fronted element carries a strong stress, and often a second stress follows later.

New and important information, by contrast, tends to come late, near the end of the Mittelfeld or in the right bracket. So *Ein Staubsauger lag auf dem Tisch* sounds odd as the first sentence of a story, while *Auf dem Tisch lag ein Staubsauger* introduces it naturally.

## Cleft sentences: Es war seine Frau, die …

A **[[cleft sentence]]** (*Spaltsatz*) splits one sentence in two to put a single element in focus:

- *Seine Frau hat ihn überredet.* → *Es war seine Frau, die ihn überredet hat.* — It was his wife who persuaded him.

The pattern is *es* + *sein* + focused element + relative clause. It says: this one, and nobody else. Notes:

- *sein* agrees with the focused element: *Es waren die Nachbarn, die geholfen haben.* — It was the neighbours who helped.
- The relative pronoun takes its case from the relative clause: *Es war der Hausmeister, dem wir den Schlüssel gegeben haben.*
- The tense of *sein* usually matches the relative clause: past in a story (*Es war …, die … hat*), present for the present (*Es ist der Preis, der die Leute abschreckt*).
- In German, clefts are used less than in English. Often stress or the Vorfeld does the same job: *SEINE FRAU hat ihn überredet.* Use clefts for strong contrast, in writing especially, where stress isn't heard.

## Pseudo-cleft sentences: Was mich stört, ist …

A **[[pseudo-cleft sentence]]** (*Sperrsatz*) puts a w-clause first and the important part after *sein*, at the end, where it gets the most weight:

- *Was hier zählt, ist nicht der Preis, sondern die Frage, ob …*
- *Was die Helferinnen und Helfer fordern, ist ein Recht auf Reparatur.*
- *Was mich stört, ist die Verpackungsflut.* — What bothers me is the flood of packaging.

The w-word must fit the verb's valency, so verbs with a preposition need a *wo(r)-* word:

| Verb | Pseudo-cleft |
|---|---|
| *etwas brauchen* | *Was wir brauchen, ist mehr Zeit.* |
| *gegen etwas sein* | *Wogegen ich bin, ist die Plastiktüte an der Kasse.* |
| *auf etwas ankommen* | *Worauf es ankommt, ist die Reparierbarkeit.* |
| *sich für etwas interessieren* | *Wofür ich mich interessiere, ist Upcycling.* |
| *jemand + Verb* | *Wer am meisten profitiert, sind die Hersteller.* |

When the focused part is a whole clause, there is a comma on both sides of *ist*: *Was mich ärgert, ist, dass die Leute so schnell aufgeben.* In speech, the pseudo-cleft often becomes a question and answer: *Wissen Sie, was mich am meisten ärgert? Dass die Leute so schnell aufgeben.*

## The Nachfeld: after the right bracket

The **[[Nachfeld]]** is the space after the right part of the verb bracket (the participle, infinitive, separable prefix or, in subordinate clauses, the finite verb). Moving something there is Ausklammerung. Some elements go there by rule, others by choice.

**Almost always in the Nachfeld:** subordinate and infinitive clauses, and comparisons with *als* and *wie*.

- *Wir haben heute mehr Geräte repariert als im letzten Monat.* (not usually ~~… mehr Geräte als im letzten Monat repariert~~, which is possible but heavy)
- *Sie hat das Gerät genauso schnell repariert wie er.*
- *Ich habe den Mann getroffen, der den Toaster gebracht hat.*

**Often in the Nachfeld, for weight and readability:** long prepositional phrases and added information.

- *Wir haben lange diskutiert über die Frage, ob man alte Akkus noch verwenden darf.* (spoken; in writing equally common: *Wir haben lange über die Frage diskutiert, ob …*)
- *Viele Geräte landen auf der Deponie, und zwar ohne jede Prüfung.*

Ausklammerung keeps the verb bracket short, so the listener hears the main verb sooner. In formal writing, put only comparisons, clauses and genuinely long additions in the Nachfeld; in speech, people move more there.

## Right dislocation: Der ist gut, der Kompost

In speech, a noun phrase is often added after the sentence to make clear what a pronoun refers to, or to add it as an afterthought. This is **[[right dislocation]]** (*Rechtsversetzung*):

- *Der ist doch nicht kaputt, der Toaster.* — It isn't broken, this toaster.
- *Die hält ewig, diese Lampe.* — It lasts for ever, this lamp.

The pronoun (usually *der, die, das*) stands in the sentence; the full noun phrase comes after a short pause, in the same case. The mirror image, left dislocation, is just as common in speech: *Der Kompost, der ist richtig gut geworden.* Both belong to spoken German; in writing, use the simple sentence.

## Negation: nicht, kein and their scope

You know that *kein* negates nouns with an indefinite or no article and *nicht* the rest. At C1, the important question is **[[scope]]**: what exactly is being denied.

**[[Sentence negation]]** (*Satznegation*) denies the whole statement. *nicht* goes as far right in the Mittelfeld as it can: after definite objects, pronouns and most time adverbs, but before the right bracket and before predicatives, directional phrases and most prepositional objects.

- *Er hat den Toaster gestern nicht repariert.*
- *Der Toaster ist nicht kaputt.*
- *Ich warte nicht auf den Techniker.*

**[[Constituent negation]]** (*Sondernegation*) denies one element only, and usually a *sondern* follows. *nicht* stands directly before the negated element, and that element is stressed.

- *Er hat nicht den Toaster repariert, sondern die Lampe.*
- *Es geht uns nicht ums Basteln, sondern um Ressourcen.*
- *Ich komme nicht morgen, sondern übermorgen.*

The position of *nicht* changes the meaning: *Wir haben nicht alle Geräte repariert* means "some, but not all". *Wir haben alle Geräte nicht repariert* is unusual and ambiguous; to say "none of them", use *Wir haben keins der Geräte repariert*.

## Stronger and finer negation

| Word | Meaning | Register and use |
|---|---|---|
| *keineswegs* | by no means, not at all | neutral to formal; denies a claim strongly: *Das ist keineswegs sicher.* |
| *keinesfalls* (B2) | on no account | often in rules and decisions: *Akkus dürfen keinesfalls in den Hausmüll.* |
| *mitnichten* | not in the least | elevated and a little old-fashioned, often emphatic or ironic; also as a one-word answer: *Mitnichten!* |
| *nicht einmal* | not even | before the element in focus: *Er hat nicht einmal angerufen.* Colloquially *nicht mal*. |
| *geschweige denn* | let alone | only after a negative or restrictive statement, with a comma: *Ersatzteile gibt es keine, geschweige denn eine Anleitung.* |
| *keinerlei* | no … whatsoever | before a noun, never takes an ending: *keinerlei Hinweise, mit keinerlei Mitteln* |
| *kaum* | hardly, barely | *Das Gerät ist kaum benutzt worden.* |
| *weder … noch* (B1) | neither … nor | *Es gab weder Ersatzteile noch eine Anleitung.* |

*keineswegs* and *keinesfalls* overlap, and many speakers use them interchangeably. The tendency: *keineswegs* says that something is not true (*Das ist keineswegs die ganze Wahrheit*); *keinesfalls* says that something must not happen (*Das darf keinesfalls passieren*).

*geschweige denn* can also introduce a clause: *Ich glaube nicht, dass er anruft, geschweige denn, dass er vorbeikommt.* (The comma after *denn* is optional.)

Notice the split negative noun in the report: *Ersatzteile gibt es keine.* This is normal, especially in speech: the noun goes to the Vorfeld for contrast and *keine* stays behind.

## Litotes: nicht unwichtig

**[[Litotes]]** (*die Litotes*) says something by denying its opposite: *nicht schlecht* (quite good), *nicht unwichtig* (rather important), *nicht ganz unschuldig* (partly to blame). It sounds understated, polite or ironic, depending on the tone. Litotes is very common in German academic and political language (*Es ist nicht auszuschließen, dass …*: it cannot be ruled out that …, i.e. it is possible). Two colloquial ones: *Die Prüfung ist nicht ohne* (the exam is quite tough), *Das ist nicht ohne Reiz* (that has a certain appeal).

## Double negation

In standard German, two negations in one clause either cancel out (that is litotes: *nicht unwichtig*) or are simply wrong: ~~Ich habe keine Zeit nicht.~~ ~~Ohne keinerlei Hilfe~~ → *Ohne jede Hilfe* (*ohne* is already negative). In several dialects, especially in the south, two negations reinforce each other instead: *Da hat keiner nix gesagt* (nobody said anything). You will hear it in films and in the street; don't use it in standard German.

## The words of this lesson: waste, recycling and repair

- *die Kreislaufwirtschaft* (circular economy) keeps materials in use as long as possible. German waste law (§ 6 Kreislaufwirtschaftsgesetz) ranks the options in this order: avoiding waste (*die Abfallvermeidung*), preparing for reuse (*die Vorbereitung zur Wiederverwendung*; *die Wiederverwendung* is reuse), recycling (*das Recycling*, B1; more formal *die Wiederverwertung*), other recovery, above all energy recovery (as when *die Müllverbrennung* generates power), and finally disposal, for example on a landfill (*die Deponie*).
- *der Wertstoff* is any material that can be recycled (paper, glass, metal, packaging); *der Wertstoffhof* is the municipal recycling centre where you bring them, along with *der Elektroschrott* and *der Sperrmüll* (bulky waste such as furniture), which in many towns is also collected from the kerb on request.
- *das Upcycling* turns waste into something of higher value (pallets into furniture), *das Downcycling* into something of lower value (high-quality plastic into park benches).
- *die Mehrwegflasche* is refilled many times; *die Einwegverpackung* is used once. Germany's *Pfandsystem* charges a deposit on most drinks containers (as of 2026: 25 cents on single-use bottles and cans, less on most refillable bottles).
- *die Ökobilanz* (life-cycle assessment) compares a product's environmental effects from production to disposal.
- *die Obsoleszenz* is a product's becoming obsolete; *geplante Obsoleszenz* (planned obsolescence) is the suspicion that manufacturers build in an early end on purpose. How often this really happens is disputed.
- *langlebig* (durable, long-lasting) and *kurzlebig* (short-lived), *ressourcenschonend* (resource-saving), *die Reparierbarkeit* (repairability), *die Wegwerfgesellschaft* (throwaway society), *die Sammelquote* (collection rate), *das Mikroplastik* (microplastics, no plural), *der Kompost* and *kompostieren*.

## Pronunciation

- *die Obsoleszenz*: ob-so-les-TSENZ. *die Deponie*: de-po-NIE (stress on the last syllable, *-ie* as long *i*).
- *der Kompost*: kom-POST; *kompostieren*: kom-pos-TIE-ren.
- *mitnichten*: mit-NICH-ten. *keinerlei*: KEI-ner-lei.
- *das Reparaturcafé*: re-pa-ra-TUR-ka-fe, with the main stress on *-tur-*.
- In cleft and pseudo-cleft sentences, the focused element carries the main stress: *Es war seine FRAU, die …*; *Was mich stört, ist die VerPAckungsflut.*

## Common mistakes

- Using the wrong w-word in a pseudo-cleft: ~~Was ich dagegen bin, ist …~~ → *Wogegen ich bin, ist …*; ~~Was es ankommt, …~~ → *Worauf es ankommt, …*
- Leaving out a comma: ~~Was mich ärgert ist dass …~~ → *Was mich ärgert, ist, dass …*
- Squeezing a comparison into the bracket: *Wir haben mehr als im letzten Monat repariert* is possible but heavy; the normal order is *Wir haben mehr repariert als im letzten Monat*.
- Putting *nicht* before a definite object when you mean the whole sentence. *Ich habe nicht den Toaster repariert* means "it wasn't the toaster I repaired" and leads the listener to expect *sondern …*; for "I didn't repair the toaster", say *Ich habe den Toaster nicht repariert*.
- *geschweige denn* after a positive statement: ~~Er kann gut Englisch, geschweige denn Französisch.~~ It needs a negative first part: *Er kann kaum Englisch, geschweige denn Französisch.*
- Declining *keinerlei*: ~~keinerleien Hinweise~~ → *keinerlei Hinweise*; double negation with *ohne*: ~~ohne keinerlei~~ → *ohne jede*.

## Key points

- The Vorfeld takes the link to the previous sentence, a scene-setter or a contrast (*Bereut hat er es keineswegs*); new information tends to come late.
- Cleft sentences (*Es war seine Frau, die …*) and pseudo-cleft sentences (*Was mich stört, ist …*; *Worauf es ankommt, ist …*) put one element in focus; the w-word follows the verb's valency.
- The Nachfeld takes comparisons with *als/wie*, clauses and long additions, which keeps the verb bracket short.
- Right dislocation (*Der ist gut, der Kompost*) is spoken German.
- Sentence negation puts *nicht* late in the Mittelfeld; constituent negation puts it before the denied element, usually with *sondern*.
- *keineswegs* (by no means), *mitnichten* (elevated), *nicht einmal* (not even), *geschweige denn* (let alone, after a negative), *keinerlei* (no … whatsoever, no ending).
- Litotes (*nicht unwichtig*) understates; double negation is standard only as litotes and otherwise dialectal.

lessons.title: Framing and euphemism: the language of politics
lessons.body:
## Words that steer

Lesson 18 showed that words carry connotations as well as meanings. In politics, business and administration this is not an accident: whoever names a thing first often decides how people think about it. A tax can be a *Steuerlast* (a burden) or a *Steuerbeitrag* (a contribution); job cuts can be *Entlassungen* or a *Personalanpassung*. This honors lesson gives you the tools to notice such choices: **[[framing]]**, **[[euphemism]]**, catchwords and combative terms, and the grammar that hides who did something. It also introduces the German *Unwort des Jahres*.

The aim is analysis, not taking sides. Every party, company and institution uses these techniques; the examples below come from many directions.

## A press release and what it means

Read this (invented) press release from a manufacturer, and then the journalist's plain-German version.

> **Pressemitteilung der Hollmann Haushaltsgeräte GmbH**
>
> Im Zuge einer strategischen Neuausrichtung wird die Hollmann GmbH ihre Strukturen am Standort Bielefeld an die veränderten Marktbedingungen anpassen. Die Produktion der Kühlgeräte wird bis Ende 2027 an einen Partnerstandort in Polen verlagert. Von der Maßnahme sind rund 180 Stellen betroffen. Selbstverständlich wird der Prozess sozialverträglich gestaltet. Zugleich passen wir unsere Preise moderat an, um auch künftig die gewohnte Qualität sicherzustellen. Die Geschäftsführung bedauert, dass dieser Schritt notwendig geworden ist, und sieht das Unternehmen gut aufgestellt für die Zukunft.

> **Was gemeint ist (aus einem Zeitungsbericht):** Hollmann schließt die Kühlgeräteproduktion in Bielefeld und verlegt sie nach Polen, wo die Löhne niedriger sind. Etwa 180 Beschäftigte verlieren ihre Arbeit. Gleichzeitig werden die Geräte teurer.

*Press release:* As part of a strategic realignment, Hollmann GmbH will adapt its structures at the Bielefeld site to changed market conditions. Production of refrigerators will be relocated to a partner site in Poland by the end of 2027. Around 180 positions are affected by the measure. Of course, the process will be carried out in a socially responsible way. At the same time, we are moderately adjusting our prices in order to ensure the usual quality in future. The management regrets that this step has become necessary and sees the company as well positioned for the future.
*What it means:* Hollmann is closing refrigerator production in Bielefeld and moving it to Poland, where wages are lower. About 180 employees will lose their jobs. At the same time, the appliances are getting more expensive.

Look at how the release works:

- **[[Euphemisms]]**: *Strukturen anpassen* and *verlagern* for closing a plant; *Stellen sind betroffen* for people losing their jobs; *Preise moderat anpassen* for raising prices.
- **No agent**: *wird verlagert, wird gestaltet* (passive), *von der Maßnahme sind … betroffen* (nominal style). Nobody decides anything; things happen.
- **Positive frame**: *strategische Neuausrichtung, gut aufgestellt für die Zukunft*: the closure is presented as progress.
- **Empty phrases** (*Worthülsen*): *sozialverträglich gestaltet* doesn't say what will be done (a severance scheme? early retirement? transfers?).

Nothing in the release is false. That is exactly why such language is effective: it isn't lying, it is choosing.

## Euphemism: making things sound better

A **[[euphemism]]** (*der Euphemismus*, plural *die Euphemismen*; adjective *euphemistisch*) replaces an unpleasant word with a milder one. Dictionaries mark many with the label *verhüllend* (veiling). Some are kind and expected (*entschlafen* for *sterben* in a death notice, honors lesson 20h2). In politics and business they often serve to *beschönigen* (gloss over) or *verharmlosen* (play down).

| Euphemism | Plain word | Where you meet it |
|---|---|---|
| *Mitarbeiter freisetzen* | *entlassen* | business |
| *Personalanpassung, Stellenabbau* | *Entlassungen* | business |
| *Preisanpassung* | *Preiserhöhung* | business, utilities |
| *Nullwachstum, negatives Wachstum* | *Stagnation, Schrumpfung* | economics |
| *Kollateralschaden* | civilians killed or hurt as a side effect of military action | military |
| *Sondervermögen* | a fund financed by extra borrowing | public finance |

*Kollateralschaden* was chosen as the *Unwort des Jahres* 1999, *Sondervermögen* as the one for 2025 (see below).

The opposite of a euphemism, a deliberately harsh word, is called a *Dysphemismus*: calling a tax a *Strafsteuer* (punitive tax) or a regulation a *Bürokratiemonster*.

## Framing: the frame decides the picture

**[[Framing]]** (*das Framing*, also *die Rahmung*) means presenting an issue through a particular image or category so that some conclusions seem natural and others hardly occur to the listener. The term comes from communication research and cognitive linguistics.

- *Steuerlast* frames taxes as a burden you'd like to put down; *Steuerbeitrag* or *Steuergeld* frame them as a contribution to shared goods.
- *Klimawandel* (climate change) sounds like a natural process; *Klimakrise* or *Klimanotstand* demand action.
- Water metaphors for people (*Flut, Welle, Strom, Zustrom*) frame migration as a natural disaster to be dammed. This was one reason the Unwort jury criticized *Zustrombegrenzungsgesetz* in January 2026.
- *Rettungsschirm* (rescue umbrella) for a financial aid package frames it as protection, not as a cost.

Framing is not lying either. Every description needs some frame. The critical question is whether the frame fits the facts and what it leaves out.

## Catchwords, combative terms and empty phrases

- *das Schlagwort* (catchword): a short word that sums up a programme and is easy to repeat: *Nachhaltigkeit, Bürokratieabbau, Digitalisierung, Chancengleichheit*. The plural is *die Schlagwörter* or *die Schlagworte*.
- *der Kampfbegriff* (combative term): a word used to attack or discredit an opponent, not to describe. *Lügenpresse* (Unwort 2014) and *Gutmensch* (Unwort 2015) were chosen largely because the jury saw them as words used to defame whole groups.
- *die Worthülse* (hollow phrase): a phrase that sounds meaningful but says nothing checkable: *Wir müssen die Menschen mitnehmen*, *zukunftsfähig aufstellen*, *ein starkes Signal senden*.
- *die Sprachregelung*: an agreed or prescribed way of naming something, for example inside a ministry or a company (*Laut interner Sprachregelung spricht man nicht von Kündigungen, sondern von Trennungen*).

When such language is used systematically to steer opinion, critics speak of *Manipulation* (*manipulieren*) and, for state campaigns, of *Propaganda*. Calling something euphemistic is a description; calling it *zynisch* (cynical) is already an evaluation: it means the speaker seems to care nothing for the people affected.

## Grammar that hides the agent

Some of the most effective framing is grammatical. You know the tools from modules 2 and 3; here is what they do in political language.

- **Agentless passive**: *Es wurden Fehler gemacht.* (Mistakes were made, but by whom?) *Die Gebühren werden erhöht.*
- **Nominal style**: *Die Entscheidung zur Schließung des Standorts …* turns a decision someone took into a thing that exists.
- **Impersonal and reflexive constructions**: *Es kam zu Ausschreitungen* (riots occurred), *Die Lage hat sich verschärft* (the situation has worsened).
- **Inanimate subjects**: *Der Markt verlangt Anpassungen.* The market can't demand anything; people can.

When you read a political text, ask: Who acts? Who is affected? Which images are used? What is left out? A plain-German paraphrase, like the journalist's in the example, is the best test.

## The Unwort des Jahres

Since 1991, a jury of linguists (with a journalist and a changing guest member) has chosen a German *Unwort des Jahres*: a word or phrase from public language that it considers misleading, euphemistic, discriminatory or contrary to human dignity. The campaign was started by the linguist Horst Dieter Schlosser in Frankfurt; today it is run as the *Sprachkritische Aktion Unwort des Jahres*, and the result is announced each January for the previous year. Anyone can send in suggestions.

The most recent choice (checked in November 2026) is *Sondervermögen* for 2025. The jury called it a euphemism: *Vermögen* (assets) sounds positive and hides that the money is borrowed, which, in the jury's view, hinders an open debate about the debt. Earlier choices include *biodeutsch* (2024), *Remigration* (2023), *alternativlos* (2010) and *notleidende Banken* (2008).

The 2025 choice was announced on 13 January 2026; second place went to *Zustrombegrenzungsgesetz*, criticized for its water metaphor. Because the jury's reasons are detailed and sometimes disputed, read them on the official website (unwortdesjahres.net) before quoting them, and treat the choice as one voice in a debate, not as a verdict.

The *Unwort* is different from the *Wort des Jahres*, chosen by the Gesellschaft für deutsche Sprache (lesson 19), which picks words that characterized the year without judging them.

## Analysing political language: a checklist

1. Who is speaking, to whom, with what interest?
2. Which words are evaluative (*Last, Monster, Rettung*)? What would a neutral word be?
3. Which images (water, war, illness, rescue) frame the issue?
4. Who is the grammatical subject? Is anyone left out (passive, nominal style)?
5. Which phrases can't be checked (*Worthülsen*)?
6. Paraphrase the key sentence in plain German. What is left?

## Common mistakes

- Treating every euphemism as a lie: many are politeness (*verstorben*, *Sie hat uns verlassen*). The question is whether information is being hidden.
- Confusing *Unwort* with "non-word": an *Unwort* is a real word, judged ill-chosen; a word that doesn't exist is *kein Wort* or *ein Nichtwort*.
- Using *zynisch* as a synonym for *kritisch* or *skeptisch*: it means disregarding other people's suffering or values.

## Key points

- Euphemisms make the unpleasant sound milder (*freisetzen, Preisanpassung, Sondervermögen*); in politics and business they often gloss over (*beschönigen*) or play down (*verharmlosen*).
- Framing chooses the image through which an issue is seen (*Steuerlast* vs *Steuerbeitrag*, *Klimawandel* vs *Klimakrise*).
- *Schlagwörter* sum up programmes, *Kampfbegriffe* attack opponents, *Worthülsen* say nothing checkable.
- The agentless passive, nominal style and inanimate subjects can hide who is responsible.
- The *Unwort des Jahres* (since 1991) is chosen by an independent jury each January; 2025: *Sondervermögen*.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete the lesson.

lessons.title: Words for solemn occasions: condolence, congratulation, tribute
lessons.body:
## When the register is fixed

Most texts let you choose your style. A few don't: a letter of condolence, a death notice, an obituary, a speech in honour of someone. Here German expects an elevated, restrained style (*gehoben*, lesson 18), a small set of fixed phrases and a few grammatical forms you rarely use elsewhere, such as the wish with *möge*. Getting these texts right matters more than in almost any other situation, because people remember what was written to them in grief or at a celebration.

This honors lesson covers the condolence letter and card, the death notice, the obituary and the laudation (*die Laudatio*), with the phrases that belong to each and the ones to avoid.

## A condolence letter

A colleague of the late Dr. Ingrid Brenner writes to her husband. They know each other a little, so the letter uses *Sie*.

> Lieber Herr Brenner,
>
> mit großer Bestürzung haben wir vom plötzlichen Tod Ihrer Frau erfahren. Es fällt uns schwer, die richtigen Worte zu finden.
>
> Ingrid war über zwanzig Jahre lang ein Teil unseres Instituts. Wir haben ihre Klugheit geschätzt, ihre Geduld mit jungen Kolleginnen und Kollegen und ihren trockenen Humor, der so manche lange Sitzung gerettet hat. Viele von uns verdanken ihr mehr, als wir ihr je gesagt haben.
>
> In diesen schweren Tagen sind wir in Gedanken bei Ihnen und Ihrer Familie. Wenn wir Ihnen in irgendeiner Weise helfen können, lassen Sie es uns bitte wissen.
>
> Wir werden Ingrid ein ehrendes Andenken bewahren.
>
> In stiller Anteilnahme
> Ihre Petra Lindqvist, im Namen des ganzen Teams

*Dear Mr Brenner, we were deeply shocked to learn of your wife's sudden death. It is hard for us to find the right words. Ingrid was part of our institute for more than twenty years. We valued her intelligence, her patience with young colleagues and her dry humour, which saved many a long meeting. Many of us owe her more than we ever told her. In these difficult days our thoughts are with you and your family. If we can help you in any way, please let us know. We will always remember Ingrid with honour. With deepest sympathy, Petra Lindqvist, on behalf of the whole team.*

The letter has a typical structure:

1. **The news and the reaction**: *Mit großer Bestürzung / Mit tiefer Betroffenheit haben wir … erfahren.* Or: *Die Nachricht vom Tod … hat uns tief getroffen.*
2. **A personal memory** of the person who died: this is the part that matters most. One concrete detail is worth more than three general adjectives.
3. **Sympathy and an offer of help**: *Wir sind in Gedanken bei Ihnen. Wenn wir etwas für Sie tun können, …* Only offer what you mean.
4. **A closing line** and sign-off: *In stiller Anteilnahme, In tiefer Verbundenheit, Mit herzlichem Beileid, In Trauer*.

Short cards follow the same pattern in two or three sentences: *Liebe Familie Brenner, zum Tod von Ingrid möchten wir Ihnen unser aufrichtiges Beileid aussprechen. Wir werden sie sehr vermissen.*

## Phrases for condolence

| Purpose | Phrases |
|---|---|
| Expressing condolence | *Mein / Unser (aufrichtiges, herzliches, tief empfundenes) Beileid. Ich möchte Ihnen mein Beileid aussprechen.* (*Herzliches Beileid!* is the spoken formula you met at A2.) |
| Reaction to the news | *Mit großer Bestürzung / tief betroffen haben wir erfahren, dass … Die traurige Nachricht hat uns sehr erschüttert.* |
| Remembering | *Wir werden ihn / sie sehr vermissen. Wir werden ihr ein ehrendes Andenken bewahren. Er wird uns als … in Erinnerung bleiben.* |
| Sympathy | *Wir fühlen mit Ihnen. In Gedanken sind wir bei Ihnen. Wir wünschen Ihnen viel Kraft.* |
| Closing | *In stiller Anteilnahme. In tiefer Trauer* (for close family). *Mit stillem Gruß.* |

The verb *kondolieren* (to offer one's condolences) takes the dative: *Wir kondolieren der Familie.* It is formal; in a personal letter you write *Ich möchte Ihnen mein Beileid aussprechen*. *Die Anteilnahme* is the sympathy shown by others: in thank-you notes, families write *Für die vielen Zeichen der Anteilnahme danken wir herzlich.*

## What not to write

Condolence letters fail most often through well-meant clichés (*Floskeln*) and false cheer:

- ~~Kopf hoch, das Leben geht weiter!~~ dismisses the grief.
- ~~Sie hatte ja ein langes Leben.~~ or ~~Wenigstens musste er nicht lange leiden.~~ Even if true, it isn't yours to say.
- ~~Ich weiß genau, wie Sie sich fühlen.~~ Nobody does. Better: *Ich kann nur ahnen, wie schwer diese Zeit für Sie ist.*
- Long descriptions of your own grief or your own losses.
- Excessive pathos (*unermesslicher, unbeschreiblicher, nie endender Schmerz*): restraint is part of the style.

A handwritten card or letter is still the norm for condolences in Germany; an e-mail is acceptable among colleagues who rarely meet, a text message only among close friends.

## The death notice

The *Traueranzeige* in a newspaper, and the printed card sent to friends (*die Trauerkarte*), have a fixed layout: often a short quotation or verse, the name with dates of birth and death, a line such as *In Liebe und Dankbarkeit nehmen wir Abschied von …* or *Wir trauern um …*, the names of the *Hinterbliebenen* (the bereaved: *In stiller Trauer: Thomas Brenner, Lea und Jonas mit Familien*), and the details of the funeral service (*die Trauerfeier*) and burial (*die Beisetzung*).

Death notices use the most elevated vocabulary in the language: *entschlafen* (to pass away), *von uns gegangen*, *nach langer, schwerer Krankheit*, *das Ableben* (decease, in formal and official texts: *Nach dem Ableben des Stifters ging das Vermögen an die Stiftung*). Firms announcing the death of an employee often write: *Wir trauern um unsere Kollegin … Wir werden ihr ein ehrendes Andenken bewahren.*

## The obituary

A *Nachruf* (obituary) in a newspaper or a professional journal tells the life of the person who died and appraises their work. It is written in the **Präteritum**, with the Plusquamperfekt for earlier events, like any written narrative:

> Ingrid Brenner wurde 1961 in Görlitz geboren. Nach dem Studium der Biologie in Leipzig kam sie 1993 an unser Institut, das sie bis zuletzt prägte. Ihre Forschung zur Bodenökologie fand international Beachtung. Wer mit ihr gearbeitet hatte, wusste, dass sie keine Frage unbeantwortet ließ. Sie starb am 3. Mai nach kurzer, schwerer Krankheit.

*Ingrid Brenner was born in Görlitz in 1961. After studying biology in Leipzig, she came to our institute in 1993 and shaped it until the end. Her research on soil ecology received international recognition. Anyone who had worked with her knew that she left no question unanswered. She died on 3 May after a short, serious illness.*

Obituaries often end with a sentence of tribute: *Mit ihr verlieren wir eine herausragende Wissenschaftlerin und einen warmherzigen Menschen.*

## The laudation: honouring someone

A *Laudatio* (plural *die Laudationes* or *Laudationen*) is a speech in praise of someone, given at a *Festakt* (formal ceremony): a prize, an anniversary, a retirement. The key verb is *würdigen* (to honour, to pay tribute to; noun *die Würdigung*): *Mit dem Preis würdigt die Stadt ihr Engagement.* The person's achievements are their *Verdienste*: *Sie hat sich große Verdienste um die Stadt erworben.*

Watch the gender: *das Verdienst* (plural *die Verdienste*) is a merit or achievement; *der Verdienst* (from *verdienen*, A2) is what you earn, income. In a laudation, it is always *das Verdienst*.

A laudation typically:

1. opens with the occasion and a personal note: *Es ist mir eine große Ehre, heute die Laudatio auf Frau Dr. Okafor zu halten.*
2. traces the person's path with concrete examples (Präteritum or Perfekt, depending on how spoken the speech is);
3. names what makes the achievement special: *Was Frau Okafor auszeichnet, ist …* (a pseudo-cleft, lesson 20);
4. ends with a direct address and a wish: *Liebe Frau Okafor, herzlichen Glückwunsch zu dieser verdienten Auszeichnung!*

## Wishes with the Konjunktiv I: Möge …

In elevated wishes German uses the Konjunktiv I, mostly with *mögen* in first position. You know the Konjunktiv I from reported speech (B2); here it expresses a wish, and you will find it in speeches, congratulations and inscriptions.

- *Möge das neue Lebensjahr dir viel Freude bringen!* — May the new year of your life bring you much joy!
- *Mögen Sie noch viele gesunde Jahre im Kreis Ihrer Familie verbringen.*
- *Möge sie in Frieden ruhen.* — May she rest in peace.

A few fixed formulas use the Konjunktiv I without *mögen*: *Gott sei Dank, Es lebe die Freiheit!, Hoch lebe das Brautpaar!*, and on gravestones and in death notices *Er ruhe in Frieden*. (The more familiar *Ruhe in Frieden* is an imperative addressed to the dead person.) In everyday congratulations people simply write *Ich wünsche dir …* or *Alles Gute zum …!*; the *möge* form adds solemnity and suits speeches and cards for big occasions.

## Common mistakes

- *der Verdienst* for merit: ~~Sein großer Verdienst ist …~~ → *Sein großes Verdienst ist …* (but *Der Verdienst in der Branche ist niedrig*: earnings).
- *kondolieren* with the accusative: ~~Wir kondolieren die Familie~~ → *der Familie*.
- Mixing registers: ~~Mit großer Bestürzung haben wir erfahren, dass Ihr Mann abgekratzt ist.~~ (a shocking Stilbruch; lesson 18) → *verstorben ist*.
- False cheer and clichés in condolences (*Kopf hoch!*).
- Using the Perfekt throughout a written obituary: the Präteritum is the norm in written narrative.

## Key points

- Condolence letters: news and reaction (*Mit großer Bestürzung …*), a personal memory, sympathy and an honest offer of help, a closing (*In stiller Anteilnahme*).
- Avoid clichés, false comfort and your own story; restraint is part of the elevated style.
- Death notices and cards name the *Hinterbliebenen* and announce the *Trauerfeier* and *Beisetzung*; *das Ableben* and *entschlafen* belong to this register.
- Obituaries (*Nachrufe*) narrate in the Präteritum and end with a tribute.
- A *Laudatio* at a *Festakt* *würdigt* someone's *Verdienste* (*das Verdienst* = merit).
- Elevated wishes use the Konjunktiv I: *Möge …!*

lessons.title: Wer erbt? Reading legal texts
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Module 4 was about style: idiom, register, word formation, emphasis. Module 5 applies everything you have learned so far to the texts that specialists write for each other and for the public: statutes, central-bank statements, science, social policy and the arts pages. Each lesson takes one kind of specialised text and the grammar it relies on most.

Legal German comes first, because it is the most extreme case. A statute packs a whole "if …, then …" into one sentence, often without a single *wenn*; it defines its own terms in brackets; and it uses words that look familiar (*Abkömmling, Ehegatte, unberührt*) in a narrow technical sense. Once you can read a paragraph of the BGB (*Bürgerliches Gesetzbuch*, the Civil Code), a contract, a court letter or the small print of an insurance policy is much less frightening.

The theme is inheritance and family law: who inherits when there is no will, what a will can and can't change, and the documents that people sign for the case that they can no longer decide for themselves. You met *der Erbe, die Erbin, das Testament* and *der Nachlass* at B1. Everything in this lesson about the law is checked against the current BGB; it explains how the texts work, and it isn't legal advice.

## How a statute is built

### Tatbestand and Rechtsfolge

Almost every legal rule has two halves. The **[[Tatbestand]]** describes a situation: who, what, under which conditions. The **[[Rechtsfolge]]** says what follows legally when the situation applies: a right, a duty, a consequence. In English legal theory the halves are often called "facts" (or "conditions") and "legal consequence".

> *Ist ein Abkömmling des Erblassers durch Verfügung von Todes wegen von der Erbfolge ausgeschlossen,* (Tatbestand) *so kann er von dem Erben den Pflichtteil verlangen.* (Rechtsfolge) — § 2303 Abs. 1 Satz 1 BGB

The skill of reading a statute is to find the two halves, then check each element of the Tatbestand one by one: Is the person an *Abkömmling* (a descendant)? Of the *Erblasser* (the deceased)? Excluded by a *Verfügung von Todes wegen* (a will or an inheritance contract)? Only if every element is there does the Rechtsfolge apply.

### Paragraf, Absatz, Satz, Nummer

German statutes are divided into numbered sections, each marked with the sign §. Lawyers cite them from the large unit to the small:

| citation | read as | meaning |
|---|---|---|
| § 1924 BGB | Paragraf 1924 BGB | section 1924 of the Civil Code |
| § 1924 Abs. 3 BGB | Paragraf 1924, Absatz 3 | subsection 3 |
| § 2303 Abs. 1 Satz 2 BGB | … Absatz 1, Satz 2 | the second sentence of subsection 1 |
| § 16 Abs. 1 Nr. 2 ErbStG | … Nummer 2 | item 2 of a list in subsection 1 |
| §§ 1924 ff. BGB | Paragrafen 1924 folgende | section 1924 and the following ones |
| § 1931 i. V. m. § 1371 BGB | … in Verbindung mit … | section 1931 read together with section 1371 |
| Art. 20 Abs. 1 GG | Artikel 20, Absatz 1 Grundgesetz | the Basic Law (and EU law) has *Artikel*, not §§ |

Duden's main spelling is *der Paragraf* (also *Paragraph*); plural *die Paragrafen*, and a weak noun: *des Paragrafen*. You met *der Absatz* (paragraph of a text) at B1; in a statute it means "subsection".

### Legal definitions in brackets

Statutes define their own vocabulary. The most compact way is a word in brackets right after the thing it names. From then on, the word means exactly that, in the whole law. This is a **[[Legaldefinition]]** (legal definition):

> *Mit dem Tode einer Person (Erbfall) geht deren Vermögen (Erbschaft) als Ganzes auf eine oder mehrere andere Personen (Erben) über.* — § 1922 Abs. 1 BGB

One sentence, three definitions: *der Erbfall* is the death of a person, *die Erbschaft* is the whole of their property, *die Erben* are the people it passes to. Other formulas you will see: *… im Sinne dieses Gesetzes sind …* ("… within the meaning of this Act are …"), *i. S. d.* (*im Sinne des/der*), and *Als … gilt …* (lesson 23).

## Text 1: Five paragraphs of the BGB

Here are the core rules of German inheritance law, quoted word for word from the BGB as published by the Federal Ministry of Justice on gesetze-im-internet.de (checked November 2026; statutes are free to quote under § 5 UrhG). The old dative *-e* (*dem Tode*) and the expression *von Todes wegen* ("by reason of death") are typical of the Code, which dates from 1900.

> **§ 1922 Gesamtrechtsnachfolge**
>
> (1) Mit dem Tode einer Person (Erbfall) geht deren Vermögen (Erbschaft) als Ganzes auf eine oder mehrere andere Personen (Erben) über.
>
> (2) Auf den Anteil eines Miterben (Erbteil) finden die sich auf die Erbschaft beziehenden Vorschriften Anwendung.
>
> **§ 1924 Gesetzliche Erben erster Ordnung**
>
> (1) Gesetzliche Erben der ersten Ordnung sind die Abkömmlinge des Erblassers.
>
> (2) Ein zur Zeit des Erbfalls lebender Abkömmling schließt die durch ihn mit dem Erblasser verwandten Abkömmlinge von der Erbfolge aus.
>
> (3) An die Stelle eines zur Zeit des Erbfalls nicht mehr lebenden Abkömmlings treten die durch ihn mit dem Erblasser verwandten Abkömmlinge (Erbfolge nach Stämmen).
>
> (4) Kinder erben zu gleichen Teilen.
>
> **§ 1931 Abs. 1 Satz 1** (Gesetzliches Erbrecht des Ehegatten)
>
> Der überlebende Ehegatte des Erblassers ist neben Verwandten der ersten Ordnung zu einem Viertel, neben Verwandten der zweiten Ordnung oder neben Großeltern zur Hälfte der Erbschaft als gesetzlicher Erbe berufen.
>
> **§ 1944 Abs. 1** (Ausschlagungsfrist)
>
> Die Ausschlagung kann nur binnen sechs Wochen erfolgen.
>
> **§ 2303 Pflichtteilsberechtigte; Höhe des Pflichtteils**
>
> (1) Ist ein Abkömmling des Erblassers durch Verfügung von Todes wegen von der Erbfolge ausgeschlossen, so kann er von dem Erben den Pflichtteil verlangen. Der Pflichtteil besteht in der Hälfte des Wertes des gesetzlichen Erbteils.
>
> (2) Das gleiche Recht steht den Eltern und dem Ehegatten des Erblassers zu, wenn sie durch Verfügung von Todes wegen von der Erbfolge ausgeschlossen sind. Die Vorschrift des § 1371 bleibt unberührt.

In English (a working translation, not an official one):

> **§ 1922 Universal succession.** (1) On the death of a person (succession), their property (the estate) passes as a whole to one or more other persons (heirs). (2) The provisions on the estate apply to the share of a co-heir (share of the inheritance).
>
> **§ 1924 Statutory heirs of the first order.** (1) Statutory heirs of the first order are the descendants of the deceased. (2) A descendant who is alive at the time of the succession excludes the descendants related to the deceased through him or her. (3) A descendant who is no longer alive at the time of the succession is replaced by the descendants related to the deceased through him or her (succession by lines of descent). (4) Children inherit in equal shares.
>
> **§ 1931(1), first sentence.** The surviving spouse of the deceased is called to inherit as a statutory heir to one quarter of the estate alongside relatives of the first order, and to one half alongside relatives of the second order or alongside grandparents.
>
> **§ 1944(1).** The inheritance can only be disclaimed within six weeks.
>
> **§ 2303 Persons entitled to a compulsory portion; amount.** (1) If a descendant of the deceased is excluded from the succession by a disposition mortis causa, he or she can demand the compulsory portion from the heir. The compulsory portion consists of half the value of the statutory share. (2) The parents and the spouse of the deceased have the same right if they are excluded from the succession by a disposition mortis causa. The provision of § 1371 remains unaffected.

Things to notice:
