- Putting the verb second: ~~…, weshalb die Kosten sind gestiegen.~~ → *weshalb die Kosten gestiegen sind*.
- Mixing up cause and effect: *weshalb* introduces the consequence (*Er war krank, weshalb er fehlte*), *weil* the cause (*Er fehlte, weil er krank war*).
- Starting a sentence with a continuing clause. It always follows what it refers to.
- Still calling the benefit *Bürgergeld*. Since 1 July 2026 it is *das Grundsicherungsgeld*.
- Reading *armutsgefährdet* as "poor". The statistic measures relative income, not deprivation.

## Key points

- A continuing relative clause comments on the whole main clause: *…, was zu Kritik führte*. A relative clause on a noun describes that noun: *die Reform, die …*.
- *was* when no preposition is needed; *wo(r)-* + the verb's preposition otherwise (*wodurch, womit, worüber, woraufhin*); *weshalb / weswegen* for "which is why"; *wobei* for a detail or restriction.
- Always after the main clause, verb at the end, always a comma. Don't chain them.
- *welch-* after prepositions is a formal variant of *der, die, das* (*innerhalb welcher*).
- A political text: Textsorte and Verfasser, Adressat, Intention, sprachliche Mittel (Hochwertwörter, Stigmawörter, *wir*, contrast pairs, selected numbers). Describe them neutrally.
- Since 1 July 2026 the basic benefit for people who can work is *das Grundsicherungsgeld* (*Grundsicherung für Arbeitsuchende*), replacing the *Bürgergeld*.

lessons.title: Der Direktor, ein erfahrener Kurator: museums, heritage and the apposition
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

The last specialised text of this module comes from the arts pages: the **[[Feuilleton]]** of a German newspaper, where exhibitions, books, theatre and architecture are reviewed. Its style is dense in a different way from a statute or a central-bank statement. It names people and things and in the same breath says who or what they are: *Clara Ost, die neue Direktorin*; *das Landesmuseum, ein wuchtiger Bau aus dem Jahr 1890*; *der Kurator Jonas Brehm*. These inserted noun phrases are **[[appositions]]**, and German, unlike English, makes them agree in case with the noun they describe. That is where learners make mistakes even at C1.

This lesson covers loose and close appositions, the case of *als* phrases, and the choice between an apposition, a relative clause and a participial attribute. It ends with the style of the Feuilleton itself.

The theme is museums and cultural heritage: exhibitions, collections, restoration, monument protection, and provenance research, the question of where works of art came from and whether they were taken from their owners.

## Text: an exhibition review

From the arts section of a regional daily (original text, written for this course; the museum, the people and the painting are invented).

> **Wem gehört das Bild?**
>
> *Das Landesmuseum zeigt, was Provenienzforschung leisten kann und wo sie an Grenzen stößt*
>
> Wer das Landesmuseum betritt, einen wuchtigen Bau aus dem Jahr 1890, erwartet Gold, Waffen und Altäre. Die neue Sonderausstellung im Erdgeschoss, die erste unter der Leitung von Clara Ost, kommt dagegen beinahe karg daher: dreißig Exponate, viel Weiß, lange Texte. Und doch gehört sie zu den spannendsten Schauen des Jahres.
>
> Im Mittelpunkt steht eine unscheinbare Frage: Woher stammt ein Kunstwerk, und auf welchem Weg ist es ins Museum gelangt? Jahrzehntelang hat man sie in vielen Häusern lieber nicht gestellt. Erst seit den Washingtoner Prinzipien von 1998 wird von öffentlichen Museen erwartet, ihre Bestände systematisch auf Raubkunst zu überprüfen, also auf Werke, die ihren meist jüdischen Eigentümern in der NS-Zeit entzogen worden waren.
>
> Der Kurator der Schau, der Kunsthistoriker Jonas Brehm, erzählt diese Geschichte an einzelnen Objekten. Da ist etwa die „Bäuerin am Fenster“, ein kleines Ölbild des Leipziger Malers Ernst Haller, das 1941 versteigert wurde und erst 1963 als Schenkung eines Sammlers ins Museum kam. Brehm und sein Team haben die Spur des Bildes über Auktionskataloge, Briefe und Steuerakten zurückverfolgt, bis zu einem Berliner Arzt, dem ersten Eigentümer, der 1939 emigrieren musste. Im vergangenen Jahr wurde das Bild an seine Enkelin zurückgegeben; sie hat es dem Museum als Leihgabe überlassen.
>
> Nicht jede Geschichte endet so eindeutig. Bei vielen Exponaten klaffen Lücken von Jahrzehnten, und die Ausstellung zeigt auch diese Leerstellen: Rahmen ohne Bild, Karteikarten mit Fragezeichen. Darin liegt ihre eigentliche Stärke. Sie präsentiert das Museum nicht als Tempel des Schönen, sondern als Ort, an dem sich Geschichte ablesen lässt, auch unbequeme.
>
> Wer nach dem Rundgang noch Zeit hat, sollte ins Depot hinuntersteigen, das zum ersten Mal mit Führungen zugänglich ist. Dort lagern rund neun Zehntel der Sammlung, denn wie fast jedes Museum zeigt auch dieses in seiner Dauerausstellung nur einen Bruchteil seiner Bestände.

> **Whose picture is it?**
>
> *The state museum shows what provenance research can achieve and where it reaches its limits*
>
> Anyone who enters the state museum, a massive building from 1890, expects gold, weapons and altarpieces. The new special exhibition on the ground floor, the first under Clara Ost's direction, comes across as almost austere by contrast: thirty exhibits, a lot of white, long texts. And yet it is one of the most exciting shows of the year.
>
> At its centre is an inconspicuous question: where does a work of art come from, and how did it get into the museum? For decades, many institutions preferred not to ask it. Only since the Washington Principles of 1998 have public museums been expected to check their holdings systematically for looted art, that is, for works that were taken from their owners, most of them Jewish, during the Nazi period.
>
> The show's curator, the art historian Jonas Brehm, tells this story through individual objects. There is, for example, "Peasant Woman at the Window", a small oil painting by the Leipzig painter Ernst Haller, which was auctioned in 1941 and only came to the museum in 1963 as a gift from a collector. Brehm and his team traced the painting's path through auction catalogues, letters and tax files back to a Berlin doctor, its first owner, who had to emigrate in 1939. Last year the picture was returned to his granddaughter; she has lent it to the museum.
>
> Not every story ends so clearly. For many exhibits there are gaps of decades, and the exhibition shows these blanks too: frames without pictures, index cards with question marks. That is its real strength. It presents the museum not as a temple of beauty but as a place where history can be read, including uncomfortable history.
>
> If you still have time after the tour, go down to the storerooms, which are open to guided tours for the first time. Around nine tenths of the collection are kept there, because like almost every museum, this one shows only a fraction of its holdings in its permanent exhibition.

Find the appositions before you read on. There are five noun phrases that rename the noun before them: *einen wuchtigen Bau …*, *die erste unter der Leitung …*, *der Kunsthistoriker Jonas Brehm*, *ein kleines Ölbild …*, *dem ersten Eigentümer*. Each is in the same case as the noun it follows.

## What an apposition is

An apposition is a noun phrase placed next to another noun phrase that refers to the same person or thing. It adds information without a verb: *Clara Ost, die neue Direktorin* = *Clara Ost, die die neue Direktorin ist*. German distinguishes two kinds.

### Loose apposition: after the noun, with commas, same case

A **[[loose apposition]]** (*lockere Apposition*) follows its noun and is separated by commas (one comma if it ends the sentence). It takes the same case as the noun it refers to:

| case | example |
|---|---|
| nominative | *Clara Ost, die neue Direktorin, eröffnet die Ausstellung.* |
| accusative | *Wir treffen Clara Ost, die neue Direktorin.* / *Wer das Landesmuseum betritt, einen wuchtigen Bau aus dem Jahr 1890, …* |
| dative | *ein Gespräch mit Clara Ost, der neuen Direktorin* / *bis zu einem Berliner Arzt, dem ersten Eigentümer* |
| genitive | *die Fassade des Museums, eines wuchtigen Baus aus dem Jahr 1890* / *die Pläne der Direktorin, einer erfahrenen Kuratorin* |

In speech, and often in careless writing, the apposition slips into the nominative: ~~mit Clara Ost, die neue Direktorin~~; ~~des Museums, ein Bau aus dem Jahr 1890~~. Standard written German keeps the case, and in exam writing the nominative counts as a mistake. Ask: which case is the first noun in? Then put the apposition in that case.

The genitive is the hardest, because the adjective endings are easy to get wrong: *des Museums, eines wuchtigen Baus*; *der Malerin, einer der wichtigsten Expressionistinnen*.

Dates are a special case. After a day of the week with *am*, Duden accepts two forms:

- *am Montag, dem 3. März* (dative, agreeing with *am Montag*)
- *am Montag, den 3. März* (accusative, the form of a date on its own, as in a letterhead)

Both are standard. Without *am* the date is in the accusative or nominative as usual: *Montag, den 3. März* / *Montag, 3. März*.

### Close apposition: no commas, usually before the name

A **[[close apposition]]** (*enge Apposition*) is joined to its noun without commas. The most common type is a title, profession or classifying noun before a name:

- *der Kurator Jonas Brehm, die Restauratorin Lea Kim, der Maler Ernst Haller, Direktorin Ost*
- *die Stadt Leipzig, das Museum Folkwang, der Monat Mai, das Wort „Provenienz“*
- *Karl der Große, Friedrich der Zweite* (an epithet after a name)

How they decline:

- With an article, the noun with the article is declined and the name stays as it is: *die Bilder des Malers Ernst Haller* (not ~~Ernst Hallers~~); *im Museum Folkwang*; *in der Stadt Leipzig*.
- Without an article, only the name takes the genitive *-s*: *Ernst Hallers Bilder*, *Direktorin Osts Pläne* (correct, but *die Pläne von Direktorin Ost* sounds more natural).
- An epithet after a name declines fully: *die Krönung Karls des Großen*, *unter Karl dem Großen*.
- *Herr* always declines: *ein Brief an Herrn Brehm*, *die Ausstellung Herrn Brehms* (rare; *von Herrn Brehm*).

Quantities belong here too: *ein Glas Wein, eine Gruppe Studenten, drei Kisten Bücher*. The second noun stays uninflected (*mit einem Glas Wein*). With an adjective it normally takes the same case as the first noun (*mit einem Glas kühlem Wein*), or, in elevated style, the genitive (*ein Glas kühlen Weines*).

### Recognizing apposition vs list

A comma after a noun can introduce an apposition or the next item of a list. *Wir haben mit der Kuratorin, der Restauratorin und dem Direktor gesprochen*: three people. *Wir haben mit der Kuratorin, einer Expertin für Raubkunst, gesprochen*: one person, described. The test: does the second phrase rename the first? Is there a closing comma before the sentence continues? Then it is an apposition.

## als phrases: in the role of

An *als* phrase says in what role or capacity someone acts or something is seen. Like an apposition, it agrees in case with the noun it refers to:

| refers to | example | case |
|---|---|---|
| the subject | *Als Kuratorin hat sie die Ausstellung konzipiert.* | nominative |
| an accusative object | *Man kennt ihn als großen Sammler.* | accusative |
| a dative | *Ihr als Direktorin fällt die Entscheidung nicht leicht.* | dative (no visible ending without an article) |
| a genitive | *die Rolle des Museums als Lernort* | genitive, usually without an ending |

After a genitive, the *als* phrase normally drops its genitive ending when it has no article or adjective: *die Bedeutung des Museums als Lernort*. With an adjective, both a nominative and a genitive occur: *die Rolle Goethes als bedeutender Sammler* / *als bedeutenden Sammlers*, and many writers avoid the problem by rephrasing: *die Rolle, die Goethe als Sammler spielte*.

Don't confuse *als* (in the role of) with *wie* (like, comparison):

- *Sie arbeitet als Restauratorin.* — She works as a restorer (that's her job).
- *Sie arbeitet wie eine Restauratorin.* — She works like a restorer (she isn't one).

In the text: *als Schenkung eines Sammlers ins Museum kam* (came as a gift), *dem Museum als Leihgabe überlassen* (left it to the museum as a loan), *nicht als Tempel des Schönen, sondern als Ort, …*.

## Apposition, relative clause or participial attribute?

The same information can usually be packed in three ways:

| form | example | effect |
|---|---|---|
| apposition | *Clara Ost, die neue Direktorin, …* | short, neutral; for who or what someone is |
| relative clause | *Clara Ost, die das Museum seit März leitet, …* | for an action or anything with a verb; easiest to read |
| participial attribute (lesson 8) | *die seit März amtierende Direktorin Clara Ost* | densest; typical of news and the Feuilleton |

Choose the apposition for identity (*die neue Direktorin*, *ein Bau aus dem Jahr 1890*), the relative clause when there is a verb, a time or a reason, and the participial attribute when you need to be brief and the attribute is short. Don't stack all three on one noun.

## Feuilleton style

The review shows the typical features of a German arts page:

- Evaluative adjectives that a news report would avoid: *wuchtig* (massive), *karg* (austere), *unscheinbar* (inconspicuous), *spannend*, *unbequem*. The reviewer judges.
- Metaphors and images: *Tempel des Schönen*, *die Spur zurückverfolgen*, *Lücken klaffen* (gaps yawn), *Leerstellen*. *daherkommen* (*kommt … karg daher*) is a favourite Feuilleton verb for how something presents itself.
- Appositions and participles to identify people and works in passing, so the sentences can carry the argument.
- A thesis: the review doesn't just describe; its fourth paragraph says what the exhibition is worth (*Darin liegt ihre eigentliche Stärke*).
- Address to the reader at the end: *Wer … noch Zeit hat, sollte …*.

An exhibition text on the museum wall (*der Wandtext, die Objektbeschriftung*) does the opposite: it describes without judging, in short sentences, with the facts of each object (*Ernst Haller (1871–1938), Bäuerin am Fenster, um 1910, Öl auf Leinwand, Leihgabe aus Privatbesitz*).

## Museums and heritage: the words

- *das Kulturerbe*: cultural heritage; *das Welterbe*: World Heritage (UNESCO's list under the World Heritage Convention of 1972; a single site is *eine Welterbestätte*).
- *der Kurator, die Kuratorin*: curator; *kuratieren*: to curate (*eine Ausstellung kuratieren*). *die Dauerausstellung* (permanent exhibition) and *die Sonderausstellung* (special, temporary exhibition); *das Exponat*: exhibit; *die Leihgabe*: loan (an object lent to a museum); *die Schenkung*: donation, gift; *der Mäzen, die Mäzenin*: patron of the arts (from Maecenas, the patron of Horace and Virgil).
- *die Restaurierung, restaurieren, der Restaurator, die Restauratorin*: restoration and the people who do it. Note the spelling: *Restaurator* has no *n* (not like *das Restaurant*).
- *die Provenienz*: provenance; *die Provenienzforschung*: provenance research. *die Raubkunst*: looted art, especially art taken from Jewish owners under National Socialism; the official term is *NS-verfolgungsbedingt entzogenes Kulturgut*. *die Rückgabe*: return, restitution. In Germany, the federal government, the Länder and the local authorities committed themselves to the Washington Principles in a joint declaration in 1999; the German Lost Art Foundation (*Deutsches Zentrum Kulturgutverluste*), founded in 2015 and based in Magdeburg, supports this research and, since 2019, also research into objects from colonial contexts.
- *der Denkmalschutz*: protection of historic monuments; *denkmalgeschützt*: listed, protected. In Germany it is a matter for the Länder, each with its own law.
- *das Artefakt*: artefact (an object made by people, especially in archaeology). *das Depot*: storeroom (of a museum); also "depository, securities account" at a bank.
- *die Vernissage*: opening of an exhibition (from French); *der Kunsthandel*: the art trade; *die Auktion*, *versteigern*, *die Versteigerung*: auction, to auction, auctioning. *Die Auktion* is the event, *die Versteigerung* the act (they often overlap).
- *der Museumsbesuch*: visit to a museum; *die Museumspädagogik*: museum education (programmes for schools and families); *die Kunstsammlung*: art collection; *das Freilichtmuseum*: open-air museum (historic buildings moved to one site).
- *der Nachlassverwalter*: administrator of an estate (lesson 21: *der Nachlass*); in the art world, the person who manages an artist's estate.

## Pronunciation

- *die Provenienz*: pro-ve-NJENTS; the *-ie-* is one syllable *[jɛ]*.
- *das Exponat*: ek-spo-NAHT; *das Artefakt*: ar-te-FAKT.
- *die Vernissage*: ver-ni-SAH-zhe (French *-age* with a soft *zh*, as in *Garage*).
- *der Mäzen*: mä-TSEHN, stress on the second syllable.
- *der Kurator*: ku-RAH-tor, plural *Kuratoren*: ku-ra-TOH-ren (the stress moves, as in *Doktor – Doktoren*).

## Common mistakes

- Putting a loose apposition in the nominative after another case: ~~mit dem Kurator, ein erfahrener Kunsthistoriker~~ → *mit dem Kurator, einem erfahrenen Kunsthistoriker*.
- Forgetting the closing comma: ~~Clara Ost, die neue Direktorin eröffnet heute.~~ → *Clara Ost, die neue Direktorin, eröffnet heute.*
- Declining the name after an article: ~~die Bilder des Malers Ernst Hallers~~ → *des Malers Ernst Haller*.
- Using commas in a close apposition: ~~der Maler, Ernst Haller, …~~ means "the painter, (namely) Ernst Haller", which is only right if the painter has already been mentioned.
- Confusing *als* and *wie*: ~~Sie arbeitet wie Kuratorin.~~ → *als Kuratorin* (her job).
- Writing *Restaurateur* for a restorer of art: that is a restaurant owner (French loan). The art restorer is *der Restaurator*.

## Key points

- An **[[apposition]]** renames a noun. A **[[loose apposition]]** follows with commas and takes the same case: *mit Frau Ost, der neuen Direktorin*; *des Museums, eines Baus aus dem Jahr 1890*.
- Dates: *am Montag, dem 3. März* and *am Montag, den 3. März* are both standard.
- A **[[close apposition]]** has no commas: *der Maler Ernst Haller*. With an article, the name stays uninflected (*des Malers Ernst Haller*); without one, the name takes *-s* (*Ernst Hallers*); epithets decline (*Karls des Großen*).
- *als* phrases agree with the noun they refer to (*Man kennt ihn als großen Sammler*); after a genitive they usually stay without an ending (*des Museums als Lernort*). *als* = role, *wie* = comparison.
- Apposition for identity, relative clause for actions, participial attribute for brevity.
- The **[[Feuilleton]]** judges: evaluative adjectives, metaphors, a thesis, address to the reader. The museum wall text describes.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete the lesson.

lessons.title: Ihre Daten: reading a privacy notice
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Every German website, app, doctor's surgery and employer gives you a *Datenschutzerklärung* (privacy notice), and most people scroll past it. It is worth reading at least once, because it is a perfect small specimen of everything module 5 has practised: legal conditions (lesson 21), formal prepositions (lesson 22), definitions (lesson 23) and dense nominal style, all in a text addressed to ordinary people.

This honors lesson reads the key articles of the EU's General Data Protection Regulation in German, takes a model privacy notice apart, and ends with a short letter that you can actually use: a request to a company to tell you what data it holds about you.

## The DSGVO in brief

The General Data Protection Regulation is called *Datenschutz-Grundverordnung* in German, abbreviated DSGVO (also written *DS-GVO*). It is Regulation (EU) 2016/679 and has applied since 25 May 2018. As an EU *Verordnung* (regulation) it applies directly in every member state; in Germany the *Bundesdatenschutzgesetz* (BDSG) supplements it. It is cited like a German statute but with articles: *Art. 6 Abs. 1 lit. a DSGVO*. *lit.* is Latin *litera* (letter) and refers to the lettered items in a list; the official German text itself says *Buchstabe a*.

The quotations below are from the German version as published in the Official Journal of the EU (ABl. L 119 of 4 May 2016; EU legislation may be reproduced with the source). As of November 2026, the EU is negotiating a "digital omnibus" package that would change some details (the Commission's proposal also redefined personal data, which the Council's position of October 2026 leaves unchanged); it has not been adopted.

### Five provisions

> **Art. 4 Nr. 1** „personenbezogene Daten“ alle Informationen, die sich auf eine identifizierte oder identifizierbare natürliche Person (im Folgenden „betroffene Person“) beziehen; …
>
> **Art. 6 Abs. 1** Die Verarbeitung ist nur rechtmäßig, wenn mindestens eine der nachstehenden Bedingungen erfüllt ist: a) Die betroffene Person hat ihre Einwilligung zu der Verarbeitung der sie betreffenden personenbezogenen Daten für einen oder mehrere bestimmte Zwecke gegeben; …
>
> **Art. 7 Abs. 3** Die betroffene Person hat das Recht, ihre Einwilligung jederzeit zu widerrufen. […] Der Widerruf der Einwilligung muss so einfach wie die Erteilung der Einwilligung sein.
>
> **Art. 15 Abs. 1** Die betroffene Person hat das Recht, von dem Verantwortlichen eine Bestätigung darüber zu verlangen, ob sie betreffende personenbezogene Daten verarbeitet werden; …
>
> **Art. 33 Abs. 1** (on a data breach, the controller must notify the supervisory authority) … unverzüglich und möglichst binnen 72 Stunden, nachdem ihm die Verletzung bekannt wurde, …

> **Art. 4(1)** "personal data" means any information relating to an identified or identifiable natural person ("data subject"); …
>
> **Art. 6(1)** Processing shall be lawful only if and to the extent that at least one of the following applies: (a) the data subject has given consent to the processing of his or her personal data for one or more specific purposes; …
>
> **Art. 7(3)** The data subject shall have the right to withdraw his or her consent at any time. […] It shall be as easy to withdraw as to give consent.
>
> **Art. 15(1)** The data subject shall have the right to obtain from the controller confirmation as to whether or not personal data concerning him or her are being processed; …
>
> **Art. 33(1)** … without undue delay and, where feasible, not later than 72 hours after having become aware of it, …

(The English is the official English version of the same articles, slightly shortened where the German is.)

Notes on the language:

- Art. 4 is a list of legal definitions (lesson 21), but in a different format from the BGB: the term in quotation marks, then the definition with no verb (*„personenbezogene Daten“ alle Informationen, die …*). Read an implicit *sind* after the term. Inside the definition is a second, bracketed one: *(im Folgenden „betroffene Person“)*, "hereinafter 'data subject'".
- *die sie betreffenden personenbezogenen Daten* is a participial attribute: the data *die sie betreffen*, "which concern her". *sie* is the *betroffene Person*. Compare Art. 15: *ob sie betreffende personenbezogene Daten verarbeitet werden* (whether data concerning her are processed), the same attribute without an article.
- German generalizes with the feminine: *die betroffene Person … ihre Einwilligung*. The pronoun follows the grammatical gender of *Person*, so the German text never needs "his or her".
- *der Verantwortliche* (the controller) is an adjectival noun, declined like an adjective: *von dem Verantwortlichen, ein Verantwortlicher*. It is the person or organization that decides why and how data are processed.
- *binnen 72 Stunden* is the formal *binnen* of lesson 22; *unverzüglich* means "without undue delay" (in German law: *ohne schuldhaftes Zögern*).

## Text: a model privacy notice

A short, invented privacy notice for an online bookshop (original text, written for this course; the company doesn't exist). Real ones are longer, but they are built from the same blocks.

> **Datenschutzerklärung der Lesefuchs GmbH** (Auszug)
>
> **1. Verantwortlicher**
> Verantwortlicher im Sinne der DSGVO ist die Lesefuchs GmbH, Am Markt 4, 99999 Musterstadt. Unseren Datenschutzbeauftragten erreichen Sie unter datenschutz@lesefuchs.example.
>
> **2. Zwecke und Rechtsgrundlagen der Verarbeitung**
> Wir verarbeiten Ihre personenbezogenen Daten (Name, Anschrift, E-Mail-Adresse, Zahlungsdaten) zum Zweck der Abwicklung Ihrer Bestellung auf Grundlage von Art. 6 Abs. 1 lit. b DSGVO. Die Angabe dieser Daten ist für den Vertragsschluss erforderlich; ohne sie können wir Ihre Bestellung nicht ausführen.
> Sofern Sie in den Empfang unseres Newsletters eingewilligt haben, verarbeiten wir Ihre E-Mail-Adresse auf Grundlage Ihrer Einwilligung (Art. 6 Abs. 1 lit. a DSGVO). Die Einwilligung ist freiwillig und kann jederzeit mit Wirkung für die Zukunft widerrufen werden, etwa über den Abmeldelink am Ende jedes Newsletters.
>
> **3. Weitergabe an Dritte**
> Eine Weitergabe Ihrer Daten an Dritte erfolgt nur, soweit dies zur Vertragserfüllung erforderlich ist, insbesondere an das mit der Lieferung beauftragte Versandunternehmen.
>
> **4. Speicherdauer**
> Ihre Daten werden gelöscht, sobald sie für den jeweiligen Zweck nicht mehr erforderlich sind, es sei denn, gesetzliche Aufbewahrungsfristen stehen der Löschung entgegen.
>
> **5. Ihre Rechte**
> Sie haben das Recht auf Auskunft, Berichtigung, Löschung und Einschränkung der Verarbeitung sowie auf Datenübertragbarkeit. Darüber hinaus steht Ihnen ein Beschwerderecht bei einer Datenschutzbehörde zu.

> **Privacy notice of Lesefuchs GmbH** (extract)
>
> **1. Controller.** The controller within the meaning of the GDPR is Lesefuchs GmbH, Am Markt 4, 99999 Musterstadt. You can reach our data protection officer at datenschutz@lesefuchs.example.
>
> **2. Purposes and legal bases of processing.** We process your personal data (name, address, e-mail address, payment details) for the purpose of handling your order on the basis of Art. 6(1)(b) GDPR. Providing these data is necessary to conclude the contract; without them we can't carry out your order. If you have consented to receiving our newsletter, we process your e-mail address on the basis of your consent (Art. 6(1)(a) GDPR). Consent is voluntary and can be withdrawn at any time with effect for the future, for example via the unsubscribe link at the end of every newsletter.
>
> **3. Disclosure to third parties.** Your data are only passed on to third parties to the extent that this is necessary to perform the contract, in particular to the delivery company commissioned with the delivery.
>
> **4. Storage period.** Your data are deleted as soon as they are no longer needed for the purpose in question, unless statutory retention periods prevent deletion.
>
> **5. Your rights.** You have the right of access, rectification, erasure and restriction of processing, and to data portability. You also have the right to lodge a complaint with a data protection authority.

## How the notice is built

### Nominal style with an empty verb

Many sentences put the action into a noun and use a "light" verb: *Eine Weitergabe … erfolgt nur, soweit …* (= *Wir geben Daten nur weiter, soweit …*); *Die Angabe dieser Daten ist … erforderlich* (= *Sie müssen diese Daten angeben*). *erfolgen* is the typical empty verb of administrative German (lesson 7 on FVG); it has no meaning of its own beyond "take place".

### Purpose and basis

- *zum Zweck der* + genitive (*zum Zweck der Abwicklung*), more formally *zu Zwecken der*, shortest *zwecks* (B2): purpose.
- *auf Grundlage von* + dative / *auf (der) Grundlage* + genitive (*auf Grundlage Ihrer Einwilligung*); also *gestützt auf*, *nach Maßgabe von*: legal basis.
- *mit Wirkung für die Zukunft*: "with effect for the future", the standard formula for a revocation that doesn't undo what happened before (as Art. 7 Abs. 3 says: processing until then stays lawful).

### Conditions and limits

*Sofern Sie … eingewilligt haben* (a yes/no condition), *soweit dies … erforderlich ist* (to the extent necessary), *es sei denn, gesetzliche Aufbewahrungsfristen stehen der Löschung entgegen* (an exception): the trio from lesson 21, used exactly as in a statute.

### Rights as nouns

Section 5 lists the data subject's rights as nouns with *auf*: *das Recht auf Auskunft, Berichtigung, Löschung …*. One *auf* governs the whole list. *Ihnen steht … zu* (lesson 21) = "you are entitled to".

### sein + zu and its alternatives

Privacy notices also use the passive substitutes of lesson 9: *Die Einwilligung ist jederzeit widerrufbar* (-bar), *kann … widerrufen werden* (modal passive), *Der Widerruf ist an … zu richten* (sein + zu). They say the same thing; *-bar* is the shortest.

## Writing an Auskunftsersuchen

Under Art. 15 DSGVO you can ask any company or authority whether it processes data about you, and if so, which data, for what purposes, to whom it has passed them on and how long it will keep them. The answer has to come without undue delay and in any case within a month of receiving the request (Art. 12 Abs. 3), with a possible extension in complex cases; the first copy of the data is free. A request doesn't need a reason and doesn't need a lawyer. A model (original):

> **Betreff: Auskunftsersuchen nach Art. 15 DSGVO**
>
> Sehr geehrte Damen und Herren,
>
> hiermit bitte ich Sie um Auskunft darüber, ob Sie personenbezogene Daten über mich verarbeiten. Sollte dies der Fall sein, bitte ich um eine Kopie dieser Daten sowie um Angaben zu den Verarbeitungszwecken, zu etwaigen Empfängern und zur geplanten Speicherdauer. Bitte teilen Sie mir außerdem mit, woher die Daten stammen, sofern Sie sie nicht bei mir selbst erhoben haben.
>
> Zur Identifizierung gebe ich meine Kundennummer 4711-23 an. Ich bitte um Antwort binnen eines Monats, wie in Art. 12 Abs. 3 DSGVO vorgesehen.
>
> Mit freundlichen Grüßen
> Mira Kowalski

What makes it work: the subject line cites the article; *hiermit bitte ich Sie um* + accusative is the standard opening of a formal request; *Sollte dies der Fall sein* is the verb-first *sollte* condition of lesson 22; *etwaig* (any, possible) is a typical official adjective (*etwaige Empfänger* = any recipients there may be); and *binnen eines Monats* shows *binnen* with the genitive, which suits the formal register of the letter (*binnen einem Monat* would also be correct).

## The words: data protection

- *personenbezogen*: personal, relating to a person (*personenbezogene Daten*). *die Verarbeitung*: processing (in the DSGVO it covers everything: collecting, storing, using, passing on, deleting). *der Verantwortliche*: controller (adjectival noun; *die Verantwortliche* for a woman; as an organization, always *der Verantwortliche* in the legal sense). You know the adjective *verantwortlich* (responsible) from B1.
- *die Einwilligung*: consent; *einwilligen in* + accusative: to consent to (separable: *willigt ein, hat eingewilligt*). Everyday German says *zustimmen*; *einwilligen* is the legal and medical term (*in eine Operation einwilligen*).
- *widerrufen*: to revoke, withdraw (inseparable and strong: *widerruft, widerrief, hat widerrufen*); *der Widerruf*: revocation. Also used for withdrawing from a contract (*das Widerrufsrecht*, the right to cancel an online purchase).
- *das Auskunftsrecht*: right of access; *die Löschung*: deletion, erasure; *die Speicherdauer*: storage period; *die Weitergabe*: passing on, disclosure.
- *der/die Datenschutzbeauftragte*: data protection officer (adjectival noun: *ein Datenschutzbeauftragter*). *die Datenschutzbehörde*: data protection authority; in Germany each Land has its own, plus the federal commissioner, so the word is often in the plural.
- *die Datenpanne*: data breach (informal but common in the press; the legal term is *die Verletzung des Schutzes personenbezogener Daten*). *die Datenschutzerklärung*: privacy notice.

## Key points

- The DSGVO (Regulation (EU) 2016/679, applies since 25 May 2018) is cited by article: *Art. 6 Abs. 1 lit. a DSGVO*.
- Its definitions put the term in quotation marks with no verb: *„personenbezogene Daten“ alle Informationen, die …*.
- Privacy notices use nominal style with *erfolgen*, purpose phrases (*zum Zweck der, auf Grundlage von*), the legal trio *sofern / soweit / es sei denn*, and rights as *das Recht auf* + nouns.
- Consent can be withdrawn at any time (*jederzeit widerrufen*), with effect for the future.
- An *Auskunftsersuchen* under Art. 15 needs no reason; the answer is due within a month (Art. 12 Abs. 3).

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete the lesson.

lessons.title: Doppelblind und randomisiert: reading about clinical trials
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

"New drug halves the risk!" Headlines like this appear every week, and German has its own versions: *Neues Medikament halbiert das Risiko*, *Durchbruch in der Krebsforschung*. Behind them is usually a study whose authors wrote something much more careful. This honors lesson compares the two kinds of text: the press release that announces a result and the study abstract that reports it. You'll learn the vocabulary of clinical research, the cautious verbs with which scientists state findings, and the difference between relative and absolute risk, which is where most misleading headlines come from.

It builds on lesson 23 (science writing), lesson 4 (Konjunktiv I in academic reports) and B2's numbers and percentages.

## How a clinical trial works

Before a new medicine is approved, it is tested on people in several phases (*Studienphasen*). The scheme below is the usual one; the details vary:

| phase | who takes part | main question |
|---|---|---|
| Phase I | a small number of mostly healthy volunteers | Is it safe? How does the body handle it? |
| Phase II | a few hundred patients | Does it work, and at what dose? |
| Phase III | often thousands of patients | Does it work better than a placebo or the standard treatment? What are the side effects? |
| Phase IV | patients after approval | rare side effects and long-term use |

A trial in the EU needs the approval of the competent authority and a positive opinion from an independent *Ethikkommission* (ethics committee); since 31 January 2022 the EU Clinical Trials Regulation (Regulation (EU) No 536/2014) has applied. Participants (*Probandinnen und Probanden*) give their informed consent and can withdraw at any time.

Three words describe a good design:

- randomisiert: chance decides who gets the new treatment and who is in the *Kontrollgruppe* (control group), so that the groups are comparable.
- doppelblind: neither the participants nor the doctors know who gets what, so expectations can't distort the results. (*einfach verblindet*: only the participants don't know.)
- placebokontrolliert: the control group gets a dummy (*das Placebo*, lesson 9).

The *Endpunkt* (endpoint) is what the trial measures to decide whether the treatment works: a *primärer Endpunkt* is fixed in advance (for example, strokes within two years), *sekundäre Endpunkte* are further outcomes. *Die Fallzahl* is the number of participants, which has to be large enough for a result to be *aussagekräftig* (meaningful); *die Abbruchquote* is the share of participants who drop out.

## Two texts about one study

Both texts are invented for this course (the substance, the institute and the figures don't exist), but they are modelled on how such texts are typically written.

### Text 1: the press release

> **Neuer Wirkstoff senkt Schlaganfallrisiko um ein Drittel**
>
> Ein am Institut für Herz-Kreislauf-Forschung entwickelter Wirkstoff könnte die Vorbeugung von Schlaganfällen grundlegend verändern. In einer großen Studie mit 4.000 Teilnehmenden senkte die Substanz KR-27 das Risiko eines Schlaganfalls um 33 Prozent. „Diese Ergebnisse sind ein Meilenstein“, sagte Studienleiterin Prof. Dr. Hanna Sommer. Für Millionen Patientinnen und Patienten mit Vorhofflimmern eröffne sich damit eine neue Perspektive. Die Zulassung soll im kommenden Jahr beantragt werden.

> **New substance cuts the risk of stroke by a third**
>
> A substance developed at the Institute for Cardiovascular Research could fundamentally change stroke prevention. In a large study with 4,000 participants, the substance KR-27 reduced the risk of a stroke by 33 percent. "These results are a milestone," said the head of the study, Prof. Hanna Sommer. For millions of patients with atrial fibrillation, she said, this opens up a new prospect. Approval is to be applied for next year.

### Text 2: the abstract

> **Wirksamkeit und Verträglichkeit von KR-27 bei Vorhofflimmern: eine randomisierte, doppelblinde, placebokontrollierte Studie der Phase III**
>
> **Methoden:** 4.000 Patientinnen und Patienten mit Vorhofflimmern wurden randomisiert und erhielten über zwei Jahre entweder KR-27 oder ein Placebo (je n = 2.000). Primärer Endpunkt war das Auftreten eines Schlaganfalls innerhalb von 24 Monaten.
>
> **Ergebnisse:** Ein Schlaganfall trat in der KR-27-Gruppe bei 40 Teilnehmenden (2,0 %) auf, in der Placebogruppe bei 60 (3,0 %). Dies entspricht einer relativen Risikoreduktion von 33 % und einer absoluten Risikoreduktion von 1,0 Prozentpunkten. Bei den sekundären Endpunkten (Gesamtsterblichkeit, Herzinfarkt) ließ sich kein signifikanter Unterschied nachweisen. 12 % der Teilnehmenden in der KR-27-Gruppe brachen die Studie vorzeitig ab, vorwiegend wegen Magen-Darm-Beschwerden, gegenüber 7 % in der Placebogruppe.
>
> **Schlussfolgerung:** Die Ergebnisse deuten darauf hin, dass KR-27 das Schlaganfallrisiko bei Vorhofflimmern senken kann. Angesichts der erhöhten Abbruchquote sind weitere Studien zur Langzeitverträglichkeit erforderlich.

> **Efficacy and tolerability of KR-27 in atrial fibrillation: a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase III trial**
>
> **Methods:** 4,000 patients with atrial fibrillation were randomized and received either KR-27 or a placebo for two years (n = 2,000 each). The primary endpoint was the occurrence of a stroke within 24 months.
>
> **Results:** A stroke occurred in 40 participants (2.0%) in the KR-27 group and in 60 (3.0%) in the placebo group. This corresponds to a relative risk reduction of 33% and an absolute risk reduction of 1.0 percentage point. No significant difference could be shown for the secondary endpoints (all-cause mortality, heart attack). 12% of participants in the KR-27 group discontinued the study early, mainly because of gastrointestinal complaints, compared with 7% in the placebo group.
>
> **Conclusion:** The results suggest that KR-27 can reduce the risk of stroke in atrial fibrillation. In view of the higher dropout rate, further studies on long-term tolerability are needed.

## Relative and absolute risk

Both texts are "true". The difference is in what they choose to say:

- **[[Absolute risk]]**: the share of people in a group to whom something happens. Here 3.0 % without the drug, 2.0 % with it.
- **[[Absolute risk reduction]]**: the difference, 3.0 − 2.0 = 1.0 *Prozentpunkt* (B2: percentage points, not percent).
- **[[Relative risk reduction]]**: the difference as a share of the original risk, 1.0 ÷ 3.0 ≈ 33 *Prozent*. This is the "one third" of the headline.

A relative figure sounds much bigger, which is why press releases prefer it. A useful third number is the *Number needed to treat* (NNT; German texts mostly use the English term): how many people must take the drug for one of them to benefit. Here: 1 ÷ 0.01 = 100 people for two years to prevent one stroke. None of the three numbers is wrong; a fair text gives the absolute figures too.

| how a text can say it | what it means |
|---|---|
| *senkt das Risiko um ein Drittel* | relative: from 3 % to 2 % |
| *senkt das Risiko um einen Prozentpunkt* | absolute: from 3 % to 2 % |
| *senkt das Risiko auf 2 Prozent* | the new absolute risk |
| *Von 100 Behandelten bleibt einem ein Schlaganfall erspart.* | NNT 100 |

Note the prepositions: *um* gives the size of the change, *auf* the new value, *von … auf* the change from one value to another (*von 3 auf 2 Prozent*).

## Stating findings cautiously

A scientific conclusion is only as strong as its data, and German academic writing has a graded set of verbs and phrases for this, from weak to strong:

| strength | phrases | example |
|---|---|---|
| a hint | *deuten darauf hin, dass …*; *weisen auf … hin* | *Die Ergebnisse deuten darauf hin, dass KR-27 wirkt.* |
| a reasonable conclusion | *legen nahe, dass …* (*nahelegen*, separable); *sprechen dafür, dass …* | *Die Daten legen nahe, dass die Dosis zu hoch war.* |
| a demonstration | *belegen, zeigen, bestätigen* | *Die Studie zeigt, dass …* |
| no effect found | *ließ sich nicht nachweisen*; *fand sich kein Hinweis auf* | *Ein Einfluss auf die Sterblichkeit ließ sich nicht nachweisen.* |

*Es ließ sich kein Unterschied nachweisen* is not the same as *Es gibt keinen Unterschied*: a study can fail to show an effect that exists (for example because the *Fallzahl* was too small). Watch for the difference when you summarize.

Other hedges: *möglicherweise, vermutlich, offenbar*; the subjective modal *dürfte* (lesson 2); *Die Ergebnisse sind mit Vorsicht zu interpretieren*; *Weitere Studien sind erforderlich.*

### Konjunktiv I for others' claims

When you report what someone else claims, the Konjunktiv I (lesson 4) keeps the distance: *Die Studienleiterin sagte, für Millionen Patienten eröffne sich eine neue Perspektive* (as in Text 1). In a critical article you might write: *Das Mittel senke das Risiko um ein Drittel, heißt es in der Pressemitteilung. Absolut betrachtet sinkt es allerdings nur um einen Prozentpunkt.* The Konjunktiv I marks the press release's claim; the indicative in the second sentence is the journalist's own statement of fact.

## Press release and abstract compared

| | press release | abstract |
|---|---|---|
| figures | relative (*um ein Drittel*) | absolute and relative |
| side effects | not mentioned | dropout rate and its cause |
| secondary endpoints | not mentioned | no significant difference |
| verbs | *senkte*, *könnte … grundlegend verändern* | *deuten darauf hin*, *ließ sich nicht nachweisen* |
| quotation | *ein Meilenstein* | none |
| aim | attention | information |

The press release isn't false, but it selects: it reports the most impressive number and leaves out the rest. When you read about a study, look for the absolute figures, the control group, the size of the trial and whether the authors themselves speak of *Hinweisen* or *Belegen*.

## The words: clinical research

- *doppelblind*, *randomisiert* (from *randomisieren*, to randomize): adjectives of study design; *das Studiendesign*: study design.
- *die Kontrollgruppe*: control group; *der Proband, die Probandin*: participant, test subject (a weak noun: *des Probanden*). *die Versuchsperson* (B2) is the general word in experiments; *Proband* is usual in medicine.
- *die Studienphase*: phase of a trial; *die Wirksamkeitsstudie*: efficacy study; *der Endpunkt*: endpoint.
- *die Fallzahl*: number of cases, sample size; *die Abbruchquote*: dropout rate.
- *die Ethikkommission*: ethics committee.
- *das Risiko senken*: to reduce the risk (also *verringern*; the opposite is *erhöhen*). *Risiko* has two plurals, *die Risiken* (usual) and *die Risikos*.
- *die Aussagekraft*: significance, informative value (*Die Studie hat wenig Aussagekraft* = it doesn't tell us much); *aussagekräftig*: meaningful, conclusive.

## Key points

- Phases I–IV; good trials are *randomisiert*, *doppelblind* and often *placebokontrolliert*, with a *primärer Endpunkt* fixed in advance; they need an *Ethikkommission*.
- Relative risk reduction (*um ein Drittel*) sounds bigger than absolute risk reduction (*um einen Prozentpunkt*); NNT says how many must be treated for one to benefit.
- *um* = by (size of the change), *auf* = to (new value), *von … auf* = from … to.
- Cautious verbs, weak to strong: *deuten darauf hin – legen nahe – belegen*; *ließ sich nicht nachweisen* ≠ "there is no effect".
- Report others' claims in the Konjunktiv I; state your own facts in the indicative.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete the lesson.

lessons.title: Brötchen, Semmel, Schrippe: regional German in Germany
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

The last module of the course looks outward and forward: at the German you will meet outside textbooks (this lesson), at literature (27 and the honors lessons), at speaking and mediation at C1 (28, 29), and at the exam (30).

At B2 you learned that German is a pluricentric language, with standard varieties in Germany, Austria and Switzerland. This lesson stays inside Germany, and that is where many learners get their first shock. You can follow the news on Deutschlandfunk without trouble, then you buy bread in Berlin and are told *Dit is ne Schrippe*, or a colleague from Stuttgart says she is going to *schwätzen* with the neighbours. Nobody is speaking "bad German". You are hearing regional German, and at C1 you are expected to understand it in everyday situations, even if you never use it yourself.

You will learn:

- how standard German, everyday speech, regional speech and dialect relate to each other;
- the three big dialect areas of Germany and what separates them;
- the most common regional words for food, people and time, with the region each belongs to;
- regional grammar you should recognize (but not copy): *tun* + infinitive, *am* + infinitive, *dem Vater sein Auto*, the missing Präteritum in the south, *der Peter*, and tags such as *gell* and *wa*;
- what to imitate and what only to recognize.

## From dialect to standard: a continuum

German speakers don't switch between two clear-cut codes, "dialect" and "standard". They move along a scale, and most people use several points on it in a single day.

| level | German term | what it is | example (Swabia) |
|---|---|---|---|
| dialect | *der Dialekt, die Mundart* | the traditional local speech, with its own sounds, words and grammar; often hard to follow for outsiders | *I gang jetzt hoim.* |
| regional speech | *der Regiolekt*, *die Regionalsprache* | everyday speech of a larger region: close to the standard, but with regional sounds, words and some grammar | *Ich geh jetzt heim.* |
| colloquial standard | *die Umgangssprache* | relaxed spoken German heard everywhere (*ich hab, haste, 'n bisschen*) | *Ich geh jetzt nach Hause.* |
| standard | *die Standardsprache, das Hochdeutsch* | the written norm and the language of news, schools and offices | *Ich gehe jetzt nach Hause.* |

All four mean "I'm going home now". You learned *der Dialekt* and *die Mundart* at B1. The adjective is *mundartlich*: *mundartliche Ausdrücke*, expressions from a dialect. A **[[Regiolekt]]** sits between dialect and standard. It is what you will hear most often in practice: a doctor in Munich, a teacher in Hamburg and a shop assistant in Leipzig all speak standard German, but each with a regional colouring.

Two notes on terms. *Hochdeutsch* has two meanings: "standard German" in everyday speech, and, among linguists, "the dialects of the higher, southern part of the country" as opposed to Low German. And *Umgangssprache* in German grammar books means colloquial speech in general, not a particular region.

Over the last hundred years the traditional dialects have lost speakers (*Dialektsprecher* and *Dialektsprecherinnen*) almost everywhere, fastest in the north and slowest in the south, where many families still speak Bavarian, Swabian or Alemannic at home. Regional speech has not disappeared with them: its words and sounds live on in the Regiolekte.

## The three big dialect areas

Linguists divide the German dialects of Germany into three belts from north to south.

| area | German term | where | typical feature |
|---|---|---|---|
| Low German | *Niederdeutsch*, *Plattdeutsch* | the northern lowlands: Schleswig-Holstein, Hamburg, Bremen, Lower Saxony, Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, Westphalia, northern Saxony-Anhalt and Brandenburg | old consonants kept: *maken, Water, Appel, dat, ik* |
| Central German | *Mitteldeutsch* | a band across the middle: most of the Rhineland, Hesse, Thuringia, Saxony | some consonants shifted, some not: Cologne *dat, wat* but *machen* |
| Upper German | *Oberdeutsch* | the south: Bavaria, Baden-Württemberg (and Austria, Switzerland) | consonants fully shifted: *machen, Wasser, Apfel, das, ich* |

The line between Low and Central German is called the Benrath line, after a district of Düsseldorf where it crosses the Rhine: north of it people traditionally said *maken*, south of it *machen*. You will learn the history behind these sound changes in the honors lesson on the history of German (92). For now it is enough to know that the standard language took its consonants from the south (*machen, Wasser*), while its pronunciation is often said to be closest to the speech of the north.

The adjectives are *niederdeutsch* and *oberdeutsch*: *ein niederdeutsches Wort, die oberdeutschen Mundarten*. **[[Plattdeutsch]]** (also simply *Platt*) is the everyday name for Low German. Low German is protected in Germany as a regional language under the European Charter for Regional or Minority Languages; there is radio and theatre in Platt, and a living *Mundartdichtung* (dialect poetry and prose). In the west, *Platt* is also used loosely for local dialects that are not Low German at all, such as the dialects of the Moselle region.

## Regional words

Regional words are the part of regional German you will meet most often, because they survive even in people who no longer speak dialect. The best-known example is the bread roll.

| standard or general | region | regional word |
|---|---|---|
| *das Brötchen* | Berlin, Brandenburg | *die Schrippe* |
| | Bavaria, Austria (and parts of Saxony) | *die Semmel* (you met it at A1) |
| | Swabia, Baden, Franconia, Hesse, the Palatinate | *der Weck* (Swabian *das Weckle*) |
| | Hamburg | *das Rundstück* |
| *der Samstag* | north and east | *der Sonnabend* |
| *der Metzger* (south, west) | east (and the trade's official name) | *der Fleischer* |
| | north | *der Schlachter* |
| *die Frikadelle* (west, north) | Berlin | *die Bulette* |
| *der Rotkohl* (north) | south, Austria | *das Blaukraut* |
| *die Möhre*, *die Karotte* | north, east | *die Mohrrübe* |
| | south | *die gelbe Rübe* |
| *der Berliner* (doughnut) | Bavaria, Austria | *der Krapfen* |
| *die Sahne* | south, Austria, Switzerland | *der Rahm* |
| *der Kloß* | south, Austria | *der Knödel* |
| *der Junge* | south | *der Bub* |
| *das Mädchen* | south, east (colloquial) | *das Mädel* |
| *dieses Jahr* | south, Austria, Switzerland | *heuer* |
| *das Butterbrot* | Berlin, the north-east | *die Stulle* |
| *das Endstück des Brotes* | north | *der Knust* |
| *der Imbiss*, *die Zwischenmahlzeit* | Bavaria | *die Brotzeit* |
| | Swabia, Baden | *das Vesper* |
| *reden, sich unterhalten* | Swabia, the south-west | *schwätzen* |
| *schauen* (south) | north, centre (colloquial) | *gucken* |

Some of these words are completely standard in their region and belong to the regional standard: a Bavarian newspaper writes *Semmel* and *heuer* without quotation marks, and a Berlin bakery sells *Schrippen*. Others are colloquial everywhere (*gucken, Mädel*). Some notes:

- *der Berliner* is a doughnut almost everywhere except in Berlin and much of eastern Germany, where it is called *der Pfannkuchen*; elsewhere a *Pfannkuchen* is a pancake. This is a famous trap.
- *der Fleischer* is the official name of the trade in Germany (*das Fleischerhandwerk*), even though *Metzger* is more common in the south and west.
- *das Vesper* (neuter) is a snack or light meal in Swabia; *die Vesper* (feminine) is the evening service in church.
- *der Weck* is also used for the whole bread roll family in the south-west (*Weckle, Wecken*). In Bavaria a *Brotzeit* can be anything from a sandwich to a plate of sausage, cheese and radish.
- *schwätzen* is the standard verb *schwatzen* with an umlaut. In Swabia it is just the normal word for "to talk": *Mir schwätzet Schwäbisch.* Elsewhere *schwatzen* or *quatschen* means "to chatter".

There is no need to learn all the regions by heart. What helps is a sense of north versus south: *Sonnabend, Schlachter, Knust, gucken* point north; *heuer, Bub, Knödel, Rahm, Brotzeit* point south.

## Telling the time the regional way

Clock times are a famous regional difference, and a practical one, because you may miss an appointment.

| time | understood everywhere | the east, parts of the south, Austria |
|---|---|---|
| 2:15 | *Viertel nach zwei* | *viertel drei* |
| 2:30 | *halb drei* | *halb drei* |
| 2:45 | *Viertel vor drei* | *drei viertel drei* |

*viertel drei* means "a quarter of the way to three", not "a quarter to three". If a colleague from Dresden or Würzburg says *Wir treffen uns um viertel drei*, be there at 2:15. *halb drei* means 2:30 everywhere.

## Regional grammar: recognize, don't copy

Regional German also has grammar of its own. You should recognize these patterns when you hear them, and know that they don't belong in formal writing.

### tun + infinitive

In many regions, especially the south and the west, *tun* is used as an auxiliary with an infinitive (the **[[tun-periphrasis]]**):

- *Ich tu grad kochen.* — I'm cooking right now. (standard: *Ich koche gerade.*)
- *Tust du das Fenster aufmachen?* — Will you open the window?

The only use that is widely accepted beyond casual speech is with the infinitive fronted for emphasis: *Kochen tut er gern, aber abwaschen nicht.* (He likes cooking, but not washing up.) Otherwise school grammar and editors mark it as colloquial or regional.

### am + infinitive: the progressive

*Ich bin am Arbeiten* (I'm working, I'm in the middle of work) is called the **[[am-progressive]]**, or in German *die rheinische Verlaufsform*, because it was first typical of the Rhineland and the Ruhr. It has spread across the country, and it is now normal in relaxed spoken German almost everywhere:

- *Sie ist gerade am Telefonieren.* — She's on the phone right now.
- *Wir sind noch am Überlegen.* — We're still thinking about it.

The infinitive is written with a capital letter, because *am* (= *an dem*) makes it a noun. With an object the form gets awkward: in the west you may hear *Ich bin die Wohnung am Putzen*, which is clearly regional. In formal writing use *gerade* or a noun: *Sie telefoniert gerade.*

### dem Vater sein Auto: the possessive dative

You may have met the possessive dative in a B1 honors lesson: *dem Vater sein Auto* (Father's car), *der Oma ihr Garten* (Grandma's garden). It is common in speech in many regions and in some dialects is the only way to express possession. Standard written German uses the genitive or *von*: *das Auto des Vaters, der Garten von Oma*.

### No Präteritum in the south

In the south (and in Austria and Switzerland) the simple past has almost disappeared from speech: people say *Ich bin gestern ins Kino gegangen*, hardly ever *ich ging*. Linguists call this **[[Präteritumschwund]]** (the loss of the Präteritum). Mostly only *war* survives, in some areas also the Präteritum of the modal verbs (*wollte, musste*). In the north, *ich ging, ich kam* still occur in conversation. For you this means: in speech everywhere, the Perfekt is never wrong; in writing, the Präteritum remains the narrative tense in every region.

### der Peter, die Anna: articles before names

In the south and in colloquial German generally, first names often take the definite article: *Der Peter kommt später. Hast du die Anna gesehen?* In standard written German the article before a name is avoided, except to show the case (*Sie zieht Goethe dem Schiller vor*) or with an adjective (*der junge Goethe*).

### Tags: gell, wa, ne, oder

You met the regional tag questions at B2: *gell?* (*gelle?*) in the south and Austria, *wa?* in Berlin, *ne?* or *nich?* in the north and centre, *oder?* everywhere, *nicht wahr?* formal. They are among the quickest clues to where a speaker comes from.

### Other things you may hear

- *wo* as a relative pronoun in the south: *der Mann, wo gestern da war* (standard: *der Mann, der gestern da war*).
- *Die Kinder sind am Schlafen, gell?* Several regional features often appear together.
- In Berlin: *ick* or *icke* for *ich*, *wat, dit, det* for *was, das*, and *j* for *g*: *Det is jut.* (That's good.) These keep the older, unshifted consonants of the Low German area that surrounds Berlin.
- In much of the north and centre, *-ig* at the end of a word is pronounced [ɪç], like *ich*: *König, wichtig*. This is the pronunciation in Duden's standard. In the south (and in Austria and Switzerland) [ɪk] is usual and accepted: *Kö-nik, wich-tik*. Such differences are called *Aussprachevarianten* (pronunciation variants).

## Reading: a bakery in Neukölln

An original feature article (*Feuilleton*, the culture pages of a newspaper). Read it first for the main point, then look for the regional words.

> **Weckle in Neukölln**
>
> Als Katrin Hägele vor drei Jahren ihre Bäckerei in Berlin-Neukölln eröffnete, hatte sie mit vielem gerechnet: mit hohen Mieten, mit Personalmangel, mit der Konkurrenz der Ketten. Womit sie nicht gerechnet hatte, war die Tafel über der Theke. „Weckle 0,60 €“ stand da in ihrer Handschrift, und die Kundschaft stand ratlos davor. „Dit is ne Schrippe, junge Frau“, erklärte ihr gleich am ersten Morgen ein älterer Herr, bevor er zwei davon bestellte.
>
> Hägele stammt aus Esslingen am Neckar, wo man beim Bäcker Weckle und Brezeln holt, das Vesper mit zur Arbeit nimmt und mit den Nachbarn über den Gartenzaun schwätzt. In Berlin gibt es stattdessen Schrippen und Stullen, und das Endstück des Brotes heißt Knust. Inzwischen hat sie zwei Tafeln aufgehängt. Auf der einen steht „Schrippe“, auf der anderen „Weckle“, und beide meinen dasselbe Gebäck.
>
> Was in Hägeles Laden so heiter wirkt, beschäftigt die Sprachwissenschaft seit rund 150 Jahren. Schon in den 1870er-Jahren begann der Sprachforscher Georg Wenker, Fragebögen an Schulen zu verschicken, um die Mundarten zu erfassen; daraus entstand der erste deutsche Sprachatlas. Heute fragen Forschungsprojekte im Internet, wie man in der eigenen Stadt das Brötchen nennt oder was man sagt, wenn es Viertel nach zwei ist. Die Karten zeigen, dass die alten Dialektgrenzen zwar verblassen, aber nicht verschwinden. Die Dialekte selbst werden seltener, doch ihre Wörter leben in den Regiolekten weiter, jener Umgangssprache, die man noch hört, wenn jemand längst Hochdeutsch spricht.
>
> „Ich rede mit meinen Kunden kein Schwäbisch“, sagt Hägele, „aber man hört halt, wo ich herkomm.“ Ihre Stammkundschaft stört das nicht. Ein Junge aus der Nachbarschaft bestellt neuerdings „zwei Weckle, bitte“ und grinst dabei. Und der ältere Herr vom ersten Morgen? Der sagt immer noch Schrippe. Aber er kommt jeden Tag.

**Translation.** *Weckle in Neukölln.* When Katrin Hägele opened her bakery in Berlin-Neukölln three years ago, she had expected a lot of things: high rents, a shortage of staff, competition from the chains. What she hadn't expected was the board above the counter. "Weckle 0.60 €" it said, in her handwriting, and the customers stood in front of it, puzzled. "That's a Schrippe, young lady," an older gentleman explained to her on the very first morning, before ordering two of them.

Hägele comes from Esslingen on the Neckar, where you buy Weckle and pretzels at the baker's, take your Vesper to work and chat (*schwätzen*) with the neighbours over the garden fence. In Berlin there are Schrippen and Stullen instead, and the end of the loaf is called the Knust. She has now put up two boards. One says "Schrippe", the other "Weckle", and both mean the same roll.

What seems so cheerful in Hägele's shop has occupied linguistics for about 150 years. As early as the 1870s the linguist Georg Wenker began sending questionnaires to schools in order to record the dialects; the first German linguistic atlas grew out of them. Today research projects on the internet ask what people in their own town call a bread roll, or what they say when it is a quarter past two. The maps show that the old dialect boundaries are fading, but not vanishing. The dialects themselves are becoming rarer, but their words live on in regional speech, the everyday language you still hear when someone has long since switched to standard German.

"I don't speak Swabian with my customers," says Hägele, "but you can tell where I'm from." Her regulars don't mind. A boy from the neighbourhood has recently started ordering "two Weckle, please", grinning as he does. And the older gentleman from the first morning? He still says Schrippe. But he comes every day.

Notice how the article works. The anecdote comes first, then the general point (*Was in Hägeles Laden so heiter wirkt, beschäftigt die Sprachwissenschaft …*), then a return to the anecdote. The customer's *Dit is ne Schrippe* is Berlin speech (*dit* for *das*, *ne* for *eine*), and Hägele's *wo ich herkomm* (standard *woher ich komme*) is regional too: a split *wo … her* and a dropped *-e*. A journalist quotes this to give the people a voice; in her own sentences she writes standard German. *Der Sprachatlas* is a dialect atlas, a set of maps showing where which form is used, and *die Dialektgrenze* the line on such a map.

## Listening: regional standard

You will hear regional German most of all from speakers who think they are speaking standard. Listen to the dialogue below: a Bavarian colleague and a colleague from Hamburg plan a lunch break. The voice is a standard German one, but the words and grammar are regional.

```dialogue lang=de-DE
# Mittagspause in München
Vroni: Du, heuer hab ich noch gar keine Brotzeit mit dir gemacht, gell? Gehst mit?
= Hey, we haven't had a snack together at all this year, have we? Are you coming?
Hauke: Gern, ich bin nur grad noch am Telefonieren. Wohin denn?
= Happily, I'm just still on the phone. Where to?
Vroni: Zum Metzger ums Eck. Der macht die besten Leberkässemmeln.
= To the butcher's round the corner. He makes the best Leberkäse rolls.
Hauke: Bei uns hieße das Schlachter und Brötchen, aber egal. Treffen wir uns um Viertel nach zwölf?
= Back home that would be Schlachter and Brötchen, but never mind. Shall we meet at a quarter past twelve?
Vroni: Viertel nach zwölf, passt. Und der Bub von der Huber kommt auch mit.
= Quarter past twelve, fine. And the Huber woman's boy is coming too.
```

Vroni's *heuer, Brotzeit, gell, Gehst mit?* (without *du*), *ums Eck* (standard *um die Ecke*), *Metzger*, *Semmel*, *Bub* and *die Huber* (article + surname) all mark her as southern. Hauke's *am Telefonieren* is the colloquial progressive; *Schlachter* and *Brötchen* are northern and general.

## What to imitate and what to recognize

At C1 the rule is simple: **recognize everything, imitate almost nothing.**

- Write standard German. In formal writing (the exam, an application, a report) regional grammar counts as a mistake: no *tun* + infinitive, no *dem Vater sein*, no *wo* as a relative pronoun.
- In speech, the Perfekt for past events, *gucken*, *am Arbeiten sein* and a tag like *oder?* are fine everywhere. They make you sound natural, not regional.
- If you live in a region, you can adopt the regional standard words (*Semmel* in Munich, *Sonnabend* in Rostock); people will take it as a friendly gesture. Avoid imitating dialect sounds and grammar, which easily sounds like parody.
- When you don't understand a regional word, ask: *Wie sagt man dazu bei Ihnen?* or *Was ist denn ein Knust?* People are usually happy to explain.

## Pronunciation

- *die Schrippe*, *die Stulle*, *der Knust*: short vowels before double or clustered consonants. *Knust* has a pronounced *K* before *n*, as in *Knie*.
- *das Plattdeutsch*: stress on the first syllable, PLATT-deutsch.
- *der Regiolekt*: re-gi-o-LEKT, stress on the last syllable, like *Dialekt*.
- *heuer*: HOI-er, two syllables.
- *gucken*: the *u* is short; the spelling *kucken* is also standard (Duden lists both).

## Common mistakes

- ~~Treffen wir uns um viertel drei? = 2:45~~. *viertel drei* is 2:15; 2:45 is *drei viertel drei* or *Viertel vor drei*.
- Thinking a *Pfannkuchen* is the same everywhere: in Berlin it's a doughnut, elsewhere a pancake.
- Using regional grammar in writing: ~~Ich tu den Bericht noch schreiben.~~ → *Ich schreibe den Bericht noch.*
- ~~Dem Chef sein Büro ist im dritten Stock.~~ in an e-mail → *Das Büro des Chefs* / *Das Büro vom Chef* (colloquial) *ist im dritten Stock.*
- Mixing up *die Vesper* (evening church service) and *das Vesper* (a snack in Swabia).
- Treating *Plattdeutsch* as "bad German". It is a language variety with its own history and literature, in many of its sounds closer to Dutch and English than to standard German.

## Key points

- German in Germany is a continuum: dialect (*Dialekt, Mundart*), regional speech (*Regiolekt, Regionalsprache*), colloquial standard (*Umgangssprache*) and the written standard.
- Three dialect belts: Low German (*Niederdeutsch, Plattdeutsch*) in the north, Central German in the middle, Upper German (*Oberdeutsch*) in the south. The Benrath line (*maken/machen*) separates Low from Central German.
- Regional words survive best: *Schrippe, Semmel, Weck* for *Brötchen*; *Sonnabend*; *Fleischer, Schlachter*; *Bulette*; *Blaukraut*; *heuer, Bub, Brotzeit, Vesper*.
- *viertel drei* = 2:15; *drei viertel drei* = 2:45.
- Regional grammar to recognize: *tun* + infinitive, *am* + infinitive (now widespread in speech), the possessive dative, the loss of the Präteritum in the south, articles with names, *wo* as a relative pronoun, tags (*gell, wa, ne, oder*).
- Write standard German; in speech, use what is common everywhere, and ask when a regional word is new to you.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete the lesson.

lessons.title: Vers, Reim und Metapher: reading poems and stylistic devices
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Poems are the densest texts a language has. Every word is chosen, sentences are bent to fit a rhythm, and older forms survive that you won't find in a newspaper. That makes poetry hard for learners, but it is also why it is worth reading at C1: if you can follow a poem, you can follow the long sentences of a Feuilleton article, the metaphors of a political speech and the word play of advertising.

This lesson gives you the tools:

- the vocabulary for talking about the form of a poem (*Strophe, Vers, Reimschema, Metrum, Enjambement, Zäsur*);
- the main **[[stylistic devices]]** (*Stilmittel*), with a reference sheet;
- the poetic syntax that makes older poems hard: inversion, ellipsis, the genitive before its noun, the dative *-e*, shortened words;
- a short map of the literary epochs;
- a method for writing a *Gedichtinterpretation* in five steps.

The poems are by Goethe, Rilke and Trakl. All three died long ago (1832, 1926 and 1914), so their texts are in the public domain and can be quoted in full. The English versions are prose translations written for this course, to help you understand, not to replace the German.

## The form of a poem

*die Lyrik* is poetry as a genre (next to *die Epik*, narrative prose, and *die Dramatik*, drama); the adjective *lyrisch* means "of poetry", and also "lyrical, tender" in everyday use. *die Dichtung* is literature in general, especially poetry, and *dichten* is to write poetry. A single poem is *das Gedicht* (A2).

### Who speaks: the lyrisches Ich

The voice that speaks in a poem is the **[[lyrisches Ich]]** (the lyrical I, the speaker). It is not the same as the poet: Goethe was not a tired wanderer on a hill every time he wrote *ich*. In an interpretation you write *Das lyrische Ich beschreibt …*, never *Goethe beschreibt, wie er …*. Some poems have no *ich* at all and describe a scene or a thing; then you speak of *der Sprecher* or simply of *das Gedicht*.

### Lines, stanzas and rhyme

A line of a poem is *der Vers* (also *die Verszeile*); a group of lines is *die Strophe* (B1). In English *verse* can mean a whole stanza; in German *Vers* is only ever one line. The pattern of rhymes is *das Reimschema*, written with letters:

| name | scheme | example endings |
|---|---|---|
| *der Paarreim* | aabb | *Haus – Maus – Wald – kalt* |
| *der Kreuzreim* | abab | *Stäbe – hält – gäbe – Welt* |
| *der umarmende Reim* | abba | *fällt – läutet – bereitet – wohlbestellt* |

A line can end on a stressed syllable (*hält, Welt*: a masculine ending, *männliche Kadenz*) or on an unstressed one (*Stäbe, gäbe*: a feminine ending, *weibliche Kadenz*). The **[[sonnet]]** (*das Sonett*) has fourteen lines in two stanzas of four lines (*Quartette*) and two of three (*Terzette*). A **[[ballad]]** (*die Ballade*) is a poem that tells a story, often a dramatic or eerie one, such as Goethe's *Erlkönig*.

### Metre: the rhythm of stressed and unstressed syllables

German verse is built on stress. The regular pattern of stressed and unstressed syllables is the **[[metre]]** (*das Metrum*, also *das Versmaß*). Its units are called feet (*Versfüße*). A stressed syllable is often written x́ and an unstressed one x; in the examples the stressed syllables are in capitals:

| foot | German | pattern | example word |
|---|---|---|---|
| iamb | *der Jambus* | x x́ | *ge-DICHT, ver-STEHT* |
| trochee | *der Trochäus* | x́ x | *FENS-ter, KIN-der* |
| dactyl | *der Daktylus* | x́ x x | *KÖ-ni-gin, WUN-der-bar* |
| anapaest | *der Anapäst* | x x x́ | *me-lo-DIE* |

A line is described by its foot and the number of stresses: *fünfhebiger Jambus* (iambic pentameter, five stresses), *vierhebiger Trochäus* (trochaic tetrameter). To find the metre, read the line aloud with natural word stress and mark the stressed syllables. Don't force the pattern: real poems vary it, and the variations are often where the meaning is.

### Where a sentence and a line part company

When a sentence runs on beyond the end of a line, that is an **[[enjambment]]** (*das Enjambement*, also *der Zeilensprung*; pronounced in the French way, *ã-schã-bə-MÃ*). It creates tension: the reader expects a pause and has to go on. The opposite case, a pause inside a line, usually marked by a comma, dash or full stop, is a **[[caesura]]** (*die Zäsur*).

## Reading a poem: Rilke, *Der Panther*

Rainer Maria Rilke (1875–1926) wrote *Der Panther* in Paris in 1902 or 1903, after watching the animals in the zoo of the Jardin des Plantes; it was published in his *Neue Gedichte* (1907). It is one of the best-known examples of a *Dinggedicht* (a "thing poem"), which looks so closely at an object or animal that it seems to see from inside it. The text keeps Rilke's spelling (*daß*).

> **Der Panther**
> *Im Jardin des Plantes, Paris*
>
> Sein Blick ist vom Vorübergehn der Stäbe
> so müd geworden, daß er nichts mehr hält.
> Ihm ist, als ob es tausend Stäbe gäbe
> und hinter tausend Stäben keine Welt.
>
> Der weiche Gang geschmeidig starker Schritte,
> der sich im allerkleinsten Kreise dreht,
> ist wie ein Tanz von Kraft um eine Mitte,
> in der betäubt ein großer Wille steht.
>
> Nur manchmal schiebt der Vorhang der Pupille
> sich lautlos auf –. Dann geht ein Bild hinein,
> geht durch der Glieder angespannte Stille –
> und hört im Herzen auf zu sein.

**Prose translation.** His gaze has grown so tired from the passing of the bars that it holds nothing any more. It seems to him as if there were a thousand bars, and behind a thousand bars no world. — The soft walk of supple, powerful strides, turning in the very smallest circle, is like a dance of strength around a centre in which a great will stands stunned. — Only now and then the curtain of the pupil slides up without a sound. Then an image goes in, goes through the tense stillness of the limbs, and in the heart ceases to be.

### Form

Three stanzas of four lines, *Kreuzreim* throughout (*Stäbe – hält – gäbe – Welt*), alternating feminine and masculine endings. The metre is the iambic pentameter: *sein BLICK ist VOM vor-Ü-ber-GEHN der STÄ-be* (eleven syllables, five stresses). The very last line breaks the pattern: *und HÖRT im HER-zen AUF zu SEIN* has only four stresses. The line itself stops short, just as the image "stops being" in the panther's heart. Form and content say the same thing.

### Language

- **Reversed perspective.** It is not the panther that walks past the bars: *das Vorübergehn der Stäbe* (the passing of the bars). We see the cage as the panther experiences it, as a world that moves while he stays.
- **Repetition and exaggeration.** *tausend Stäbe … tausend Stäben* (a hyperbole), *im allerkleinsten Kreise* (a superlative strengthened with *aller-*).
- **Comparison and metaphor.** *ist wie ein Tanz von Kraft* is a simile (*ein Vergleich*, with *wie*); *der Vorhang der Pupille* (the curtain of the pupil) is a **[[metaphor]]** (*die Metapher*), a comparison without *wie*.
- **Paradox.** *Tanz von Kraft* and *betäubt ein großer Wille* put strength and helplessness side by side; *weiche … starker* and *angespannte Stille* combine opposites.
- **Enjambment and caesura.** *der Stäbe / so müd geworden* runs over the line; *sich lautlos auf –. Dann geht ein Bild hinein* has a hard caesura in the middle of the line: the pupil opens, and everything stops for a moment.

### Poetic syntax

- *Vorübergehn, müd*: shortened forms (standard *Vorübergehen, müde*), common in verse for the rhythm.
- *im allerkleinsten Kreise*: the old dative ending *-e* (*im Kreis* in today's German).
- *durch der Glieder angespannte Stille*: the genitive *der Glieder* stands **before** its noun, a form that is now only poetic or very formal (standard: *durch die angespannte Stille der Glieder*). You also know it from fixed phrases: *des Rätsels Lösung, Gottes Wille*.
- *Ihm ist, als ob …*: an impersonal construction with the dative (it seems to him) and an *als ob* clause in Konjunktiv II (*gäbe*).

## Stylistic devices

*das Stilmittel* (also *die rhetorische Figur*) is a deliberate use of language for effect. If you took the B2 honors lesson on rhetoric, you know the rhetorical ones (anaphora, climax, tricolon, the rhetorical question). Poetry uses them all, and a few more. The reference sheet for this lesson lists them all with examples; here are the most important, with original examples.

| device | German | what it does | example |
|---|---|---|---|
| metaphor | *die Metapher* | a word used in a transferred sense, comparison without *wie* | *das Meer der Zeit; sein Herz aus Stein* |
| simile | *der Vergleich* | comparison with *wie* or *als ob* | *still wie ein Grab* |
| personification | *die Personifikation* | a thing or idea acts like a person | *Der Abend legt sich müde auf das Dorf.* |
| alliteration | *die Alliteration* | words that begin with the same sound | *mit Kind und Kegel; Milch und Mehl* |
| anaphora | *die Anapher* | the same word(s) at the start of lines or clauses | *Kein Laut im Hof. Kein Licht im Haus.* |
| antithesis | *die Antithese* | two opposites placed side by side | *Der Tag ist laut, die Nacht ist leer.* |
| oxymoron | *das Oxymoron* | two contradictory words joined in one phrase | *beredtes Schweigen; bittersüß* |
| chiasmus | *der Chiasmus* | crossed order: A B / B A | *Die Nacht ist kurz, lang ist der Weg.* |
| synaesthesia | *die Synästhesie* | one sense described with the words of another | *ein warmes Gelb; schreiende Farben* |
| onomatopoeia | *die Lautmalerei* | words that imitate a sound | *Es knistert, zischt und rauscht.* |
| ellipsis | *die Ellipse* | a sentence with words left out | *Kein Licht. Nur Schnee.* |
| inversion | *die Inversion* | unusual word order for emphasis or rhythm | *Golden blüht der Baum.* |
| symbol | *das Symbol* | a concrete thing that stands for an idea | *die Taube für den Frieden* |

Two distinctions that matter:

- A **[[metaphor]]** works on one word or phrase (*der Vorhang der Pupille*); a **[[symbol]]** is a thing in the poem that keeps its literal meaning and also stands for something else (the cage in *Der Panther* is a real cage and also a symbol of imprisonment). The adjectives are *metaphorisch* (*ein metaphorischer Ausdruck*) and *symbolisch* (*eine symbolische Bedeutung*).
- An **[[oxymoron]]** joins contradictory words in a single phrase (*bittersüß*); an **[[antithesis]]** sets two ideas against each other in a sentence or a pair of lines. **[[Synaesthesia]]** mixes the senses (*ein warmes Gelb*: a colour described as a temperature). A **[[chiasmus]]** crosses the order of two parallel phrases: *Die Nacht ist kurz* (subject, adjective) / *lang ist der Weg* (adjective, subject).

When you name a device, always say what it does. *In Vers 3 steht eine Antithese* is only half an observation; *Die Antithese von Tag und Nacht zeigt die Zerrissenheit des lyrischen Ichs* is an interpretation.

## Two more poems

### Trakl, *Ein Winterabend*

Georg Trakl (1887–1914), born in Salzburg, is one of the first poets of German Expressionism (*der Expressionismus*). This is the second version of the poem, published in *Sebastian im Traum* (1915).

> **Ein Winterabend**
>
> Wenn der Schnee ans Fenster fällt,
> Lang die Abendglocke läutet,
> Vielen ist der Tisch bereitet
> Und das Haus ist wohlbestellt.
>
> Mancher auf der Wanderschaft
> Kommt ans Tor auf dunklen Pfaden.
> Golden blüht der Baum der Gnaden
> Aus der Erde kühlem Saft.
>
> Wanderer tritt still herein;
> Schmerz versteinerte die Schwelle.
> Da erglänzt in reiner Helle
> Auf dem Tische Brot und Wein.

**Prose translation.** When the snow falls against the window and the evening bell rings long, for many the table is laid and the house is well provided. — Many a one on his wanderings comes to the gate on dark paths. Golden blooms the tree of grace from the cool sap of the earth. — Wanderer steps quietly in; pain turned the threshold to stone. There, in pure brightness, bread and wine shine on the table.

Things to notice:

- **Form.** Three stanzas, each with the rhyme scheme abba (*fällt – läutet – bereitet – wohlbestellt*), in trochees with four stresses: *WENN der SCHNEE ans FENS-ter FÄLLT*.
- **Inversion.** *Golden blüht der Baum der Gnaden* puts the adjective first, where the stress falls.
- **Genitive before the noun** again: *aus der Erde kühlem Saft* (= *aus dem kühlen Saft der Erde*); and the dative *-e* in *auf dem Tische*.
- **Metaphor.** *Schmerz versteinerte die Schwelle*: pain turned the threshold to stone. It is also the only verb in the past tense, in the middle of a present-tense poem: a moment of past suffering inside a timeless scene.
- **Symbol.** *Brot und Wein* are an ordinary meal and also the bread and wine of the Christian communion. The wanderer without a home finds a table laid for him.
- **No article.** *Wanderer tritt still herein* leaves out the article, as if *Wanderer* were a name. The figure becomes general: any wanderer, anyone.

### Goethe, *Wandrers Nachtlied* (*Ein Gleiches*)

Johann Wolfgang von Goethe (1749–1832) wrote these eight lines on the wooden wall of a hut on the Kickelhahn, a hill near Ilmenau, in September 1780. He printed them in his collected works of 1815 under the title *Ein Gleiches* ("another of the same kind"), after an earlier poem called *Wandrers Nachtlied*; today the poem is usually known by that earlier title. Editions differ slightly in punctuation (some print *Warte nur! Balde*); this is a common version.

> Über allen Gipfeln
> Ist Ruh,
