> In allen Wipfeln
> Spürest du
> Kaum einen Hauch;
> Die Vögelein schweigen im Walde.
> Warte nur, balde
> Ruhest du auch.

**Prose translation.** Over all the hilltops is peace; in all the treetops you feel hardly a breath; the little birds are silent in the wood. Only wait, soon you too will rest.

The movement goes from the mountains (*Gipfel*) to the trees (*Wipfel*) to the birds and finally to *du*: from the inanimate world to the living and then to the human being. The last line can be read as rest after a day's walk or as death. Notice the older forms: *Ruh* (= *Ruhe*), *spürest* (an older, fuller form of *spürst*), *Vögelein* (a diminutive of *Vogel*), *balde* (= *bald*), *im Walde*. *Gipfeln – Wipfeln* is a rhyme that changes a single sound.

## The epochs in brief

*die Epoche* (an epoch) is a period of literature with shared ideas and forms. The dates are approximate and the epochs overlap; use them as a map, not as a law.

| epoch | about | key idea | authors |
|---|---|---|---|
| *die Aufklärung* (Enlightenment) | 1720–1790 | reason, tolerance, education | Lessing, Kant |
| *der Sturm und Drang* | 1765–1785 | feeling, genius, revolt | the young Goethe and Schiller |
| *die Klassik* (Weimar Classicism) | 1786–1805 | harmony, humanity, classical form | Goethe, Schiller |
| *die Romantik* (Romanticism) | 1795–1835 | longing, night, nature, the infinite | Novalis, Eichendorff, the Grimms |
| *der Realismus* (Realism) | 1850–1890 | ordinary life, society, restraint | Fontane, Storm |
| *die Moderne* (Modernism) | from about 1890 | crisis of language and the self, new forms | Rilke, Hofmannsthal, Thomas Mann |
| *der Expressionismus* (Expressionism) | 1910–1925 | the big city, war, inner chaos, strong images | Trakl, Heym, Lasker-Schüler |

*die Moderne* is the broadest of these terms: it covers several movements from the end of the 19th century on, Expressionism among them. Christian Morgenstern (1871–1914) belongs here too, with his comic *Galgenlieder* (1905); one of them, *Fisches Nachtgesang*, consists only of the signs for stressed and unstressed syllables, arranged in the shape of a fish: a poem about metre made of nothing but metre.

## A Gedichtinterpretation in five steps

A **[[Gedichtinterpretation]]** is the classic German essay on a poem. It is not a summary: it shows how the form and language of the poem create its meaning. A workable plan:

1. **Introduction.** Author, title, year, epoch, theme, and a first thesis about the meaning (*Deutungshypothese*). *Das Gedicht „Der Panther“ von Rainer Maria Rilke aus dem Jahr 1902/03 beschreibt einen Panther im Pariser Zoo. Es zeigt, wie Gefangenschaft ein lebendiges Wesen innerlich auslöscht.*
2. **Content.** What happens, stanza by stanza, in the present tense and in your own words. *In der ersten Strophe wird der Blick des Tieres beschrieben, …*
3. **Form.** Stanzas, lines, rhyme scheme, metre, endings, and especially the places where the form breaks its own pattern.
4. **Language.** Stylistic devices, word fields, sentence structure, tense, always with their effect. *Die Metapher „Vorhang der Pupille“ lässt das Auge wie eine Bühne erscheinen, auf der nichts mehr gespielt wird.*
5. **Conclusion.** Return to your thesis, confirm or refine it, and place the poem in its epoch or in today's world.

Useful phrases:

- *Das Gedicht handelt von … / thematisiert … / Im Mittelpunkt steht …*
- *Das lyrische Ich wendet sich an … / spricht aus der Sicht von …*
- *Auffällig ist …; Dies unterstreicht / verstärkt / verdeutlicht …*
- *Das Enjambement in Vers 2 bewirkt, dass …*
- *Man könnte die letzte Zeile auch als … deuten.*

Quote exactly, give the line (*V. 3* = Vers 3), and use the present tense throughout.

## Pronunciation

- *das Enjambement*: French, ã-schã-bə-MÃ, with nasal vowels.
- *die Zäsur*: tsä-SUR, stress on the second syllable.
- *der Daktylus*: DAK-ty-lus, stress on the first syllable. *der Jambus*: JAM-bus. *der Trochäus*: tro-CHÄ-us, with *ch* as in *ach*.
- *das Oxymoron*: o-XY-mo-ron. *die Synästhesie*: sü-näs-te-SIE, four syllables and a long final *-ie* (not like *Tragödie*).
- *die Personifikation*: per-so-ni-fi-ka-TSION.

## Common mistakes

- Calling a line a *Strophe*: in German *der Vers* is one line, *die Strophe* a group of lines.
- Treating the speaker as the poet: ~~Rilke ist traurig, weil er …~~ → *Das Gedicht vermittelt …* / *Das lyrische Ich …*
- Naming a device without its effect. Always add *dadurch*, *dies bewirkt*, *so wird deutlich*.
- Mixing up *Metapher* and *Vergleich*: *wie ein Tanz* is a simile (*Vergleich*), *der Vorhang der Pupille* a metaphor.
- Reading the genitive before the noun as a subject: in *durch der Glieder angespannte Stille* the subject of the clause is still *ein Bild*; *der Glieder* belongs to *Stille*.
- Retelling in the past tense. Interpretations use the present: *In der zweiten Strophe beschreibt das Gedicht …*

## Key points

- Talk about form with *Vers* (line), *Strophe*, *Reimschema* (*Paarreim* aabb, *Kreuzreim* abab, *umarmender Reim* abba), *Metrum* (*Jambus, Trochäus, Daktylus*), *Enjambement* and *Zäsur*.
- The voice of a poem is the *lyrisches Ich*, not the author.
- Stylistic devices: *Metapher, Vergleich, Personifikation, Alliteration, Anapher, Antithese, Oxymoron, Chiasmus, Synästhesie, Lautmalerei, Ellipse, Inversion, Symbol*. Always name the effect.
- Poetic syntax: inversion, ellipsis, the genitive before the noun (*der Erde kühlem Saft*), the dative *-e* (*im Walde*), shortened words (*müd, Ruh*).
- Epochs (approximate): Aufklärung, Klassik, Romantik, Realismus, Moderne, Expressionismus.
- A *Gedichtinterpretation*: thesis, content, form, language, conclusion, in the present tense with exact quotations.

lessons.title: Talk and discussion at C1: presenting, rephrasing, holding your ground
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

At B2 you learned to give a short presentation and to take part in a discussion. At C1 the bar rises in three ways. You speak for longer and on more abstract questions; you are expected to structure what you say so that a listener can follow without effort; and when a word is missing, you don't stop, you find another way to say it. In a discussion you build on what the other person said, concede a point without giving up your position, and help the conversation reach a result.

This lesson covers:

- the speaking part of the Goethe-Zertifikat C1, as the official model test describes it;
- structuring a five-minute talk, with signposting phrases at C1 level;
- rephrasing strategies (*Umschreibungsstrategien*) for when a word is missing;
- taking up, interrupting and building on your partner's points;
- relativizing and conceding without giving in, and reaching an agreement.

The theme is life in rural areas: people moving away, closing shops and surgeries, poor mobile reception, and the villages that are coming back to life.

## The speaking exam at a glance

The Goethe-Zertifikat C1 speaking module (*Sprechen*) is normally taken in pairs. According to the Durchführungsbestimmungen (Stand 1 September 2023) it lasts about 20 minutes for a pair, or about 15 minutes in the rare case that a candidate is examined alone, plus 20 minutes of preparation. You prepare alone; you may make notes, but in the exam you speak freely. There are two parts:

| part | what you do | length |
|---|---|---|
| Teil 1: *Vortrag* | You choose one of two topics. Each comes with four points to cover (for example: give an example, argue for and against, propose measures or alternatives). You give a talk; then your partner asks you questions about it, and you ask your partner about theirs. | talk about 5 minutes; questions about 2 minutes |
| Teil 2: *Diskussion* | You and your partner get a short input text on a controversial question and four points to discuss. You exchange views, react to each other and, as one of the points, agree on something together. | about 5 minutes |

Two examiners mark parts 1 and 2 separately, and the result is the average of their marks, out of 100 (pass mark 60). The model test's marking sheet looks at how well you fulfil the task, coherence, fluency, vocabulary, grammar and pronunciation, and in Teil 2 at interaction; the questions and answers after the talk count too. The introductory chat at the start is not scored.

What this means in practice:

- **Cover all four points.** A brilliant talk that leaves one out loses marks for task fulfilment.
- **Structure aloud.** The listener can't see your notes, so say where you are: *Ich komme nun zum zweiten Punkt.*
- **Interaction is part of the mark.** In Teil 2, a monologue is a weakness even if every sentence is correct.

Always check the current Modellsatz on goethe.de before an exam; formats are revised from time to time.

## Structuring a talk

At B2 you learned the basic phrases (*Ich möchte über … sprechen; zum Schluss …*). At C1 you vary them and use them to show the logic of the talk, not just its order.

| function | C1 phrases |
|---|---|
| opening, stating the question | *Ich möchte heute eine Frage aufgreifen, die viele Gemeinden beschäftigt: …* · *Im Folgenden möchte ich zunächst kurz umreißen, worum es geht.* |
| outline | *Mein Vortrag gliedert sich in drei Teile.* · *Zunächst …, dann …, und abschließend …* |
| moving on | *Damit komme ich zum zweiten Punkt.* · *Das führt mich direkt zur Frage, …* · *Lassen Sie mich nun auf … eingehen.* |
| the core | *Damit komme ich zum Kern des Problems.* · *Entscheidend ist meines Erachtens …* |
| example | *Ein Beispiel aus meinem Heimatland mag das veranschaulichen: …* · *Nehmen wir etwa …* |
| weighing | *Auf der einen Seite …, auf der anderen …* · *Dem steht gegenüber, dass …* |
| own view | *Ich persönlich halte … für den sinnvolleren Weg, und zwar aus zwei Gründen.* |
| summing up | *Fassen wir zusammen: …* · *Unterm Strich lässt sich sagen, dass …* |
| inviting questions | *Damit bin ich am Ende. Ich bin gespannt auf Ihre Fragen.* |

*umreißen* (to outline, sketch) is an inseparable verb: *Ich umreiße kurz das Problem; sie hat die Lage knapp umrissen.* (Separable *UMreißen* is to knock down: *Der Sturm hat den Zaun umgerissen.*)

## A model talk

An original transcript of a C1-level talk of about four minutes. The topic: should the state do more to bring doctors to the countryside? Notice the signposting, and how each of four points is covered.

> Ich möchte heute eine Frage aufgreifen, die vor allem in strukturschwachen Regionen viele Menschen beschäftigt: Wie lässt sich die medizinische Versorgung auf dem Land sichern? Dazu möchte ich zunächst kurz umreißen, wo das Problem liegt, dann ein Beispiel aus meinem Heimatland geben, anschließend Vor- und Nachteile staatlicher Förderung abwägen und zum Schluss sagen, welchen Weg ich für sinnvoll halte.
>
> Zunächst zum Problem. In vielen Landgemeinden gehen die Hausärztinnen und Hausärzte in den nächsten Jahren in Rente, und Nachfolger sind kaum zu finden. Junge Medizinerinnen ziehen lieber in die Städte oder in den Speckgürtel, wo es Schulen, Kultur und schnelles Internet gibt. Die Folge ist ein Teufelskreis: Wo der Landarzt fehlt, ziehen auch Familien weg, und wo Familien wegziehen, schließen Dorfladen, Bank und Schule. Der Ortskern verödet.
>
> Ein Beispiel aus meinem Heimatland mag das veranschaulichen. In der Region, aus der ich komme, hat die Kommune vor einigen Jahren eine Praxis gebaut und sie jungen Ärztinnen mietfrei angeboten. Inzwischen arbeiten dort drei Ärztinnen in Teilzeit, und es gibt sogar wieder Zuzug.
>
> Damit komme ich zum Kern der Frage: Sollte der Staat solche Modelle fördern? Dafür spricht, dass medizinische Versorgung zur Daseinsvorsorge gehört; niemand sollte wegen seiner Postleitzahl schlechter versorgt werden. Dem steht gegenüber, dass Geld allein niemanden aufs Land lockt. Wer dort keine Arbeit für den Partner und keinen Kitaplatz findet, kommt auch für eine mietfreie Praxis nicht.
>
> Ich persönlich halte deshalb ein Gesamtpaket für den sinnvolleren Weg: Förderung der Praxen ja, aber nur zusammen mit Investitionen in Mobilfunk, Kinderbetreuung und Busverbindungen. Unterm Strich lässt sich sagen: Den Landarzt holt man nicht mit einem Scheck zurück, sondern mit einem Dorf, in dem man gern lebt. Damit bin ich am Ende und freue mich auf Ihre Fragen.

**Translation.** Today I'd like to take up a question that concerns many people, especially in structurally weak regions: how can medical care in the countryside be secured? I'd like first to outline briefly where the problem lies, then give an example from my home country, then weigh up the advantages and disadvantages of state support, and finally say which path I think makes sense.

First, the problem. In many rural communities the family doctors will retire in the next few years, and successors are hard to find. Young doctors prefer to move to the cities or to the commuter belt, where there are schools, culture and fast internet. The result is a vicious circle: where the country doctor is missing, families move away too, and where families move away, the village shop, the bank and the school close. The village centre becomes deserted.

An example from my home country may illustrate this. In the region I come from, the local authority built a surgery a few years ago and offered it rent-free to young doctors. Three doctors now work there part-time, and people are even moving in again.

That brings me to the heart of the question: should the state support such models? In favour is the fact that medical care is part of the basic public services; nobody should get worse care because of their postcode. Against that is the fact that money alone doesn't attract anyone to the countryside. Someone who finds no job there for their partner and no nursery place won't come even for a rent-free surgery.

Personally, I therefore think a complete package is the more sensible way: support for surgeries, yes, but only together with investment in mobile networks, childcare and bus connections. All in all one can say: you don't bring the country doctor back with a cheque, but with a village people like living in. That brings me to the end, and I look forward to your questions.

The four points are each announced in the first paragraph and then signalled: *Zunächst zum Problem* · *Ein Beispiel … mag das veranschaulichen* · *Damit komme ich zum Kern* · *Ich persönlich halte deshalb …*. *mag … veranschaulichen* is the concessive or modest *mögen* of formal speech ("may illustrate"). The last sentence uses a contrast (*nicht mit einem Scheck, sondern mit einem Dorf*) to give the listener something to remember.

Some of the words: *die Landflucht* (the movement of people from the country to the towns), *der Strukturwandel* (structural change, when an economy's old industries decline), *strukturschwach* (structurally weak, with few jobs and poor infrastructure), *die Daseinsvorsorge* (the basic public services a state must provide: water, energy, health, transport), *die Nahversorgung* (shops for daily needs within reach), *der Speckgürtel* (literally "bacon belt", the prosperous suburbs around a city; colloquial), *abgehängt* (left behind, cut off), and *das Funkloch* (a spot with no mobile reception). *die Kommune* is the local authority (municipality), with the adjective *kommunal*: *die kommunalen Finanzen*. *die Provinz* means the provinces, everything outside the big cities, and the adjective *provinziell* is pejorative (narrow-minded, small-town): *Das ist mir zu provinziell.* People who praise *das Landleben* (country life) and talk about *die Landbevölkerung* (the rural population) often want to *wiederbeleben* (revive) the village centre: *die Wiederbelebung der Ortskerne* is a common goal of local politics.

## When a word is missing: rephrasing strategies

Even at C1 you will sometimes not know a word, or it won't come. Stopping or switching to English costs marks for fluency; an elegant **[[Umschreibung]]** (circumlocution, paraphrase) costs nothing and even shows skill. Five strategies:

| strategy | how | example (target: *das Funkloch*) |
|---|---|---|
| general word + relative clause | name the category, then define | *eine Stelle, an der man kein Netz hat* |
| function | what it does or what you do with it | *das, womit man …* · *ein Gerät, mit dem man …* |
| *so etwas wie* | an approximate word | *so etwas wie ein toter Winkel fürs Handy* |
| opposite or comparison | *das Gegenteil von …* · *ähnlich wie …* | *das Gegenteil von gutem Empfang* |
| example | name a case | *wie bei uns im Tal, wo das Handy nie geht* |

Signal phrases buy you time and tell the listener what you are doing:

- *Wie soll ich sagen …* · *Ich komme gerade nicht auf das Wort …* · *Wie nennt man das noch?*
- *…, also, sagen wir mal, …* · *…, oder anders formuliert: …*
- *Ich meine diese Läden, die … – ja, genau, Dorfläden.*

To **[[paraphrase]]** (*paraphrasieren*) is to say the same thing in other words; you also do it to check that you understood your partner: *Wenn ich Sie richtig verstehe, meinen Sie, dass …* · *Sie wollen also sagen, …?*

## Discussion: taking up and building on points

In Teil 2 you are marked for interaction. That means more than taking turns: you refer to what your partner said and develop it. Useful verbs:

- *an etwas anknüpfen* (to link up with, follow on from): *Ich möchte an das anknüpfen, was Sie eben über die Busverbindungen gesagt haben.*
- *etwas aufgreifen* (to take up a point): *Sie haben das Thema Mobilfunk angesprochen; das würde ich gern aufgreifen.*
- *einhaken* (to cut in, take up a point immediately, colloquial but common): *Darf ich da kurz einhaken?*
- *der Einwurf* (an interjection, a brief objection): *Wenn ich einen kurzen Einwurf machen darf: …*
- *den Gesprächsfaden wieder aufnehmen* (to pick up the thread again): *Um den Gesprächsfaden wieder aufzunehmen: Wir waren bei den Kosten.*

*das Gegenüber* is the person opposite you in a conversation (*Hören Sie Ihrem Gegenüber genau zu*), a noun formed from the preposition *gegenüber* (A1).

### Holding your ground politely

At C1 you can concede part of an argument and still keep your position. The pattern is: acknowledge, limit, counter.

| step | phrases |
|---|---|
| acknowledge | *Da ist durchaus etwas dran.* · *Das ist ein berechtigter Einwand.* · *Zugegeben, …* |
| limit | *Das mag für die Städte gelten, auf dem Land aber …* · *Ich gebe Ihnen insofern recht, als …* · *Das trifft nur zum Teil zu.* |
| counter | *Trotzdem/Dennoch bin ich der Meinung, dass …* · *Entscheidend scheint mir aber …* · *Man darf dabei nicht vergessen, dass …* |

Konjunktiv II and modal particles soften without weakening: *Wäre es nicht sinnvoller, zuerst …?* · *Ich würde das eher anders sehen.* · *Das ist ja gerade das Problem.* · *Das kann man so doch nicht sagen.*

### Reaching an agreement

The discussion task usually asks you to agree on something. Leave a minute for it:

- *Können wir uns darauf einigen, dass …?*
- *Wir sind uns also zumindest darin einig, dass …*
- *Ein Kompromiss könnte so aussehen: …*
- *Dann halten wir fest: …*

### A model discussion

```dialogue lang=de-DE
# Soll das Dorf einen eigenen Laden bekommen?
Jana: Ich finde, ein genossenschaftlicher Dorfladen ist die beste Lösung. Die Leute kaufen da, wo sie sich kennen.
= I think a cooperative village shop is the best solution. People shop where they know each other.
Malte: Darf ich da kurz einhaken? Das klingt schön, aber viele dieser Läden schließen nach zwei, drei Jahren wieder.
= May I cut in there? That sounds nice, but many of these shops close again after two or three years.
Jana: Da ist durchaus etwas dran. Aber die meisten scheitern, weil sie nur Lebensmittel verkaufen. Wenn es dort auch Post, Café und einen Paketdienst gibt, sieht die Sache anders aus.
= There's certainly something in that. But most of them fail because they only sell food. If there's also a post office, a café and a parcel service, things look different.
Malte: An den Punkt würde ich gern anknüpfen: Dann ist der Laden eigentlich ein Treffpunkt, nicht nur ein Geschäft.
= I'd like to follow on from that point: then the shop is really a meeting place, not just a business.
Jana: Genau. Und das stärkt die Dorfgemeinschaft.
= Exactly. And that strengthens the village community.
Malte: Können wir uns darauf einigen, dass ein Laden nur dann Sinn hat, wenn er mehr bietet als Einkaufen?
= Can we agree that a shop only makes sense if it offers more than shopping?
Jana: Ja, darauf können wir uns einigen.
= Yes, we can agree on that.
```

Malte interrupts politely (*Darf ich da kurz einhaken?*), Jana concedes and limits (*Da ist durchaus etwas dran. Aber …*), Malte builds on her point (*An den Punkt würde ich gern anknüpfen*), and Malte proposes the agreement. Neither simply repeats their opening position.

## Questions after the talk

After the talk in Teil 1 your partner asks you questions, and you ask about theirs. Good questions show that you listened:

- *Sie haben gesagt, dass … Könnten Sie das noch etwas genauer erklären?*
- *Mich würde interessieren, wie Sie zu … stehen.*
- *Gilt das, was Sie beschrieben haben, auch für …?*

When you are asked something you hadn't thought about, take a second: *Das ist eine gute Frage. Darüber habe ich, ehrlich gesagt, noch nicht nachgedacht, aber ich würde sagen …*

## Pronunciation and fluency

- Pause at the end of a thought, not in the middle of a phrase. A pause before *Damit komme ich zum Kern …* sounds deliberate; a pause between *der* and *Daseinsvorsorge* sounds lost.
- Stress the new information: *Nicht das GELD fehlt, sondern die INFRASTRUKTUR.*
- *die Daseinsvorsorge*: DA-seins-vor-sor-ge, main stress on the first syllable. *strukturschwach*: struk-TUR-schwach. *die Kommune*: ko-MU-ne.
- Fillers such as *also, sagen wir mal, wie soll ich sagen* are normal in moderation; *äh* after every third word is not.

## Common mistakes

- Reading the talk from notes. Write key words, not sentences; the examiners mark fluency.
- Leaving out one of the four points, or spending four minutes on the first.
- Treating Teil 2 as two short talks. React: *Sie haben vorhin gesagt …*
- Stopping when a word is missing, or switching to English. Paraphrase: *so etwas wie …, also eine Stelle, an der …*
- Over-politeness that never commits: *Vielleicht könnte man eventuell möglicherweise …* At C1, soften once and then say what you think.
- *umreißen* as separable: ~~Ich reiße kurz das Problem um.~~ → *Ich umreiße kurz das Problem.*

## Key points

- Goethe C1 Sprechen (according to the official model test and rules): about 20 minutes in pairs, 20 minutes' preparation alone; Teil 1 a talk of about 5 minutes on one of two topics with four points, then questions; Teil 2 a discussion of about 5 minutes with an input text, ending in an agreement.
- Announce the structure and signpost each step: *zunächst kurz umreißen; Damit komme ich zum Kern; Unterm Strich …*
- When a word is missing, paraphrase: category + relative clause, function, *so etwas wie*, opposite, example.
- Take up and build on your partner's points: *anknüpfen, aufgreifen, einhaken, einen Einwurf machen, den Gesprächsfaden wieder aufnehmen*.
- Concede and limit, then counter: *Da ist etwas dran, aber … · Das mag für … gelten, … · Dennoch …*
- Leave time to agree: *Können wir uns darauf einigen, dass …?*

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete the lesson.

lessons.title: Passing it on: mediation at C1
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

*Sprachmittlung* (mediation) means passing on content to someone who can't access it themselves: because the text is too technical, too long, in the wrong register, or because two people are talking past each other. At B2 you passed on information at work. At C1 the tasks get harder. You summarize a specialist text for a particular reader, shift the register (specialist → lay, formal → informal), explain figures out loud, and mediate between two people who disagree, without adding a view of your own.

You will practise:

- analysing what a reader needs (*adressatengerecht formulieren*);
- condensing a dense legal or specialist text into its *Kernbotschaft* (core message);
- rewriting the same content for three different readers;
- explaining a chart orally;
- mediating between two positions, in speech and in written minutes with Konjunktiv I;
- choosing neutral reporting verbs, so that your own opinion doesn't slip in.

The theme is development cooperation and global justice: supply chains, child labour, fair trade and the question of who carries responsibility for working conditions on the other side of the world.

## What a mediator does

Every mediation task has the same three questions behind it:

1. **Who is the reader or listener?** *der Adressat, die Adressatin.* What do they already know, and what is their relationship to you?
2. **What do they need?** Not everything in the source, only what serves their purpose. The *Kernbotschaft* comes first.
3. **How do they need it?** Register, length, form (chat message, e-mail, short talk), and which terms need explaining.

To write *adressatengerecht* means to write in a way that fits the addressee. It is the most important criterion in mediation, in the exam and in real life: a correct summary in the wrong register for the reader has failed.

The verb *übermitteln* (to pass on, transmit, convey) is the formal word for what a mediator does with information: *Ich übermittle Ihnen die wichtigsten Punkte.*

## The source: a supply-chain law

Here is the kind of text you might have to pass on. First, one sentence from a German statute, quoted verbatim (statutes are not protected by copyright in Germany, § 5 UrhG):

> „Unternehmen sind dazu verpflichtet, in ihren Lieferketten die in diesem Abschnitt festgelegten menschenrechtlichen und umweltbezogenen Sorgfaltspflichten in angemessener Weise zu beachten mit dem Ziel, menschenrechtlichen oder umweltbezogenen Risiken vorzubeugen oder sie zu minimieren oder die Verletzung menschenrechtsbezogener oder umweltbezogener Pflichten zu beenden.“
>
> (§ 3 Abs. 1 Satz 1 Lieferkettensorgfaltspflichtengesetz, gesetze-im-internet.de)

Plain English: companies must take appropriate care, in their supply chains, to prevent or reduce risks to human rights and the environment, or to end violations. One sentence, 42 words, one main clause and an infinitive group (*mit dem Ziel, … vorzubeugen oder … zu minimieren oder … zu beenden*), with the key information packed into adjectives (*menschenrechtlich, umweltbezogen*) and nouns (*Sorgfaltspflichten, Risiken, Verletzung*).

Second, an original briefing text in the style of a business association's newsletter (the association is invented). The facts are as of November 2026; laws in this field are changing, so check the current state before you rely on it.

> **Sorgfaltspflichten in der Lieferkette: der Stand der Dinge**
>
> Seit dem 1. Januar 2023 gilt in Deutschland das Lieferkettensorgfaltspflichtengesetz (LkSG), meist kurz Lieferkettengesetz genannt. Erfasst waren zunächst Unternehmen mit mindestens 3.000 Beschäftigten im Inland, seit 2024 sind es Unternehmen ab 1.000 Beschäftigten. Sie müssen unter anderem ein Risikomanagement einrichten, regelmäßig Risikoanalysen durchführen, Präventions- und Abhilfemaßnahmen ergreifen und ein Beschwerdeverfahren anbieten, über das etwa Beschäftigte eines Zulieferers auf Menschenrechtsverletzungen wie Kinderarbeit oder die Ausbeutung von Arbeitskräften hinweisen können. Die Einhaltung überwacht das Bundesamt für Wirtschaft und Ausfuhrkontrolle (BAFA).
>
> Im September 2025 beschloss die Bundesregierung einen Gesetzentwurf, der die jährliche Berichtspflicht abschaffen und Bußgelder auf schwere Verstöße beschränken soll; an den Sorgfaltspflichten selbst soll sich nichts ändern. Der Bundestag beriet den Entwurf im Januar 2026 in erster Lesung und überwies ihn an die Ausschüsse; verabschiedet ist er bis heute nicht. Im Juli 2026 kündigte die Koalition zudem an, den Anwendungsbereich noch im Herbst 2026 gesetzlich auf Unternehmen mit mindestens 5.000 Beschäftigten und mehr als 1,5 Milliarden Euro Umsatz zu beschränken; ein Entwurf dafür lag Ende Oktober 2026 noch nicht vor. Die Prüfung der Berichte hat das BAFA bereits im Herbst 2025 eingestellt.
>
> Auf europäischer Ebene wurde die EU-Lieferkettenrichtlinie (CSDDD) durch das sogenannte Omnibus-I-Paket deutlich abgeschwächt. Nach der im Februar 2026 veröffentlichten Änderungsrichtlinie erfasst sie nur noch Unternehmen mit mehr als 5.000 Beschäftigten und über 1,5 Milliarden Euro weltweitem Nettoumsatz. Die Mitgliedstaaten müssen sie bis Juli 2028 umsetzen, angewendet wird sie ab Juli 2029. Mit der Umsetzung soll das LkSG durch ein neues Gesetz abgelöst werden. Für Unternehmen heißt das: Die Pflichten des LkSG gelten fort, bis der Gesetzgeber etwas anderes beschließt.

**Translation.** *Due diligence in the supply chain: where things stand.* The Supply Chain Due Diligence Act (LkSG), usually just called the supply chain law, has applied in Germany since 1 January 2023. At first it covered companies with at least 3,000 employees in Germany; since 2024 it has covered companies with 1,000 or more. Among other things they must set up risk management, carry out regular risk analyses, take preventive and remedial measures, and offer a complaints procedure through which, for example, a supplier's employees can report human rights violations such as child labour or the exploitation of workers. Compliance is monitored by the Federal Office for Economic Affairs and Export Control (BAFA).

In September 2025 the federal government adopted a bill that is to abolish the annual reporting obligation and limit fines to serious violations; the due diligence obligations themselves are to remain unchanged. The Bundestag debated the bill at first reading in January 2026 and referred it to committees; it has still not been passed. In July 2026 the coalition also announced that it would restrict the law's scope by statute in autumn 2026 to companies with at least 5,000 employees and more than 1.5 billion euros in turnover; at the end of October 2026 there was no draft for this yet. BAFA stopped checking the reports in autumn 2025.

At European level the EU supply chain directive (CSDDD) was considerably weakened by the so-called Omnibus I package. Under the amending directive published in February 2026 it now covers only companies with more than 5,000 employees and more than 1.5 billion euros in worldwide net turnover. Member states must transpose it by July 2028, and it will apply from July 2029. When it is transposed, the LkSG is to be replaced by a new law. For companies this means: the LkSG's obligations continue to apply until the legislature decides otherwise.

Notice the register: nominal style (*die Einhaltung überwacht …*, *Präventions- und Abhilfemaßnahmen*), the passive (*wurde … abgeschwächt*, *angewendet wird sie ab …*), *soll* for a plan that is not yet law (*der … abschaffen … soll*), long compounds (*Lieferkettensorgfaltspflichtengesetz*: *Liefer-ketten-sorgfalts-pflichten-gesetz*, "supply-chain due-diligence-obligations law"), and the abbreviations specialists use (*LkSG, BAFA, CSDDD*).

## Three readers, three texts

Now pass the same content on to three different people.

### 1. A friend asks in a chat

Your friend Can writes: *Sag mal, gilt dieses Lieferkettengesetz eigentlich noch? Ich hab gelesen, das wird abgeschafft.*

> Hi Can, nee, abgeschafft ist es nicht. Große Firmen (ab 1.000 Leuten) müssen weiterhin prüfen, ob bei ihren Zulieferern Kinder arbeiten oder Leute ausgebeutet werden, und was dagegen tun. Geplant ist, dass sie keinen jährlichen Bericht mehr schreiben müssen, dass es Strafen nur noch bei schweren Verstößen gibt und dass das Gesetz bald nur noch für richtig große Konzerne gilt. Beschlossen ist das aber noch nicht. Und irgendwann kommt eh eine EU-Regel, die das deutsche Gesetz ersetzt. LG

Everything technical is gone: no *Sorgfaltspflichten*, no *BAFA*, no *CSDDD*. The *Kernbotschaft* comes first (*abgeschafft ist es nicht*), then the planned changes in everyday words, then the open status. The register is informal (*nee, Leute, eh, LG*), but the facts are exact.

### 2. A managing director asks by e-mail

Frau Brandl runs a family company with 400 employees that supplies parts to a car manufacturer. She asks whether the new rules affect her firm.

> Sehr geehrte Frau Brandl,
>
> vielen Dank für Ihre Anfrage. Kurz zusammengefasst: Unmittelbar gilt das Lieferkettengesetz nur für Unternehmen ab 1.000 Beschäftigten, Ihre Firma ist also nicht direkt verpflichtet. Mittelbar können Sie aber betroffen sein, weil große Kunden ihre Anforderungen häufig über Verträge und Fragebögen an ihre Zulieferer weitergeben.
>
> An diesen Pflichten soll sich auch nach der geplanten Gesetzesänderung nichts ändern; entfallen soll vor allem die jährliche Berichtspflicht der großen Unternehmen. Außerdem will die Koalition das Gesetz künftig nur noch für Unternehmen ab 5.000 Beschäftigten gelten lassen; ein Entwurf liegt dazu aber noch nicht vor. Die EU-Richtlinie, die das deutsche Gesetz ab 2028/29 ablösen soll, wird nach der jüngsten Änderung nur noch sehr große Konzerne erfassen.
>
> Gern stelle ich Ihnen die wichtigsten Punkte in einem kurzen Gespräch genauer vor.
>
> Mit freundlichen Grüßen
> Jonas Feld

Here the reader is a decision-maker. She doesn't need the history; she needs the answer to her question (*nicht direkt, aber möglicherweise mittelbar*), the reason, and what the changes mean for her. The register is semi-formal and precise (*unmittelbar / mittelbar, entfallen, erfassen*), with short paragraphs and an offer at the end.

### 3. A class of fifteen-year-olds

You visit a school class during a project week on *Entwicklungszusammenarbeit*. You say:

> Stellt euch vor, euer T-Shirt wurde in einer Fabrik genäht, in der Kinder arbeiten. Wer ist dafür verantwortlich? Nur die Fabrik? Oder auch die Firma in Deutschland, die das T-Shirt verkauft? Das Lieferkettengesetz sagt: auch die große Firma hier muss hinschauen. Sie muss prüfen, wo Gefahren für Menschenrechte bestehen, und etwas dagegen unternehmen. Und Arbeiterinnen in der Fabrik müssen sich bei ihr beschweren können.

For young listeners the abstract law becomes a concrete case (the T-shirt), questions involve them, and the key duties appear as verbs (*hinschauen, prüfen, etwas unternehmen, sich beschweren*). Details such as thresholds and dates are left out because they don't serve this audience.

The lesson: **select, then reformulate.** Nominal style becomes verbal style; specialist terms are replaced or explained; and the order follows the reader's question, not the source.

## Explaining a chart out loud

In oral mediation you may have to explain figures to someone who can't see them, for example on the phone. The chart below is invented for this lesson.

| year | share of fair-trade bananas in banana sales (invented country) |
|---|---|
| 2016 | 6 % |
| 2020 | 11 % |
| 2025 | 14 % |

> Also, die Grafik zeigt, wie viel Prozent der verkauften Bananen fair gehandelt waren. 2016 war es nur etwa jede siebzehnte Banane, sechs Prozent. Bis 2020 hat sich der Anteil fast verdoppelt, auf elf Prozent, und 2025 lag er bei vierzehn Prozent. Der Anteil steigt also, aber seit 2020 langsamer. Und selbst heute ist es nur ungefähr jede siebte Banane.

Out loud you round, translate percentages into pictures (*jede siebte Banane*), give the trend before the details and finish with what it means. You met the written Grafikbeschreibung in lesson 13; the oral version is shorter and more concrete.

## Mediating between two people

The hardest form of mediation is between two people who disagree. Your job is not to decide who is right but to make each position clear to the other and to find common ground. A meeting of a volunteer association that runs a *Weltladen* (a fair-trade shop):

```dialogue lang=de-DE
# Sitzung im Weltladen
Leonie: Wir sollten nur noch Produkte mit Fairtrade-Siegel verkaufen. Alles andere ist unglaubwürdig.
= We should only sell products with a Fairtrade label from now on. Anything else isn't credible.
Herr Demir: Dann verdoppeln sich bei manchen Waren die Preise, und die Kundschaft bleibt weg. Ein leerer Laden hilft niemandem im Globalen Süden.
= Then the prices of some goods double, and the customers stay away. An empty shop doesn't help anyone in the Global South.
Sophie: Darf ich kurz zusammenfassen? Leonie, dir geht es darum, dass der Laden glaubwürdig bleibt. Herr Demir, Ihnen geht es darum, dass er wirtschaftlich überlebt. Beide wollen Sie also, dass der Laden den Produzentinnen und Produzenten möglichst viel nützt.
= May I briefly sum up? Leonie, what matters to you is that the shop stays credible. Mr Demir, what matters to you is that it survives economically. So you both want the shop to benefit the producers as much as possible.
Herr Demir: Ja, so kann man das sagen.
= Yes, you could put it that way.
Sophie: Wäre es dann ein Kompromiss, bei Kaffee und Schokolade nur noch Siegelware anzubieten und bei den anderen Produkten schrittweise umzustellen?
= Would it then be a compromise to offer only certified goods for coffee and chocolate and to switch gradually for the other products?
```

Sophie does four things: she asks permission to sum up, paraphrases each position by its **interest** (*dir geht es darum, dass …*), names what both share (*Beide wollen Sie also …*), and only then proposes a compromise, as a question in Konjunktiv II. She doesn't say who is right. Notice she switches between *du* (Leonie) and *Sie* (Herr Demir): a mediator respects each person's form of address.

### Written minutes: Konjunktiv I

When you report the same meeting in writing, for people who weren't there, you use reported speech with Konjunktiv I (B2, and lesson 04 at C1). The minutes call the speakers by their surnames: Leonie is Frau Wolf, Sophie is Frau Yıldız.

> Frau Wolf sprach sich dafür aus, künftig nur noch Produkte mit Fairtrade-Siegel anzubieten; alles andere sei unglaubwürdig. Herr Demir gab zu bedenken, dass sich dann bei manchen Waren die Preise verdoppelten und Kundschaft verloren gehe. Frau Yıldız schlug als Kompromiss vor, bei Kaffee und Schokolade sofort und bei den übrigen Produkten schrittweise umzustellen.

*verdoppelten* is Konjunktiv II, because the Konjunktiv I *verdoppeln* looks like the indicative (replacement rule). The minutes keep the order of the discussion, name each speaker and give no verdict.

## Keeping your own view out

The quickest way to take sides by accident is the reporting verb. Compare:

| neutral | what it adds |
|---|---|
| *Er sagt / erklärt / betont, dass …* | nothing |
| *Sie weist darauf hin, dass …* | that it is a fact worth noticing |
| *Er gibt zu bedenken, dass …* | a careful objection |
| *Sie wendet ein, dass …* | an objection |

| loaded | what it suggests |
|---|---|
| *Er behauptet, dass …* | that the claim may be false |
| *Sie gibt zu, dass …* | that she admits a fault |
| *Er räumt ein, dass …* | that he concedes a point against his own position |
| *Sie unterstellt, dass …* | that she insinuates something unfair |

None of the loaded verbs is wrong; they are wrong only when the source doesn't support them. If Herr Demir simply said the prices would double, *Herr Demir behauptete …* adds your doubt, and *Herr Demir gab zu …* turns his argument into a confession.

Other ways your view slips in: adjectives (*das naive Argument*), particles (*Er meint ja, …*), and selection (leaving out the strongest point of one side). Read your text once only to check for these.

## The vocabulary of development

A few distinctions that a mediator needs to get right:

- *die Entwicklungshilfe* (development aid) is the older term; many organisations now prefer *die Entwicklungszusammenarbeit* (development cooperation), because "aid" suggests one side giving and the other receiving. The ministry speaks of *Entwicklungszusammenarbeit*; in everyday speech *Entwicklungshilfe* is still common. *die Entwicklungspolitik* is the policy field as a whole.
- *das Entwicklungsland* (developing country), *das Schwellenland* (emerging economy: "threshold country", on the threshold of industrialization), *der Globale Süden* (the Global South: a term for poorer countries, chosen because it describes a position in the world economy rather than a stage of development). *das Geberland* is a donor country.
- *das Wohlstandsgefälle* (the gap in prosperity, literally "prosperity gradient"), *die Verteilungsgerechtigkeit* (distributive justice, fairness in how wealth is shared).
- *die Nachhaltigkeitsziele* (the Sustainable Development Goals: seventeen goals adopted by the United Nations in 2015 as the 2030 Agenda), among them *Armutsbekämpfung* (fighting poverty) and *Ernährungssicherheit* (food security).
- *humanitär* refers to emergency help in crises (*humanitäre Hilfe, Hilfslieferungen, Hilfsgüter*), as opposed to long-term development work. *die Ernährungskrise* is a food crisis.
- *der Mikrokredit* (a very small loan, typically to start a small business), *die Selbsthilfe* (self-help), *der Schuldenerlass* (debt relief), *der Klimafonds* (a climate fund), *die Projektförderung* (project funding), *die Entwicklungsagentur* (a development agency).
- *korrupt* (corrupt) and *ausbeuten* (to exploit) are strong words; in mediation use them only when the source does.

## Pronunciation

- *das Lieferkettensorgfaltspflichtengesetz*: main stress on the first part, LIE-fer-ket-ten-…; read it in its parts, and in speech say *das Lieferkettengesetz*.
- *humanitär*: hu-ma-ni-TÄR, stress on the last syllable.
- *der Adressat*: a-dres-SAT, stress on the last syllable; *adressatengerecht*: a-dres-SA-ten-ge-recht.
- *der Fairtrade*: English pronunciation, roughly FÄHR-treit.

## Common mistakes

- Summarizing everything instead of selecting what the reader needs.
- Keeping the source's nominal style for a lay reader: ~~die Einrichtung eines Beschwerdeverfahrens~~ → *Arbeiter müssen sich beschweren können.*
- Adding facts or opinions that aren't in the source (*Das Gesetz bringt sowieso nichts*).
- Loaded reporting verbs: ~~Herr Demir behauptete, die Preise würden steigen~~ when he only said so.
- Forgetting the open status: a planned change (*soll abgeschafft werden*) is not a decided one (*ist abgeschafft*).
- Using one register for everybody: the chat to a friend and the e-mail to a managing director can't be the same text with a different greeting.

## Key points

- Mediation = passing content on: select what the reader needs, then reformulate for them (*adressatengerecht*).
- Put the *Kernbotschaft* first; follow the reader's question, not the source's order.
- Shift register: nominal → verbal, specialist terms → explanation or example, abbreviations → full words.
- Orally: round figures, give the trend first, make numbers concrete.
- Between people: summarize each position by its interest, name what they share, propose a compromise as a question.
- In written reports use Konjunktiv I and neutral reporting verbs (*sagen, betonen, hinweisen, zu bedenken geben, einwenden*); *behaupten, zugeben, unterstellen* take sides.
- Supply-chain facts as of November 2026: the LkSG applies to companies with 1,000 or more employees in Germany; a bill to drop the reporting duty was still in committee in the Bundestag, and the coalition had announced (July 2026) a law limiting the LkSG to companies with at least 5,000 employees and 1.5 billion euros' turnover; the amended EU directive (CSDDD) is to be transposed by July 2028 and applied from July 2029 to companies with more than 5,000 employees and 1.5 billion euros' turnover.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete the lesson.

lessons.title: The Goethe-Zertifikat C1 and review
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

This is the last core lesson of German C1. It says in plain words what C1 means, describes the best-known exam at this level, the Goethe-Zertifikat C1, with a strategy for each part, and reviews the grammar of the course with a table that points back to the lessons. Its questions mix exam knowledge with review from all six modules.

You don't need an exam to have reached C1. But C1 is the level many universities in German-speaking countries ask for, and many employers and professional bodies too, so it is worth knowing how the exam works. Requirements, fees and rules change: always check with the institution that asks for the certificate and with the exam centre.

## What C1 means

C1 is the fifth of the six CEFR levels, the lower of the two "proficient user" levels. In plain words, at C1 you:

- understand long, demanding texts and talks, including what is only implied, and recognize the writer's or speaker's attitude;
- speak fluently and spontaneously, without obviously searching for words, and when a word is missing, you find another way to say it;
- use German flexibly for social, academic and professional purposes, in the register that fits;
- write clear, well-structured texts on complex subjects, and control the connectors and pointing words that hold a text together.

Compared with B2, the difference is less about new grammar and more about range, precision and control. At B2 you could report what someone said; at C1 you report a whole argument across a paragraph and show your distance from it (04). At B2 you used the passive; at C1 you choose between the passive and five alternatives according to register (09). At B2 you could give your opinion; at C1 you concede part of the other side's case and still hold your ground (14, 28).

## The Goethe-Zertifikat C1

The exam for adults is modular: four separate *Module*, which you can take together or separately. The facts below come from the official Modellsatz (2nd edition, February 2024) and the Durchführungsbestimmungen (Stand 1 September 2023, valid for exams from 1 January 2024).

| module | time | parts and items | what you do |
|---|---|---|---|
| Lesen | 65 minutes | 4 parts, 30 items | a popular-science article with gaps (4 options each); a magazine or online article with 3-option multiple choice; a commentary with 8 gaps for 10 sentences (2 are extra); three short contributions by academics, with statements to match to them (2 statements fit nobody) |
| Hören | about 40 minutes | 4 parts, 30 items | a podcast presenting three books, heard once (match statements to the books); a radio interview with a scientist, heard twice (*stimmt / stimmt nicht / dazu wird nichts gesagt*); a discussion with a host and two guests, heard once in four sections (3-option multiple choice); a lecture, heard twice (3-option multiple choice) |
| Schreiben | 75 minutes | 2 parts | a forum post of about 230 words on a social question, with four content points (about 50 minutes); a half-formal message of about 120 words to a person in a hierarchy, such as a superior, with four points (about 25 minutes) |
| Sprechen | about 20 minutes in pairs (about 15 alone), plus 20 minutes' preparation | 2 parts | a talk of about 5 minutes on one of two topics, then questions; a discussion of about 5 minutes on a controversial question with a short input text |

The three written modules together take about 180 minutes, not counting breaks; if you take them on one day, the usual order is Lesen, Hören, Schreiben, and the Sprechen module normally comes after them. In Hören you have three minutes at the end to transfer your answers to the answer sheet, and you read the questions before each part.

### Points and grades

Each module is scored out of 100 and passed with 60. In Lesen and Hören each of the 30 items is worth one point, and the raw score is multiplied by 3.33 and rounded. Schreiben is marked by two raters independently and the average is taken (a third rater is called in for borderline cases); in Sprechen, two examiners mark the two parts separately, and the average counts.

| points | grade |
|---|---|
| 90–100 | sehr gut |
| 80–89 | gut |
| 70–79 | befriedigend |
| 60–69 | ausreichend |
| 0–59 | nicht bestanden |

Because the modules are separate, you can repeat only the one you didn't pass, as often as the exam centre's schedule allows. How results from different dates can be combined on certificates is governed by the exam regulations (*Prüfungsordnung*); ask the centre before you register.

The Goethe-Institut publishes the official materials for free:

- [Modellsatz Goethe-Zertifikat C1 (PDF)](https://www.goethe.de/pro/relaunch/prf/materialien/C1_modular/c1-modular_modellsatz.pdf), with answers, transcripts and marking criteria
- [Durchführungsbestimmungen Goethe-Zertifikat C1 (PDF)](https://www.goethe.de/pro/relaunch/prf/fr/Durchfuehrungsbestimmungen_C1_neu.pdf)

Do the whole Modellsatz once under exam conditions, about four weeks before the exam, and once more a few days before. The rest of this lesson tells you what to practise in between.

## Strategies: Lesen

Read the instructions and the example (*Beispiel 0*) of each part: they show exactly what counts as an answer. You may do the parts in any order; the recommended times add up to 65 minutes, so keep an eye on the clock.

| part | what helps | lessons |
|---|---|---|
| Teil 1: gap text, 4 options (about 10 min) | The gaps test grammar and fixed combinations: prepositions with verbs and nouns, connectors, *dazu/darauf*, FVG (*in Betracht ziehen*). Read the whole sentence, including what follows the gap. | 07, 10, 11, 22 |
| Teil 2: article, 3-option multiple choice (about 20 min) | Read the questions first, then the text. The right option usually paraphrases the text; an option that repeats the text's words exactly is often a trap. | 12, 24 |
| Teil 3: commentary, 8 of 10 sentences (about 20 min) | The sentences fit through cohesion: a pronoun (*dies, Letzteres*), a connector (*gleichwohl, folglich*) or a repeated idea must point to the sentence before and after the gap. Cross out sentences as you use them. | 10, 11 |
| Teil 4: three academics' contributions, 7 statements (about 15 min) | For each statement, find the passage, then check the attitude: does the author claim it, report it from others or reject it? Two statements fit nobody. | 02, 04, 05 |

In the matching parts it is often worth checking whether an author really says something or only mentions that others say it: *Manche Forscher behaupten, …* is not the author's own view. Konjunktiv I (*Es sei erwiesen, dass …*) also signals someone else's claim (04).

## Strategies: Hören

You read the questions before each part: 60 seconds before Teil 1 and Teil 2, 30 seconds before each section of Teil 3, 90 seconds before Teil 4. Use the time to underline the key words in each statement.

| part | what helps | lessons |
|---|---|---|
| Teil 1: podcast on three books, heard once | Keep a column for each book and note one or two key words while you listen. Statements often paraphrase the presenter's evaluation (*eher enttäuschend, lohnt sich vor allem für …*). | 12, 25 |
| Teil 2: radio interview, heard twice | *stimmt nicht* means the speaker says the opposite; *dazu wird nichts gesagt* means the topic comes up but not this point, or not at all. Don't choose *stimmt nicht* just because you didn't hear it. | 02, 04 |
| Teil 3: discussion with a host and two guests, heard once in four sections | Track who holds which view; listen for concession and contrast (*zwar …, aber; das mag sein, nur …*). Each section has two questions. | 14, 20, 28 |
| Teil 4: lecture, heard twice | Lectures are structured: *zunächst, im Folgenden, damit komme ich zu …* Use the first hearing for the outline and the second for details. | 08, 13, 23 |

Konjunktiv II past and Plusquamperfekt sound almost the same (*hatte/hätte, war/wäre*), and both appear in interviews: one says what happened, the other what didn't (03). Particles carry attitude: *eigentlich, ja, doch, eben* (16).

## Strategies: Schreiben

Both tasks give you four content points, and **[[Aufgabenerfüllung]]** (task fulfilment) is the first criterion: a text that covers three points well and forgets the fourth cannot get top marks. The model test's marking sheet also rates coherence (*Kohärenz*), vocabulary (*Wortschatz*) and grammar (*Strukturen*).

- **Teil 1, forum post (about 230 words, about 50 minutes).** Plan for five minutes: one sentence per point, an example for each, and your position. Use C1 connectors (*zumal, wobei, gleichwohl, insofern … als*) and pointing words (*Letzteres, dies*), but naturally, not as a list. Lesson 15 has the full method; lessons 11 and 14 the connectors.
- **Teil 2, half-formal message (about 120 words, about 25 minutes).** The register is the task: polite, clear and constructive to someone above you (*Ich würde gern anregen, …; Wäre es möglich, …?*). Address each point in a sentence or two; show understanding for the other side before you propose something (15).
- **Save ten minutes to check:** verb position after connectors, the cluster in subordinate clauses (*…, dass man es hätte vorhersehen können*), adjective endings, *dass/das*, commas before infinitive groups with *um, ohne, statt* and after a correlate (§ 73).

Word counts are guidelines (*circa*). Writing far less risks missing content; writing far more risks more mistakes and less time to check.

## Strategies: Sprechen

You prepare for 20 minutes alone and may make notes, but you speak freely. Lesson 28 has the phrases.

- **Teil 1, talk.** Choose the topic on which you have examples, not the one that sounds cleverer. Write a short outline with the four points, one example each and two or three key words per point, never full sentences. Announce the structure at the start and signpost each point. After the talk, answer your partner's questions, and ask about your partner's talk: questions and answers are part of the task, and the model test's marking sheet has a criterion for them (*Fragen/Antworten*).
- **Teil 2, discussion.** React to your partner: take up their points (*Ich möchte an das anknüpfen, was Sie gesagt haben*), concede and limit (*Da ist etwas dran, aber …*), and agree on something at the end, if the task asks for it. A discussion where each person gives a mini-talk is a weak discussion.
- **When a word is missing,** paraphrase it (*so etwas wie …; ein Gerät, mit dem man …*). Fluency counts more than one perfect word.

## Exam language

The words below come up in instructions, in descriptions of the exam and in the marking criteria. Several are general words of exam talk that you will meet in other exams' descriptions too.

- *der Prüfungsablauf* (the sequence of the exam), *die Bearbeitungszeit* (the time allowed for a task), *die Teilaufgabe* (a part of a task), *die Textsorte* (text type: *Forumsbeitrag, Kommentar, Vortrag*).
- *die Zuordnung* (matching): *Zuordnungsaufgaben*, tasks in which you match statements to texts or people.
- *der Hörtext*, *der Lesetext*; *der Vortragsteil* (the talk part of the speaking exam); *die Einleitungsfrage* (an opening question to warm up); *der Diskussionspartner, die Diskussionspartnerin*.
- *die Aufgabenerfüllung* (task fulfilment), *die Angemessenheit* (appropriateness, of register), *die Sprachrichtigkeit* (grammatical and lexical accuracy), *die Spannbreite* (range: *die Spannbreite des Wortschatzes*), *die Ausdrucksfähigkeit* (the ability to express oneself), *der Gesamteindruck* (overall impression).
- *die Gewichtung* (weighting) and *gewichten* (to weight): *Beide Teile werden gleich gewichtet* means both parts count equally. Check the current rules for the weighting of each module's parts; the model test shows the marking sheets.
- *die Prüfungsvorbereitung*, *die Lösungsstrategie* (a strategy for solving a task), *die Selbsteinschätzung* (self-assessment), *das Redemittel* (a useful phrase, the standard term in German language teaching), *das Sprachniveau* (level of language).

## Course review: where to look again

| topic | lessons |
|---|---|
| Modal verbs in every tense; subjective modals about the past (*Sie muss es gewusst haben*) | 01, 02 |
| Konjunktiv II of the past with modals and passive; irreal wishes, comparisons, consequence | 03 |
| Konjunktiv I in academic and extended reports; KI vs KII vs indicative as distance | 04 |
| Focus particles (*sogar, ausgerechnet, erst, lediglich*); modal particles at C1 | 05, 16 |
| Modality in rules; probability in forecasts | 05h1, 05h2 |
| Nominal style and back; Funktionsverbgefüge by function | 06, 07 |
| Participial attributes and participial clauses | 08 |
| Every alternative to the passive | 09 |
| *es*, correlates and pointing words | 10 |
| Cohesion: connectors, *Letzteres*, Thema-Rhema | 11 |
| Summary, graph description, Erörterung, forum post, message | 12–15 |
| Idioms, register, word formation | 17–19 |
| Information structure (Spaltsätze, Nachfeld) and negation | 20 |
| Legal conditionals, written-language prepositions, definitions | 21–23 |
| Continuing relative clauses (*was, weshalb, wodurch, wobei*); appositions | 24, 25 |
| Regional German; poetry and stylistic devices | 26, 27 |
| Speaking at C1; mediation | 28, 29 |

A good way to review: take one Modellsatz part, note every item you got wrong, and decide for each whether it was vocabulary, grammar, strategy or time. Then go back to the lesson in the table.

## Beyond C1

The next level, C2, is the highest on the CEFR scale; the Goethe-Institut offers an exam for it as well. For university admission in Germany there are also two exams designed for that purpose, TestDaF and the DSH (*Deutsche Sprachprüfung für den Hochschulzugang*). Which one a university accepts, and with which result, depends on the university and the programme. Their formats differ from the Goethe exam and have been revised in recent years, so check the current information from the providers before you prepare.

More important than the next certificate is the next book. At C1 you can read most of what native speakers read. The reading list for this course suggests newspapers, podcasts and literature to go on with.

## Common mistakes

- Treating the Modellsatz topics as predictions. Every exam has new topics; practise the task types, not the themes.
- In Hören Teil 2, choosing *stimmt nicht* when the point simply wasn't mentioned (that is *dazu wird nichts gesagt*).
- In Lesen Teil 3, choosing a sentence because it shares a word with the text, without checking that its pronoun or connector fits.
- In Schreiben, forgetting one of the four points, or writing the half-formal message in the register of a chat.
- In Sprechen, reading out full sentences from the notes, or not reacting to the partner.
- Not transferring the answers in Lesen: only the answer sheet is marked.

## Key points

- Goethe-Zertifikat C1, modular: Lesen 65 min (4 parts, 30 items), Hören about 40 min (4 parts, 30 items), Schreiben 75 min (forum post about 230 words, message about 120 words), Sprechen about 20 min in pairs plus 20 min preparation (talk about 5 min with questions, discussion about 5 min).
- Each module out of 100, pass at 60; grades at 90, 80, 70 and 60. Modules can be taken and repeated separately.
- Lesen: grammar in the gaps, paraphrase in the options, cohesion in the sentence gaps, attitude in the academic texts.
- Hören: read the questions first; *stimmt nicht* ≠ *dazu wird nichts gesagt*; track who says what.
- Schreiben and Sprechen: cover all four points, signpost, react to your partner, paraphrase when a word is missing.
- Review with the table, using your mistakes in the Modellsatz to choose what to repeat.

lessons.title: Kleist, Michael Kohlhaas: the long sentence
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Heinrich von Kleist (1777–1811) wrote some of the most gripping and most difficult prose in German. His sentences are long, packed with clauses and insertions, and they hold back the decisive word until the last moment. Learning to read one of them is the best training there is for the long periods of legal, academic and literary German.

This honors lesson reads the opening of *Michael Kohlhaas* (1810), Kleist's novella about a horse dealer whose sense of justice turns him into a robber and murderer. You will:

- map a long period into its main and subordinate clauses;
- recognize the insertions (appositions, adverbials between commas) that make it long;
- read the Konjunktiv II of the past with modal verbs in an older order (*würde … haben gelten können*);
- rewrite a period in modern German;
- learn the vocabulary of justice and revenge.

Kleist died in 1811, so his text is in the public domain. It is quoted from Projekt Gutenberg-DE (based on a Diogenes edition that follows the 1810 text), with Kleist's spelling (*Roßhändler, Rechtgefühl*) and punctuation; some modern editions normalize the commas.

## The novella and its background

*Michael Kohlhaas* has the subtitle *Aus einer alten Chronik* ("from an old chronicle"). A first part appeared in 1808 in the journal *Phöbus*; the complete text was published in 1810 in the first volume of Kleist's *Erzählungen*. The story is based on a real case: Hans Kohlhase, a merchant from Cölln near Berlin, who in the 1530s waged a private feud against Saxony after being wronged, and who was executed in Berlin in 1540.

In Kleist's version the story begins with a small injustice. On his way to a market in Saxony, Kohlhaas is stopped at the castle of the Junker Wenzel von Tronka and told he needs a pass. There is no such rule, but he has to leave two black horses and a servant behind as a pledge. When he returns, the horses have been worked half to death and the servant has been beaten and driven away. Kohlhaas goes to court, but the Junker's relatives at the court in Dresden make sure the complaint goes nowhere. His wife tries to hand a petition to the *Kurfürst* (the Elector, the ruler of a German state who took part in electing the emperor) and is fatally injured.

Then Kohlhaas declares a *Fehde* (a private feud, a medieval form of armed self-help), burns the Junker's castle and sets fire to Wittenberg and Leipzig. *Selbstjustiz* (taking the law into one's own hands) becomes *Rache* and *Vergeltung* (revenge and retribution). Martin Luther himself publishes an appeal to him and then receives him; an amnesty follows and fails; and at the end, in Berlin, Kohlhaas receives both justice and punishment: his horses are restored to him in their old condition and the Junker is punished, and Kohlhaas is executed for breaking the public peace.

The question Kleist asks is still open: when the state acts with *Willkür* (arbitrariness) and refuses justice, how far may a person go? Kohlhaas is *unbeugsam* (unbending), and his revenge becomes *maßlos* (without measure). The narrator calls him one of the most upright and at the same time most terrible men of his time.

## The opening paragraph

> An den Ufern der Havel lebte, um die Mitte des sechzehnten Jahrhunderts, ein Roßhändler, namens Michael Kohlhaas, Sohn eines Schulmeisters, einer der rechtschaffensten zugleich und entsetzlichsten Menschen seiner Zeit. – Dieser außerordentliche Mann würde, bis in sein dreißigstes Jahr für das Muster eines guten Staatsbürgers haben gelten können. Er besaß in einem Dorfe, das noch von ihm den Namen führt, einen Meierhof, auf welchem er sich durch sein Gewerbe ruhig ernährte; die Kinder, die ihm sein Weib schenkte, erzog er, in der Furcht Gottes, zur Arbeitsamkeit und Treue; nicht einer war unter seinen Nachbarn, der sich nicht seiner Wohltätigkeit, oder seiner Gerechtigkeit erfreut hätte; kurz, die Welt würde sein Andenken haben segnen müssen, wenn er in einer Tugend nicht ausgeschweift hätte. Das Rechtgefühl aber machte ihn zum Räuber und Mörder.

**Translation (written for this course).** On the banks of the Havel there lived, around the middle of the sixteenth century, a horse dealer by the name of Michael Kohlhaas, the son of a schoolmaster, one of the most upright and at the same time most terrible men of his age. — This extraordinary man could have passed, until his thirtieth year, for the model of a good citizen. In a village that still bears his name he owned a farm, on which he made a quiet living from his trade; the children his wife bore him he brought up, in the fear of God, to be hard-working and loyal; there was not one among his neighbours who had not enjoyed his kindness or his fairness; in short, the world would have had to bless his memory, had he not gone to excess in one virtue. But his sense of justice made him a robber and a murderer.

Some older words:

- *der Roßhändler*: today spelled *der Rosshändler* (*das Ross*, a horse, now poetic or regional, + *der Händler*).
- *rechtschaffen*: upright, honest. *entsetzlich*: terrible, dreadful.
- *der Meierhof*: a large farm (historical).
- *das Weib*: wife, woman. In Kleist's time a neutral word in this sense; today it is pejorative (except in fixed phrases).
- *ausschweifen*: to go to excess (today mostly as the adjective *ausschweifend*, dissolute).
- *das Rechtgefühl*: Kleist's form. Today's word is *das Rechtsgefühl*, with a linking *-s*: a sense of right and wrong, of justice.

## Mapping the period

Kleist's style is **[[hypotaxis]]** (*die Hypotaxe*): sentences built from a main clause and layers of subordinate clauses and insertions. Its opposite is **[[parataxis]]** (*die Parataxe*): short main clauses side by side. A main clause with its subordinate clauses is a **[[Satzgefüge]]** (complex sentence); a sentence in which clauses are nested inside each other, so that the reader has to hold the beginning in mind until the end, is a *Schachtelsatz* ("box sentence"), a word often used with a critical edge.

Take the paragraph apart sentence by sentence.

**Sentence 1** is a single main clause with no subordinate clause at all. It is long because of what is inserted:

| part | function |
|---|---|
| *An den Ufern der Havel* | place, in the Vorfeld |
| *lebte* | finite verb in position 2 |
| *, um die Mitte des sechzehnten Jahrhunderts,* | time, between commas |
| *ein Roßhändler* | the subject, held back until after the verb |
| *, namens Michael Kohlhaas,* | his name |
| *Sohn eines Schulmeisters,* | apposition 1 |
| *einer der rechtschaffensten zugleich und entsetzlichsten Menschen seiner Zeit.* | apposition 2: the judgement |

The order is that of a chronicle: place, time, person, name, origin, and then, at the very end, the paradox that drives the whole story: *rechtschaffen* and *entsetzlich* at once. The word *zugleich* is placed between the two adjectives, which makes the reader stop at the contradiction.

**Sentence 2** has a Konjunktiv II of the past with a modal verb: *würde … haben gelten können* (would have been able to pass for). Today you would write *hätte … gelten können* (lesson 03). Kleist uses *würde* + *haben* + double infinitive, a form that was possible in his time and survives only in very formal style. The meaning is the same: he could have been regarded as a model citizen, but he wasn't, as we are about to learn.

**Sentence 3** is the longest: four main clauses joined by semicolons, each a step in the portrait.

1. *Er besaß … einen Meierhof, auf welchem er sich … ruhig ernährte;* with a relative clause on *Dorfe* (*das noch von ihm den Namen führt*) and one on *Meierhof* with *welcher* (formal).
2. *die Kinder, die ihm sein Weib schenkte, erzog er … zur Arbeitsamkeit und Treue;* the object *die Kinder* comes first, with its relative clause, then the verb.
3. *nicht einer war unter seinen Nachbarn, der sich nicht seiner Wohltätigkeit … erfreut hätte;* a double negation that means "everyone". The relative clause is in Konjunktiv II (*erfreut hätte*) because it depends on a negated main clause: there was no one of whom this would not be true. *sich einer Sache erfreuen* (genitive) is formal for "to enjoy".
4. *kurz, die Welt würde sein Andenken haben segnen müssen, wenn er in einer Tugend nicht ausgeschweift hätte.* An irreal condition (lesson 03): the world would have had to bless his memory, *if he had not gone to excess in one virtue*. Again *würde … haben … müssen* where today we'd write *hätte … segnen müssen*.

**Sentence 4** is suddenly short: *Das Rechtgefühl aber machte ihn zum Räuber und Mörder.* After a whole paragraph of praise, nine words reveal that the virtue in sentence 3 is his sense of justice, and that it is his ruin. The long period builds tension; the short sentence releases it. *aber* after the subject (not at the start) stresses *Das Rechtgefühl*: it was precisely his sense of justice that did it.

Notice too what Kleist's commas do. Many of them would not be required, or even allowed, today (*würde, bis in sein dreißigstes Jahr für …*; *seiner Wohltätigkeit, oder seiner Gerechtigkeit*). They are rhetorical: they mark pauses for breath and emphasis rather than grammar. That is why quotations keep them exactly, and why you should not copy them in your own writing.

## Rewriting a period in modern German

A useful exercise with any long sentence is to rewrite it as several modern sentences. That shows you understood it, and it is the skill you need when you summarize a dense text for someone else (lesson 29). Sentence 3 in modern German might read:

> Er besaß einen Bauernhof in einem Dorf, das heute noch seinen Namen trägt, und verdiente dort mit seinem Handel ruhig seinen Lebensunterhalt. Seine Kinder erzog er gottesfürchtig, fleißig und treu. Alle seine Nachbarn hatten seine Hilfsbereitschaft oder seine Gerechtigkeit erfahren. Kurz: Man hätte ihn in guter Erinnerung behalten müssen, wenn er es mit einer Tugend nicht übertrieben hätte.

Compare what is lost. The modern version is clearer, but the suspense is gone: Kleist's reader has to wait for the verb, the subject and the point, and that waiting is part of the meaning. When you rewrite, keep the facts and the logic, and say in a sentence what the original's form achieves.

A method for any long period:

1. Find the finite verbs and mark the main clause(s).
2. Bracket the insertions between commas or dashes; read the sentence once without them.
3. Identify each subordinate clause and what it depends on (*der, welcher, wenn, dass*).
4. Note the mood (indicative, Konjunktiv) and what it tells you about reality.
5. Rewrite as short sentences, then compare.

## Justice and revenge: talking about the theme

- *die Selbstjustiz*: taking the law into one's own hands. *Kohlhaas übt Selbstjustiz, weil die Gerichte versagen.*
- *die Rache* (revenge), *sich an jemandem für etwas rächen* (to take revenge on someone for something), *jemanden/etwas rächen* (to avenge): *Er will den Tod seiner Frau rächen.*
- *die Vergeltung*: retribution, repayment of a wrong (more formal than *Rache*).
- *die Willkür*: arbitrariness, arbitrary use of power; *willkürlich*: arbitrary. *die Willkür der Behörden.*
- *die Fehde*: a feud; in the Middle Ages a recognized form of private war, banned in the Holy Roman Empire by the Ewiger Landfriede of 1495.
- *das Rechtsgefühl*: a sense of justice. *Sein Rechtsgefühl ist verletzt.*
- *unbeugsam* (unbending, uncompromising), *maßlos* (immoderate, without limits): *maßlose Rache*.
- *der Kurfürst*: an Elector, one of the princes who elected the emperor. In the story two of them play a part: the Elector of Saxony and the Elector of Brandenburg.

Useful frames for discussing the story:

- *Kohlhaas' Rache ist zwar verständlich, aber maßlos.*
- *Man kann die Novelle als Frage nach dem Verhältnis von Recht und Gerechtigkeit lesen.*
- *Ab dem Moment, in dem …, schlägt sein Rechtsgefühl in Rache um.*

## Common mistakes

- Reading *würde … haben gelten können* as a future. It is Konjunktiv II of the past: "could have passed for".
- Taking *nicht einer …, der sich nicht … erfreut hätte* as negative. Two negations: everyone had enjoyed his kindness.
- Copying Kleist's commas into your own texts. Quote them exactly; write today's rules yourself.
- Writing *Rechtgefühl* in your own text: the modern word is *Rechtsgefühl*.
- Confusing *rächen* (avenge) and *sich rächen* (take revenge): *Er rächt seine Frau* vs *Er rächt sich an dem Junker*.

## Key points

- *Michael Kohlhaas* (complete 1810): a horse dealer's sense of justice turns into revenge when the state refuses him justice.
- Kleist's style is hypotaxis: long *Satzgefüge*, insertions between commas, the decisive word held back; then a short sentence for the turn.
- Map a period: finite verbs, main clauses, insertions, subordinate clauses, mood; then rewrite in short sentences.
- *würde … haben gelten können / segnen müssen* is an older form of the Konjunktiv II past with a modal (today *hätte … gelten können*).
- The KII in *nicht einer war …, der … erfreut hätte* comes from the negated main clause.
- Kleist's punctuation is rhetorical: keep it in quotations, don't imitate it.
