lessons.title: Einstellung, Schnitt, Rückblende: talking about film
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Talking about a film you liked is B1. Analysing how a film creates its effect, how the camera, the editing and the sound make you feel what you feel, needs a vocabulary of its own. German film criticism, school film analysis and the Feuilleton all use it, and it is also handy in conversation (*Hast du die Szene mit der Rückblende gesehen?*).

This honors lesson teaches you:

- the terms for shot sizes, camera angles and camera movement;
- editing, flashbacks, sound and the arc of suspense;
- how to describe a scene: present tense, *man sieht*, Zustandspassiv, participles;
- a short introduction to the cinema of the Weimar Republic, one of the great periods of German film;
- how to write a short sequence analysis (*Sequenzanalyse*).

## Shot sizes: how close is the camera?

You know *die Einstellung* (B2) as the hiring of staff and as an attitude. In film it means a shot: one uninterrupted piece of film between two cuts. The **[[shot size]]** (*die Einstellungsgröße*) says how much of the scene the frame shows. German film analysis usually distinguishes these:

| German | English | what you see | typical effect |
|---|---|---|---|
| *die Totale* | long shot, establishing shot | a whole landscape, a street, a room with people in it | overview, orientation; people look small |
| *die Halbtotale* | full shot | people from head to foot, with some surroundings | action, movement |
| *die Halbnahe* | medium shot | people from the knees or hips up | conversation, interaction |
| *die Nahaufnahme* (*die Nahe*) | close shot | head and shoulders | facial expression, emotion |
| *die Großaufnahme* | close-up | the face fills the frame | intense emotion, closeness |
| *die Detailaufnahme* | extreme close-up | a part of the face, an object | attention to one detail |

*die Großaufnahme* is the term most often used in conversation; in English it is a "close-up". The *Nahaufnahme* is a little further away. The words combine with *in*: *in der Totale, in Großaufnahme* (often without the article).

## Camera angle and movement

The **[[camera angle]]** (*die Kameraperspektive*) is the height from which the camera looks:

- *die Normalsicht*: at eye level; the neutral angle.
- *die Froschperspektive* (*die Untersicht*): from below, "frog's perspective". The person filmed looks big, powerful or threatening.
- *die Vogelperspektive* (*die Aufsicht*): from above, "bird's perspective". People look small, lost or controlled.

*die Kameraführung* is how the camera is handled as a whole, and especially how it moves:

- *der Schwenk*: the camera turns on the spot, left and right or up and down (*die Kamera schwenkt über den Platz*).
- *die Kamerafahrt*: the camera itself moves (*die Kamera fährt auf das Haus zu*, moves towards the house; *fährt zurück*, pulls back).
- *der Zoom*: the lens changes the shot size without the camera moving.
- *die Handkamera*: a hand-held camera; the image shakes slightly, which suggests immediacy or nervousness.

## Editing, time and sound

- *der Schnitt* is both the cut between two shots and editing as a whole (*Der Film hat einen schnellen Schnitt*). *die Montage* is editing as an art, the way shots are put together to create meaning; at B2 you learned that *die Montage* is also the assembly of parts in a factory.
- *die Rückblende* is a flashback: the film jumps back in time. The opposite, a jump forward, is *die Vorausblende*.
- *der Spannungsbogen* is the arc of suspense: how tension builds, peaks and is released over a scene or a whole film.
- *der Vorspann* comes before the film (opening titles), *der Abspann* after it (end credits). *Wir sind bis zum Ende des Abspanns sitzen geblieben.*
- *die Filmmusik* is the soundtrack music; *die Geräusche* are the sound effects; *die Stimme aus dem Off* is a voice-over, a voice whose speaker you don't see.
- *die Kulisse* is the set or scenery (also on stage); *vor einer gemalten Kulisse* is in front of painted scenery.

## Describing a scene

A scene description uses the present tense, whatever the time of the story, and a small set of constructions. Lesson 15h2 used the same tools for pictures.

- *man sieht / ist zu sehen*: *In der ersten Einstellung sieht man eine leere Straße.* · *Im Hintergrund ist ein Bahnhof zu sehen.*
- the Zustandspassiv and participles: *Der Raum ist nur schwach beleuchtet.* · *Die von unten gefilmte Figur wirkt bedrohlich.*
- the camera as subject: *Die Kamera fährt langsam auf das Fenster zu. · Die Kamera folgt der Frau durch die Menge.*
- effect: *Dadurch entsteht der Eindruck, dass … · Die Froschperspektive lässt den Mann übermächtig erscheinen. · Die Musik verstärkt die Spannung.*
- hedging the interpretation: *Man könnte die Einstellung so deuten, dass … · Offenbar soll gezeigt werden, wie …*

Keep description and interpretation apart: first what is on screen, then what it does.

## A sequence analysis

An original analysis of a scene from an invented short film, *Die letzte Fähre*. Notice the order: context, description shot by shot, interpretation.

> In der Schlüsselsequenz des Kurzfilms „Die letzte Fähre“ wartet die Hauptfigur Mara nachts am Ufer auf die Fähre, mit der ihr Bruder zurückkehren soll. Die Sequenz beginnt mit einer Totale: Der Anleger liegt im Nebel, Mara ist nur als kleine Gestalt am Bildrand zu sehen. Die Kamera bleibt lange statisch; man hört nur das Wasser und in der Ferne ein Signalhorn. Dann folgt ein Schnitt auf eine Großaufnahme ihres Gesichts. In einer kurzen Rückblende, die in warmen Farben gehalten ist, sieht man die Geschwister als Kinder auf derselben Fähre. Zurück in der Gegenwart fährt die Kamera langsam zurück, bis Mara wieder in der Totale verschwindet. Die Fähre kommt nicht.
>
> Die Sequenz lebt vom Kontrast der Einstellungsgrößen. Die Totale zeigt Maras Einsamkeit, die Großaufnahme ihre Hoffnung; die Rückfahrt der Kamera nimmt diese Hoffnung wieder zurück. Auch die Farben sind gegensätzlich gestaltet: Die Vergangenheit erscheint warm, die Gegenwart kalt und grau. Weil auf Filmmusik verzichtet wird, wirkt die Stille umso bedrückender. Der Spannungsbogen der Sequenz endet bewusst ohne Auflösung; der Zuschauer bleibt wie Mara im Ungewissen.

**Translation.** In the key sequence of the short film *The Last Ferry*, the main character Mara waits on the shore at night for the ferry on which her brother is supposed to return. The sequence begins with a long shot: the landing stage lies in the fog; Mara can be seen only as a small figure at the edge of the frame. The camera stays still for a long time; all you hear is the water and, in the distance, a horn. Then there is a cut to a close-up of her face. In a short flashback, kept in warm colours, we see the brother and sister as children on the same ferry. Back in the present, the camera slowly pulls back until Mara disappears again in the long shot. The ferry doesn't come.

The sequence lives from the contrast of shot sizes. The long shot shows Mara's loneliness, the close-up her hope; the camera's pulling back takes this hope away again. The colours are designed as opposites too: the past appears warm, the present cold and grey. Because there is no film music, the silence feels all the more oppressive. The sequence's arc of suspense deliberately ends without resolution; like Mara, the viewer is left in uncertainty.

Notice: present tense throughout; *ist … zu sehen*; the Zustandspassiv *ist … gehalten*, *sind … gestaltet*; the passive *wird … verzichtet* (*auf etwas verzichten*: to do without something, here with an impersonal passive); and the link between each technical observation and its effect (*zeigt Maras Einsamkeit; wirkt … bedrückender*).

## Weimar cinema in brief

In the years of the Weimar Republic (1918–1933), German cinema was one of the most inventive in the world. A few landmarks, all silent films (*Stummfilme*) except the last:

- *Das Cabinet des Dr. Caligari* (Robert Wiene, 1920): the classic of film Expressionism. The town is a painted *Kulisse* of crooked houses, slanting streets and painted shadows; the sets show the inner world of the characters, not a real place.
- *Nosferatu – Eine Symphonie des Grauens* (Friedrich Wilhelm Murnau, 1922): an early vampire film, famous for its use of shadows.
- *Der letzte Mann* (Murnau, 1924): the story of a hotel doorman who loses his post, told almost without intertitles. The camera moves freely through the rooms and streets; critics spoke of the *entfesselte Kamera*, the "unchained camera".
- *Metropolis* (Fritz Lang, 1927): a vast vision of a future city divided between the rich above and the workers below, with huge sets and crowds.
- *M* (Fritz Lang, 1931): an early sound film about the hunt for a child murderer. Lang uses sound as a means of storytelling: the murderer is recognized by a melody he whistles.

Many of the people who made these films, Lang among them, left Germany after 1933, and several shaped Hollywood cinema afterwards.

When you write about these films, describe what you see and refer to scenes by their content; don't quote intertitles or screenplays at length.

## Pronunciation

- *die Totale*: to-TA-le, stress on the second syllable.
- *die Kulisse*: ku-LIS-se.
- *die Froschperspektive*: FROSCH-per-spek-ti-ve, main stress on *Frosch*.
- *Nosferatu*: nos-fe-RA-tu. *Murnau*: MUR-nau.

## Common mistakes

- Telling the story instead of analysing it. A sequence analysis describes how the film shows something, not only what happens.
- Using the past tense: ~~Die Kamera fuhr auf das Haus zu.~~ → *Die Kamera fährt auf das Haus zu.*
- Calling every close shot a *Totale*: *die Totale* is the widest shot, the opposite of the *Großaufnahme*.
- Mixing up *Vorspann* (before) and *Abspann* (after).
- Naming a technique without its effect: *eine Froschperspektive* alone is not yet an analysis; *die Froschperspektive lässt ihn übermächtig wirken* is.

## Key points

- Shot sizes: *Totale, Halbtotale, Halbnahe, Nahaufnahme, Großaufnahme, Detailaufnahme*.
- Angles: *Normalsicht, Froschperspektive* (from below), *Vogelperspektive* (from above); movement: *Schwenk, Kamerafahrt, Zoom, Handkamera*; all together: *die Kameraführung*.
- Editing and time: *Schnitt, Montage, Rückblende*; structure: *Spannungsbogen, Vorspann, Abspann*; sound: *Filmmusik, Geräusche, Stimme aus dem Off*.
- Describe in the present, with *man sieht / ist zu sehen*, the Zustandspassiv and the camera as subject; then interpret, with hedges.
- Weimar cinema: *Caligari* (1920), *Nosferatu* (1922), *Der letzte Mann* (1924), *Metropolis* (1927), *M* (1931).

lessons.title: Kant, Was ist Aufklärung?: reading philosophical German
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

This honors module reads German that thinks: a philosopher, two collectors of fairy tales who became the founders of German linguistics, the history of the language itself, and a scientist who wanted to describe the whole of nature in one book. Each lesson combines short quotations from public-domain originals with original texts and practice written for this course.

The first text is one of the most quoted essays in German: Immanuel Kant's answer to the question *Was ist Aufklärung?* (What is Enlightenment?), published in December 1784. Its first paragraph contains the most famous definition in German philosophy and a motto that is still printed on posters, mugs and university buildings.

You will read the opening and three key passages with notes; learn to cope with older spelling (*Muth, Theil, seyn*) and older grammar (genitive objects, a finite verb left out, *derselbe* as a pronoun); and paraphrase, summarize (lesson 12) and comment on (lesson 14) Kant's argument.

## Kant and the question of 1784

Immanuel Kant (1724–1804) spent his whole life in and around Königsberg in East Prussia (today Kaliningrad), where he taught at the university. His *Kritik der reinen Vernunft* (1781) is famously hard to read; the essay on enlightenment is short and almost conversational in places, written for the readers of a monthly magazine, the *Berlinische Monatsschrift*.

The magazine had printed an article on marriage in which a Berlin pastor, Johann Friedrich Zöllner, asked in a footnote what "enlightenment" actually was, since everyone used the word. Several writers answered; Kant's answer appeared in the December issue of 1784 under the title *Beantwortung der Frage: Was ist Aufklärung?* Kant died in 1804, so the text has long been in the public domain.

The quotations below follow the text of the 1913 edition of Kant's works by Ernst Cassirer (Project Gutenberg no. 30821). That edition modernizes the spelling and some of the punctuation (*Mut* for *Muth*), but keeps Kant's words and sentence structure. Further down you'll see what the 1784 print looks like.

## The opening: a definition in four steps

> „Aufklärung ist der Ausgang des Menschen aus seiner selbstverschuldeten Unmündigkeit. Unmündigkeit ist das Unvermögen, sich seines Verstandes ohne Leitung eines anderen zu bedienen. Selbstverschuldet ist diese Unmündigkeit, wenn die Ursache derselben nicht am Mangel des Verstandes, sondern der Entschließung und des Mutes liegt, sich seiner ohne Leitung eines andern zu bedienen. Sapere aude! Habe Mut, dich deines eigenen Verstandes zu bedienen! ist also der Wahlspruch der Aufklärung.“

> "Enlightenment is man's emergence from his self-incurred immaturity. Immaturity is the inability to make use of one's understanding without the guidance of another. This immaturity is self-incurred when its cause lies not in a lack of understanding but in a lack of resolution and courage to use it without the guidance of another. Sapere aude! Have the courage to use your own understanding! is therefore the motto of enlightenment."

(The English is a translation for this course.)

### How the paragraph is built

Look at how each sentence picks up the end of the one before:

1. *Aufklärung ist … Unmündigkeit.* The new word comes last.
2. *Unmündigkeit ist das Unvermögen, …* The last word of sentence 1 becomes the subject of sentence 2 and is defined.
3. *Selbstverschuldet ist diese Unmündigkeit, wenn …* Now the adjective *selbstverschuldet* from sentence 1 is explained. Kant puts it in the Vorfeld, before the verb, to link back.
4. *Sapere aude! … ist also der Wahlspruch der Aufklärung.* The word *also* (therefore) draws the conclusion, and the paragraph ends with *Aufklärung*, the word it began with.

This is the known-before-new order of lesson 11 (Thema-Rhema), used with great discipline, and one reason the passage is easy to remember.

The key terms:

- *die Unmündigkeit*: from *der Mund*? No: from the old word *die Munt*, protection or guardianship (as in *der Vormund*, guardian). *mündig* means "of age", legally able to act for oneself; *unmündig* is someone who still needs a guardian, such as a child. Kant turns the legal word into a description of the mind. Today *mündig* is a common word in politics and education: *der mündige Bürger*, *Erziehung zur Mündigkeit*.
- *der Verstand*: understanding, intellect (*Hast du den Verstand verloren?* Have you lost your mind?). In Kant's technical philosophy *Verstand* and *Vernunft* (reason) are different faculties; this essay uses them in a looser, everyday way.
- *die Leitung*: guidance. *das Unvermögen*: inability. *die Entschließung*: resolution, decision (today *der Entschluss*; *die Entschließung* now means a resolution passed by a parliament).
- *Sapere aude*: Latin, "dare to be wise", a line from the Roman poet Horace. Kant translates it freely as *Habe Mut, dich deines eigenen Verstandes zu bedienen!*

### sich einer Sache bedienen: verbs with a genitive object

The phrase that occurs three times in the paragraph is *sich seines Verstandes bedienen*: to make use of one's understanding. The verb *sich bedienen* takes a **[[genitive object]]**:

- *sich seines Verstandes bedienen* — to use one's understanding
- *sich seiner bedienen* — to use it (*seiner* is the genitive of *er*, referring back to *der Verstand*)

In modern German the genitive object is rare and mostly formal. The few verbs that still take one are worth recognizing, because they appear in exactly the kind of text this module reads:

| verb | example | everyday alternative |
|---|---|---|
| *sich einer Sache bedienen* | *Er bediente sich eines Tricks.* | *einen Trick benutzen* |
| *einer Sache bedürfen* (gehoben) | *Das bedarf einer Erklärung.* | *Das braucht eine Erklärung.* |
| *jemandes / einer Sache gedenken* | *Wir gedenken der Opfer.* | *an die Opfer erinnern* |
| *sich einer Sache enthalten* | *Sie enthielt sich der Stimme.* | *Sie stimmte nicht ab.* |
| *jemanden einer Sache beschuldigen* | *Man beschuldigte ihn des Diebstahls.* | *Man warf ihm Diebstahl vor.* |

*sich der Stimme enthalten* (to abstain in a vote) and *der Opfer gedenken* are standard in news German; the others sound bookish in conversation. For a genitive pronoun like *seiner* (of him/it) or *ihrer* (of her/them), ask what masculine or neuter noun came before: in *sich seiner … zu bedienen*, it is *der Verstand*.

### derselbe as a pronoun

*die Ursache derselben*: the cause of it, its cause. *derselben* is the genitive feminine of *derselbe* (the same), used here simply as a pronoun for *diese Unmündigkeit*. Today you would write *ihre Ursache* or *die Ursache dafür*. This use of *derselbe / dieselbe / dasselbe* as a plain "it" survives in old-fashioned official German (*Der Antrag ist vollständig auszufüllen; eine Kopie desselben ist beizulegen.*), and style guides advise against it. In lesson 11 you meet *derselbe* in its living sense, "the same one".

### A modern paraphrase

One good way to check that you've understood a difficult text is to paraphrase it in plain, modern German:

> Aufklärung bedeutet, dass Menschen aufhören, sich von anderen sagen zu lassen, was sie denken sollen. Wer nicht selbstständig denkt, ist unmündig. Daran ist man selbst schuld, wenn man durchaus denken könnte, sich aber nicht traut oder sich nicht entscheiden kann. Deshalb lautet das Motto der Aufklärung: Trau dich, selbst zu denken!

> Enlightenment means that people stop letting others tell them what to think. Anyone who doesn't think independently is immature. It is your own fault if you could think perfectly well but don't dare to or can't make up your mind. That's why the motto of enlightenment is: Dare to think for yourself!

Genitive objects become ordinary verbs, abstract nouns become clauses (*Mangel der Entschließung* → *sich nicht entscheiden können*): the reverse of the nominal style of module 2.

## Why people stay immature

The second paragraph asks why so many people remain in this state:

> „Faulheit und Feigheit sind die Ursachen, warum ein so großer Teil der Menschen, nachdem sie die Natur längst von fremder Leitung freigesprochen (naturaliter maiorennes), dennoch gerne zeitlebens unmündig bleiben; und warum es anderen so leicht wird, sich zu deren Vormündern aufzuwerfen. Es ist so bequem, unmündig zu sein.“

> "Laziness and cowardice are the reasons why so great a part of mankind, after nature has long since released them from the guidance of others (naturaliter maiorennes: of age by nature), nevertheless gladly remain immature for life; and why it is so easy for others to set themselves up as their guardians. It is so comfortable to be immature."

Three things in this sentence are typical of 18th-century German and confuse modern readers.

**1. The missing auxiliary.** *nachdem sie die Natur längst von fremder Leitung freigesprochen* — where is the finite verb? In today's German it would be *freigesprochen **hat***. Writers of the 18th and 19th centuries often left out the auxiliary *haben* or *sein* at the end of a subordinate clause. This **[[dropped auxiliary]]** (*afinite Konstruktion*) is not an error but a feature of the written style of the period; you'll find it in Kant, Goethe and Kleist. When a subordinate clause seems to end without a finite verb, supply *hat/haben* or *ist/sind* in your head:

- *…, nachdem er das Haus verlassen (hatte), …*
- *…, als die Nachricht eingetroffen (war), …*

In *sie die Natur*, *sie* (the people) is the object and *die Natur* the subject: pronouns come first in the Mittelfeld. *freisprechen* (normally "to acquit") here means "to declare free".

**2. Agreement by sense.** *ein so großer Teil der Menschen … bleiben*: the subject is singular (*ein Teil*), but the verb is plural because Kant is thinking of the people (*sie*). Today the singular is the norm (*ein großer Teil der Menschen bleibt*), though Duden also accepts the plural after such phrases.

**3. *deren* and *es wird leicht*.** *sich zu deren Vormündern aufzuwerfen*: to set themselves up as *their* guardians; *sich zu etwas aufwerfen* is still used, always critically. *es wird anderen leicht* is older German for *es fällt anderen leicht*.

Then the short sentence that everyone remembers: *Es ist so bequem, unmündig zu sein.* After the long period, four words of everyday German.

Kant then gives examples of the guardians we choose ourselves:

> „Habe ich ein Buch, das für mich Verstand hat, einen Seelsorger, der für mich Gewissen hat, einen Arzt, der für mich die Diät beurteilt usw., so brauche ich mich ja nicht selbst zu bemühen.“

> "If I have a book that has understanding for me, a pastor who has a conscience for me, a doctor who decides on my diet for me, and so on, then I need not trouble myself."

This is a verb-first conditional (B2) resumed by *so*: *Habe ich …, so brauche ich …* = *Wenn ich … habe, (dann) brauche ich …*; the *so* is typical of older and legal German (lesson 21). Note the modal particle *ja* (of course): Kant speaks ironically in the voice of the comfortable reader. *nicht zu … brauchen* is the negative of *müssen*.

What the guardians practise is what German today calls *die Bevormundung*: treating adults like children. *bevormunden* is common in political debate, always as a reproach: *Die Bürger wollen nicht bevormundet werden.*

## Public and private use of reason

The heart of the essay is a distinction that surprises modern readers, because Kant uses "public" and "private" almost the other way round from how we use them today.

> „Der öffentliche Gebrauch seiner Vernunft muß jederzeit frei sein, und der allein kann Aufklärung unter Menschen zustande bringen; der Privatgebrauch derselben aber darf öfters sehr enge eingeschränkt sein, ohne doch darum den Fortschritt der Aufklärung sonderlich zu hindern.“

> "The public use of one's reason must always be free, and it alone can bring about enlightenment among men; the private use of it, however, may often be very narrowly restricted without particularly hindering the progress of enlightenment."

He defines both:

> „Ich verstehe aber unter dem öffentlichen Gebrauche seiner eigenen Vernunft denjenigen, den jemand als Gelehrter von ihr vor dem ganzen Publikum der Leserwelt macht. Den Privatgebrauch nenne ich denjenigen, den er in einem gewissen ihm anvertrauten bürgerlichen Posten oder Amte von seiner Vernunft machen darf.“

> "By the public use of one's own reason I mean that use which anyone makes of it as a scholar before the entire reading public. I call private use that which one may make of one's reason in a certain civil post or office entrusted to him."

So:

| | **[[public use of reason]]** (*öffentlicher Vernunftgebrauch*) | **[[private use of reason]]** (*Privatgebrauch der Vernunft*) |
|---|---|---|
| who | anyone, speaking as a *Gelehrter* (scholar), i.e. writing for the reading public | the same person in an office or job (officer, civil servant, clergyman, taxpayer) |
| freedom | must always be free | may be restricted |
| Kant's example | an officer may publish a critique of military mistakes | the same officer must obey an order on duty |

A *Gelehrter* in Kant's sense is not only a professor but anyone who writes for the public in their own name. Note the function-verb phrase behind the definitions: *von etwas Gebrauch machen* (to make use of something).

Grammar notes: *muß* is the pre-1996 spelling of *muss*; *dem Gebrauche, im Amte* show the old dative *-e* (lesson 91); *der allein kann* uses *der* as a stressed demonstrative (this use alone); *denjenigen, den …* is formal "the one that"; *einem gewissen ihm anvertrauten bürgerlichen Posten* contains a participle attribute (module 2); *sonderlich* is old-fashioned for *besonders* and survives mainly in the negative (*nicht sonderlich begeistert*).

Kant sums up the political side with a remark he attributes to his king, Frederick II of Prussia:

> „Räsonniert, soviel ihr wollt und worüber ihr wollt, aber gehorcht!“

> "Argue as much as you like and about whatever you like, but obey!"

*räsonnieren* (from French *raisonner*) meant to reason, to discuss. Today the word is spelled *räsonieren* and means mainly "to grumble, to hold forth" (umgangssprachlich); the old sense is marked as dated. Kant's point: a ruler who lets people think and publish freely can still expect obedience in their duties. For him, freedom of thought (*die Gedankenfreiheit*) means little without the freedom to publish one's thoughts.

The essay ends with a cautious diagnosis of its time:

> „Wenn denn nun gefragt wird: leben wir jetzt in einem aufgeklärten Zeitalter? so ist die Antwort: Nein, aber wohl in einem Zeitalter der Aufklärung.“

> "If it is now asked: do we live in an enlightened age? the answer is: No, but certainly in an age of enlightenment."

*aufgeklärt* (enlightened, a finished state) versus *der Aufklärung* (of enlightenment, a process still going on): one of the most quoted distinctions in German. Note the *so* again after the conditional clause, and *wohl* in its older sense of "certainly, indeed".

## Reading the 1784 print

In the original print of 1784 the motto looks like this:

> „Habe Muth dich deines eigenen Verstandes zu bedienen!“

and the sentence about comfort reads *Es ist so bequem, unmündig zu seyn.* Modern editions differ in how much they modernize, so it helps to know the main features of 18th-century spelling:

| 18th century | today | rule of thumb |
|---|---|---|
| *Muth, Theil, Noth, thun* | *Mut, Teil, Not, tun* | the *h* after *t* was dropped in 1901 (in German words) |
| *seyn, bey, Freyheit* | *sein, bei, Freiheit* | *y* for *i* in many words |
| *räsonniren, studiren* | *räsonieren, studieren* | verbs in *-iren* now *-ieren* |
| *daß, muß* | *dass, muss* | *ß* after short vowels until the reform of 1996 |
| *Habe Muth dich … zu bedienen!* | *Habe Mut, dich … zu bedienen!* | commas followed the rhythm of the sentence more than the grammar |
| *zu Stande, in Ansehung* | *zustande, hinsichtlich* | spelling and vocabulary of the period |

Punctuation needs a warning too: 18th-century commas and semicolons often marked pauses for the reader rather than grammatical boundaries, and Kant uses semicolons to hold together long periods, often two halves of one argument (as in the *öffentlich/privat* sentence). The quotations here keep the punctuation of their edition; don't use it as a model for modern commas.

Lesson 92 tells the story of how German spelling became standardized.

## A modern text: *Mündig im Netz?*

Kant's essay is still a reference point in German public debate, especially when people discuss whether citizens are being treated as adults. Read this commentary, written for this course in the style of a newspaper opinion page.

> **Mündig im Netz?**
>
> Es ist so bequem, unmündig zu sein: Kaum ein Satz der deutschen Philosophie ist so aktuell geblieben. Navigationsdienste wählen unseren Weg, Empfehlungssysteme unsere Lektüre, und auf jede Frage formuliert uns eine Software die Antwort. Kant hätte gesagt: Wir haben ein Buch, das für uns Verstand hat.
>
> Daraus folgt allerdings nicht, dass wir die Technik abschaffen sollten. Unmündig ist nicht, wer sich beraten lässt, sondern wer das Urteilen ganz anderen überlässt. Ebenso falsch wäre es, den Staat zum Vormund zu machen, der seine Bürger vor jeder falschen Information schützt. Wer Menschen für unfähig hält, sich ein eigenes Urteil zu bilden, betreibt Bevormundung, auch wenn er es gut meint. Mündigkeit lässt sich nicht verordnen; sie muss geübt werden.
>
> Leben wir also in einem aufgeklärten digitalen Zeitalter? Nein, aber vielleicht in einem Zeitalter der digitalen Aufklärung. Vorausgesetzt, wir haben den Mut, uns unseres eigenen Verstandes zu bedienen, und nicht nur den unseres Telefons.

> **Mature online?**
>
> It is so comfortable to be immature: hardly any sentence in German philosophy has stayed so topical. Navigation services choose our route, recommendation systems our reading, and software words the answer to every question for us. Kant would have said: we have a book that has understanding for us.
>
> It doesn't follow, however, that we should abolish technology. The immature person is not someone who takes advice, but someone who leaves judging entirely to others. It would be just as wrong to make the state into a guardian who protects its citizens from every piece of false information. Anyone who considers people incapable of forming their own judgement is practising paternalism, even with good intentions. Maturity cannot be decreed; it has to be practised.
>
> So do we live in an enlightened digital age? No, but perhaps in an age of digital enlightenment. Provided we have the courage to use our own understanding, and not just our phone's.

Things to notice:

- The text alludes to Kant without quotation marks (*Es ist so bequem …*; *ein Buch, das für uns Verstand hat*), as opinion pages often do with classics.
- *Kant hätte gesagt*: Konjunktiv II of the past for an imagined statement (lesson 03).
- *Unmündig ist nicht, wer …, sondern wer …*: a free relative clause (*wer* = the person who) in a *nicht … sondern* contrast, a classic structure of definitions and commentary.
- *Mündigkeit lässt sich nicht verordnen*: *sich lassen* + infinitive as a passive with "can" (lesson 09).
- *den Mut, uns unseres eigenen Verstandes zu bedienen, und nicht nur den unseres Telefons*: the genitive object, and *den* (= *den Verstand*) as a demonstrative pronoun with a genitive after it. The last sentence also lacks a main verb: an ellipsis for effect.
- The structure of a *Kommentar*: a hook, a concession (*Daraus folgt allerdings nicht …*), a rejected counter-position (*Ebenso falsch wäre es …*), a conclusion that echoes the opening.

## Summarizing an argument

Lesson 12 teaches the *Zusammenfassung*: source, topic, main thesis, the arguments in order, the conclusion, no opinion of your own, present tense, and reported speech where you want distance. Here is a short summary of the first part of Kant's essay at C1:

> In seinem Aufsatz „Beantwortung der Frage: Was ist Aufklärung?“, der 1784 in der Berlinischen Monatsschrift erschien, bestimmt Immanuel Kant Aufklärung als den Ausgang des Menschen aus seiner selbstverschuldeten Unmündigkeit. Unmündig sei, wer nicht fähig sei, seinen Verstand ohne die Anleitung anderer zu gebrauchen; selbstverschuldet sei dieser Zustand dann, wenn es nicht an Verstand, sondern an Entschlossenheit und Mut fehle. Als Ursachen nennt Kant Faulheit und Feigheit: Es sei bequem, anderen das Denken zu überlassen, und diese machten sich bereitwillig zu Vormündern. Aufklärung setze vor allem Freiheit voraus, und zwar die Freiheit, von seiner Vernunft öffentlich Gebrauch zu machen. Während man in einem Amt gehorchen müsse, dürfe man als Gelehrter vor dem Lesepublikum frei urteilen und Kritik üben. Kant kommt zu dem Schluss, dass seine Zeit noch kein aufgeklärtes Zeitalter sei, wohl aber ein Zeitalter der Aufklärung.

Notice:

- The first sentence names author, title, date, place of publication and the thesis.
- Konjunktiv I (*sei, fehle, setze voraus, müsse, dürfe*) for Kant's claims, alternating with indicative reporting verbs (*bestimmt, nennt, kommt zu dem Schluss*). Where the Konjunktiv I would look like the indicative, the summary avoids it (*diese machten sich …* is Konjunktiv II for *machen*).
- No comment, and the famous sentences are paraphrased, not copied (*seinen Verstand ohne die Anleitung anderer zu gebrauchen*).

## Commenting on it

A comment (*Stellungnahme*, lesson 14) then takes a position, for example: *Kants Unterscheidung ist auch heute noch aufschlussreich, weil …* (still illuminating today because …); *Man könnte ihm entgegenhalten, dass …* (one could object that …); *Was Kant nicht vorhersehen konnte, ist …* (what Kant could not foresee is …). A fair objection: Kant's reading public was small, most people in 1784 could not read, women were largely excluded, and the freedom he praises depended on a king's goodwill. A good comment concedes this without dismissing the text: *Gleichwohl bleibt der Grundgedanke gültig, dass …*

## Pronunciation

- *Philosoph, philosophisch*: stress on *-soph*: phi-lo-SOPH, phi-lo-SO-phisch; *ph* = [f].
- *Kant*: short *a*, [kant].
- *mündig, Mündigkeit*: MÜN-dig, MÜN-dig-keit; final *-ig* as [ɪç] in standard German.
- *Sapere aude*: German speakers usually say SA-pe-re AU-de.
- *räsonieren*: rä-so-NIE-ren, from French *raisonner*.

## Common mistakes

- Reading *Privatgebrauch der Vernunft* as "private life". In Kant, "private" means using one's reason in an office or job, where obedience is required; "public" means writing for the public as a scholar.
- Taking *derselben* as "of the same". In *die Ursache derselben* it simply means "its cause" (*ihre Ursache*).
- Looking for a missing word when an older subordinate clause ends with a participle: *nachdem sie die Natur … freigesprochen* has a dropped *hat*.
- Using genitive objects in conversation. *Ich bediene mich eines Kugelschreibers* sounds pompous; say *Ich nehme einen Kuli*. In formal writing, *sich einer Sache bedienen* is fine.
- Confusing *aufgeklärt* (enlightened, a state already reached) with *Aufklärung* (the process): *kein aufgeklärtes Zeitalter, aber ein Zeitalter der Aufklärung*.
- Copying 18th-century commas. *Habe Muth dich deines eigenen Verstandes zu bedienen!* has no comma in the original; modern rules require one before an infinitive group that depends on a noun (*Mut, dich … zu bedienen*).
- *der Verstand* vs *die Vernunft* vs *der Grund*: *Verstand* is understanding or intellect, *Vernunft* is reason or good sense (*Sei doch vernünftig!*), and *der Grund* is a reason in the sense of a cause (*aus diesem Grund*).

## Key points

- Kant's essay (Berlinische Monatsschrift, December 1784) defines enlightenment as *der Ausgang des Menschen aus seiner selbstverschuldeten Unmündigkeit*; its motto is *Sapere aude! Habe Mut, dich deines eigenen Verstandes zu bedienen!*
- People remain immature out of *Faulheit und Feigheit*; others are happy to act as their *Vormünder*. *Bevormundung* is still the word for this in modern debate.
- The **[[public use of reason]]** (as a scholar, before the reading public) must be free; the **[[private use of reason]]** (in an office) may be restricted.
- Older philosophical German uses verbs with a genitive object (*sich einer Sache bedienen*), *derselbe* as a pronoun, the **[[dropped auxiliary]]** in subordinate clauses, verb-first conditions resumed by *so*, and 18th-century spelling (*Muth, seyn, Theil*).
- To understand a difficult text, paraphrase it in modern verbal style; to summarize it, report its thesis and arguments in the present tense with Konjunktiv I where distance matters; to comment on it, concede and object with the connectors of lessons 11 and 14.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete the lesson.

lessons.title: Die Brüder Grimm: fairy tales and a dictionary
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Jacob and Wilhelm Grimm are known all over the world for one book, the *Kinder- und Hausmärchen*. In Germany they are also remembered for two others: the *Deutsches Wörterbuch*, the largest historical dictionary of the language, and Jacob's *Deutsche Grammatik*, which founded the scientific study of the Germanic languages. This lesson looks at all three.

You'll see how the brothers collected and rewrote their tales between 1812 and 1857, read short passages from three of them, and learn the grammar of the fairy-tale style: the narrative Präteritum, the opening and closing formulas, and older forms such as *ward*, the dative *-e* and a *dessen* that starts a main clause. At the end you retell a tale in modern German. Lesson 92 then follows Jacob Grimm into the history of German sounds.

The Grimms died in 1863 (Jacob) and 1859 (Wilhelm), so their works are in the public domain. The quotations from the final edition of 1857 follow the text on Projekt Gutenberg-DE; the 1812 opening of *Der Froschkönig* is quoted from D. L. Ashliman's side-by-side edition of both versions. Editions differ slightly in spelling (*daß/dass*, *fünfzehnten/funfzehnten*); the quotations keep the spelling of these sources.

## Two brothers, two libraries

Jacob Grimm was born in 1785 and Wilhelm in 1786, in Hanau near Frankfurt; they grew up in Steinau and Kassel. Both studied law in Marburg, where the legal historian Friedrich Carl von Savigny showed them his library of old manuscripts. That changed their lives: they became librarians and scholars of old German literature, law and language.

They worked together almost all their lives. In 1830 both moved to Göttingen as university librarians; Jacob was made a professor at once, Wilhelm a few years later. In 1837 both were dismissed: they were among the *Göttinger Sieben*, seven professors who protested publicly when the new king of Hanover abolished the constitution. In 1841 the king of Prussia invited them to Berlin, where they spent their last years working on the dictionary.

## The Kinder- und Hausmärchen

The first volume of the *Kinder- und Hausmärchen* appeared at the end of 1812, the second in 1815. Seven editions of the full collection followed in the brothers' lifetime; the last, of 1857, is called the *Ausgabe letzter Hand* (the final edition authorized by the authors) and contains 200 tales and ten children's legends. A cheaper *Kleine Ausgabe* with 50 tales (first published in 1825) made the book a family classic.

### Folk tale or literary tale?

The Grimms presented their tales as **[[folk tales]]** (*Volksmärchen*): stories passed on orally among the people, which they had only written down. A **[[literary fairy tale]]** (*Kunstmärchen*), by contrast, is invented by a known author, such as Wilhelm Hauff or Hans Christian Andersen. The truth about the Grimms lies in between. Many of their storytellers were not peasants but young women from educated middle-class families in Kassel, some of them of French Huguenot descent, who knew the French tales of Charles Perrault. The best-known storyteller from outside the city, Dorothea Viehmann from Niederzwehren, was a tailor's wife who sold produce in Kassel. And Wilhelm, in particular, rewrote the tales from edition to edition.

### How Wilhelm rewrote them

Compare the opening of the first tale, *Der Froschkönig oder der eiserne Heinrich*, in the first edition and in the last.

1812:

> „Es war einmal eine Königstochter, die ging hinaus in den Wald und setzte sich an einen kühlen Brunnen.“

> "Once upon a time there was a king's daughter who went out into the forest and sat down by a cool well."

1857:

> „In den alten Zeiten, wo das Wünschen noch geholfen hat, lebte ein König, dessen Töchter waren alle schön …“

> "In the old days, when wishing still helped, there lived a king whose daughters were all beautiful …"

The 1857 sentence goes on to say that the youngest was so beautiful that the sun itself, which had seen so much, was amazed whenever it shone on her face. The plain report of 1812 has become a poetic opening with a reflection on time and a rhythm meant for reading aloud. That is typical of Wilhelm's work: he added atmosphere, direct speech, proverbs and fixed phrases; he made the tales more moral and more suitable for children. Two well-known changes: in the first edition the jealous queen in *Schneewittchen* is the girl's own mother, later her stepmother; and details that hinted at sex disappeared after the first edition.

Even the ending of *Der Froschkönig* is gentler than many people remember: the princess does not kiss the frog. In both versions she throws him against the wall in disgust, and that is what breaks the spell.

The brothers were open about their method in their prefaces: they wanted to keep the content of what they heard but give it a form of their own. For readers today the *Märchensammlung* is therefore two things at once: a record of older storytelling and a 19th-century literary work.

## The language of the fairy tale

### The narrative Präteritum

Fairy tales are told in the Präteritum from beginning to end: *es war einmal, lebte, ging, setzte sich*. In everyday speech, especially in the south, people use the Perfekt for the past (*Sie ist in den Wald gegangen*); in a written story, the Präteritum is the tense of narration. Children in German-speaking countries know Präteritum forms like *sprach, ward, rief, fiel* from fairy tales long before they learn them at school. That's why this course calls it the **[[narrative preterite]]**: the Präteritum as the default tense of storytelling.

Notice also *wo das Wünschen noch geholfen hat*. Inside the past narration, the narrator steps out and comments in the Perfekt: those times, from today's point of view. And *wo* is used for time (*in den Zeiten, wo* = when). That's common in speech today (*in dem Moment, wo …*); in careful writing *als* or *in denen* is preferred.

### Opening and closing formulas

A Märchen announces itself with an **[[opening formula]]** and closes with a **[[closing formula]]**:

| opening | closing |
|---|---|
| *Es war einmal …* | *… und wenn sie nicht gestorben sind, (dann) leben sie noch heute.* |
| *Vor Zeiten war …* | *… und sie lebten glücklich bis an ihr Ende.* |
| *In den alten Zeiten, wo …* | *Mein Märchen ist aus.* |

The Grimms' own wording varies from tale to tale. *Fundevogel* (No. 51) ends: *„… und wenn sie nicht gestorben sind, leben sie noch.“* *Dornröschen* ends *„und sie lebten vergnügt bis an ihr Ende.“* The modern standard form, *Und wenn sie nicht gestorben sind, dann leben sie noch heute*, is used jokingly in everyday German for anything that has gone on for a long time: *Die Baustelle? Und wenn sie nicht gestorben sind …*

### Older forms you will meet

**ward** for *wurde*. In older German the Präteritum of *werden* in the singular was *ward* (*ich ward, er ward*); *wurde* won in the 18th and 19th centuries. The Grimms use both. You'll still find *ward* in poetry and in deliberately old-fashioned style (*Und es ward Licht* in older Bible translations).

**The dative -e.** Masculine and neuter nouns of one syllable used to take *-e* in the dative singular: *im Walde, dem Könige, zu Hause, in seinem Reiche*. Today it survives in fixed phrases (*zu Hause, im Grunde, nach Hause, auf dem Lande*) and in elevated style. Don't add it to modern nouns; recognize it when you read.

**ihrer as a partitive genitive.** In *Dornröschen*, the king wants to invite the wise women to his daughter's christening:

> „Es waren ihrer dreizehn in seinem Reiche …“

> "There were thirteen of them in his kingdom …"

*ihrer* is the genitive of *sie* (them): "thirteen of them". Modern German says *Es gab dreizehn davon* or simply *Es gab dreizehn weise Frauen*. The structure survives in a few phrases (*Wir waren unser drei*: there were three of us), which sound old-fashioned or regional.

**A dessen that starts a main clause.** Look again at *lebte ein König, dessen Töchter waren alle schön*. If *dessen Töchter* introduced a relative clause, the verb would go to the end: *dessen Töchter alle schön waren*. Here the verb is in second position. The clause is not a relative clause but a main clause, and *dessen* works like a demonstrative: "his daughters were all beautiful". This construction, a d-word with main-clause order, is a feature of older narrative German; in modern writing it would be a mistake.

## Dornröschen: curse and release

*Dornröschen* (No. 50, the Grimms' version of *Sleeping Beauty*) shows the motifs of the fairy tale in a few lines. The king has only twelve golden plates, so one of the thirteen wise women is not invited. She appears at the feast anyway and calls out:

> „Die Königstochter soll sich in ihrem fünfzehnten Jahre an einer Spindel stechen und tot hinfallen.“

> "In her fifteenth year the king's daughter shall prick herself on a spindle and fall down dead."

The twelfth woman has not yet spoken her wish. She cannot lift the curse, only soften it:

> „Es soll aber kein Tod sein, sondern ein hundertjähriger tiefer Schlaf, in welchen die Königstochter fällt.“

> "But it shall not be death, rather a deep sleep of a hundred years into which the king's daughter falls."

Grammar:

- *soll* in both sentences expresses the will of the speaker: what she decrees will happen. This is the *soll* of commands, laws and curses (compare lesson 05h1 on *soll* in rules), not the *soll* of hearsay.
- *in ihrem fünfzehnten Jahre*: in her fifteenth year; note the dative *-e*.
- *kein Tod …, sondern ein … Schlaf*: *kein … sondern* corrects a noun.
- *in welchen*: a relative pronoun with *welch-*, formal (lesson 24); modern German would usually say *in den*.

Note that the Grimms speak of *weise Frauen* (wise women), not of a *Fee* (fairy). Fairies belong to the French tradition: in Perrault's *La Belle au bois dormant* they are *fées*. German retellings, films and children's books often turn the Grimms' wise women into *Feen*, and most German readers would call the thirteenth one *die böse Fee*.

The story's key words have remained part of the language:

- *der Fluch* (curse), *verfluchen* (to curse); in fairy tales also *verwünschen* (to put under a spell), from which comes the adjective *verwunschen* (enchanted): *ein verwunschenes Schloss*, used today for any romantic, overgrown place.
- *der Zauberer* (wizard) and *die Zauberin* (sorceress) cast the spells; *verzaubern* (to put a spell on, to turn into something by magic: *in einen Frosch verzaubert*); figuratively "to enchant, to delight": *Die Pianistin hat das Publikum verzaubert.*
- *erlösen* (to release from a spell) and *die Erlösung*. In everyday German *eine Erlösung* is any great relief: *Das Ende der Prüfungswoche war eine Erlösung.*
- *das Zauberwort*: the magic word that opens doors (*Sesam, öffne dich!*); figuratively a word that is expected to solve everything: *Digitalisierung heißt das Zauberwort.* And parents ask children: *Wie heißt das Zauberwort?* (answer: *Bitte!*).

## An original tale in the Grimm style

The following tale was written for this course in the style of the 1857 edition: Präteritum, short main clauses joined by *und* and *da*, the rule of three, a curse and a release. It is not a Grimm tale.

> **Das verwunschene Spinnrad**
>
> Es war einmal eine arme Witwe, die hatte eine einzige Tochter, und die Tochter konnte so fein spinnen, dass man ihr Garn im ganzen Land rühmte. Eines Tages ging das Mädchen in den Wald, um Holz zu sammeln, und fand unter einer alten Eiche ein Spinnrad aus Silber. Daneben saß ein Zwerg und weinte.
>
> „Warum weinst du?“, fragte das Mädchen. Da sprach der Zwerg: „Ein böser Zauberer hat meinen Herrn, den Sohn des Königs, in einen Stein verwandelt und das Spinnrad verwünscht. Nur wer auf ihm drei Spindeln Mondlicht spinnt, kann ihn erlösen. Aber wer es versucht und dabei ein Wort spricht, den trifft der Fluch selbst.“
>
> Das Mädchen setzte sich an das Rad und spann, drei Nächte lang, und sprach kein Wort. In der ersten Nacht kam ein Sturm, in der zweiten ein Feuer, in der dritten erschien der Zauberer selbst und verfluchte sie mit lauter Stimme. Sie aber schwieg und spann. Als die dritte Spindel voll war, zersprang der Stein, und der Königssohn stand vor ihr.
>
> Da war die Freude groß, der Zauberer aber verlor alle Macht. Die Witwe zog mit ins Schloss, der Zwerg wurde Hofmeister, und das Mädchen heiratete den Königssohn. Und wenn sie nicht gestorben sind, so leben sie noch heute.

> **The Enchanted Spinning Wheel**
>
> Once upon a time there was a poor widow who had an only daughter, and the daughter could spin so finely that her yarn was praised throughout the land. One day the girl went into the forest to gather wood and found a spinning wheel made of silver under an old oak tree. Beside it sat a dwarf, weeping.
>
> "Why are you crying?" asked the girl. Then the dwarf said: "An evil wizard has turned my master, the king's son, into a stone and put a spell on the spinning wheel. Only someone who spins three spindles of moonlight on it can set him free. But whoever tries and says a word while doing so is struck by the curse themselves."
>
> The girl sat down at the wheel and spun for three nights and said not a word. On the first night a storm came, on the second a fire, on the third the wizard himself appeared and cursed her in a loud voice. But she kept silent and spun. When the third spindle was full, the stone burst apart, and the king's son stood before her.
>
> Then there was great joy, but the wizard lost all his power. The widow moved into the castle with them, the dwarf became steward of the household, and the girl married the king's son. And if they haven't died, they are living still.

Find the features of the style:

- Präteritum throughout the narration (*war, ging, fand, saß, spann, zersprang*), Perfekt only in direct speech (*hat … verwandelt*), as in conversation.
- *die hatte eine einzige Tochter*, *und die Tochter konnte …*: demonstrative *die* at the start of a main clause, linking like a relative pronoun. Same structure as *dessen Töchter waren alle schön*.
- *Da sprach der Zwerg*: *da* + verb + subject, the typical way a Märchen moves on (*da* = then). *sprechen* for *sagen* is part of the style.
- *wer es versucht …, den trifft der Fluch selbst*: a free relative clause with *wer* picked up by *den* in the main clause (accusative, because *der Fluch trifft ihn*).
- The rule of three: three spindles, three nights, three trials. The silence is the test; the release (*die Erlösung*) is the reward.
- *Und wenn sie nicht gestorben sind, so leben sie noch heute*: the closing formula with *so*, as in older conditionals (lesson 90).

## Retelling a tale in modern German

At C1 you should be able to retell a story in more than one register. Here is the beginning of the tale above in three versions.

A written plot summary (*Inhaltsangabe*): present tense, neutral, no direct speech, Konjunktiv I for what characters say:

> In dem Märchen „Das verwunschene Spinnrad“ erlöst ein armes Mädchen einen verzauberten Königssohn, indem es drei Nächte lang schweigend spinnt. Im Wald trifft das Mädchen einen Zwerg, der ihm erklärt, ein Zauberer habe seinen Herrn in einen Stein verwandelt; nur wer drei Spindeln Mondlicht spinne, ohne ein Wort zu sagen, könne ihn retten.

Retold orally to a friend: Perfekt, colloquial words, particles:

> Also, da ist ein Mädchen in den Wald gegangen und hat so ein silbernes Spinnrad gefunden. Daneben saß ein Zwerg und hat geheult, weil ein Zauberer den Prinzen in einen Stein verwandelt hatte. Und das Mädchen sollte halt drei Nächte durchspinnen, ohne was zu sagen …

Read aloud to a child: the fairy-tale Präteritum is kept, but sentences are shorter and the vocabulary simpler.

Note in the oral version that *saß* stays in the Präteritum: *sein, haben*, the modal verbs and a few frequent verbs such as *sitzen, stehen, liegen* are often used in the Präteritum even in speech (B1 grammar). *heulen* is the colloquial word for *weinen*; *ohne was zu sagen* (*was* = *etwas*) is colloquial for *ohne ein Wort zu sagen*.

## The Deutsches Wörterbuch

In 1838 the brothers, who had lost their professorships, signed a contract for a dictionary of the German language "from Luther to Goethe" and beyond. They planned a few volumes and a few years of work. The first volume came out in 1854. Wilhelm wrote the letter D; Jacob completed A, B, C and E, and died in 1863 while he was working on the entry *Frucht*. Generations of scholars continued the work, which was finished in 1961: 32 volumes and a source index published in 1971, about 320,000 headwords in all. It is freely searchable online (for example via the *Wörterbuchnetz* of the University of Trier and the DWDS).

The *Deutsches Wörterbuch* (*DWB*, or simply *der Grimm*) is a historical dictionary: for each word it gives its forms, its origin and its senses through the centuries, with quotations from texts of every period. It is the place to look when you find a word in Kant or Goethe that no modern dictionary explains. One thing will surprise you when you open it: the Grimms wrote nouns with a small letter (*die frucht*), because Jacob considered the capitalization of nouns an unnecessary late habit.

## Jacob Grimm and the sound laws

Jacob Grimm's other great work was the *Deutsche Grammatik* (from 1819), a comparative grammar of all the Germanic languages. In its second edition (1822) he described a regular correspondence between consonants in Germanic languages and in related languages such as Latin and Greek: where Latin has *p*, Germanic has *f*; where Latin has *t*, Germanic has *th*; where Latin has *c* [k], Germanic has *h*.

| Latin | English | German |
|---|---|---|
| *pater* | father | *Vater* |
| *tres* | three | *drei* |
| *cornu* | horn | *Horn* |

This correspondence, which the Danish scholar Rasmus Rask had also observed a few years earlier, is called **[[Grimm's law]]** in English (*das Grimmsche Gesetz* or *die erste (germanische) Lautverschiebung* in German). It showed that sound change is regular, not random, and it made historical linguistics a science. Lesson 92 explains it and the second consonant shift, which separates High German from Low German and English.

## Pronunciation

- *Grimm*: short *i*: [ɡrɪm]. The usual name is *die Brüder Grimm* (also *die Gebrüder Grimm*).
- *die Fee*: one long *e*, [feː]; plural *Feen* [ˈfeːən], two syllables.
- *der Zwerg*: [tsvɛrk], the *g* is devoiced at the end.
- *verwunschen*: ver-WUN-schen, short *u*; compare *verwünschen*, ver-WÜN-schen.
- *das Spinnrad*: SPINN-rad, stress on the first part of the compound.

## Common mistakes

- Telling a fairy tale in the Perfekt when you write it. Written stories use the Präteritum (*Sie ging in den Wald*); the Perfekt belongs to conversation (*Sie ist in den Wald gegangen*).
- Reading every *dessen* or *die* after a comma as a relative pronoun. If the verb is in second position (*dessen Töchter waren alle schön*), it's an older main clause: "his daughters were …".
- Adding the dative *-e* to modern nouns: ~~im Büroe~~, ~~mit dem Handye~~. It belongs to fixed phrases (*zu Hause, im Grunde*) and old texts.
- Mixing up *verwunschen* (enchanted) and *verwünscht* (cursed, damned): *ein verwunschener Garten* is romantic; *dieser verwünschte Regen!* is a complaint.
- *der Fluch* (curse, swear word) is not *die Flucht* (escape).
- Treating the Grimms' tales as unchanged oral folk tales. They are folk material in a literary form shaped mainly by Wilhelm.
- Confusing Grimm's law (the first consonant shift: Latin *pater* – German *Vater*) with the second, High German consonant shift (English *apple* – German *Apfel*), lesson 92.

## Key points

- The *Kinder- und Hausmärchen* (1812/1815; final edition 1857 with 200 tales and ten legends) present **[[folk tales]]** (*Volksmärchen*), but Wilhelm Grimm rewrote them over 45 years; a **[[literary fairy tale]]** (*Kunstmärchen*) is invented by a known author.
- Fairy tales use the **[[narrative preterite]]** throughout, an **[[opening formula]]** (*Es war einmal …*) and a **[[closing formula]]** (*… und wenn sie nicht gestorben sind, leben sie noch heute*).
- Older forms: *ward* for *wurde*, the dative *-e* (*im Walde*), the partitive genitive *ihrer* (*Es waren ihrer dreizehn*), and d-words with main-clause order (*dessen Töchter waren alle schön*).
- Fairy-tale words live on in modern German: *der Fluch, verwünschen, verwunschen, verzaubern, erlösen, die Erlösung, das Zauberwort*.
- The Grimms began the *Deutsches Wörterbuch* in 1838; it was completed in 1961. Jacob Grimm's *Deutsche Grammatik* described the regular sound correspondences now called **[[Grimm's law]]**.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete the lesson.

lessons.title: From Althochdeutsch to today: a short history of German
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Why does German say *Apfel* where English says *apple* and Low German *Appel*? Why is *Haus* spelled with *au* when a Swiss German speaker says *Huus*? Why did Kant write *Muth* and Luther *Vnd*? This lesson tells the story of the German language in about 3,000 words: where it comes from, how its sounds changed, what it looked like in four periods, how printing, Luther and the chanceries pushed it towards one written standard, how spelling was regulated, and which languages it borrowed from.

You'll read one short sample from each older period, all of them centuries in the public domain, with notes and a modern German translation written for this course. The aim is not to learn Old or Middle High German, but to recognize them, and to understand modern German better: many irregularities of today's language are fossils of this history.

## The family: Indo-European and Germanic

German belongs to the **[[Indo-European]]** language family (*indogermanisch*; also *indoeuropäisch*), which stretches from Iceland to northern India: Latin and the Romance languages, Greek, the Slavic and Celtic languages, Persian, Sanskrit and many more. The family was discovered around 1800 by comparing words and grammar; the common ancestor, *Proto-Indo-European* (*das Urindogermanische*), is not written down anywhere but reconstructed.

Within this family German is a Germanic (*germanisch*) language, together with English, Dutch, Frisian, the Scandinavian languages and the extinct Gothic. The Germanic branch is set apart above all by the first consonant shift, which Jacob Grimm described in 1822 (lesson 91): Indo-European *p, t, k* became Germanic *f, th, h*.

| Latin | Germanic: English | German |
|---|---|---|
| *pater* | father | *Vater* |
| *piscis* | fish | *Fisch* |
| *tres* | three | *drei* |
| *cor (cordis)* | heart | *Herz* |

Words that German has had since Germanic or Indo-European times are called **[[inherited words]]** (*Erbwörter*): *Vater, Mutter, Hand, Haus, Herz, drei*. Words taken from other languages later are loanwords (*Lehnwörter*, B2) or, if they still look foreign, *Fremdwörter*. More on these below.

Look at the last line of the table: English *heart* has *t*, German *Herz* has *z*. That difference belongs to a second, later shift, which happened only in German.

## The second consonant shift: why German is "High" German

Between about the 6th and the 8th century, the speakers of the southern Germanic dialects changed the consonants *p, t, k* once more. This **[[High German consonant shift]]** (*die zweite* or *hochdeutsche Lautverschiebung*) is what separates High German from all other Germanic languages, including English, Dutch and the Low German of northern Germany.

| before the shift (English, Low German) | after the shift (Standard German) | position |
|---|---|---|
| *apple / Appel*, *pound / Pund* | *Apfel*, *Pfund* | *p* → *pf* at the start of a word, after *m*, and when doubled |
| *ship / Schipp*, *open / open* | *Schiff*, *offen* | *p* → *ff/f* after a vowel |
| *ten / tein*, *tide / Tied*, *heart / Hart* | *zehn*, *Zeit*, *Herz* | *t* → *z* [ts] at the start of a word, after a consonant and when doubled |
| *water / Water*, *that / dat* | *Wasser*, *das* | *t* → *ss/s* after a vowel |
| *make / maken*, *book / Book*, *I (ik)* | *machen*, *Buch*, *ich* | *k* → *ch* after a vowel |

Two further changes belong to the same process but spread less far. In parts of the south, *k* at the start of a word became [kx] or [x]: Swiss German *Chind* for *Kind*. And *d* became *t* in High German: English *daughter, deep*, German *Tochter, tief*.

"High" here is geographical: it refers to the higher land of central and southern Germany, Austria and Switzerland, not to a higher style. Low German (*Niederdeutsch, Plattdeutsch*) is spoken in the lowlands of the north and kept the old consonants: *Water, maken, ik, dat, Appel*.

The shift did not spread evenly. The further north, the fewer of its changes appear, and the boundaries for individual words fan out across the Rhineland like the ribs of a fan. The most important line is the **[[Benrath line]]** (*die Benrather Linie*), named after a district of Düsseldorf. It marks *maken* north of it and *machen* south of it, and it is the traditional boundary between Low German and the High German dialects. A few kilometres further north, the Uerdingen line separates *ik* from *ich*; much further south, around Speyer, *Appel* gives way to *Apfel*. The region in between, where some changes happened and others didn't, is called *Mitteldeutsch* (Central German). Lesson 26 shows the dialect map of Germany as it is today.

Standard German is based on High German dialects, which is why it has *Apfel, Wasser, machen*. That's also why the language is called *Hochdeutsch* even when people mean "Standard German": in everyday speech *Hochdeutsch* has come to mean the standard language as opposed to any dialect.

## Four periods

German historians of language usually divide the history of German into four periods. The dates are conventions and differ a little from book to book.

| period | German | roughly | key texts |
|---|---|---|---|
| Old High German | *Althochdeutsch* (ahd.) | c. 750 – 1050 | glosses, prayers, the *Hildebrandslied* |
| Middle High German | *Mittelhochdeutsch* (mhd.) | c. 1050 – 1350 | courtly epics, the *Nibelungenlied*, Minnesang |
| Early New High German | *Frühneuhochdeutsch* (frnhd.) | c. 1350 – 1650 | chancery documents, Luther's Bible |
| New High German | *Neuhochdeutsch* (nhd.) | from c. 1650 | Kant, Goethe and everything since |

### Althochdeutsch: the Hildebrandslied

The oldest German texts are mostly translations and glosses (German words written between the lines of Latin manuscripts) made in monasteries. The one surviving heroic poem is the *Hildebrandslied*, written down in the 830s at the monastery of Fulda on two spare leaves of a religious book; the manuscript is in Kassel. Its 68 lines tell of a father, Hildebrand, who returns after thirty years and meets his son Hadubrand between two armies; the son doesn't believe who he is, and they fight. The text breaks off in the middle of the battle. It begins:

> Ik gihorta ðat seggen,
> ðat sih urhettun ænon muotin,
> Hiltibrant enti Haðubrant untar heriun tuem.

(Line division and spelling as in modern editions, which follow Braune's *Althochdeutsches Lesebuch*.)

A modern German rendering: *Ich hörte erzählen, dass zwei Herausforderer allein aufeinandertrafen, Hildebrand und Hadubrand, zwischen zwei Heeren.* In English: "I heard it told that two challengers met alone, Hildebrand and Hadubrand, between two armies."

Notes:

- *ik, ðat, seggen* look northern, almost English: the scribes mixed Old High German with Old Saxon (the ancestor of Low German), and nobody is sure why. *ð* is the letter "eth", pronounced like English *th*.
- *gihorta*: Präteritum of *hōren*; *gi-* is the ancestor of the prefix *ge-*.
- *enti*: *und*. *untar heriun tuem*: *unter Heeren zwei*, between two armies, with *heriun* a dative plural (*das Heer*) and *tuem* the dative of "two".
- *urhettun*: challengers; *ænon muotin*: met alone, in single combat (*ænon* is related to *ein*, *muotin* to English *meet*). *urhettun* and *muotin* have no modern German descendants, which is why Old High German needs a dictionary.

Old High German still had full vowels in its endings (*gihorta, heriun*), where modern German has a weak *-e* or nothing (*hörte, Heeren*). The weakening of endings marks the transition to Middle High German.

### Mittelhochdeutsch: Walther von der Vogelweide

Around 1200, poets at the courts of southern Germany and Austria wrote in a language that was remarkably uniform over large areas: the poetic Middle High German of the *Nibelungenlied*, of Wolfram von Eschenbach's *Parzival* and of the love songs (*Minnesang*). The best-known lyric poet is Walther von der Vogelweide (c. 1170 – c. 1230). One of his poems begins:

> Under der linden
> an der heide,
> dâ unser zweier bette was,
> dâ mugt ir vinden
> schône beide
> gebrochen bluomen unde gras.

Modern German: *Unter der Linde auf der Heide, wo unser beider Lager war, da könnt ihr, schön geknickt, beides finden, Blumen und Gras.* In English: "Under the linden on the heath, where the two of us had our bed, there you may find, nicely broken, both flowers and grass." A woman speaks, remembering a meeting with her lover; the poem survives in two medieval manuscripts.

Notes:

- The circumflex (*dâ, schône*) is a convention of modern editors: it marks long vowels. Medieval manuscripts don't use it consistently.
- *unser zweier*: the genitive "of the two of us", like *ihrer dreizehn* in Grimm (lesson 91).
- *mugt ir*: you can (*mügen, mugen* = to be able). Middle High German *mugen* meant "can"; the old sense survives in *Das mag sein* (that may be) and in *vermögen* (to be able to).
- *vinden*: *finden*. *v* and *f* were both used for [f]; modern *Vater, viel, vor* keep the *v*.
- *bluomen*: *Blumen*. The *uo* was a diphthong, [uə]; it became the long vowel *u* in modern German.

That last point leads to the two great vowel changes that turned Middle into New High German:

- **[[Diphthongization]]**: long *î, û, iu* [yː] became *ei, au, eu*: *mîn niuwez hûs* → *mein neues Haus*; *wîn* → *Wein*; *zît* → *Zeit*.
- **[[Monophthongization]]**: the diphthongs *ie, uo, üe* became long *i, u, ü*: *liebe* [liə-] → *Liebe* [iː]; *guot* → *gut*; *brüeder* → *Brüder*.

The spelling *ie* in *Liebe, lieben, die* is a fossil of the old diphthong: the pronunciation changed, the spelling stayed, and *ie* became the normal way to write long *i*. And Swiss German, which did not take part in the diphthongization, still says *Huus, Ziit, miin* (and *Wii*): Walther's vowels, in a modern Swiss mouth.

### Frühneuhochdeutsch: printing, chanceries and Luther

In the late Middle Ages there was no single written German but many regional written forms. Two developments brought them closer.

First, the chanceries (*Kanzleien*), the writing offices of princes and cities, produced documents that had to be understood beyond their own region. Two chancery languages became especially influential: that of the Saxon electors in Meissen and that of the imperial chancery under Emperor Maximilian I (around 1500).

Second, printing. After Johannes Gutenberg's invention in Mainz around 1450, printers wanted to sell their books as widely as possible and avoided purely local forms. When the Reformation began in 1517, pamphlets and Bibles spread in hundreds of thousands of copies.

Martin Luther (1483–1546) translated the New Testament in 1521–22 (the *Septembertestament*, 1522); the complete Bible followed in 1534. He based his written German on the East Central German of the Saxon chancery, and he wrote about his method in the *Sendbrief vom Dolmetschen* (1530): a translator, he argued, should not follow the Latin word for word but listen to how the mother at home, the children in the street and the common man at the market speak. Modern German has made this into a saying: *dem Volk aufs Maul schauen* (to listen to how ordinary people talk; *aufs Maul* is colloquial).

Here are the first verses of St John's Gospel in the 1545 edition, the last printed in Luther's lifetime (Wittenberg, Hans Lufft), as reproduced by stilkunst.de from the original print, with the long *ſ* written as *s*:

> IM anfang war das Wort / Vnd das wort war bey Gott / vnd Gott war das Wort. Das selbige war im anfang bey Gott. Alle ding sind durch dasselbige gemacht / vnd on dasselbige ist nichts gemacht / was gemacht ist.

Modern Luther Bible: *Im Anfang war das Wort, und das Wort war bei Gott, und Gott war das Wort. Dasselbe war im Anfang bei Gott. Alle Dinge sind durch dasselbe gemacht, und ohne dasselbe ist nichts gemacht, was gemacht ist.*

Notes:

- The slash, the virgule (/), does the job of the comma. The full stop is already used as today.
- *Vnd, vnd*: *u* and *v* were two shapes of one letter; *v* was used at the start of a word, *u* inside it, whatever the sound.
- Capitals are not yet systematic: *das Wort* and *das wort* in the same verse, *anfang, ding* in lower case. Capitalizing all nouns became the rule only in the 17th and 18th centuries.
- *bey*: the *y* spelling Kant still used (*seyn*). *on*: *ohne*. *dasselbige*: an older, longer form of *dasselbe*.

The idea that Luther "created" Standard German is a popular simplification. Historians of language today stress that the chanceries, the printers and many other writers prepared the ground; but the enormous circulation of his Bible made one form of written German familiar everywhere, including the Catholic south, which resisted it for a long time.

### Neuhochdeutsch: norms and dictionaries

From the 17th century, grammarians and language societies worked to describe and standardize the written language; in the 18th century the Leipzig professor Johann Christoph Gottsched and the lexicographer Johann Christoph Adelung were the leading authorities. By the time of Kant and Goethe, educated Germans from Königsberg to Zurich wrote essentially the same language. Spelling, however, still varied.

## Spelling: from Duden to the reform

In 1880 the schoolmaster Konrad Duden published a spelling dictionary, the *Vollständiges Orthographisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache*. At a conference in Berlin in 1901, the German states agreed on common spelling rules, which Austria and Switzerland also adopted; they came into force in 1902–03. One visible change: the *h* after *t* disappeared from German words (*Thür, Theil, Muth* → *Tür, Teil, Mut*); *Theater* and *Thema* keep it because they come from Greek.

For most of the 20th century the Duden dictionary was the reference for German spelling; from 1955 it was officially binding in doubtful cases in West Germany. The *Rechtschreibreform* of 1996, agreed by Germany, Austria, Switzerland and other German-speaking countries, replaced that role with an official set of rules (*das Amtliche Regelwerk*). Its best-known changes:

- *ss* after a short vowel, *ß* only after a long vowel or diphthong: *daß* → *dass*, *Fluß* → *Fluss*, but *Straße, groß, heißen*;
- spelling by word family: *Stängel* (from *Stange*, formerly *Stengel*), *nummerieren* (from *Nummer*);
- three identical letters kept in compounds: *Schifffahrt*;
- more capitals for nominalized words: *im Allgemeinen, des Weiteren*.

The reform caused years of public controversy. The *Rat für deutsche Rechtschreibung*, set up in 2004, revised the most criticized parts in 2006 and has updated the rules since; the current version of the *Amtliches Regelwerk* is from 2024. In several cases two spellings are now correct, and Duden marks the one it recommends: *Orthografie* (also *Orthographie*), *Fotografie* (also *Photographie*).

## Loanwords: a history in layers

Every period of contact left words in German. The older the loan, the less foreign it looks.

| period | from | examples |
|---|---|---|
| Roman times | Latin | *Mauer* (*murus*), *Fenster* (*fenestra*), *Keller* (*cellarium*), *Wein* (*vinum*), *Straße* (*strata*) |
| Christianization | Church Latin | *Kloster, Mönch, schreiben, Schule, Tafel* |
| Middle Ages, courtly culture | Old French | *Abenteuer* (*aventure*), *Turnier, Lanze*, and the suffix *-ieren* |
| Renaissance, trade | Italian | *Bank, Konto, Kredit, brutto, netto, Risiko* |
| 17th–18th century | French | *Mode, Möbel, Onkel, Tante, Etage, Perücke* |
| science and scholarship | Latin and Greek | *Universität, Philosophie, Methode, Atom* |
| 19th century to today | English | *Sport, Streik, Computer, Team, Handy* (a German creation) |

Loans that came early were absorbed completely: nobody hears Latin in *Fenster* or *Keller*, which have German stress and German plurals. *Fremdwörter* such as *Universität* or *Etage* keep foreign stress or sounds.

There is a quieter kind of borrowing too: the **[[loan translation]]** (*die Lehnübersetzung*), in which a foreign word is translated part by part with German material. *Wolkenkratzer* translates English *skyscraper*; *Halbinsel* translates Latin *paeninsula*; *Mitleid* is modelled on Latin *compassio*. These words look native, but their pattern is borrowed.

## A lecture excerpt: *Vom hûs zum Haus*

Read this excerpt from an introductory lecture on the history of German, written for this course in the style of a university lecture (the format of Goethe C1 Hören Teil 4, lesson 30).

> Meine Damen und Herren, beginnen wir mit einem ganz unscheinbaren Wort: *Haus*. Im Mittelhochdeutschen, also um 1200, sprach man es mit einem langen *u* aus, *hûs*, und genau so klingt es noch heute in weiten Teilen der Schweiz und im Niederdeutschen. Dass wir im Standarddeutschen *Haus* sagen, verdanken wir einem Lautwandel, der als neuhochdeutsche Diphthongierung bezeichnet wird. Er setzte vermutlich schon im 12. Jahrhundert im Südosten des Sprachgebiets ein, also im heutigen Österreich, und breitete sich von dort im Laufe mehrerer Jahrhunderte nach Norden und Westen aus.
>
> Wichtig ist dabei zweierlei. Erstens verläuft Lautwandel regelmäßig: Nicht nur *hûs* wurde zu *Haus*, sondern auch *mûs* zu *Maus* und *bûch* zu *Bauch*. Zweitens erreicht er nie alle Mundarten. Viele alemannische Dialekte im Südwesten, vor allem in der Schweiz, haben die alten langen Vokale bewahrt, und deshalb sagt man in Zürich bis heute *Huus*.
>
> Wie lässt sich das alles überhaupt wissen, obwohl es keine Tonaufnahmen gibt? Zum einen aus Reimen: Wenn ein Dichter zwei Wörter reimt, müssen sie für ihn ähnlich geklungen haben. Zum anderen aus Schreibungen, die sich in den Handschriften einer Region allmählich verändern. Und schließlich aus dem Vergleich mit den heutigen Dialekten, die man gewissermaßen als lebende Archive betrachten kann.

> Ladies and gentlemen, let's start with a quite inconspicuous word: *Haus*. In Middle High German, that is around 1200, it was pronounced with a long *u*, *hûs*, and that's exactly how it still sounds today in large parts of Switzerland and in Low German. That we say *Haus* in Standard German is due to a sound change known as the New High German diphthongization. It probably began as early as the 12th century in the south-east of the language area, in today's Austria, and from there spread north and west over several centuries.
>
> Two things are important here. First, sound change is regular: not only did *hûs* become *Haus*, but *mûs* also became *Maus* and *bûch* became *Bauch*. Second, it never reaches all dialects. Many Alemannic dialects in the south-west, especially in Switzerland, have kept the old long vowels, and that's why people in Zurich still say *Huus* today.
>
> How can we know any of this, when there are no sound recordings? Firstly from rhymes: if a poet rhymes two words, they must have sounded similar to him. Secondly from spellings that gradually change in a region's manuscripts. And finally from comparison with today's dialects, which can be regarded, as it were, as living archives.

Things to notice: the lecture's signposting (*beginnen wir mit, Wichtig ist dabei zweierlei. Erstens … Zweitens, Zum einen … zum anderen … und schließlich*), the hedges of scholarly German (*vermutlich*, *gewissermaßen*), the passive substitute *Wie lässt sich das wissen?* (lesson 09), and the subjective *müssen* with a perfect infinitive (*müssen … geklungen haben*, lesson 02).

## Pronunciation

- *Althochdeutsch*: ALT-hoch-deutsch, main stress on *alt-*. Likewise *MIT-tel-hoch-deutsch*, *FRÜH-neu-hoch-deutsch*.
- *indogermanisch*: in-do-ger-MA-nisch.
- *die Orthografie*: or-to-gra-FIE, stress on the last syllable, like most nouns in *-ie* that come from Greek (*Philosophie, Geografie*; but *Tragödie, Komödie* with unstressed *-ie*, [-di̯ə]).
- *die Lautverschiebung*: LAUT-ver-schie-bung.

## Common mistakes

- Calling Low German "a dialect of Standard German". Low German never went through the second consonant shift; it is closer to Dutch in its sounds and is officially recognized as a regional language.
- Thinking "High German" means "posh German". *Hoch* refers to the geography of the dialects that underwent the second shift.
- Mixing up the two consonant shifts: the first (Grimm's law) separates Germanic from Latin (*pater – father, Vater*); the second separates High German from English and Low German (*water – Wasser*).
- Treating *ie* in *Liebe* as two vowels. In modern German it is one long [iː]; the spelling remembers a Middle High German diphthong.
- Assuming that every English-looking word in German is borrowed from English. *Haus, Hand, Wasser* are inherited words that German and English share from Germanic; *Handy* is a German invention.
- *Orthografie* vs *Rechtschreibung*: both mean spelling, but *Orthografie* is the technical term (and the system of rules); in conversation say *Rechtschreibung*.

## Key points

- German is an **[[Indo-European]]** and Germanic language; **[[inherited words]]** (*Erbwörter*) like *Vater, Herz, drei* go back to that past.
- The **[[High German consonant shift]]** (6th–8th century) turned *p, t, k* into *pf/f, z/ss, ch* (*Apfel, Wasser, machen*); Low German and English kept the old sounds. The **[[Benrath line]]** (*maken/machen*) is the traditional boundary between Low and High German.
- Four periods: Althochdeutsch (c. 750–1050, *Hildebrandslied*), Mittelhochdeutsch (c. 1050–1350, Walther von der Vogelweide), Frühneuhochdeutsch (c. 1350–1650, chanceries, printing, Luther's Bible of 1534/1545), Neuhochdeutsch.
- **[[Diphthongization]]** (*hûs → Haus*) and **[[monophthongization]]** (*guot → gut*) shaped the vowels of modern German; Swiss German kept the old long vowels.
- Spelling was unified in 1901 and reformed in 1996 (revised 2006 and since); the reform's best-known rule is *ss* after short vowels (*dass*).
- Loanwords came in layers: Latin, Church Latin, French, Italian, French again, Latin and Greek, English. A **[[loan translation]]** (*Wolkenkratzer*) borrows the pattern, not the word.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete the lesson.

lessons.title: Alexander von Humboldt: science, travel and the essay
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Alexander von Humboldt is probably the most famous German scientist few people have read. Mountains, rivers, an ocean current, a penguin, a squid, universities and hundreds of streets are named after him; Charles Darwin wrote that reading Humboldt's travel account as a young man had shaped the whole course of his life. His idea that nature is a single connected system, in which climate, plants, animals and people depend on one another, sounds strikingly modern.

This lesson tells the story of his American expedition (1799–1804), reads short passages from *Ansichten der Natur* and *Kosmos*, and looks briefly at his brother Wilhelm and the university that bears both their names.
