The grammar is the grammar of narrating and describing at C1: the Präteritum and Plusquamperfekt in a sequence of events, participial attributes and participial clauses (lesson 08), and the long nominal sentences of 19th-century scientific prose.

Alexander von Humboldt died in 1859, so his works are in the public domain. The quotation from *Ansichten der Natur* follows the 3rd edition of 1849 in a modern-spelling edition (Anaconda, 2022); the quotations from *Kosmos* follow the first volume (Cotta, 1845) as reprinted in the German History in Documents collection of the German Historical Institute, Washington, which keeps the old spelling (*todt*).

## Two brothers

The Humboldt brothers grew up in Berlin and at the family estate of Tegel. **Wilhelm** (1767–1835) became a diplomat, a scholar of language and, for little more than a year (1809–1810), the head of education in the Prussian government. In that short time he began a reform of the Prussian school system and prepared the founding of the University of Berlin, which opened in 1810. The idea associated with his name is the **[[unity of research and teaching]]** (*die Einheit von Forschung und Lehre*): professors should teach what they themselves are researching, and students should take part in research rather than just learn finished knowledge. Since 1949 the university has been called the Humboldt-Universität zu Berlin, after both brothers. Wilhelm also wrote on the diversity of human languages; his saying that language makes "infinite use of finite means" is still quoted by linguists.

**Alexander** (1769–1859) studied finance, natural science and mining, worked for some years as an inspector of mines in Prussia, and experimented on himself with electricity. When his mother died in 1796 he inherited enough money to finance a large expedition at his own expense. He was a *Naturforscher* in the broadest sense: botanist, geologist, geographer, astronomer and physicist at once. German calls such a person a *Universalgelehrter* (polymath), and Humboldt is often described as one of the last.

## The American journey, 1799–1804

In June 1799 Humboldt and the young French botanist Aimé Bonpland sailed from A Coruña in Spain to the Spanish colonies in America. The Spanish king had given them an unusual permission to travel and do research freely. The expedition lasted five years:

1. **Venezuela (1799–1800).** They landed at Cumaná and spent months on the coast and in the llanos, the grass plains. In 1800 they travelled by canoe up the Orinoco and showed that a natural channel, the Casiquiare, connects the Orinoco with the river system of the Amazon.
2. **Cuba (1800–1801).** A stay in Havana, where Humboldt studied the economy of the island and, later, wrote sharply against slavery.
3. **The Andes (1801–1802).** From Cartagena through Bogotá to Quito. In June 1802 they climbed Chimborazo, then believed to be the highest mountain in the world, and reached a height that no European was known to have reached before, without getting to the summit.
4. **Peru and Mexico (1802–1804).** On the Pacific coast Humboldt measured the temperature of the cold ocean current that is named after him today. A year in Mexico followed, with work in the archives and the mines.
5. **The United States (1804).** On the way home Humboldt visited Washington, D.C. and met President Thomas Jefferson. In August 1804 the travellers landed in Bordeaux.

They brought back a herbarium with many thousands of dried plants, including species unknown in Europe, as well as rock samples, drawings and notebooks full of measurements. Humboldt travelled with dozens of instruments: barometers to determine altitude, thermometers, a sextant and chronometer to determine latitude (*den Breitengrad*) and longitude (*den Längengrad*), and instruments for measuring the magnetism of the earth and the blue of the sky. His measurements corrected the maps of the regions he crossed: the *Vermessung* of the land was as important to him as the description of its plants.

He spent the next two decades in Paris writing up the results. The travel work appeared mostly in French, in some thirty volumes. In German, he published shorter books for a wider public.

## The Naturgemälde

One of the first results was a single large picture: a cross-section of Chimborazo and its neighbour Cotopaxi, on which the names of plants are written at the altitudes where they grow, from the tropical forest at the foot to the lichens below the snow line. Columns on both sides give temperature, air pressure, humidity and other values for each altitude. Humboldt called it a **[[Naturgemälde]]** (a "painting of nature"): a picture that shows at a glance how plants depend on climate and altitude. It was published in 1807 with his essay on the geography of plants, and it is often counted among the first modern infographics.

The idea behind it runs through all of Humboldt's work: to understand a plant, you have to know the climate, the soil, the altitude and the neighbours it lives with. Today we would call that thinking in ecosystems; the word *Ökologie* was coined only in 1866, by Ernst Haeckel.

## Ansichten der Natur: science for readers

*Ansichten der Natur* (Views of Nature, first edition 1808, extended in 1826 and 1849) is said to have been Humboldt's favourite among his books. It contains essays on the grasslands of South America, the waterfalls of the Orinoco and the life of the tropical forest at night. Each essay is written for general readers, in carefully composed prose; the scientific details are added in long notes at the end. The essay on the steppes and deserts begins *„Am Fuße des hohen Granitrückens, welcher im Jugendalter unseres Planeten …“* and only arrives at its main verb several lines later.

In the preface to the first edition Humboldt says what he wants to achieve:

> „Überblick der Natur im Großen, Beweis von dem Zusammenwirken der Kräfte, Erneuerung des Genusses, welchen die unmittelbare Ansicht der Tropenländer dem fühlenden Menschen gewährt, sind die Zwecke, nach denen ich strebe.“

> "An overview of nature on a grand scale, proof of the interaction of its forces, a renewal of the pleasure that the direct sight of tropical lands gives to the feeling human being: these are the aims I strive for."

How the sentence works:

- The subject is a list of three noun phrases without a conjunction: *Überblick …, Beweis …, Erneuerung …*. Only after all three does the verb come: *sind die Zwecke*. Plural verb, because three things are the subject.
- The nouns have no article: in lists and headings, German often drops the article (*Überblick der Natur im Großen*), which gives the sentence the weight of a programme.
- *welchen … gewährt*: a relative clause with *welch-* (formal, lesson 24), masculine accusative, referring to *der Genuss*. *gewähren* (to grant, to give) is formal.
- *dem fühlenden Menschen*: Partizip I as an attribute: the human being who feels. Humboldt wants to reach the feelings and the understanding at once; that is the programme of the whole book.
- *nach denen ich strebe*: *streben nach* (to strive for) with the preposition moved in front of the relative pronoun.

This is the C1 skill of reading long nominal sentences in a nutshell: find the verb (*sind*), find out what it agrees with (the three nouns), and then unpack each noun phrase.

## Kosmos: nature as a whole

Humboldt's last great work, *Kosmos. Entwurf einer physischen Weltbeschreibung* (Cosmos: Sketch of a Physical Description of the World), grew out of lectures he gave in Berlin in 1827–28, which were open to a broad public, not only to students. The first volume appeared in 1845, when Humboldt was 75; the fifth was published after his death, in 1862. The book attempts nothing less than a description of the whole universe, from the stars to the distribution of plants, and of the history of how people have seen nature.

Early in the first volume he defines his subject:

> „Die Natur ist für die denkende Betrachtung Einheit in der Vielheit, Verbindung des Mannigfaltigen in Form und Mischung …“

> "Nature, for the contemplative mind, is unity in diversity, a connection of the manifold in form and composition …"

And a little later:

> „Nicht ein todtes Aggregat ist die Natur …“

> "Nature is not a dead aggregate …"

Grammar notes:

- *Einheit in der Vielheit*: two abstract nouns in *-heit*, a typical pattern of philosophical German (lesson 90). *das Mannigfaltige* (the manifold, the many different things) is a nominalized adjective; *mannigfaltig* (varied, diverse) is still used in formal writing.
- *für die denkende Betrachtung*: for thoughtful contemplation, again a Partizip I attribute.
- *Nicht ein todtes Aggregat ist die Natur*: the subject (*die Natur*) comes last and the negated predicate first. Putting the negated element in the Vorfeld makes a strong contrast: "a dead aggregate is exactly what nature is not" (lesson 20 on information structure). *todt* is the old spelling of *tot*, like *Muth* and *Theil* in Kant (lesson 92). *nicht ein* instead of *kein* is contrastive negation: it rejects one description to make room for another, and Humboldt goes straight on (after a colon) to say what nature is instead, in Schelling's words: "the holy, eternally creating primal force of the world".

*Kosmos* was a bestseller; the first volume is reported to have sold out within weeks. Humboldt's ideal of a *Naturbeschreibung* that is both exact and beautiful, measured and felt, influenced writers and painters as much as scientists.

## Telling the story of an expedition

Here is an original text written for this course in the style of a popular-science magazine. It describes one episode of the journey. Notice the tenses and the participial constructions.

> **Mit Messgeräten in den Urwald**
>
> Als Alexander von Humboldt und Aimé Bonpland im Frühjahr 1800 zu ihrer Fahrt auf dem Orinoco aufbrachen, hatten sie bereits Monate in Venezuela verbracht. Sie hatten Pflanzen gesammelt, Höhlen erkundet und in den Llanos Zitteraale untersucht, Fische, die starke elektrische Schläge austeilen können. Nun wollten sie eine Frage klären, über die die Geografen in Europa seit Langem stritten: ob es zwischen dem Orinoco und dem Amazonas tatsächlich eine natürliche Wasserverbindung gebe.
>
> Die Reise im Kanu dauerte mehrere Wochen. Tagsüber vermaß Humboldt den Fluss, bestimmte mit seinen Instrumenten Breitengrade und notierte Temperaturen; nachts, von Moskitos geplagt, beobachtete er die Sterne, um die Längengrade zu berechnen. Die von Bonpland gesammelten Pflanzen wurden in Papier gepresst und in Kisten verstaut, die man vor der feuchten Luft kaum schützen konnte.
>
> Im Mai 1800 erreichten die beiden Forschungsreisenden den Casiquiare. Nachdem sie den Fluss befahren und seine Richtung gemessen hatten, stand fest, was bis dahin nur Gerücht gewesen war: Der Casiquiare verbindet die beiden großen Flusssysteme. Humboldt trug die Verbindung in seine Karten ein, die später die Kartografie der Region verändern sollten.
>
> Zurück in Angostura, erschöpft und vom Fieber geschwächt, musste Bonpland wochenlang das Bett hüten. Humboldt dagegen begann, seine Messungen auszuwerten.

> **With instruments into the jungle**
>
> When Alexander von Humboldt and Aimé Bonpland set off on their journey up the Orinoco in the spring of 1800, they had already spent months in Venezuela. They had collected plants, explored caves and examined electric eels in the llanos, fish that can deliver strong electric shocks. Now they wanted to settle a question that geographers in Europe had been arguing about for a long time: whether there really was a natural waterway between the Orinoco and the Amazon.
>
> The journey by canoe took several weeks. During the day Humboldt surveyed the river, determined degrees of latitude with his instruments and noted temperatures; at night, plagued by mosquitoes, he observed the stars in order to calculate longitude. The plants collected by Bonpland were pressed in paper and stowed in boxes that could hardly be protected from the damp air.
>
> In May 1800 the two explorers reached the Casiquiare. After they had travelled along the river and measured its direction, what until then had only been rumour was established: the Casiquiare connects the two great river systems. Humboldt entered the connection in his maps, which were later to change the cartography of the region.
>
> Back in Angostura, exhausted and weakened by fever, Bonpland had to stay in bed for weeks. Humboldt, by contrast, began to evaluate his measurements.

### Tenses: Präteritum and Plusquamperfekt

The text is a narrative, so the main line of events is in the Präteritum: *aufbrachen, dauerte, vermaß, erreichten, trug ein*. Whenever the text looks back from a point in the story to something that happened before it, it uses the Plusquamperfekt: *hatten … verbracht, hatten … gesammelt, … gewesen war, nachdem sie … gemessen hatten*. This relation, "earlier than the point in the story", is called **[[anteriority]]** (*die Vorzeitigkeit*). Three typical places for the Plusquamperfekt:

- after *nachdem*: *Nachdem sie den Fluss befahren hatten, stand fest, …* (*nachdem* + Plusquamperfekt, main clause in the Präteritum, is the standard pattern);
- in the background at the start of an episode: *Als sie aufbrachen, hatten sie bereits Monate … verbracht;*
- in relative clauses about earlier states: *was bis dahin nur Gerücht gewesen war*.

A common mistake is to use the Plusquamperfekt as a "more past" tense for everything long ago. If events simply follow one another, the Präteritum is enough, however long ago they happened.

Two further time references:

- *die später die Kartografie der Region verändern sollten*: *sollen* in the Präteritum + infinitive for the "future in the past", what was going to happen (were later to change). It's typical of historical narration and biography: *Er sollte seine Heimat nie wiedersehen.*

### Participial constructions

The text uses the participle structures of lesson 08:

- Participial attribute: *die von Bonpland gesammelten Pflanzen* = *die Pflanzen, die Bonpland gesammelt hatte*. The attribute contains its own agent (*von Bonpland*).
- Participial clauses (*Partizipialsätze*) as adverbials: *nachts, von Moskitos geplagt, beobachtete er …* (while plagued by mosquitoes); *Zurück in Angostura, erschöpft und vom Fieber geschwächt, musste Bonpland …* The implicit subject of the participle is the subject of the main clause (Humboldt in the first, Bonpland in the second). Commas with participle groups are often optional (§ 72), unless the group is announced by a reference word or trails after the clause (lesson 08); in long sentences like these they make reading easier.

In German academic biography and popular-science writing, these structures make it possible to pack a lot of background into one sentence without a string of subordinate clauses. Used too often, they make a text heavy; a good C1 text mixes them with ordinary clauses, as above.

### An indirect question in Konjunktiv I

*ob es … tatsächlich eine natürliche Wasserverbindung gebe*: the indirect question reports what the geographers were asking, so it takes the Konjunktiv I (*gebe*), as in news German. *gibt* (indicative) would also be correct; *gebe* sounds more formal and keeps the question at a distance.

## Writing about an expedition yourself

Useful phrases for describing a scientific journey or biography at C1:

- *Die Expedition führte ihn von … über … bis nach …* — The expedition took him from … via … to …
- *Nachdem er …, brach er zu … auf.* — After he had …, he set off for …
- *Zu den wichtigsten Ergebnissen zählt …* — Among the most important results is …
- *Er gilt als Begründer der …* — He is regarded as the founder of …
- *Seine Messungen ermöglichten es erstmals, … zu kartieren.* — His measurements made it possible for the first time to map …
- *Was ihn von anderen Forschungsreisenden unterschied, war …* — What distinguished him from other explorers was … (a Sperrsatz, lesson 20)

Be careful with superlatives and "firsts" in biographies: *als einer der Ersten*, *gilt als* and *wird oft als … bezeichnet* are safer than *als Erster*, unless you have checked the fact.

## Pronunciation

- *Humboldt*: HUM-bolt; the *dt* is pronounced [t], as in *Stadt*.
- *die Expedition*: ex-pe-di-TSION, stress on the last syllable, like all nouns in *-tion*.
- *das Herbarium*: her-BA-ri-um; plural *Herbarien*: her-BA-rjen, three syllables (the *i* is not a separate syllable, as in *Familie*).
- *die Kartografie*: kar-to-gra-FIE.
- *Chimborazo*: German speakers usually say tschim-bo-RA-so.

## Common mistakes

- Using the Plusquamperfekt for every past event, however long ago: ~~Humboldt war 1769 in Berlin geboren worden.~~ → *Humboldt wurde 1769 in Berlin geboren.* The Plusquamperfekt needs a later point in the story to look back from.
- *nachdem* with the Präteritum in both clauses: ~~Nachdem sie den Fluss befuhren, stand fest …~~ → *Nachdem sie den Fluss befahren hatten, stand fest …*
- A participial clause with the wrong implicit subject: ~~Von Moskitos geplagt, waren die Sterne gut zu sehen.~~ (the stars were not plagued by mosquitoes) → *Von Moskitos geplagt, beobachtete Humboldt die Sterne.*
- Confusing *vermessen* (to survey, to measure precisely) with *messen* (to measure): *die Temperatur messen*, but *ein Land vermessen*. *sich vermessen* means to make a mistake in measuring.
- *Breitengrad* vs *Längengrad*: latitude (north–south position, parallel to the equator) vs longitude (east–west position).
- *der/die Forschungsreisende* is an adjectival noun: *ein Forschungsreisender, eine Forschungsreisende, die Forschungsreisenden*, and *mit einem Forschungsreisenden*.

## Key points

- Alexander von Humboldt (1769–1859) travelled through Spanish America with Aimé Bonpland from 1799 to 1804, measured, mapped and collected, and saw nature as one connected whole; his **[[Naturgemälde]]** of the Andes shows plants by altitude and climate.
- *Ansichten der Natur* (1808, 3rd ed. 1849) combines literary essays and scientific notes; *Kosmos* (1845–1862) describes the whole universe as *Einheit in der Vielheit*.
- His brother Wilhelm (1767–1835) prepared the founding of the University of Berlin (1810); the **[[unity of research and teaching]]** is the principle associated with his name.
- To narrate an expedition: Präteritum for the main events, Plusquamperfekt for **[[anteriority]]** (especially after *nachdem*), *sollte* + infinitive for the future in the past, Konjunktiv I for reported words.
- Participial attributes (*die von Bonpland gesammelten Pflanzen*) and participial clauses (*von Moskitos geplagt, …*) condense background information; their implicit subject must be the subject of the main clause.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete the lesson.

sections.name: Varieties, literature and the C1 exam
Honors: Denken, Sprache und Geschichte (thought, language and history)

questions.stem: Kant: "Selbstverschuldet ist diese Unmündigkeit, wenn die Ursache derselben nicht am Mangel des Verstandes, sondern der Entschließung und des Mutes liegt …" When, according to Kant, is immaturity self-incurred?
choices: When a person lacks the intelligence to think for themselves
When a person could think for themselves but lacks the resolution and courage to do so
When a person is still legally under age
When the state forbids people to publish their thoughts
questions.explanation: The cause lies "nicht am Mangel des Verstandes, sondern der Entschließung und des Mutes": not in a lack of understanding, but in a lack of resolution and courage. Someone who really lacks understanding is not to blame. Legal age is only where the word mündig comes from, and censorship is a separate topic of the essay.

questions.stem: In "… des Mutes liegt, sich seiner ohne Leitung eines andern zu bedienen", what does "seiner" refer to?
choices: die Leitung
der Mut
der Mensch
der Verstand
questions.explanation: "sich einer Sache bedienen" takes a genitive object, and "seiner" is the genitive pronoun for a masculine or neuter noun: the courage to use it, i.e. one's understanding (der Verstand), exactly as in the previous sentence ("sich seines Verstandes … zu bedienen"). Mut is masculine too, but one doesn't "use courage without guidance"; die Leitung is feminine (it would be "ihrer"), and a person is not what is being used.

questions.stem: Complete with the article (genitive object): "Bei der Abstimmung im Rat enthielt sie sich ___ Stimme."
questions.explanation: "sich einer Sache enthalten" (to abstain from something) takes the genitive: "sich der Stimme enthalten", to abstain in a vote. "die" would be the accusative, which this verb doesn't take.

questions.stem: Which sentence means the same as "Dieser Vorschlag bedarf einer gründlichen Prüfung."?
choices: Dieser Vorschlag braucht eine gründliche Prüfung.
Dieser Vorschlag hat eine gründliche Prüfung bestanden.
Dieser Vorschlag ist das Ergebnis einer gründlichen Prüfung.
Dieser Vorschlag verdient keine gründliche Prüfung.
questions.explanation: "einer Sache bedürfen" (formal, with the genitive) means "to need, to require": the proposal needs a thorough examination. It says nothing about an examination already passed or already done, and it isn't negative.

questions.stem: In an 18th-century text: "Der Fürst lobte den Minister, nachdem dieser die Reform durchgeführt, vor dem ganzen Hof." Which word would modern German need after "durchgeführt"?
choices: worden
zu
hatte
nothing: the participle is used as an adjective here
questions.explanation: This is the dropped auxiliary of older written German: the finite auxiliary at the end of the subordinate clause is left out. Modern German needs "nachdem dieser die Reform durchgeführt hatte" (Plusquamperfekt with haben after nachdem). "worden" would make a passive, which doesn't fit because "dieser" is the agent, and "zu" would make an infinitive.

questions.stem: Kant's distinction: is each activity a public or a private use of reason?
left: Ein Offizier führt im Dienst einen Befehl aus, den er für falsch hält.
Derselbe Offizier veröffentlicht unter seinem Namen einen Aufsatz über Fehler im Kriegsdienst.
Ein Pfarrer lehrt im Gottesdienst, was seine Kirche vorschreibt.
Ein Bürger, der seine Steuern pünktlich zahlt, kritisiert sie in einer Zeitschrift als ungerecht.
choices: private use of reason
public use of reason
questions.explanation: For Kant, "private" means using one's reason in an office or post (officer on duty, pastor in church), where obedience may be required. "Public" means speaking as a scholar to the reading public, for example in a published article, and that must always be free. The taxpayer pays (duty) but may criticize the tax in print: the criticism is the public use.

questions.stem: Listen to part of a radio interview with a philosopher. Statement: "Kant hielt seine eigene Zeit für ein bereits aufgeklärtes Zeitalter."

audio.text: Viele vergessen, dass Kants Aufsatz eigentlich eine Antwort war. Ein Berliner Pfarrer hatte in einer Fußnote gefragt, was Aufklärung denn überhaupt sei. Kant antwortet darauf erstaunlich bescheiden. Er sagt nicht: Wir haben es geschafft. Er sagt im Gegenteil, man lebe noch nicht in einem aufgeklärten Zeitalter, wohl aber in einem Zeitalter der Aufklärung. Das heißt: Der Prozess hat begonnen, aber er ist längst nicht abgeschlossen. Und ich würde sagen, das gilt heute genauso.

choices: stimmt
stimmt nicht
dazu wird nichts gesagt
questions.explanation: The philosopher stresses that Kant said the opposite: "man lebe noch nicht in einem aufgeklärten Zeitalter, wohl aber in einem Zeitalter der Aufklärung" – the process had begun but was far from complete. So the statement is false (stimmt nicht).

questions.stem: Listen to a contribution to a radio discussion. What is the speaker's position on the planned ban?

audio.text: Ich verstehe ja, dass die Stadt etwas gegen den Zuckerkonsum tun will. Aber ein Verbot von Süßgetränken in allen öffentlichen Gebäuden, also auch für Erwachsene? Das ist für mich Bevormundung. Erwachsene können selbst entscheiden, was sie trinken. Was ich dagegen sofort unterschreiben würde: klare Warnhinweise und mehr Aufklärung in den Schulen. Mündige Bürger brauchen Informationen, keine Verbote.

choices: She supports the ban because sugar consumption is dangerous.
She has not made up her mind yet.
She rejects the ban for adults as paternalism but supports warnings and education.
She thinks people are not able to make their own decisions about food.
questions.explanation: She calls the ban "Bevormundung" (paternalism) because adults can decide for themselves, but would "sofort unterschreiben" clear warnings and more education. She understands the city's concern but doesn't support the ban, and she says the opposite of the last choice: "Mündige Bürger brauchen Informationen, keine Verbote."

questions.stem:
Read the text. According to the writer, in which situation could the teacher criticize the curriculum freely under Kant's distinction?

"Darf eine Lehrerin ihre Schulbehörde öffentlich kritisieren? Wer Kants Aufsatz von 1784 liest, findet darauf eine erstaunlich moderne Antwort. Nach Kants Unterscheidung müsste sie im Unterricht den Lehrplan befolgen, denn das gehört zu ihrem Amt; hier ist der Gebrauch der Vernunft eingeschränkt. Schreibt sie aber unter ihrem eigenen Namen einen Zeitungsartikel über die Mängel dieses Lehrplans, so spricht sie als Gelehrte zum Publikum, und daran dürfte sie niemand hindern. Manche Arbeitgeber sehen das heute anders und verlangen von ihren Beschäftigten, sich öffentlich zurückzuhalten. Gerade deshalb lohnt es sich, den alten Text wieder zu lesen."
choices: In class, when she explains the curriculum to her pupils
In a newspaper article written under her own name
Only in an anonymous letter to the authority
In no situation, because she is a civil servant
questions.explanation: "Schreibt sie aber unter ihrem eigenen Namen einen Zeitungsartikel …, so spricht sie als Gelehrte zum Publikum, und daran dürfte sie niemand hindern": that is Kant's public use of reason. In class she uses her reason "privately", in her office, and must follow the curriculum. The text says nothing about anonymous letters, and Kant's point is precisely that holding an office doesn't forbid public criticism.

questions.stem: In the same text: "Gerade deshalb lohnt es sich, den alten Text wieder zu lesen." What does "deshalb" refer to?
choices: That some employers today expect their staff to keep quiet in public
That Kant wrote the essay in 1784
That teachers must follow the curriculum in class
That the essay is difficult to read
questions.explanation: "deshalb" points back to the sentence just before it: "Manche Arbeitgeber sehen das heute anders und verlangen …, sich öffentlich zurückzuhalten." Because of this modern pressure, the writer finds Kant's text worth rereading. The date and the duty in class are mentioned earlier but are not the reason given, and the text never says the essay is hard to read.

questions.stem: Build Kant's kind of sentence (condition without wenn, resumed by so).
questions.prompt: If I have a doctor who decides for me, I needn't trouble myself.
questions.explanation: The verb-first conditional ("Habe ich …") replaces "wenn ich … habe"; the main clause can start with "so" (older and formal) or directly with the verb ("brauche ich"), so both are accepted. "nicht … zu bemühen brauchen" is the negative of "müssen"; "muss" can't be combined with "zu bemühen".

questions.stem: Kant's contemporaries wrote "Muth", "Theil" and "seyn". What are the modern spellings?
choices: Muht, Teihl, sein
Mut, Theil, sein
Muth, Teil, sein
Mut, Teil, sein
questions.explanation: The th in German words lost its h in the 1901 spelling rules (Muth → Mut, Theil → Teil), and the y in seyn had already given way to i (sein). The other choices keep one of the old spellings or put the length h in the wrong place.

questions.stem: Which statement about the Kinder- und Hausmärchen is correct?
choices: The Grimms wrote down each tale exactly as they heard it and never changed it.
Most tales were invented by Jacob Grimm himself.
Wilhelm Grimm in particular reworked the style of the tales from edition to edition until 1857.
The first edition already contained the final version of every tale.
questions.explanation: Wilhelm rewrote the tales over seven editions (1812/15 to 1857): he added atmosphere, dialogue and fixed phrases and made them more suitable for children, as the two openings of Der Froschkönig show. So the tales were neither recorded unchanged nor invented by Jacob, and the first edition was not final.

questions.stem: "In den alten Zeiten, wo das Wünschen noch geholfen hat, lebte ein König, dessen Töchter waren alle schön." What is unusual about "dessen Töchter waren alle schön"?
choices: It is a relative clause with a word-order mistake that the Grimms overlooked.
It is a main clause (verb second) in which "dessen" works like a demonstrative: "his daughters were all beautiful".
It is a question without a question mark.
"dessen" is the genitive of "die Töchter".
questions.explanation: A relative clause would end with the verb ("dessen Töchter alle schön waren"). Here the verb is in second position, so it is an older type of main clause introduced by a d-word, meaning "his daughters …". It is a deliberate feature of the style, not an error, and "dessen" refers to "ein König" (masculine), not to the daughters (that would be "deren").

questions.stem: Complete in the narrative tense of the fairy tale: "Da ___ der Zwerg: „Ein böser Zauberer hat meinen Herrn verzaubert.“" (sprechen)
questions.explanation: Fairy tales are narrated in the Präteritum: "Da sprach der Zwerg". The Perfekt ("hat … gesprochen") belongs to conversation and appears in a Märchen only inside direct speech, as in the dwarf's own words.

questions.stem: Dornröschen: "Es waren ihrer dreizehn in seinem Reiche." What does this mean?
choices: There were thirteen of them in his kingdom.
Thirteen of her people lived in his kingdom.
They had been in his kingdom for thirteen years.
Their thirteen children were rich.
questions.explanation: "ihrer" is the genitive of "sie" (them), used partitively: "thirteen of them", referring to the wise women. "Reiche" is "Reich" with the old dative -e, not the adjective "reich". Today you would say "Es gab dreizehn weise Frauen in seinem Reich."

questions.stem: Complete the closing formula: "Und wenn sie nicht gestorben sind, …"
choices: … dann sind sie noch heute gestorben.
… so lebten sie bis heute.
… dann hätten sie noch heute gelebt.
… dann leben sie noch heute.
questions.explanation: The formula is "Und wenn sie nicht gestorben sind, dann (or so) leben sie noch heute": if they haven't died, they are still alive today, hence the present tense. The Präteritum "lebten" and the Konjunktiv II "hätten … gelebt" don't fit the logic, and the first choice contradicts itself.

questions.stem: Match each word with its meaning.
choices: enchanted (under a spell)
cursed, damned
to release from a spell
to put a spell on
to escape
questions.explanation: "verwunschen" is the old participle of verwünschen, now an adjective for something enchanted (ein verwunschenes Schloss); "verwünscht" is the modern participle and means cursed or damned (dieser verwünschte Regen). "erlösen" ends a spell, "verzaubern" casts one. "to escape" would be flüchten (die Flucht), not der Fluch.

questions.stem: The thirteenth wise woman: "Die Königstochter soll sich in ihrem fünfzehnten Jahre an einer Spindel stechen und tot hinfallen." What does "soll" express here?
choices: Hearsay – people say that she pricked herself.
The speaker's will – she decrees that it will happen.
A polite suggestion to the king.
A regret – the princess should have been more careful.
questions.explanation: This is the "soll" of commands, laws and curses: the speaker declares what is to happen. Hearsay "soll" would refer to a past event with a perfect infinitive ("soll sich gestochen haben"); a regret would need the Konjunktiv II ("hätte … sollen"); and a curse is anything but polite.

questions.stem: Listen to an excerpt from a lecture. What does the speaker say about the idea that the Grimms' tales came "straight from the people"?

audio.text: Die Brüder Grimm haben ihre Märchen gern als Stimme des Volkes dargestellt. Schaut man sich aber an, wer ihnen die Geschichten erzählt hat, ergibt sich ein anderes Bild. Viele Beiträgerinnen waren junge Frauen aus gebildeten Kasseler Familien, einige mit französischen Vorfahren, die die Märchen von Perrault kannten. Die bekannteste Erzählerin, Dorothea Viehmann, war zwar keine Bürgerstochter, aber auch keine einfache Bäuerin. Und schließlich hat Wilhelm die Texte über Jahrzehnte sprachlich überarbeitet. Volksmärchen sind das also nur zum Teil.

choices: It is only partly true, because of who the storytellers were and how Wilhelm revised the texts.
It is completely true; the Grimms only wrote down what peasants told them.
It is false, because the Grimms invented the tales themselves.
questions.explanation: The speaker concludes: "Volksmärchen sind das also nur zum Teil." The reasons: many storytellers came from educated families and knew Perrault, and Wilhelm revised the texts for decades. The speaker doesn't say the tales were invented by the Grimms, nor that they came from peasants.

questions.stem: Listen to a radio report on the Deutsches Wörterbuch. Which statement is correct according to the report?

audio.text: Als Jacob und Wilhelm Grimm 1838 den Vertrag für ein deutsches Wörterbuch unterschrieben, rechneten sie mit wenigen Bänden. Es kam anders. Wilhelm starb 1859, Jacob vier Jahre später, mitten in der Arbeit am Artikel „Frucht“. Erst 1961, mehr als hundert Jahre nach dem ersten Band, war das Werk abgeschlossen. Wer heute wissen will, was ein Wort bei Luther oder Goethe bedeutete, findet es im „Grimm“, und zwar kostenlos im Internet.

choices: The brothers finished the dictionary shortly before their deaths.
The dictionary was completed only in 1961.
The dictionary can only be consulted in a library.
Wilhelm worked on the dictionary longer than Jacob.
questions.explanation: "Erst 1961 … war das Werk abgeschlossen." Jacob died in the middle of the entry "Frucht", so the brothers didn't finish it; Wilhelm died first (1859), four years before Jacob; and the report says the dictionary is free on the internet.

questions.stem: Put these events in time order, earliest first.
choices: The first volume of the Kinder- und Hausmärchen appears.
The brothers sign the contract for the Deutsches Wörterbuch.
The final edition of the Kinder- und Hausmärchen appears.
The Deutsches Wörterbuch is completed.
questions.explanation: Kinder- und Hausmärchen vol. 1: 1812; contract for the dictionary: 1838 (after the brothers lost their posts in Göttingen in 1837); final edition (Ausgabe letzter Hand) of the tales: 1857; completion of the dictionary: 1961.

questions.stem: Build the sentence from the tale in this lesson.
questions.prompt: She could spin so finely that her yarn was praised throughout the land.
questions.explanation: "so … dass" introduces a consequence; the finite verb goes to the end of the dass clause ("rühmte"), in the Präteritum like the rest of the narration. In the Mittelfeld, "ihr Garn" and "im ganzen Land" can change places, so both orders are accepted. "rühmt" would break the tense of the story.

questions.stem: You are retelling the tale "Das verwunschene Spinnrad" to a friend over coffee. Which sentence fits that situation best?
choices: Also, das Mädchen ist in den Wald gegangen und hat da so ein silbernes Spinnrad gefunden.
In dem Märchen findet ein armes Mädchen ein silbernes Spinnrad, neben dem ein Zwerg sitzt.
Da ging das Mädchen in den Wald und fand unter einer alten Eiche ein Spinnrad aus Silber.
Das Auffinden eines silbernen Spinnrads durch das Mädchen erfolgt im Wald.
questions.explanation: In conversation the past is usually told in the Perfekt, with colloquial markers such as "also" and "so ein". The second choice is the neutral present tense of a written plot summary, the third the fairy-tale Präteritum of the text itself, and the fourth an absurdly nominal style that fits no situation.

questions.stem: Which pair shows the effect of the High German (second) consonant shift?
choices: Latin "pater" – German "Vater"
Middle High German "hûs" – German "Haus"
English "water" – German "Wasser"
Middle High German "guot" – German "gut"
questions.explanation: In "water – Wasser", t after a vowel became ss in High German, which is the second consonant shift; English kept the old t. "pater – Vater" shows the first, Germanic shift (Grimm's law); "hûs – Haus" is the diphthongization and "guot – gut" the monophthongization, which are vowel changes.

questions.stem: Match each Low German word with its Standard German counterpart.
choices: ich
Apfel
Zeit
Wasser
Wetter
questions.explanation: Low German kept the consonants that High German shifted: k after a vowel became ch (ik – ich), p became pf (Appel – Apfel), t at the start of a word became z (Tied – Zeit), t after a vowel became ss (Water – Wasser). "Wetter" (weather) is a different word, with no shift.

questions.stem: The Benrath line, the traditional boundary between Low German and the High German dialects, separates which forms?
choices: maken (north) and machen (south)
ik (north) and ich (south)
Appel (north) and Apfel (south)
Hus (north) and Haus (south)
questions.explanation: The Benrath line, named after a district of Düsseldorf, is the maken/machen line. The ik/ich boundary is the Uerdingen line a little further north, Appel/Apfel lies much further south near Speyer, and Hus/Haus is a vowel difference, not part of the consonant shift.

questions.stem: Put the periods of German in time order, earliest first.
choices: Althochdeutsch
Mittelhochdeutsch
Frühneuhochdeutsch
Neuhochdeutsch
questions.explanation: Old High German (about 750–1050, e.g. the Hildebrandslied), Middle High German (about 1050–1350, Walther von der Vogelweide), Early New High German (about 1350–1650, Luther's Bible), New High German (from about 1650). The dates are conventions and vary slightly between books.

questions.stem: Middle High German "mîn niuwez hûs" became which phrase in modern German?
choices: mein nüwes Hus
mine neue Hus
min neues Haus
mein neues Haus
questions.explanation: Through the New High German diphthongization the long vowels î, iu and û became ei, eu and au: mîn → mein, niuwez → neues, hûs → Haus. The other choices keep at least one old long vowel, as some dialects still do (Swiss German Huus, miin).

questions.stem: Why is the long i in "Liebe" spelled "ie"?
choices: Because the word was borrowed from French.
Because the spelling keeps a Middle High German diphthong that later became a long vowel.
Because "ie" shows that the word has two syllables in the middle.
Because the 1996 spelling reform introduced it.
questions.explanation: In Middle High German "liebe" had a diphthong, [iə]. The monophthongization turned it into a long [iː], but the spelling stayed, and "ie" became the normal way to write long i. "Liebe" is an inherited Germanic word, it has two syllables (Lie-be), and the spelling is centuries older than the 1996 reform.

questions.stem: Complete: "Seit der Rechtschreibreform von 1996 schreibt man nicht mehr „daß“, sondern „___“."
questions.explanation: The reform introduced ss after a short vowel: daß → dass (also Fluß → Fluss). ß remains after a long vowel or diphthong (Straße, heißen).

questions.stem: Luther 1545: "IM anfang war das Wort / Vnd das wort war bey Gott / vnd Gott war das Wort." Which statement about this text is correct?
choices: The slash (/) does the job of today's comma.
"Vnd" is a different word from "und", meaning "but".
All nouns are already capitalized, as in modern German.
"bey" is a printing error for "bei".
questions.explanation: The virgule (/) is the comma of the period. "Vnd" is simply "und": u and v were two shapes of one letter, with v at the start of a word. Capitals are not yet systematic ("das Wort" and "das wort", "anfang"), and "bey" is the normal y spelling of the time, which Kant still used in "seyn".

questions.stem: Listen to the end of a lecture. According to the lecturer, how do we know how Middle High German sounded?

audio.text: Bleibt die Frage, woher wir eigentlich wissen, wie man um 1200 gesprochen hat. Tonaufnahmen gibt es natürlich keine. Wir haben aber die Reime der Dichter: Wenn Walther zwei Wörter aufeinander reimt, dürfen wir annehmen, dass sie für ihn ähnlich geklungen haben. Dazu kommen Schreibungen, die sich in den Handschriften einer Region allmählich verändern. Und dann gibt es die heutigen Mundarten, die manches Alte bewahrt haben. Kein einzelnes Indiz beweist etwas, aber zusammen ergeben sie ein recht verlässliches Bild.

choices: From a few early sound recordings found in monasteries.
From several kinds of evidence together, such as rhymes, spellings and today's dialects.
Only from the rhymes of the poets, which prove the pronunciation exactly.
questions.explanation: The lecturer lists rhymes, changing spellings and modern dialects, and stresses that "kein einzelnes Indiz beweist etwas, aber zusammen ergeben sie ein recht verlässliches Bild". There are no recordings ("Tonaufnahmen gibt es natürlich keine"), and rhymes alone prove nothing.

questions.stem: Listen to part of an interview with a historian of language. Statement: "Die Historikerin meint, Luther habe die deutsche Schriftsprache allein geschaffen."

audio.text: Man liest immer wieder, Luther habe das Hochdeutsche erfunden. Das ist eine schöne Legende, aber eben eine Legende. Luther hat sich an der sächsischen Kanzleisprache orientiert, die es lange vor ihm gab, und die Drucker haben ebenfalls daran gearbeitet, regionale Formen zu vermeiden. Was Luther tatsächlich geleistet hat: Seine Bibel wurde in riesigen Auflagen gedruckt und gelesen. Dadurch wurde eine bestimmte Form des Deutschen überall bekannt.

choices: stimmt
stimmt nicht
dazu wird nichts gesagt
questions.explanation: She calls this idea "eine schöne Legende, aber eben eine Legende": Luther built on the Saxon chancery language, and the printers also helped. His real contribution, in her view, was the enormous circulation of his Bible. So the statement is false.

questions.stem: Build the sentence (passive).
questions.prompt: The word "Fenster" was borrowed from Latin early on.
questions.explanation: Passive: "wurde" in second position, the participle "entlehnt" at the end. Any of the three phrases can stand in the Vorfeld, and the other two can be ordered either way in the Mittelfeld, so all six orders are accepted. "entliehen" is the participle of "entleihen" (to borrow a book or object), not the term for words: "entlehnen".

questions.stem: Which word is a loan translation (Lehnübersetzung)?
choices: Fenster (from Latin "fenestra")
Computer (from English)
Hand (Germanic)
Wolkenkratzer (from English "skyscraper")
questions.explanation: "Wolkenkratzer" translates "skyscraper" part by part with German words (Wolke + kratzen), so only the pattern is borrowed. "Fenster" is a loanword absorbed long ago, "Computer" a foreign word taken over whole, and "Hand" an inherited word.

questions.stem: Which statement about Humboldt's American journey is correct?
choices: He travelled alone and financed the journey with a grant from the Prussian king.
He showed that the Casiquiare connects the Orinoco with the river system of the Amazon.
He reached the summit of Chimborazo in 1802.
He published all his results in German immediately after his return.
questions.explanation: In 1800 Humboldt and Bonpland travelled up the Orinoco and confirmed the Casiquiare connection. Humboldt travelled with Aimé Bonpland and paid with his inheritance; on Chimborazo they reached a record height but not the summit; and the main travel work appeared over many years, mostly in French.

questions.stem: Complete: "Als sie im Frühjahr 1800 zum Orinoco aufbrachen, ___ sie bereits Monate in Venezuela ___."
choices: haben … verbracht
waren … verbracht
hatten … verbracht
verbrachten … (no second word)
questions.explanation: The months in Venezuela came before the departure, the point of reference in the story, so the Plusquamperfekt expresses anteriority: "hatten … verbracht" (verbringen takes haben). The Perfekt "haben … verbracht" doesn't fit a Präteritum narrative, "waren" is the wrong auxiliary, and "verbrachten" would put the two events on the same level.

questions.stem: Complete with the auxiliary: "Nachdem Humboldt den Fluss vermessen ___, kehrte er nach Angostura zurück."
questions.explanation: After "nachdem" the earlier action is in the Plusquamperfekt when the main clause is in the Präteritum: "nachdem er … vermessen hatte, kehrte er … zurück". vermessen takes haben, and "hat" (Perfekt) would not show that the surveying came before the return.

questions.stem: Which relative clause means the same as "die von Bonpland gesammelten Pflanzen"?
choices: die Pflanzen, die Bonpland gesammelt hatte
die Pflanzen, die Bonpland sammelten
die Pflanzen, von denen Bonpland gesammelt wurde
die Pflanzen, die Bonpland sammeln wollte
questions.explanation: The participial attribute contains a Partizip II with an agent (von Bonpland): the plants that Bonpland had collected. In the second choice the plants would be collecting Bonpland (plural verb, plants as subject), the third makes Bonpland the one collected, and the fourth only says he wanted to collect them.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses the participial clause correctly?
choices: Von Moskitos geplagt, waren die Sterne in dieser Nacht besonders klar.
Von Moskitos geplagt, war die Nacht für die Messungen zu kurz.
Von Moskitos geplagt, beobachtete Humboldt die ganze Nacht die Sterne.
Von Moskitos geplagt, gelangen Humboldt in dieser Nacht keine Messungen.
questions.explanation: The implicit subject of a participial clause is the subject of the main clause. Only in the third sentence is it the person plagued by mosquitoes: Humboldt. In the others the subject is the stars, the night or the measurements (keine Messungen gelangen ihm), so the sentences say that these were plagued by mosquitoes.

questions.stem: "Humboldt trug die Verbindung in seine Karten ein, die später die Kartografie der Region verändern sollten." What does "verändern sollten" express?
choices: What ought to change in the cartography of the region today
What would have happened if the maps had been published
What had happened before Humboldt drew the maps
What was going to happen later, seen from the time of the story
questions.explanation: In historical narration, "sollte" + infinitive (Präteritum) expresses the future in the past: the maps were later to change the cartography, and did. It isn't advice about today, and it isn't an unreal condition (that would need "hätten … verändert"); the earlier past would be the Plusquamperfekt.

questions.stem: Match each word with its meaning.
choices: to survey (measure precisely)
to map
degree of latitude
degree of longitude
altitude
questions.explanation: "vermessen" means measuring land or a region precisely (strong: vermaß, hat vermessen); "kartieren" means recording on a map. "der Breitengrad" gives the north–south position, "der Längengrad" the east–west position. Altitude is "die Höhe" or "die Höhenlage".

questions.stem: Listen to part of a radio portrait. What does the speaker mean by the "Einheit von Forschung und Lehre"?

audio.text: Wilhelm von Humboldt war nur gut ein Jahr für das preußische Bildungswesen zuständig, aber diese Zeit hat genügt, um die Gründung der Berliner Universität vorzubereiten. Mit seinem Namen verbindet man bis heute die Einheit von Forschung und Lehre. Gemeint ist: Professoren sollen nicht fertiges Wissen vortragen, das sie aus Büchern haben, sondern das lehren, woran sie selbst forschen. Und die Studierenden sollen nicht nur zuhören, sondern selbst an der Forschung beteiligt werden.

choices: Universities should teach only subjects that are useful for the state.
Professors should teach from their own research, and students should take part in research.
Research and teaching should take place in separate institutions.
questions.explanation: The speaker explains: professors should teach "das …, woran sie selbst forschen", and students "selbst an der Forschung beteiligt werden". Nothing is said about usefulness to the state, and the idea is the opposite of separating research from teaching.

questions.stem: Listen to a museum audio guide. What is the main point the speaker makes about Humboldt's Naturgemälde?

audio.text: Vor Ihnen hängt eine Reproduktion des berühmten Naturgemäldes der Anden. Auf den ersten Blick sieht man einfach einen Berg im Querschnitt. Schauen Sie aber genauer hin: In die Flanken des Berges hat Humboldt die Namen von Pflanzen geschrieben, und zwar genau in der Höhe, in der sie wachsen. Links und rechts stehen Tabellen mit Temperatur, Luftdruck und Feuchtigkeit. Humboldt wollte nicht einzelne Pflanzen beschreiben, sondern auf einen Blick zeigen, wie Pflanzenwelt, Höhe und Klima zusammenhängen.

choices: It is mainly a landscape painting made for its beauty.
It is a detailed map for climbers of the Andes.
It shows how plant life, altitude and climate are connected, all in one picture.
It shows the individual plants of the Andes in detailed drawings.
questions.explanation: The key sentence is the last one: Humboldt wanted "auf einen Blick zeigen, wie Pflanzenwelt, Höhe und Klima zusammenhängen". The speaker says the picture looks like a simple cross-section, not a landscape painting for its own sake; it gives plant names at their altitudes rather than drawings of individual plants, and it isn't a route map.

questions.stem: Build the sentence (nachdem + Plusquamperfekt).
questions.prompt: After they had travelled along the river, the connection was established.
questions.explanation: The nachdem clause comes first, with the Plusquamperfekt at its end ("befahren hatten"); the main clause then starts with the verb ("stand … fest", separable feststehen). "befahren" takes haben, so "waren" is wrong.

questions.stem: "… Erneuerung des Genusses, welchen die unmittelbare Ansicht der Tropenländer dem fühlenden Menschen gewährt, …" What does "welchen" refer to?
choices: die Ansicht
die Tropenländer
der Mensch
der Genuss
questions.explanation: "welchen" is a masculine accusative relative pronoun: the pleasure (den Genuss) that the sight of tropical lands gives to the feeling person. "die Ansicht" is the subject inside the relative clause, "die Tropenländer" are plural, and "der Mensch" is the dative object in the clause ("dem fühlenden Menschen").

questions.stem: Humboldt, Kosmos: "Nicht ein todtes Aggregat ist die Natur." Why is "Nicht ein todtes Aggregat" at the beginning?
choices: To make a question without a question mark
To put strong emphasis on what nature is not, as a contrast
Because the subject always comes last in 19th-century German
Because "todt" is the subject of the sentence
questions.explanation: Putting the negated predicate in the Vorfeld creates a strong contrast: "a dead aggregate is exactly what nature is not". The subject is "die Natur", placed at the end for weight; 19th-century German had the same word order rules as today, and "todt" is just the old spelling of "tot", an adjective.

questions.stem: Complete in the Perfekt: "Die Delegation ___ nicht früher abreisen ___."
choices: ist … dürfen
hat … dürfen
hat … gedurft
ist … gedurft
questions.explanation: With an infinitive, a modal verb forms its Perfekt with the double infinitive: hat abreisen dürfen. The auxiliary is always haben, because it belongs to the modal, even though abreisen on its own takes sein (sie ist abgereist). "gedurft" is used only when the modal stands alone (Das hat sie nicht gedurft).

questions.stem: Which is the correct subordinate-clause version of "Die Regierung hat am Ende nachgeben müssen"? "Der Diplomat räumte ein, dass …"
choices: die Regierung am Ende nachgeben müssen hat
die Regierung hat am Ende nachgeben müssen
die Regierung am Ende müssen hat nachgeben
die Regierung am Ende hat nachgeben müssen
questions.explanation: With a double infinitive the finite verb hat does not go to the very end of the subordinate clause; it comes directly in front of the two infinitives. Everything else (here: am Ende) stays before hat. "nachgeben müssen hat" puts hat at the end, and "hat am Ende nachgeben müssen" lets am Ende slip in after hat.

questions.stem: Which sentence means "The treaty had to be ratified by both parliaments"?
choices: Der Vertrag hat von beiden Parlamenten ratifiziert werden müssen.
Der Vertrag hat von beiden Parlamenten ratifiziert müssen werden.
Der Vertrag ist von beiden Parlamenten ratifiziert werden müssen.
Der Vertrag hat von beiden Parlamenten ratifizieren müssen.
questions.explanation: Modal + passive in the Perfekt: hat + Partizip II + werden + modal infinitive (read from the right: müssen → werden → ratifiziert). The order "ratifiziert müssen werden" is the English order, "ist" is the wrong auxiliary (modals always take haben), and "hat … ratifizieren müssen" is active: the treaty itself would have had to ratify something.

questions.stem: Type the missing word: "Die Vermittlerin hat die Delegationen in getrennten Räumen verhandeln ___."
questions.explanation: lassen + infinitive forms its Perfekt with the double infinitive, like a modal verb: hat … verhandeln lassen (had them negotiate). The participle gelassen is used only without an infinitive: Sie hat die Akten im Büro gelassen.

questions.stem: Which sentence means "The minister wasn't allowed to travel there"?
choices: Die Ministerin hat nicht anreisen müssen.
Die Ministerin will nicht angereist sein.
Die Ministerin hat nicht anreisen dürfen.
Die Ministerin wird nicht anreisen dürfen.
questions.explanation: nicht dürfen = not be allowed; the Perfekt is hat … anreisen dürfen. "nicht müssen" means she didn't have to travel; "will nicht angereist sein" is subjective wollen (she claims not to have travelled); "wird … dürfen" is the future (she won't be allowed).

questions.stem: You are telling a friend in Hamburg about yesterday. Which version sounds most natural in conversation there?
choices: Gestern hatte ich lange arbeiten gemusst, und dann bin ich noch einkaufen gegangen.
Gestern musste ich lange arbeiten, und dann bin ich noch einkaufen gegangen.
Gestern habe ich lange arbeiten müssen, und dann ging ich noch einkaufen.
Gestern arbeitete ich lange, und dann ging ich noch einkaufen.
questions.explanation: In northern and central German speech, modal verbs are normally in the Präteritum (musste) while other verbs are in the Perfekt (bin gegangen). "hatte … gemusst" is wrong twice (Plusquamperfekt and the participle instead of the double infinitive). The other two are correct German, but the mix of Perfekt modal and Präteritum ging is unusual, and the all-Präteritum version sounds like written narrative, not a chat with a friend.

questions.stem: Listen to the interview. Statement: "Die Vermittlerin durfte die Vorschläge nicht von einer Delegation zur anderen weitergeben." Stimmt, stimmt nicht, or is it not mentioned?

audio.text: Frau Kessler, Sie haben in Wien zwischen den beiden Delegationen vermittelt. Wie war die Stimmung? – Angespannt. Die Delegationen haben sich zwei Wochen lang kaum gesehen. Wir haben jeden Vorschlag einzeln von einem Raum in den anderen tragen müssen, und am Anfang durfte niemand mit der Presse sprechen. Das hat geholfen. – Und der Durchbruch? – Der kam in der letzten Nacht. Beide Seiten hatten verstanden, dass sie ohne Einigung nach Hause hätten fahren müssen. Und das wollte niemand.

choices: stimmt
stimmt nicht
dazu wird nichts gesagt
questions.explanation: Stimmt nicht: Frau Kessler says the opposite: "Wir haben jeden Vorschlag einzeln von einem Raum in den anderen tragen müssen" (they had to carry every proposal from one room to the other). What was not allowed at first was talking to the press.

questions.stem: Listen to the interview. Statement: "Die Regierungen haben die Einigung sofort öffentlich gefeiert." Stimmt, stimmt nicht, or is it not mentioned?

audio.text: Frau Kessler, Sie haben in Wien zwischen den beiden Delegationen vermittelt. Wie war die Stimmung? – Angespannt. Die Delegationen haben sich zwei Wochen lang kaum gesehen. Wir haben jeden Vorschlag einzeln von einem Raum in den anderen tragen müssen, und am Anfang durfte niemand mit der Presse sprechen. Das hat geholfen. – Und der Durchbruch? – Der kam in der letzten Nacht. Beide Seiten hatten verstanden, dass sie ohne Einigung nach Hause hätten fahren müssen. Und das wollte niemand.

choices: stimmt
stimmt nicht
dazu wird nichts gesagt
questions.explanation: Dazu wird nichts gesagt: the interview ends with the breakthrough in the last night and the reason for it (without an agreement they would have had to go home). How the governments reacted afterwards is not mentioned.

questions.stem: Listen to the lecture excerpt. What is its main point?

audio.text: Viele glauben, ein Vertrag sei gültig, sobald die Regierungen ihn unterschrieben haben. Das ist nicht so. Nach der Unterzeichnung muss er in den meisten Fällen noch ratifiziert werden. In Deutschland heißt das: Regelt ein Vertrag die politischen Beziehungen des Bundes oder betrifft er Gegenstände der Bundesgesetzgebung, so muss das Parlament zustimmen, und zwar in Form eines Gesetzes. Erst danach kann der Bundespräsident ratifizieren. Bei manchen Verträgen hat das Jahre gedauert, und einige sind nie in Kraft getreten, weil ein Partner nicht ratifiziert hat.

choices: Signing a treaty is usually not enough: it must also be ratified, in Germany with parliament's consent in the form of a law.
In Germany the Federal President can ratify any treaty without parliament.
A treaty comes into force as soon as the governments have signed it.
questions.explanation: The lecturer corrects the idea that a signature is enough ("Das ist nicht so"): most treaties must be ratified, and in Germany treaties on political relations or federal legislation need parliament's consent "in Form eines Gesetzes" before the Federal President ratifies. The other two options state exactly the views the lecturer rejects.

questions.stem: Match each sentence to its meaning.
choices: She had to negotiate.
She had had to negotiate.
She will have to negotiate.
She should have negotiated.
She must have negotiated.
questions.explanation: Perfekt (hat … müssen) = had to; Plusquamperfekt (hatte … müssen) = had had to; Futur I (wird … müssen) = will have to; Konjunktiv II past (hätte … müssen) = should have / would have had to (lesson 03). "She must have negotiated" is the subjective use (Sie muss verhandelt haben), which none of the sentences expresses.

questions.stem: Build the sentence in German.
questions.prompt: The last round of talks had had to be broken off without a result.
questions.explanation: Modal + passive in the Plusquamperfekt: hatte + Partizip II + werden + modal infinitive. The passive inside a modal construction uses the infinitive werden, not worden, and the modal appears as an infinitive (müssen), not as gemusst. "Ohne Ergebnis" can also open the sentence.

questions.stem: Build the sentence in German.
questions.prompt: The talks failed because the minister had not been allowed to travel there.
questions.explanation: In the weil clause the finite verb hatte comes in front of the double infinitive (anreisen dürfen), and nicht stays before hatte. The auxiliary is haben even though anreisen takes sein, and the modal stays in the infinitive (dürfen, not gedurft).

questions.stem: Which sentence means the same as "Sie mussten nicht lange warten"?
choices: Sie brauchten nicht lange zu warten.
Sie brauchten lange zu warten.
Sie durften nicht lange warten.
Sie brauchten nicht lange gewartet.
questions.explanation: brauchen + zu + infinitive replaces müssen after a negation: nicht zu warten brauchen = not have to wait. Without nicht, "brauchten lange zu warten" is not standard German; "nicht … dürfen" means they weren't allowed to wait long; and brauchen needs zu + infinitive, not a participle.

questions.stem: Which sentence is NOT standard German?
choices: Man hat die Krise kommen sehen.
Man hat die Krise kommen gesehen.
Er hat seinen Pass verlängern gelassen.
Er hat seinen Pass verlängern lassen.
questions.explanation: With an infinitive, lassen takes the double infinitive in standard German: hat … verlängern lassen. The participle gelassen is used only without an infinitive (Er hat den Pass zu Hause gelassen). With sehen and hören both forms are standard: kommen sehen and kommen gesehen.

questions.stem: "Der Diplomat hat von dem Plan wissen müssen." What does this mean?
choices: He surely knew about the plan.
It was his duty to be informed about the plan.
He wanted to know about the plan.
He is said to have known about the plan.
questions.explanation: hat … wissen müssen is the objective Perfekt of müssen: a past obligation (it was his job to know). "He surely knew" would be the subjective Der Diplomat muss von dem Plan gewusst haben (lesson 02); "wanted to" would be wollen, and "is said to" would be soll … gewusst haben.

questions.stem: Complete: "Es ist klar, dass man im Herbst ___."
choices: wird von vorn beginnen müssen
von vorn beginnen wird müssen
von vorn beginnen gemusst wird
von vorn wird beginnen müssen
questions.explanation: In a subordinate clause, werden usually goes in front of the two infinitives, like hat in the Perfekt, while the rest of the clause (von vorn) stays before it. "wird von vorn …" lets von vorn slip in after the finite verb, "beginnen wird müssen" splits the infinitives, and gemusst is not used with an infinitive. (The order "von vorn beginnen müssen wird" is also found, mainly in speech.)

questions.stem: Complete: "Die EU hat neue Sanktionen gegen das Land ___."
choices: verhängt
ratifiziert
deeskaliert
erklärt
questions.explanation: Sanktionen verhängen = to impose sanctions (also eine Strafe, eine Sperre, den Ausnahmezustand verhängen). Treaties are ratifiziert, conflicts are deeskaliert, and you erklärt a war or neutrality, not sanctions.

questions.stem:
Read the magazine article.

"Die Botschafterin
Wer an Diplomatie denkt, denkt an Gipfeltreffen und Empfänge. Der Alltag einer Botschafterin sieht meist anders aus. Ina Marquardt leitet seit drei Jahren eine deutsche Botschaft in einem kleinen Land am Rand Europas. „Den größten Teil meiner Zeit verbringe ich mit Gesprächen, die nie in der Zeitung stehen“, sagt sie. Gemeint sind Treffen mit Ministerien, Unternehmen und Vereinen, oft ohne konkretes Ergebnis.

Hinzu kommen Aufgaben, an die Außenstehende selten denken. Als im vergangenen Winter ein Erdbeben die Hauptstadt erschütterte, hat die Botschaft innerhalb weniger Stunden einen Krisenstab einrichten müssen. Mehrere Hundert Deutsche mussten erreicht, einige aus dem Land gebracht werden. „Damals sind wir drei Nächte lang kaum nach Hause gekommen“, erinnert sich Marquardt. Das Konsulat, das sonst Pässe verlängert und Visa erteilt, wurde zur Notrufzentrale.

Und die große Politik? Die werde in Berlin und Brüssel gemacht, sagt die Botschafterin ohne Bitterkeit. Ihre Aufgabe sei es, die Lage vor Ort zu erklären und Vertrauen aufzubauen, damit man im Ernstfall miteinander reden könne. Dass sie dabei manchmal Positionen vertreten muss, die sie privat anders sieht, gehört für sie zum Beruf. „Wer das nicht kann, sollte nicht in den diplomatischen Dienst gehen.“

Ob sie den Beruf noch einmal wählen würde? Marquardt zögert keine Sekunde. „Sofort. Aber ich hätte früher lernen sollen, mit wenig Schlaf auszukommen.“"

What does the article say about an ambassador's everyday work?
choices: It consists mainly of summits and receptions.
It is mainly about issuing passports and visas.
Much of it consists of talks that the public never hears about.
It is mainly about making foreign policy decisions.
questions.explanation: Marquardt says she spends most of her time on "Gesprächen, die nie in der Zeitung stehen". Summits and receptions are what people imagine ("Wer an Diplomatie denkt, denkt an …"), passports and visas are the consulate's normal job, and big policy, she says, is made in Berlin and Brussels.

How does Marquardt feel about having to represent positions she doesn't share privately?
choices: She thinks it shows that the profession is badly organized.
She sees it as part of the job.
She refuses to do it.
She finds it the hardest part of the job and would like to change it.
questions.explanation: "…, gehört für sie zum Beruf", and anyone who can't do it "sollte nicht in den diplomatischen Dienst gehen". She accepts it without complaint; nothing suggests she wants to change it or refuses.

Ob sie den Beruf noch einmal wählen würde? Marquardt zögert keine Sekunde. „Sofort. Aber ich hätte früher lernen sollen, mit wenig Schlaf auszukommen.“"

What does her last remark ("Aber ich hätte früher lernen sollen, mit wenig Schlaf auszukommen") suggest?
choices: She regrets choosing the profession.
She thinks ambassadors should sleep more.
She learned early in her career to need little sleep.
She would choose the job again, although it is very demanding.
questions.explanation: She answers "Sofort" (immediately) to the question whether she would choose the job again, then adds, with humour, a regret: hätte … lernen sollen = she should have learned (but didn't). The job is demanding (sleepless nights), but she doesn't regret it. "She learned early … to need little sleep" contradicts hätte … sollen, which refers to something that did not happen.

questions.stem: "Er muss es gewusst haben." What does this mean?
choices: He had to know it (it was his duty).
He must have known it (I'm sure he did).
He should have known it (but he didn't).
He must know it.
questions.explanation: muss + perfect infinitive (gewusst haben) is the subjective use: the speaker is sure, from evidence, that he knew. A past duty would be Er hat es wissen müssen / Er musste es wissen; "should have known" is Er hätte es wissen müssen (lesson 03); "He must know it" refers to the present (Er muss es wissen).

questions.stem: Complete so that the sentence means "The chronicler claims to have seen the siege": "Der Chronist ___ die Belagerung gesehen haben."
choices: soll
muss
mag
will
questions.explanation: Subjective wollen reports the subject's own claim, usually with doubt: Er will … gesehen haben = he claims to have seen. soll would pass on what others say (he is said to have seen); muss would be the writer's firm conclusion; mag would concede a possibility.

questions.stem: Which sentence means "The town is said to have been besieged for seven months"?
choices: Die Stadt soll sieben Monate lang belagert worden sein.
Die Stadt sollte sieben Monate lang belagert werden.
Die Stadt will sieben Monate lang belagert worden sein.
Die Stadt soll sieben Monate lang belagert sein worden.
questions.explanation: Hearsay = sollen in the present + perfect infinitive; in the passive the perfect infinitive is Partizip II + worden sein. "sollte … belagert werden" means it was supposed to be (or ought to be) besieged; wollen needs a subject that can make claims, which a town can't; and the order is worden sein, not sein worden.

questions.stem: "Der Chronist muss nicht gelogen haben." What does this mean?
choices: The chronicler can't have lied.
The chronicler mustn't lie.
The chronicler didn't necessarily lie.
The chronicler didn't have to lie.
questions.explanation: muss nicht + perfect infinitive = not necessarily: it's possible that he told the truth. "can't have lied" would be kann nicht gelogen haben; "mustn't lie" is darf nicht lügen; "didn't have to lie" is the objective past (musste nicht lügen / hat nicht lügen müssen).

questions.stem: Type the missing word: "Die Kaiserin dürfte bereits 1350 gestorben ___."
questions.explanation: sterben takes sein in the perfect (sie ist gestorben), so the perfect infinitive is gestorben sein: Die Kaiserin dürfte … gestorben sein = the empress probably died as early as 1350.

questions.stem: Which completion means "…that the charter must have been forged"? "Die Historikerin glaubt, dass …"
choices: die Urkunde muss gefälscht worden sein
die Urkunde gefälscht worden sein muss
die Urkunde gefälscht sein worden muss
die Urkunde hat gefälscht werden müssen
questions.explanation: With a perfect infinitive there is no double infinitive, so in a subordinate clause the modal goes to the very end: gefälscht worden sein muss. "muss gefälscht worden sein" is main-clause order, "sein worden" reverses the passive perfect infinitive, and "hat gefälscht werden müssen" is grammatical but objective: the charter had to be forged.

questions.stem: Which sentence expresses the least certainty that he knew?
choices: Er muss es gewusst haben.
Er dürfte es gewusst haben.
Er wird es wohl gewusst haben.
Er könnte es gewusst haben.
questions.explanation: On the scale of certainty, muss (sure) comes first, dürfte and wird wohl (probable, assumed) in the middle, and kann/könnte (possible) near the bottom, just above kann nicht (impossible).

questions.stem: "Der Bote sollte längst angekommen sein." What does the speaker mean?
choices: The messenger should have arrived long ago, and the speaker is surprised he hasn't.
The messenger is said to have arrived long ago.
The messenger was supposed to arrive long ago, but he refused.
The messenger claims to have arrived long ago.
questions.explanation: sollte (Konjunktiv II) + perfect infinitive usually expresses an expectation: by now he ought to be here. Hearsay is the present soll (Er soll angekommen sein), a claim by the subject is will, and "supposed to arrive" would be the objective Er sollte ankommen.

questions.stem: Match each sentence to its meaning.
choices: He is said to have seen nothing.
He claims to have seen nothing.
He can't have seen anything.
He probably saw nothing.
He wasn't allowed to see anything.
questions.explanation: soll = others say so (hearsay); will = the subject's own claim; kann nicht / kann nichts = impossible; dürfte = probable. "He wasn't allowed to see anything" is objective (Er durfte nichts sehen), with the modal in the past.

questions.stem: Build the sentence in German.
questions.prompt: The inscription can't have been made before 1200.
questions.explanation: kann nicht + perfect infinitive = impossible. entstehen takes sein (ist entstanden), so the perfect infinitive is entstanden sein, not haben; worden would make it passive. "Vor 1200" (or, emphatically, "Nicht vor 1200") can also open the sentence, and "kann vor 1200 nicht entstanden sein" is also correct.

questions.stem: Build the sentence in German.
questions.prompt: The documents are said to have been destroyed.
questions.explanation: Hearsay in the passive past: sollen (plural, to agree with die Dokumente) + Partizip II + worden sein. The passive uses worden, not geworden (which belongs to werden = to become), and soll doesn't agree with a plural subject.

questions.stem: Listen to the lecture excerpt. What does the lecturer conclude about the date of the sword?

audio.text: Der Fund wurde zunächst auf das zehnte Jahrhundert datiert. Inzwischen wissen wir: Das kann nicht stimmen. Die Münzen, die neben dem Schwert lagen, müssen aus dem zwölften Jahrhundert stammen, denn sie tragen das Bild eines Herrschers, der erst 1138 an die Macht kam. Das Schwert dürfte also frühestens Mitte des zwölften Jahrhunderts in den Boden gelangt sein. Ob es jemals in einer Schlacht benutzt wurde, wissen wir nicht. Es könnte auch ein Geschenk gewesen sein, ein Zeichen von Herrschaft und nicht von Krieg.

choices: It certainly dates from the 10th century.
It was certainly used in a battle after 1138.
It was probably buried no earlier than the mid-12th century.
questions.explanation: The 10th-century date "kann nicht stimmen"; the coins "müssen" come from the 12th century, so the sword "dürfte … frühestens Mitte des zwölften Jahrhunderts in den Boden gelangt sein": probably no earlier. Whether it was ever used in battle "wissen wir nicht".

questions.stem: Listen again. How sure is the lecturer that the sword was a gift?

audio.text: Der Fund wurde zunächst auf das zehnte Jahrhundert datiert. Inzwischen wissen wir: Das kann nicht stimmen. Die Münzen, die neben dem Schwert lagen, müssen aus dem zwölften Jahrhundert stammen, denn sie tragen das Bild eines Herrschers, der erst 1138 an die Macht kam. Das Schwert dürfte also frühestens Mitte des zwölften Jahrhunderts in den Boden gelangt sein. Ob es jemals in einer Schlacht benutzt wurde, wissen wir nicht. Es könnte auch ein Geschenk gewesen sein, ein Zeichen von Herrschaft und nicht von Krieg.

choices: The lecturer is certain of it.
It is only a possibility the lecturer mentions.
The lecturer rules it out.
questions.explanation: "Es könnte auch ein Geschenk gewesen sein": könnte + perfect infinitive presents a possibility, nothing more. Certainty would need muss, exclusion kann nicht.

questions.stem: Listen to the interview. Statement: "Der Historiker hält die Zahl der Toten, die die Chronik nennt, für zuverlässig." Stimmt, stimmt nicht, or is it not mentioned?

audio.text: Wie viele Menschen sind damals in der Stadt an der Pest gestorben? – Genau wissen wir das nicht. Die Chronik spricht von zwei Dritteln der Bevölkerung, aber diese Zahl dürfte stark übertrieben sein. Die Steuerlisten von 1350 verzeichnen etwa ein Drittel weniger Haushalte als vorher, und manche Familien müssen auch aufs Land geflohen sein. – Und die Hungersnot, von der die Chronik berichtet? – Die kam später, zwei Jahre danach, als niemand mehr da war, der die Felder bestellen konnte.

choices: stimmt
stimmt nicht
dazu wird nichts gesagt
questions.explanation: Stimmt nicht: he says the chronicle's figure of two thirds "dürfte stark übertrieben sein" (is probably greatly exaggerated) and points to the tax lists, which suggest about a third fewer households.

questions.stem: "Ein Heer, das monatelang vor der Stadt lag, müsste Spuren hinterlassen haben." What does the writer mean?
choices: The army should have left traces, but it was ordered not to.
The army had to leave traces behind.
The army is said to have left traces.
If an army had really been there that long, we would expect to find traces.
questions.explanation: müsste + perfect infinitive expresses what the evidence would lead us to expect. In the text the traces are missing, which counts against the chronicle. The other options read it as an obligation (objective) or as hearsay (soll).

questions.stem: Which sentence contains a mistake?
choices: Er hat es gewusst haben müssen.
Er muss den Brief geschrieben haben.
Sie dürfte schon abgereist sein.
Das kann nicht wahr gewesen sein.
questions.explanation: A subjective modal about the past stays in the present and takes the perfect infinitive: Er muss es gewusst haben. "hat … gewusst haben müssen" mixes the objective Perfekt (hat … müssen) with a perfect infinitive. The other three are correct: muss, dürfte and kann nicht + perfect infinitive.

questions.stem: What is "Quellenkritik"?
choices: A review of a new history book.
Criticism of historians in the press.
Examining who wrote a source, when, for whom and how reliable it is.
Translating old texts into modern German.
questions.explanation: die Quellenkritik is the historian's basic method: asking about the author, date, purpose and transmission of a source before trusting its content. A book review is eine Rezension.

questions.stem:
Read three experts' contributions to a journal debate: "Wie zuverlässig sind mittelalterliche Chroniken?"

Expertin A, Mediävistin: „Wir dürfen Chroniken nicht wie Zeitungsberichte lesen. Ein Chronist schrieb für einen Auftraggeber, meist einen Herrscher oder ein Kloster, und er wollte zeigen, dass Gott auf dessen Seite stand. Zahlen sind deshalb oft symbolisch gemeint. Wenn ein Heer zehntausend Mann gehabt haben soll, heißt das zunächst nur: Es war sehr groß. Wer daraus Statistik macht, hat die Quelle missverstanden.“

Experte B, Archäologe: „Ich vertraue lieber dem, was im Boden liegt. Münzen, Knochen und verbrannte Balken lassen sich datieren, oft auf wenige Jahrzehnte genau. Allerdings muss man auch hier vorsichtig sein: Ein Fund zeigt, dass etwas geschehen ist, aber nicht, warum. Erst zusammen mit den Texten ergibt sich ein Bild. Archäologie ohne Schriftquellen bleibt stumm.“

Expertin C, Archivarin: „Viele Chroniken, die wir heute lesen, sind Abschriften von Abschriften. Jeder Schreiber kann Fehler gemacht oder etwas ergänzt haben, oft in bester Absicht. Bevor man über den Inhalt urteilt, sollte man deshalb die Überlieferung klären: Welche Handschriften gibt es, wie alt sind sie, wer hat sie besessen? Diese Arbeit ist mühsam, aber ohne sie steht jede Interpretation auf Sand.“

Which expert makes each statement? One statement fits none of them.
left: Numbers in chronicles often weren't meant literally.
Physical finds and written sources should be used together.
Before interpreting a chronicle, you should find out how its text was handed down.
Chronicles are more reliable than archaeological finds.
choices: Expertin A
Experte B
Expertin C
none of them
questions.explanation: A: "Zahlen sind deshalb oft symbolisch gemeint." B: "Erst zusammen mit den Texten ergibt sich ein Bild." C: "Bevor man über den Inhalt urteilt, sollte man … die Überlieferung klären." Nobody claims chronicles are more reliable than finds; B even says he trusts finds more.
